SAMUEL E. BURKE
Grand Master
1921-1922

mi

t

Samuel Edgerton Burke
Grand Master 1921-1922

Samuel Edgerton Burke, our fifty-fifth Grand Master, was born in
the Province of Ontario, Canada, and came to the United States in
his early youth. He attended Lake Forest University, Illinois, and
graduated from that institution in 1896 with the degree of Doctor of
Dental Surgery. The call of the west brought him to Los Angeles in
1900, where he has since made his home. He was made a Master
Mason July 20, 1903, in Sunset Lodge No. 352 of Los j\ngeles, and
from the date of his admission was an active worker in the Masonic
vineyard, as he is yet. He became Master of his Lodge in 1906, and
shortly thereafter was appointed Inspector, in which capadty he served
faithfully for nine years. In relief work he has cheerfuUy given of
his time and energy and money, and served as a member of the Los
Angeles Board of Relief since 1907.
In other branches of Masonry Brother Burke has taken interest,
but never permitting such interests to interfere with his work in craft
Masonry. He received the degrees of the Royal Arch and the Council
in 1904, and was High Priest of Signet Chapter No. 57 in 1910. His
Commandery degrees date from 1905, and his Scottish Rite degrees to
the 32d were received in 1908.
He served the Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons as Grand
Chaplain in 1917, and was Grand Master of the Grand Council of California in 1919.
Brother Burke's activities in Grand Lodge, as an officer, are as
follows: Grand Chaplain 1911 ; Grand Bible Bearer 1912; Grand Ora·
tor 1915; Junior Grand Warden 1918; Senior Grand Warden 1919;
Deputy· Grand Master 1920, and in October of 1921 he was elected
Grand ~faster.
Brother B.urke's home is blessed by the presence of a wife who is
embued with the sweetest characteristics of virtue and of those attributes which go to make an ideal American home; and a daughter whose
loveliness of character and person charm all who know her. He also
has a son who was raised a Master Mason on the 24th of April, 1922,
by his father and in his father's Lodge. The young man sta.nds high
in the estimation of those who know him, and he has every prospect
of becoming a factor in the social and business life of his chosen city.
Our retiring Grand Master is an orator of no mean ability, and
his voice has never been raised except in the cause of right and justice and mercy. May he live to a green old age.

ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master then· delivered his Annual Address, as
follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of
California:
For the seventy-third time the Supreme Grand Master permits
us to meet in assembly that we may review the past, consider the
present and plan for the future of this Grand jurisdiction. Just
one short year ago I stood in this room and was invested with
the greatest honor that has ever come into my life; and now to this
same room I come this morning to render to you an account of
my stewardship and to bestow, a little later, the insignia of
authority upon my successor. To me it has been a wonderful year, a
marvelous experience, one of the happiest years in my life. It
seems to me, as I now review it, that the Grand Masters who
preceded me have, by their effort, smoothed every rough spot in
the road I travelled. The small difficulties I have at times encountered were only the merest trifles; a word of explanation on
either side usually sufficed, and then, because of the little rough~
ness encoui'ltered and safely passed, my path seemed smoother,
fairer, more alluring than ever before. It has not been necessary
for your Grand Master to so much as render a decision this year.
There have been occasions, of course, when interpretation or
explanation was desired or needed, but never any situation or
circumstance that would demand or warrant a decision on his part.

Necrology.
However, with all its smiling sunny days, the year has had
its times of passing cloud. I do not need to emphasize the shadow
cast upon us all by the death of our beloved Past Grand Master,
Alonzo Judson Monroe, one of the finest and noblest men and
Masons that ever trod this old earth of ours. Also our well-loved
Samuel David Mayer, veteran Grand Organist of this Grand Lodge,
whose golden voice has for so many, many years echoed in this
very room and whose inspired hand wakened loving melodies from
yonder organ for over fifty years, is with us no more. Another
grievous loss to our Grand body was sustained in the passing of
Harvey Davis Loveland, committeeman and Past Grand Orator.
His hearty hand-clasp and genial smile will long be missed by
his many friends in the Grand Lodge. Tomorrow morning at
half past nine o'clock we will assemble in this room for a solemn
1ervice in memory of these our departed brethren.

Just on the eve of my departure from my home to attend this
communication (and after this report was in the hands of the printer) I
received a telegram advising me of the death of our Assistant Grand
Secretary, Harry Johnson. I cannot y'et quite realize that it is truethat he is gone from us never to return; that I will never again
receive his hearty greeting from the outer room of the Grand Secretary's office. I loved Harry Johnson. I think all of us did that knew
him well. Foc almost twenty years I have been coming to the meetings
of this Grand Lodg~ and I have always looked forward to seeing Harry
in his old place. He is going to be missed, and missed, and missed
again in the haunts and by the men who have worked with him so long.

other like member missing. I have without exception denied the
requested dispensation in these cases. One of the Fifteen Articles
of the old York Constitutions of the year 926 sets forth the fact
that our candidates must be without physical blemish, and, in my
opinion, it ill behooves a Grand Master to grant a dispensation
admitting to the fraternity applicants who are so dismembered that
they cannot substantially conform to the physical requirements of
the several degrees. While it is very true that we are now speculative rather than operative Masons, yet, as I view the matter, if we
are to stand up to and live by the ancient rules and land marks
of our institution, we must abide by the laws then made and now
set forth in our• book of Constitution to be the rule and guide, not
only of the officers of subordinate Lodges, but of the officers of
the Grand Lodge as well. Moreover, since these conditions of
membership are as well known to the Masters and Wardens of our
Lodges of this jurisdiction as they are to the Grand Master, I
think such requests for dispensation ill-timed and ill-considered.

Interpretation of Section 89.
Soon after the close of the Grand Lodge last year, I began to
receive inquiries concerning the correct construction to be placed
on an amendment to Section 89 of our Constitution as adopted at
that session. Many Masters of Lodges had not a clear and definite
understanding of this amendment, which reads:
"Except, however, that the Lodge may expend twenty per cent
of its total revenue for purposes of refreshments and the promotion
of fraternal intercourse."
Having been appealed to from so many sources for an interpretation of this amendment, after conferring with Past Grand
Master Angellotti, Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee, I
caused a circular letter to be sent to all our Lodges, the text of
which was in part as follows:
"As the law now stands, twenty per cent of the total revenue
of the Lodge constitutes a fund exempt from the inhibition of
Section 88 insofar as expenditures for purposes specified in Section
89 are concerned, and available for such purposes at any time,
regardless of the year within which it was received, but not prior
'to January 1, 1920."

the possibility of securing a dispensation to confer degrees upon

Clandestine Masonry.
For some fifteen years past there has been at work in this
country a clandestine Masonic organization headed by Matthew
McBlain Thomson, formerly a member of two Lodges in Scotland,
but who came to this country later and affiliated with a Lodge in
the State of Idaho. Some time after, he took a demit from the
idaho Lodge and formed an organization which he called the
American Masonic Federation. He had paid agents scattered over
the country who organized Lodges and conferred alleged degrees.
The charge for the Craft degrees ranged from $35 to $50 and for
the Scottish Rite degrees from $135 to $200. For specified sums he
added the Commandcry and Shrine degrees. Several times these
organizers of Mr. Thomson were arrested on charges of embezzlement and obtaining money under. false pretenses, and there was an
occasional conviction. In 1915 one of the organizers named Ransom was arrested in St. Louis, Missouri, and the Postoffice Inspector
in that city evidently concluded that it was high time the United
States government took the case in hand on the basis of using the
mails for fraudulent purposes. He ordered an investigation of the
matter, and after an exhaustive inquiry into the workings of this
federation which eventually led into Scotland and France as well as
all over this country, the case was brought to trial in the United
States District Court in Salt Lake City in the spring of this present
year. Neither Judge nor any member of the jury were Masons, but
a verdict of guilty was brought in, and the Judge sentenced the

13

defendants, of whom there were three, to serve a term of two years
in the penitentiary and pay a fine of $5000 each. One of the trio is
now in prison, while Thomson and one confederate have appealed
for a new trial. Let us hope that this rings down the curtain on
the activities of Clandestine Masonry in these United States.

Extraneous Organizations.

Public Schools Week

I cannot help but view with much apprehension the introduction, growth and expansion of the many orders that profess the
furtherance of Freemasonry as their prime objective, and who are
often called "Masonic organizations" by both public and press but
whose only kinship in reality lies in the prerequisiti~n to membe;ship
of the Master Mason degree. I have made a careful survey of their
workings this year with relation to Ancient Craft Masonry, and J
believe I am justified in saying that whatever district I have visitell
this year and found none of these so-called "side orders" in operation, there I have found Masonry on a higher, more orderly, and
more dignified plane. I believe I may safely prophesy that if these
bodies are not curbed by other means, it will eventually be necessary for this Grand Lodge to enact some form of legislation looking
toward the control or retirement of these extraneous organizations.

In keeping with what is quite generally regarded as a worthy
precedent, I issued, under date of August 14th, a Proclamation
designating the week commencing September 18th as "Public
Schools Week" solely for the purpose of "more strongly cementing
the ties which now exist between the Masonic fraternity and the
Public Schools of our country." While it was suggested that "the
provisions of the Towner-Sterling bill might properly be stressed,"
it was made clear that discussions of school questions "should not
be along the lines of propaganda for the support of any particular
line of legislation except insofar as informative matter may and
should be presented for fair and full and dispassionate consideration," and further, "that only constructive, not destructive, phases
of the subject be discussed." The purpose of this action was to
awaken the craft, at this time when "many schemes are being presented to interfere with the proper operation of our system of public
education," to the importance of manifesting an active, alert, intelligent interest in the conduct of the affairs of that supremely important governmental agency which has, quite properly, been
termed "the real bulwark of this great republic," and at the same
time, to emphasize the necessity for that accurate, dependable information which is a pre-requisite to just judgments and to intelligent thought and action.
The ignorance, apathy and indifference of the average elector
regarding the administration of the affairs of our system of public
education is appalling, and those who have special interests to serve
are not slow to observe and to take advantage of this shortcoming,
which renders possible the dissemination through our public schools
of insidious propaganda which strikes at the very foundation of
our wonderful fabric of government and admits of the retention of
teachers whose Americanism is not always above reproach.
It is not unusual for members of a Board of Education or
School Trustees to be elected to office by the votes of fifteen or
t\\·enty per cent of the qualified electors of their district. It is
seldom that more than thirty-five or forty per cent of the electors
express themselves at school district elections respecting either
men or measures. Parents rarely know how or what their children

Masonic Homes.
The greatest and most enduring monuments that this Grand
Lodge can ever erect or hope to erect are those living monuments
to Masonry at Covina and Decoto-our Masonic Homes. It is not
necessary for me to deliver this morning a panegyric on either the
work or the workers in these wonderful institutions. You are all
familiar, either by report or personal visit, with the mighty work
being carried on within their walls. Tomorrow afternoon, as you
may have noted, a time is set aside for you to visit our northern
home at Decoto. I trust that any of you who are not already conversant with the work being done there will avail yourselves of this
opportunity afforded.
'
Masonic Club-House.
This Grand Lodge at its annual communication in 1921 approved
the erection of a suitable clubhouse near the campus of the University of California for the use of Master Masons and sons and
daughters of Masons at the University. It also authorized a Statewide appeal for funds to erect and equip such a building, All
Lodges of this jurisdiction have been circularized by the commit-

are being taught. There is no governmental function which so
vitally affects such a large percentage of our population and yet
there is none with respect to which there is so much ignorance or
in which there is so little apparent interest as there is regarding
matters of school administration and the expenditure of taxes
allocated to educational purposes. This, notwithstanding the fact
that, in addition to the constantly-increasing special common and
high school district taxes, I am informed that over fifty-one per
cent of all expenditures of State funds, received by indirect taxation, are apportioned to the support of our system of public instruction.
Our schools must be administered fearlessfy, efficiently, impartially and in the interest of ALL of our people, and their
administration must not be permitted to run afoul the field of
politics. The interests of no one class or group of our complex
society are not more important than are the interests of every other
class or group, and if our institutions are to endure we must be
constantly on the alert and must insist upon the unselfish and
disinterested administration of our institutions for public education
in consonance with the principles found in the great charter of
our liberties.

In the Grand Secretary's report will be found a complete statistical report covering all details of Lodges constituted, dispensations granted, special communications of this Grand Lodge for
such purposes a~ instituting Lodges, laying cornerstones and
dedicating. Masonic halls. I therefore feel that a mere summary is
all that is now requisite. The Grand Lodge of California has been
convened this year thirty-eight times for the various occasions
upon which it is fitting and proper that we should officiate.

Visits.
Likewise, in the report of our Grand Lecturer you will find
fully and specifically enumerated the official visits made by the
Grand Master this year, and I have no desire to encroach upon
your time and temper this morning with matter which, at best, can
be only amplified repetition of an official report. Again I will
summarize by saying that in this Grand jurisdiction there are
eighty-six Masonic districts and that I have been in almost all of
them. I might add that I also extended my visitation to the Lodges
of the seventy-sixth Masonic District in the Hawaiian Islands.
This year of visitation has been to me a realization of what
previously existed in my mind as an imperfect and very general

Discipline.
I have found, too, our Lodges generally ·working in full
harmony with the best traditions of our institution, but in one single
instance a condition became manifest indicating that possibly due
to .the large influx of members, an influence had been brought into
the Lodge which was not in accord with the diginity which characterizes the government of Masonic Lodges, and which condition
could not have obtained had the older and more seasoned members
attended Lodge and given more personal attention to affairs concerning the Lodge. I refer to Union Lodge No. 58. Under date of
May 2d, 1922, I caused to be sent to this Lodge as well as to all
our Lodges, a circular letter calling upon all the brethren to
carefully guard their heritage as American citizens and to be not
led away on any pretext from a strict obedience to the laws of the
land. Some ulterior and anonymous influence had apparently and
unhappily been at work among some of the members of Union
Lodge, and at the stated meeting of the Lodge held on the 7th of
June, the communication of the Grand Master w~s read and by
almost unanimous vote ordered to be returned to him. The Secretary of the Lodge thereupon, as directed by his Lodge, did return
the communication. This was an act of contumacy which could
not be overlooked, and I therefore directed the Inspector of the
District to take up the charter of the Lodge and send it to the
Grand Secretary, to be kept until the order of arrest should be
rescinded or until the Grand Lodge should take action thereon.
'The charter was arrested on June 20th. Subsequently, better counsel prevailed among the members of the Lodge, suitable apology
was made, and on the ~8th of July, I visited the brethren of this
Lodge at Sacramento and after a full and friendly. discussion of the
whole affair with a large number of the members, restored the
charter. I understand that harmony has prevailed since that time,
that Union Lodge is again working along the lines which has for so
many years characterized this old Lodge, and that it will continue
to be a large factor in the moral and social life of the city of
Sacramento.

Recommendations.

I recommend that changes in our Constitution be mitde, as

Section 73. It is almost physically impossible for the brethren
who join in the formation of a new Lodge in the larger cities to
personally visit all the Lodges in their local territorial jurisdiction,
and I therefore recommend that section 73 be amended to read
"(if from a city or town where more than one Lodge exists, then
from a majority of the Inspectors of such Lodges)." I am sure
the Grand Master can be safely informed relative to the propriety of the formation of a new Lodge, by trusting to the judgment
of the Inspectors. This amendment would not change the law
relating to communities where only one Lodge exists.
Section 96. This section now provides that a petitioner must
request in writing for a waiver of jurisdiction if and when he
desires to apply for the degrees in a Lodge. other than that of his
residence. Manifestly the petitioner cannot be said to be familiar
with Masonic law or usage, and I recommend that Section 96 be
amended to provide that the Lodge, and not the petitioner, shall
request the waiver, when desired.
Section 112. I recommend that section 112 be amended
by adding after the last word in the section as it now reads, the
following: "Any number of candidates may be examined at any
meeting, but not more than five shall be examined at any one time.
Such examinations shall be held in front of the East."
Section 161. I recommend that the first paragraph of section
161 be amended to read substantially as follows: "Section 161. A
member against whom no charges are pending, and whose dues are
paid for four months in advance, who desires to affiliate with
another Lodge, may apply for in writing, and receive from the Secretary of the Lodge of which he is a member, a duly attested certificate of his standing. ~Y presenting this certificate within two
months, a member may apply for affiliation with another Lodge
in this jurisdiction in the manner prescribed in Section 98. If
such applicant be ~lected to affiliate with a Lodge, he can become
a member thereof, only, after the Secretary of the Lodge which
issued the certificate of standing has been advised of such election,
and acknowledged the receipt of such advice. If favorable action is
not taken within four months from the date of the certificate of
standing, the applicant shall be considered a member of the Lodge
issuing the certificate and chargeable with dues therein. Nothing
in this section shall operate to change the law regarding demits or
affiliation by demit.

read '~ubstantially as follows:

If the above named sections 161 and 248 are amended, sections
l 28b, 128c, 161 a, 161 b and 161 c should be repealed.
I also recommend that our book of Constitution be revised in
order that laws that have been repealed by amendment may be
omitted and whatever else is necessary may be done that will tend
to condense and simplify its present form; also that rulings of the
Grand Master do not become a part of the Constitution.
Conclusion.
In "conclusion, I would like to summarize the strides made by
our fraternity in California for this year. As you know, my doctrine proclaimed from the snows of Siskiyou to the sands of Imperial Valley has been more Lodges, and of fewer members. This
morning I take great pleasure in telling you that during the year
there have been twenty-six dispensations granted for the formation
of new Lodges, and there are others under way who were not
sufficiently advanced to receive their dispensations by this date.
Also I believe you will be gratified in learning that the growth of
our Order this year has been eight thousand.
This report would be indeed incomplete without some recognition of the brethren who have this year so freely given of their
time and labor and have so unselfishly devoted the best interests
of their hearts to the benefit of this Grand Lodge and to the assistance of its Grand Master. To the Inspectors of the Masonic
Districts of this Grand jurisdiction I am under the deepest obligation for services faithfully, efficiently and untiringly rendered. These
brethren are the very backbone of our Masonry, and possibly do
more than any other agency to hold our Lodges together and to

keep alive the fine spirit of our Institution. In my humble qpinion they should be clothed on official visits with proper rega~fa of
their rank, the regalia to become their personal property, a~d on
the retirement from office of an Inspector he to be given pa&t rank
as such and be permitted to wear his insignia on all Masonic
occasions, including Grand Lodge communications. I believe that
if we should adopt some measure of this sort, it would not only
lend dignity to the rank of Inspector, but would tend to relieve the
Grand Master of much traveling, and accomplish results quite as
good as though the Grand Master himself c.ould personally visit
all the Lodges. Our jurisdiction is now so large, and the territory
to be covered by a general round of visitations so vast, that the
Grand Master can scarcely do justice to himself and his person:il
affairs by attempting to personally appear in many of the Lodges.
Hence I believe he can generally best be represented by the Inspectors. I do not present this idea to you in the form of a recommendation, merely a suggestion that I personally consider might
with great propriety and general good be adopted.
To the Grand Lodge officers, who have been ever willing and
ever patient in rendering assistance whenever and wherever needed,
to the Past Grand Masters whose good counsel has upheld me and
directed me, to the Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer who have
been my chart and compass from first to last and without whose
aid I would have been a very small bark adrift on a mighty seato all of these I am indebted far beyond my command of words
to express.
And, lastly, the brethren of this Grand Lodge, you who have
so kindly and courteously given me your attention this morning,
one and all, I thank you.

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
To th\; Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California;
As Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge and Treasurer of the
Masonic Homes of California, I am privileged to report having had,
during the past year, the care and custody of funds and securities to
the unprecedented amount of $714,993.61. This is due in large measure
to the accumulated fund11 of the Homes for building purposes and improvements now rapidly being paid out.
The issuanee of United States Treasury notes and certificates has
made it possible to adopt the policy, with the approval of the Grand
Master and the President of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes, of placing the surplus funds of Grand Lodge an.d the Ho~es
in that class of government securities at more than savmgs bank mterest, readily convertible into cash, and selling at a premium when it
was found necessary to increase bank balances. By this method of
handling the funds it has been made possible, during the year, to earn
for the Grand Lodge and the Masonic Homes, in interest and premiums,
over $39,000.00. The financial report is herewith attached:

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the M.".W.".Grand Lodge of California:

I present herewith my fifteenth annual report of the transactions of the Grand Secretary's office for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1922, and a detailed statement of all moneys received and
disbursed for the twelve months. I also append an account of
receipts since the close of the fiscal year to and including October
5, 1922.
Death of Harry' Johnson
The Grand Secretary's office suffered a great loss in the death
of Harry Sumner Johnson, Assistant Grand Secretary, who was
suddenly called hence just as the sun was setting on the evening
of October 1, 1922. Brother Johnson was particularly efficient and
faithful in the discharge of his duties-a very encyclopedia of Masonic law and custom-courteous always, and industrious beyond
the demands of his work. He was made a Master Mason in California Lodge No. 1, September 27, 1900, and was installed as Assistant Grand Secretary at the October Communication of Grand Lodge
following. His reappointment annually since that time is evidence
that Grand Masters appreciated his worth.
On April 30, 1904, he withdrew from California Lodge No. 1
and joined in the formation of San Francisco Lodge (now No. 360),
being named in the Dispensation as Junior Warden. At the annual
election in December, 1904, he was advanced to the station of Senior
Warden, and the following December, 1905, was elected and installed as Master, and as such served during the trying days following the great fire of April, 1906.
Brother Johnson's home life was almost ideal. Besides his wife,
he left four lovely children who idolized their father. To the widow
and the fatherless children, I know I but echo the sentiment of all
members of Grand Lodge in saying that he left a heritage greater
than material riches, the heritage of a good name.

Courtesy Degrees
The conferring degrees as a courtesy to Lodges of other jurisdictions, which if not requested too often would be a pleasure, is
still a source of expense to our Lodges, particularly in San Francisco, Los Angeles and San Diego. During the year we have conferred 675 degrees as favors to Lodges of other jurisdictions, and
have requested like favors to the number of ninety-seven.

53

Los Angeles Masonic Employment Bureau

Burials

Applications received, 3,638. Positions secured, 3,249. Temporafy
positions to the number of 2,385 were secured, not induded in the
above list. Fifteen applications were cancelled for failure to report
for duty, insubordination or failure to make good.

During the year ending August 31st, 1922, the fallowing named
Masons, or members of their families, have been given Masonic burial,
or shipped in accordance with the wishes of the relatives.
September 13, 1921, Thomas H. Bunney; Jewel No. 94, Suncook,
New Hampshire.

our endeavor to develop greater co-operation by the craft. Many calls
from employers not members of the fraternity, as our men average
well and maintain a standard of efficiency, thus developing self respect and real manhood.

Brother W. E. Metz of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296 introduced the following:
•
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Califorma:
Whereas, The three principal tenets of Masonry, Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth, have been the foundation stones of our fraternity for
countless ages, but have in ·recent years, in thickly populated centers,
commence'd to crumble into decay, due to the building up of Lodges
of large membership who remain unknown to each other; and

Resolved:' That Section 157 be amended by adding thereto, the following "Section 157 * * * except as provided for in Section 161."

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

Whereas, It is a fundamental fact that it is not in conformity with
the laws of nature to hold a sincere feeling of brotherly love for a
total stranger, and as the exercise of that principle can only be brought
about through contact, getting together, learning each other's faults and
virtues, and stimulating the practice of these tenets, it naturally follows
that we must'have smaller Lodges and more of them. It is a11; urgent
need recognized by all Masons who have given the matter consideration,
but owing to the arduous task of mastering the ritual and lectures of
the three degrees, and the reluctance (due to recognized sentiment) of
Past Masters to withdraw from their Lodges, the formation of a new
Lodge is looked upon with trepidation; and

Brother Norton Langford of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296
presented the following:

Whereas, Believing that the situation can and should be relieved
whereby the formation of new Lodges would be encouraged without
affecting a sentiment which is truly commendable, I offer the following
resolution :

Resolved: That Section 161 be amended to read as follows: "Section 161. A member in good standing whose dues are paid, who desires to affiliate with another Lodge, may apply for, and receive from
the Secretary of the Lodge of which he is a member, a duly attested
certificate of his standing. By presenting such a certificate with his
petition, a member may apply f~r affiliation with another Lodge in the
manner prescribed in Section 98. If such applicant be elected to
affiliate with a Lodge he can become a member thereof, only, after the
issuance of a certificate of his withdrawal, which shall be immediately
issued upon due notice of his election from the Lodge with which he
desires to affiliate.

PROPOSAL TO PAY INSTRUCTORS

To the 111. ost Worshipful Grand Lodge of Califorma:
Whereas, In the larger centers where Lodges have been burdened
with a vast amount of work, the instruction of candidates has been
and still is a perplexing problem; and
Whereas, In following the mode of instructipn that our law provides,
inability of Masters to secure the services of sufficient brethren who
possess the prerequisites for the work, to-wit: proficiency and time; and

Whereas, When candidates are instructed in stores, barber shops and
othe~ public places, a due regard for secrecy is seldom exercised to a
full extent, which laxness has a tendency to tacitly, if not openly advertise Masonry; and
Whereas, The instruction of candidates should be regarded as being
of as great an importance as the conferring of the degrees, yet we
have gone on year after year doing part of our work in secret and
the rest, as it were, in public ; and
~Vhereas, It has been demonstrated that where a number of candidates have been instructed collectively in a Masonic Temple, they
have not only been imbued with a higher regard for Masonry, but have
exhibited a rivalry in attaining proficiency, and through such personal
contact avenues have been opened for the formation of friendships; a
closer bond of brotherly feeling is welded, resulting in deeper interest,

64

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

more regular attendance, the making of better Masons, and in ultimately cementing the Lodges closer together; and

tary's cash book be submitted yearly to the Finance Committee,
and to publish a summary of the tr'anscript with the Proceedings. This was referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

Whereas, There are Lodges who have adopted the mode of collective instruction, imparted by a paid instructor, in order to do which,
they have resorted to such subterfuges as carrying such instruction as
an "assistant" secretary, "employment" secretary, or creating some
other fictitious position, to conceal their purpose and justify their
conduct ; and
Whereas, Believing that the more honorable, proper and Masonic
way of meeting this existing condition and finding relief, is not by
subterfuge, but by an appeal to this Grand Lodge, openly and above
board, for proper legislation, I offer the following resolution:
Resolved: That a new section be added to read as follows:
"Sec. ll ir;,;. If two or more Lodges are located within the corporate limits of any city, or Masonic district, such Lodges, for the purpose of properly instructing candidates in the lectures of the several
degrees, may enter into a compact wherein they may provide for the
employm~nt of a brother, at a salary to be agreed upon by said Lodges;
provided, that the brother 50 appointed shall be a meniber of one of
the Lodges to the compact, holds 110 other Masonic office, and certified
to as proficient, in the candidates lectures of the three degrees, by the
Grand Lecturer, or the Inspector of the District wherein such Lodges
are located, whose duties shall be:
(a) To instruct all candidates referred to him by the Masters of
the various Lodges to the compact;
(b) To devote so much of his time as may be necessary for the
proper performance of his duties; and
(c) To perform said duties only in a building which is used for
Masonic purposes.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

SUNDAY DESECRATION
Brother L. T. Cranz introduced the following:
Whereas, Freemasonry is pre-eminently a moral institution and demands 'of its votaries a strict conformity to the requirements of the
moral law and a decent regard to the conventions which regulate the
orderly conduct of society; and
Whereas, The Constitution of the Grand Lodge specifically forbids
the holding of any Lodge meeting on a Sunday except for funeral
purposes; now therefore, be it
Resolved, That no Mason or body of Masons shall advertise in the
public press the holding of any meeting or gathering for any purP.ose
whatever on a Sunday, other than for funeral purposes ; nor shall tickets be issued or posters displayed for any public function except as
hereinbefore stated.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

not only ignored this courtesy and custom, but have earned 1t to the
point of abuse by taking within their ranks, with very s.ligl'.t and of~­
times no investigation, or inquiry as tp the cause of re3ect1on, candidates who have been rejected by Lodges of concurrent jurisdiction; and
Whereas This p~rnicious practice has sometimes reached the stage
of solicitin~, thereby reducing Masonry to a commercial b~sis, causing
strife, discord and ill-feeling among the craft, and enablmg men of
doubtful character to gain admission within our ranks; and
Whereas, Believing that the fraternity as a whole is being injure~
and its high standard lowered by such practice, and that the evil
should be corrected by proper legislation, I offer the following resolution:
Resolved: That Section 97 be· amended to read as follows:
"Sec. 97. Nor shall any Lodge receive such application from any
person who, within twelve months next preceding, shall have been
rejected by any Lodge, unless by dispensation from the Grand Master,
as provided in Section 43.
Nor shall any Lodge recei~e such application from any person who,
after twelve months next preceding, shall have been rejected, unless
(a) He was rejected in the Lodge receiving the petition, or in another Lodge not having concurrent jurisdiction,
(h) By dispensation from the Grand Master, upon proper showing
that an injustice has been done,
(c) By first obtaining a waiver from the Lodge having concurrent
jurisdiction, in which he was rejected.

be no immediate prospect of its being presented on the floor of the
Congress of the United States;

jurisdiction of California, as follows:
First, That he does here and now reaffirm its endorsements of the
principles of said measure.
Second, That a committee be appointed by the M. \V. Grand Master,
charged with the duty of taking such steps as may be reasonable and
proper to the end that said measure now pending in the Congress of
the United States shall be reported out of committee and action taken
by the Congress thereon at the earliest possible moment.
Third, That there be appropriated from the Grand Treasury of this
Lodge the sum of $2000 to defray the expenses of said committee.
Fourth, That said committee be charged to report at the next annual
convocation of this Grand Lodge and to make recommendation thereto
as to any other steps which it may recommend to be taken in the
premises.
Fifth, That said committee prepare a history and synopsis of the
legislation on this subject, and also from time to time report as to
the progress being made hereafter, and that printed copies of said
documents be prepared by this Grand Lodge in sufficient numbers and
forwarded to the subordinate Lodges of this jurisdiction for distribution among their members.
Sixth, That a copy of this resolution be sent to each of the Grand
Lodges in the United States, and that the V. W. Grand Secretary be
instructed to request each of said Grand Lodges to appoint a committee to act in conjunction with the committee appointed herein.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit my fifteenth annual report, and trust that my
efforts will meet with the approbation of the Grand Lodge.
. The Loc~ges generally are in a most healthful and prosperous condition, financially and otherwise, and growing numerically. Many of the
Lodges are growing so large that they are thereby getting away from
the real fraternal spirit that should be ever present. This spirit is impossible in the Lodges that are hovering around the thousand mark
and many arc now reaching that point. It is, however, gratifying t~
report the formation of 25 new Lodges for this year. Quite a number
o.f ne:V Lodges ar: now forming, and will no doubt receive dispensations m the near tuture. But with all this, the Lodges generally are
receiving many petitions and have about all the degree work they can
handle. Several Lodges have and are now erecting beautiful and well
appointed new Masonic Temples, with all the comforts and conveniences
tha: could be desired. Others are remodeling their old Temples, prepan~g. for more commodious social quarters and club rooms, thereby
prov1dmg for the comforts and pleasures of their members. This, to
my way of thinking, is most commendable and will surely add to the
attendance of the Lodges; for after all it is the social activities that
help to bring out the true fraternal spirit and better acquaintanceship
one with the other.
The great increase in membership has been this year about the same
as the last year or two, and is fast approaching the One Hundred
Thousand mark, with 445 Lodges to date. It is essentially necessary
that the officers of Lodges, when conferring the degrees upon their

72

l'ROC'E:NDINGS OF 'l'HE

candidates, to so impress them with the high importance of Masonry,
that they will convince the world that in becoming Master Masons they
have in fact and indeed become better men.
I have visited every district in the state and have held schools of
instruction in many of the Lodges therein, both day and night sessions.
All of these meetiugs have been well attended by the Officers and many
members who were interested in the work.
The Lodges generally have worked out to a greater or less extent
a definite program of education and social entertainment monthly. This
has stimulated interest and increased the attendance materially. Many
of the Lodges publish bulletins giving the degree work and other
activities for the month.
The Grand Master has pretty thoroughly covered the jurisdiction
and has visited nearly all the districts. The brethren have been instructed and entertained by the eloquent addresses given by the Grand
Master. It has been my privilege to accompany him on many of these
visits.

ANNUAL ORATION
Brother Will H. Fischer, Grand Orator, then held Grand
Lodge for an •hour with one of the most eloquent, instructive
and timely orations ever delivered before this body, at the conclusion of which the entire membership present arose to its feet
with well-deserved and long-continued applause. And on motion the Grand Secretary was directed to cause the Oration to
be printed. in sufficient number to supply each member in the
jurisdiction with a copy. Fo!Jowing is the full text of the
Oration:
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
I thank you for this courteous reception, and trust that I may be
able to contribute to the thought of this Communication a suggestion
or two which may be of value, and which will merit your consideration
as the days speed by.
·

At the outset, Most Worshipful Grand ),faster, I desire to express
to you my thanks for the appointment given me a year ago, and also
my appreciation of the courtesy and consideration you have so unceasingly manifested toward me; and I also take this opportunity to acknowledge to my associate officers of Grand Lodge, to the Masters and Wardens here assembled, and through them to the brethren of this Grand
Jurisdiction, my profound gratitude for numberless acts of fraternal
kindness by which they have made me much their debtor.
\Ve are met to exchange fraternal salutations, to give an accounting of our stewardship, to give ear to the admonitions of our master
workmen, to enjoy for a little space the pleasure of each other's
companionship, to b.reak bread and eat meat together, to pledge our
faith anew, to kneel at our common altar, to pay Affection's tribute
to the memory of those beloved brethren who came so often into this
presence but come no more; and then, as Masons have done in all ages
before us, to go forth again unto our labors. On such occasion the
duty of my office requires that I should address you "upon matters
appertaining to the Craft."
At the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge :Ve naturally concern ourselves with an effort to chart, as best we may, our future
activities. We often hear brethren say: "vVe are not greatly interested
in the past of institutions in general; our chief concern is not even with
the present; it is the future to which we look." I make bold to suggest
to you, my brethren, that we cannot intelligently chart the future of
our own or any institution, and that we cannot discern the paths of
wisdom in the present, unless we shall have first surveyed, to some

79

extent at least, that which has taken place in the past; for it is the
experience of the past that must always serve as a guide to the development of the future.
Society in general is passing through an era of restlessness, the
effects of which are felt by Masonry as by all institutions, and as a
result we frequently encounter agitated and excited brethren who have
lost their hosp.itality for the traditional conception of Masonry's proper
sphere of action. We find these brethren, apparently prey to anxiety
and distress as they run about through the halls of Masonry pointing
out activities to which, in their opinion, the Fraternity should commit
itself, and opportunities of which they fear Masonry will fail to avail
itself. I am going to speak to you today in simple, homely phrases,
with reference to what I conceive to be the real opportunities of
Masonry and Masons.
So far as I am concerned, I frankly confess that I am slow to commit
the sanction of my individual judgment to those adventures and innovations which, in such great number, are suggested by enthusiastic
brethren; for I am persuaded that these brethren have fallen victims
to a confusion of thought, leading them to seek to impose upon the
Institution itself duties and activities which properly belong to the
individual Mason.
As I look back over the history of this Institution of ours I find
that Masonry has never paraded under a militant flag; but Masom
have bled in countless conflicts waged to advance the common sta'.~
of man. Masonry has never ruled or sought to rule at the courts of
kings, the palaces of emperors, or in the parliaments of the free. It
has never exercised or sought to exercise a temporal power; it has
requir.ed no embattled defenders by day and no masked avengers by
night. But Masons have written into codes and constitutions those
principles and laws which have lifted the eyes of bondsmen to the sunswept skies, and lighted the flaming torch of knowledge in the nigh~
of ignorance and degradation to illumine the upward-faring pathway3
of humankind. Masonry has never presumed to perform ·a churchly
office; but Masons in every country and in every clime have been
distinguished by their reverence for Deity and by the virtue of their
lives.
From time immemorial Masonry has exercised a mystically beneficent influence over human society and human history; and I am
convinced that this influence, like the Institution's age-long endurance
and the intimacy and vigor of its appeal to men living under all manner
of conditions and systems and governments, in shifting centuries and
in cha~ging times, has been due, first to its continuing and unbroken
attachment to unchallengeable fundamental principles of human conduct
and divine aspiration, and secondly, to the fact that, like a great rock

80

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GHAND LODGE OF CALII~OnNrA

lifting itself· from the sea, it has resisted in all times the fickle winds
and tides of popular fancy, passion, delusion and design.
Thus Masonry has come down to us, performing its original
functions, teaching to men the kindly, manly virtues, informing them
with a generous and exalted patriotism, instructing them in the social
sciences, and indelibly impressing on their minds a moving sense of
the power, wisdom and goodness of the Great Artificer of the Universe.
Upon that basis and with that sort of a program Masonry has ever
transmitted from the eternal sources of Truth, through her votarie>
into the world about them, the light that illumines and makes possible
the advance of civilization. Shall we now, in any rashness of inspiration
or ambition, consider a departure from the old basis of our Institution,
or innovations in its ancient and effective program? That, to me, is
the challenge of the hour, the subject which should be uppermost in
O!lr minds.

the fluttering oriflammcs of conflict are raised. There are old trails,
too, choked, it mµy be, with new. growth. There are old virtues, old
proprieties, old modesties, old truths to be conserved, and there are old
evils, old passions, old prcjmliccs and old ignorance to be overcome.
It is not strange that, in the midst of the maze and conflict of modern
thought and action he should manifest a tendency to become confused;
the age itself is confused and confusing.

I am not of that small number who insist that Masonry, as an
Institution, can take n'o action whatsoever along so-called "practical"
lines, but I am persuaded now, as ever I have been persuaded, that
every characteristic of the Institution stamps it as necessarily conservative, and that every obligation imposes upon those in control of its
destinies a solemn respect for such conservatism. It is Masonry's great
function to inform; it is the function of individual Masons to perform.
Many experiments are proposed. We have brethren who insist that
our Institution should enter the field of politics and attempt to function
as a definite political organization in support of Masons who happen to
be candidates for office. \Ve have others who believe that Masonry
should organize its forces to oppose or aid some particular class or
creed. We have others who would commit the Fraternity to the
espousal of certain specific measures of proposed legislation. · Others
would not hesitate to align the Order with one or another of the
numberless movements of the day and the times. Still others would
use the Fraternity to advance certain radical policies of public education. And so we might, if it were necessary, go through an extended
list of experiments and ideas presented for our consideration, all of
which must be and are rejected by the great body of sound, dear-thinking Masons. Remembering that harmony is "the strength and support
of all Institutions," let us examine the general conditions which surround
us, so that we may judge with some intelligence as to whether Masonry
might be successful in such adventures as have just been indicated.
The Mason coming upon the scene of life today finds that there are
new pathways winding across the world, challenging his curiosity and
daring; there are new sciences, new thoughts, new theories, new
tendencies to be tested in the laboratory of experience ; there are new
ideas knocking at the door of Time; there are new battlefields on which

The fruits of radical propaganda are making themselves apparent.
We encounter, among the people, a restive disposition. We have a
greater measure of prosperity and general comfort than can be found
elsewhere in this wide world, and yet we have a discontented people.
\Ve see these fruits in the crumbling of the home; we have but to read
divorce statistics. vVe find a people whose forefathers fought to make
this a Republic drifting from their old moorings, departing from the
system which was handed down to them as the one plan of government under which the people could escape, on the one hand the tyranny
of kings and on the other the tyranny of mobs, and surrendering their
priceless heritage for a democracy full-sown with the seeds of social
and economic revolution. Our old Americanism, which was the wonder
and admiration of the world, is shaken and corrupted. We find the
people, led by demagogic guides, demanding that government take
upon itself the exercise of functions which nature intended, and which
our ancestors fought to win, for the individual; and at the same time,
through the adoption of whimsical popular devices advertised as precursors of the millennium, they are withdrawing from government the
exercise of vital functions and prerogatives in the deprivation of which
governm'ent loses its integrity, its power and its virtue and becomes the
craven creature of the crowd.

.
Ma~onry as an Institution could scarcely be expected to interpose
itself directly among these matters; but every Mason can individually
damn t.he treacherous flatteries of the demagogue, the visionary and
the radical. And he should have no hestitancy in doing so. Let every
Mason in this jurisdiction rededicate himself to common sense to oldfashioned Americanism, and go forth to give battle to all who' counsel
the follies we have had under discussion. The society of our day
supports numb:rless institutions and organizations, each especially
crea~ed and designed te advance one particular science, to promote one
particular professi~n, to encourage one particular business or industry,
to protect one particular group of labor, to uphold the interests of one
particular church or p~rty. In those organizations the Mason has
wonderful opportunity to bring to the treatment of every problem and
activity of our times an application of the sound principles which
Masonry has instilled into his consciousness and into the impulses of
his life. There, in the busy round of every day, my brethren, is our
transcendent opportunity to win the world to that Masonry of action
and spirit which is the very heart-throb of civilization.
We hear and think much about our schools. Now, the Masonic
Fraternity is on record, and always has been, as a champion of public
education. Tfiere is not one among us who would care to take a
backward step. In a nation such as ours it is imperative that the
people should be educated. We stand always, and with all our strength,
for the protection, integrity and upbuilding of the public school system.
In that we are unanimous. But, if I be not mistaken, the individual
Mason is not committed, by reason of such loyalty, to specific measures
of education. I do not conceive it to be my Masonic duty blindly to
endorse every measure presented to me, merely .because it comes from
those who have in charge the administration of the schools. I do not
recognize. it as a Masonic duty to vote for issues of school bonds for
instance, unless I have assured myself of the public necessity ther~for.
The point I wish to make is this, that Masons should never become the
unquestioning and unreasoning bond-servants of any institution, whether
schools, or churches, or societies. It is our duty to know what we
are doing when we exercise the electoral franchise, and to realize that
those who administer human institutions are as human as ourselves,
subject to the same ambitions and faults. There is never a time when
Masons should not be particularly careful to see that the causes they
pu,blidy support )1ave real merit and deserve such support.
But speaking broadly, the cause of the schools is the cause of
Masonry, and herein, perhaps, the Institution itself, can find some
functioning scope. If Masonry is to remain, as it will, a great pillar
of support to the schools, there may be room for the application, in a
formal way, of well-considered Masonic judgment as to school admin-

istration and also as to the character and efficiency of the training
imparted to the young. Above all, Masonry might well undertake to
see that the professional school politician is driven out of our educational
system.
Our educational cost is enormous. It is of the utmost importance
to see that the expenditures along that line are made with the highest
possible degree of efficiency. I would like to see Masonry, in this
jurisdiction, through properly organized committees keep in close touch
with the schools, studying them carefully and impartially and reporting
their findings from time to time for the information and guidance of the
Craft. These investigations might especially relate to educational policies as expressed in courses of study. The spirit of our schools, and
the purposes they have in view, are of high importance. There is an
old French saying that it is impossible to make a silk purse out of a
sow's ear. If our schools are to perform their function in a manner
most useful to society they must equip the individual student with the
training he or she is qualified to ·receive. It is a useless expense to
insist on giving a large-calibre education to a small-calibre mind. It
is not only extravagant but socially dangerous to make the swivelchair the objective of all education, because there are a great many
boys and girls who do not possess swivel-chair brains, but who are
well qualified to lead socially useful and personally happy lives if given
the proper aspirations and training. Once we have passed the elementary studies we must adapt education, so far as may be possible, to the
individual, or at least to classes and types of individuals. We must
not hold up false standards of success, and we must not flatter children.
It is wrong to induce a boy, by nature intended for a mechanical
trade, to go through years of so-called higher. education to become,
ultimately, a failure in a profession to which nature has not adapted
him. It is wrong to insinuate that the purpose of modern education is
to raise the youth of the land above the necessity to labor. It is right
to dignify labor and to train the labor of the oncoming generations_ for
efficiency. There are liberal rewards for efficient labor. I would like to
see a rule enforced which would dose the doors of our free universities
to all students who had failed to manifest the highest degree of
ambition and scholarship. I would like to see those doors opened to
every student who had demonstrated his capacity for higher learning;
and if he were poor I would like to see the State advance him the
money required for his support.
Economy in school administration is required because of the vast
educational need, as may be observed from the figures on illiteracy. As
shown by the 1920 Census there were in this country over 5,000,000
people above the age of ten years unable to read or write in any
language, of which number more than 4,400,000 were above the age of

21 years. What sort of citizenship are we going to expect from men
and .women who have no means of learning our history or imbibing

of life in a complex age? Why, under moderr;t conditions they become
a p~ey to the exploiter and the agitator. Victimized, disappointed,

Masons, as good Americans, have the right and duty to demand that

Illite:acy. is !ntimately associated, as we all know, with the problem
of Amencamzat10n. It would appear that "Americanization" has become a mere slogan. Doubtless we might develop various opinions
as to how we might make good Americans of those who come from
foreign shores. The subject is too large for extended discussion but
it .challenges the extended thought of every Mason. Dismissi~g it
quickly as we hasten along, I leave this thought for your consideration:
Don't pamper the immigrant; don't entertain him with cheap movies,
for he can attend to his own entertainment; but insist that he get a
square deal and decent treatment in industry and that his children be
given a decent education. In the meantime, keep the gates of immigration closed until we have Americanized the immigrants now in our
midst, and then open them only to immigrants of the better classes.
Masonry, as an Institution, can practice no greater folly than to
consider itself a political organization. Politics is a rock upon which
wit.h haste and irrevocable disaster, the barque of Masonry would b~
split; but every Mason, my brethren, can do politics for himself, and
every Mason should be an active politician, using that word in its
best sense. Because of our adoption of popular legislation there rests
upon each of us a great responsibility. For instance, we shall find on
the ballot, on November 7th, thirty propositions, most of them proposed
amendments to the Constitution, the organic law of our State. On each
of these propositions it is our duty to vote intelligently. How many of
us can honestly say that we have studied those measures-all or any
of them-and given thought to the principles they involve? How many
of us feel that we are capable of standing here now and giving an
intelligent opinion as to the probable results, in operation, of these
amendments, some of which go to the very heart of our economic and
governmental organizations? Our duty is clear. If we fail to perform
it, .how can ~e boast of our good citizenship
Let us, my brethren,
strive to attam breadth and vision and the understanding that each of
us has a proud privilege and a great duty as a citizen of this country
of ours; that every act and policy of ,government has a meaning for
the people; that we owe it to society and to ourselves to take a little

87

time away from our auto rides and the movies and give a night occasionally to honest study and thinking and discussion relative to the welfare
of our nation and our State.
We have another great problem-the crime problem. Why, in my
cou11ty of Los Angeles, which produces so many other great fig·ures for
the edification of you gentlemen from other parts of the State, we
produced in a year more murders than in the same space of time were
committed in the British Isles. All sorts of crime are prevalent, not
only in California but throughout the nation; and the most shocking
phase of the situation lies in the fact that so many of the criminals are
mere youths. What is the cause and what is the cure? I must confess that the answer is difficult to supply. Ori. the one hand we have
our school~, and compulsory education. We have hundreds if not
thousands of philanthropic and uplift societies; we have churches and
charities; we have good men and women in all sorts of social service.
We have wealth, comfort, luxury, music, art, refinement. On the other
hand we have the multiplication of criminals, both young and old; we
have violence; we have vice; we have an increase in. the number of
feeble-minded; we have increasing insanity. The wave of crime rises
until it threatens to engulf us in general disorder and a social breakdown.
Certainly, with reference to crime, the so-called modern theories
have failed to produce results. The old, fundamental law still holds.
Naught but the fear of punishment is a deterrent to crime. Masons
can do this much; each one of us can exercise his personal influence
to impress upon jurors the folly of the prevailing idea of heroizing
criminals. We can say to the editors of our great papers that we do
not want crime capitalized at our expense; that we do not want it exploited all over the front page every day. We can signify that we are
not interested in reading, and in having our children read, the sensational exploits of boy bandits. We can say, if we will, that we do
not wish to read the salacious details of every putrid divorce case that
can be dug out of the sewers of either high or low society. Each of us
can carry that message to our editors. If the Masons of California
would act in unison along that line, the complexion of the news would
be greatly changed and improved; for let me tell you, my brethren,
that when you take the publicity out of crime and vice today, you
will go a long way toward reducing these evils. We can say to the
judges of our courts that we have had enough of this silly idea of
releasing crooks and criminals on probation; we can demand that the
criminal courts function as they were intended to function. They can
enforce the law and the penalties of the law; we need no extraneous
organizations for that purpose. And we can say to the proprietors of
moving picture houses which we attend that we want them to quit
showing pictures that breed crimes and the troop of vicious lusts. Let

us, as Masons, impress everywhere those sound, clean, right principles

We must stand a little firmer, my friends, for the integrity of the
American borne. I have suggested to you that the statistico of the
divorce courts of our Janel are very depressing. I know that this is a
delicate subject. I realize that there are many cases wherein the
severance of marital ties is justified by conditions; but in just the
measure that it is possible, Masons, who claim to be special and sworn
defenders of the home life of our countr}, should frown upon the idea
that men and women can make easy marriages and hasty separations,
leaving children orphaned while their parents yet live, cases for our
courts to handle, soil jn which the seeds of crime will flourish; and
over and above all the destruction in the minds and hearts of men and
women of those fine old ideals which have lain at the very roots of our
national life, and which are the very foundation· stones of any Christian
civilization that has hope of endurance. And along that line, my
brethren, practice as we preach.
Someone has said: "It is not the number of people that makes a
nation great, else China would be the greatest nation on the globe today.
It is not prowess that preserves empires from decay, else Rome would
have lived forever. It is not genius, else the dust of the Parthenon
would not now be mingled with the dust of Grecian art, and we might
still be enchanted with the songs of some dark-eyed Sappho and
charmed with the Iliad of some modern Homer. It is the virtue and
patriotism of the people and their faith in Almighty God, that uphold
nations and lengthen the paths of their glory."
Our late Brother, Theodore Roosevelt, gave us this utteraiice:
"We here in America hold in our hands the future of the world the
fate of the coming years; and shame and disgrace will be ours if i~ our
eyes the light of high resolve be dimmed, if we trail in the dust the
golden hopes of men."
Drawing now to a conclusion, my brethren, let us have a right conception of this Masonry of ours. Let us get away from the idea that,
as an Institution, it is militant; for it never was formed to function that
way. Let us carry in our minds and hearts an understanding of that
nobler Masonry which prompts men to manifest in their lives those
manly virtues which are the flower of a just, generous and elevated
spirit. And let us be kind.
So many gods, so many greeds,
So many paths that wind and wind,
When just the art of being kind
Is all this old world needs.

We speak of the mysteries of Masonry. The only mystery I have
ever encountered in Masonry is the fact that so many Masons fail
to understand its simplicity. Let us drink deep, my brethren, at the
fountains which spring beside our altars. Let us realize that the
teachings of Masonry, so simple, yet so sufficient, are genuine expressions of the only thoughts, the only principles, that will preserve our race
and our civilization and continue us a great and glorious nation.
Finally, I commend to you the spirit of a poem:
Let me but live my life from day to day
With forward face and unreluctant soul,
Not hastening toward or turning from the goal,
Not mourning for the things that disappear
In the dead past, or holding back in fear
From what the future veils; but with a whole
And happy heart. that pays its toll
To youth and age and journeys on with cheer.
So, let the path wind up the hill or down,
O'er rough or smooth, the journey will be joy,
Still seeking what I sought when but a boyN ew friendships, high endeavor and a crown.
And thus my heart will keep with courage to the quest,
Knowing the road's last turn will be the best.

Brother Charles M. Wollenberg, President of the Board of
Trustees of the Masonic Homes, presented t'he report of the

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

We present herewith our annual report for the fiscal year ended
July 31 as to financial matters, and to October 1, 1922, relative to the
general condition of the Homes.
On October 14, 1921, th e Board met and organized with the same
officers as reported last year. Past Grand Master Charles Albert
Adams presented his appointment as a member of the Board, vice
Charles G. Johnspn, term expired. The newly-installed Junior Grand
Warden, R.". w:. David ]. Reese, was a~so seated as a member of
the Board.
Regular meetings were held at San Francisco and Los Angeles,
as well as weekly conferences by the Trustees living in the vicinity of
the two cities.
On the 22d of January, 1922, at the invitation of the Committee
on Endowment, a joint meeting of that Committee with the Board
of Trustees was held at the city of San Francisco, full report of
which will be rendered by the Committee on Endowment.

Appointment of Superintendent at Covina
The vacancy in the office of Superintendent of the Home at Covina
was filled in N ovemher, 1921, by the appointment of Brother Leland
S . Drew, a member of Orland Lodge No. 265. He had been teacher of
manual training and principa! of a high school, and at the time of his
engagement at the Home was assistant Superintendent of Schools of
Contra Costa county. He came to us highly recommended, and his
successful administration of the Home <luring the y~ar is evidence that
the Board made no mistake in this selection. V./ e recognize that
Brother Drew was somewhat handicapped in his work because of his
.lack of personal acquaintance of conditions and with the brethren
generally in the vicinity of the Home, but we feel that he has fully
adjusted himself to his new environment, and we predict a successful
administration of the Covina Home under his superintendency.

Matrons
In November, 1921, Mrs. Maude E. Miller resnmed her duties as
Matron at the Covina Home, to the delight of the children. Mrs.

New Buildings
At the annual communication of Grand Lodge last year, the accepted plans of the proposed new buildings to be erected on the
grounds of· the Dec·oto Home were displayed. An architect was
selected in accordance . with the plan outlined in our last annual
report, Brother William Mooser of Doric Lodge No. 216 being the
winner of the contest. He was instructed to prepare detail plans for
a hundred-room building for men, a fifty-room bui'.ding for women,
and an addition to our over crowded hospital; with a causeway leading
from the hospital to the new building for women. On April 1, 1922,
bids from seventy-five contractors were received and considered for
the construction of the new buildings. Aft~r a careful analysis of the
several bids, co.ntracts were entered into.
Construction work is progressing, but not as rapidly as we wish,
owing largely to the difficulty of getting certain classes of labor to
report at the Home, many mechanics apparently preferring to work
in the cities. However, it is hoped that the bui'dings contracted for
will be completed before the middle of next summer, when the matter
of furnishing must be considered.

Home. The full capacity of the present buildings contemplates a
maximum of one hundred and twenty, but this number will necessitate
the use of rooms now assigned to the older children for study purposes. The Home cannot properly maintain more than one hundred
and eight, and your Trustees will, during the coming year, study the
scheme of operation of other similar institutions and decide whether
the present type of buildings at Covina be continued. It is possible
that the semi-cottage plan will be adopted.

Care of the Bodily Afflicted
At the last annual communication of Grand Lodge the Trustees
were authorized to assist Lodges in the care of those whose physical
infirmities precluded their admission to the Decoto Home. During
the year we have, under the authority given, assisted a number of
Lodges to properly care for men and women who would otherwise
have been too great a burden for the Lodges, and who wou'.d otherwise
have possibly been neglected. 'I'his expense has been listed in our
financial report as Outside Relief, and has added to the total sum of
maintenance, but we feel that the results have amply justified the
wisdom of the rule. lt is particularly helpful to the older and smaller
LodgeR whose funds are not too p!entiful.

The farm at Decoto is not profitable from <l monetary view,
although there is si1own a small profit on the year's operation. Uo';ever, there is · a large indirect gain which cannot be mea~ur.ed m
dollars or discussed as a commercial transaclion, ;md that is m. ~he
furnishing to the residents of fresh vegetables in gcner?us qmmt1ti:s,
fresh eggs and poultry from the chicken yard, fresh fn11ts and ~ern~s
in season of a quality and quantity that would not be possible tf
these items were required to be purchased in the markets.
The farm at the Covina Horne will not show a profit for several
years. The orange and lemon and other trees are young. and h<;ve not
come in'to full production. The heavy frosts last wmter virtually
wiped out the young orchard and it must be replan~ed. T~e. frosts also
curtailed the productivity of the older trees. This condition was an
.tnusual occurrence and we hope will not again happen. We expect
that when the orange and lemon groves come into full bearing, the
Covina farm activities will show a handsome profit.

Scholarships
Three of our children from the Covina Home are now participating in the privileges of scholarships donated for the pur?ose. ,01:e
is attrnding the Cogswell Po'.ytechnic school in San Francisco. fh.1s
young man is making good progress. in hi~ sch~ol work, and will
graduate in the early part of 1923. It 1s the mtent1on of the Board to
then send him to the University of California as a student of 1111111ng
engineering. One, a girl, is at Claremont college a_nd ~e~orts from
that institution indicate that the expense thereat is givmg proper
results. One, a boy, has matriculated at the University of Southern
California as a student of dentistry. As will be noted in the report of
the Superintendent of the Home ~t Covina, we have had .sixteen
children attending high school durmg the last year, and with the
beginning of the fall term there are twenty children from the Home
in attendance there.
We need more funds for scholarships, and it is hoped some good
brother or some generous Masonic Body will speedily add to the small
funds we now have in hand for educational purposes.

Financial Statement
The financial statement appended to this report clearly indicates
the success of the legislation requiring initiates to pay twenty dol'ars
for the benefit of the Homes. Without this scheme of raising revenue
the building programme at our two Homes would have been impossible.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRA:N'D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Decoto Home-Report of Superintendent

There has been no change in the management of the farm. The
greater part of the hill ranch has, as in the past, been leased either on
shares or cash rental. A fair crop of hay has been raised and the
surplus sold in the local market. The chicken and hog ranches, and
the berry gardens have given good returns. The vegetab'e garden
supplies a variety of fresh vegetables for the table and plenty of greens
for the farmyard. The fruit crop in the orchards has been light.
The apricots have been dried. The prune crop is now being gathered
and sent to the dryer. All dried fruit over and above our needs will
be sold in the San Francisco market.
There are now 3000 volumes on the shelves of our library. In
addition to this, our reading tables in the men's club rooms, the ladies'
social room and hospital are well supplied, through members of the
fraternity, with daily papers and periodicals from San Francisco, Oakland and other places.
The Grand Chapter Order of the Eastern Star at the Annual
Communication in October, 1921, <ippropriated $1000.00 for the furnishing of the Ladies' Social Room in the new building of 50 rooms.·
now being erected upon the grounds of the Home. This amount is
available as soon as the building is completed and ready to be occupied.
The social life of the Home has been greatly enriched during the
year by literary and musical entertainments made possible by the
interest taken in our welfare by Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters and
members of the fraternity and their ladies. These entertainments have
been factors in contributing to the pleasure and contentment of the
family ..
. A moving picture entertainment is given in the Temple every
Wednesday afternoon. A family social is held every Thursday evening. Chorus practice every Friday evening. Services are held in the
Assembly Hall every Sunday afternoon. All these gatherings are
well attended. A radio wireless equipment, complete in every detail
_has been installed where the members of the Home can "listen in" and
enjoy radio concerts which are daily given, both afternoon and evening,
·
in San Francisco and the Bay cities.
The special exercises which stand out prominently are those which
were held on Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, New Year's Day,
Lincoln's Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter Sunday, Memorial
Day, and Independence Day. The programs for these exercises were
prepared and given by the members of the Home.

To the Board of Tru·stees, Masonic Homes of California:
I herewith present for your consideration my thirteenth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decoto, California,
for the year ending August 31, 1922.
There has been the usual routine in the management of the Home,
without any special changes during the past year, which has been a
very important one in the history of the Home, as many new and necessary improvements are now being made to enlarge the usefulness of
the great benevolent work carried on here by the fraternity.
The new buildings for men and women and the additions to the
hospital now being built will, when completed, meet the requirements
of the Lodges in this jurisdiction for sometime to come and enable
the management to render a higher standard of service in ministering
to the needs of those who are enjoying the care and protection of
the Home. To care for the members of our large family, where each
one has his own individuality, his own self expression, calls for a
consecrated spirit of service in keeping with the ideals of our fraternity.
There are now at the Home 88 men and 62 women. During the
year 35 persons have been admitted, 27 have passed away and there
have been 4 departures. All the rooms for women are now occupied
and admissions are only made as vacancies occur.
The general health of the family has been good with the exception
of those who are infirm and feeble owing to advancing years. There
are 28 persons being cared for at the Coleman hospital, where they are
receiving every care and comfort our physician and nurses are able
to give them.
All the members of the Home are encouraged to render some
service in keeping with their strength for the upbuilding of the 'Home
and in their leisure hours to interest themselves in healthful and
wholesome diversions for their moral, mental· and physical wellbeing.
A number of the brethren and ladies daily assist in light work
connected with the several departments of the Home. · Three of the
brethren have so far recovered their health, that they are now on
leave of absence and are engaged in gainful occupations and for the
time being are successful in supporting themselves.
All the necessary repairs in order to keep up the physical condition of the buildings have been made. All the carpenter work and
painting is done by members of the Home.

The follO\ving is a list of those who have contributed to our
enjoym~nt.

September 17, 1921, a program of moving pictures, songs and
dances given by Victory Lodge, No. 474.
