September 24, third degree conferred by Mount Oso Lodge, No.

460.
October l, Alameda Pyramid, No. 8, A. E. 0. S. staged a farce
entitled "Oh Doctor."
October 8, Oakland Lodge, No. 188, Rockridge Lodge No. 468 and
the Alameda Pyramid of Sciots gave a luncheon in the Grove and an
entertainment in the evening.
October 9, a program of music, recitations and dancing given in
the afternoon by Albert Pike Chapter, No. 284, 0. E. S.
November 2, DeMolay Order for Boys, San Jose Chapter, conferred the first and second degrees.
February 2, 1922, DeMolay Order for Boys, Oakland Chapter, gave
a program consisting of a one-act play, music and songs.
May 6, Pacific Lodge, No. 136, third degree in the Temple. \Vork
illustrated with stereopticon pictures; afterward, accompanied by their
ladies, gave a concert in the Assembly Hall.
May 10, the Ladies' Auxiliary of Berkeley Commandery, K. T.
Basket luncheon on the grounds. An entertainment of music, readings
and dancing in the evening.
May 14, concert by 65 members of the Lockwood High School
band.
May 14, the Olympic male quartette entertained the family in the
Assembly Hall.
May 20, third degree conferred by Balder Lodge, No. 393.
May 29, Jewel Lodge, No. 374, band concert on the Horne·grounds.
June 10, luncheon in the grove in the afternoon and an entertainment in the evening given by Fruitvale Lodge, No. 336 and their
ladies.
July 15, Apollo Lodge, No. 396, band concert on the grounds,
luncheon in the Grove, entertainment in the evening.
July 29, Fellowship Lodge, No. 480, gave a luncheon in the Grove,
followed by an entertainment in the Temple.
August 5, a visit of the Grand Matron and officers of the Eastern
Star, accompanied by members of the East Bay Matrons Association.
Basket luncheon, followed by an entertainment in the Temple.
August 19, Oakland Lodge, No. 188, refreshments in the Grove
in the afternoon and a musical program in the evening.
August 26, Thousand Oaks Lodge, No. 478, conferred the second
section of the third degree, afterward accompanied by the members
of Thousand Oaks Chapter, 0. E. S. gave a program of music and
songs.

RECOMMENDATIONS.

Incinerator for the burning of refuse and garbage.
Smokehouse for the curing of ham and bacon.
Survey of the boundaries of the Home property and repairs to
fences.
A Ford truck for the hauling of light freight, express and mail.
An additional washing machine for the laundry.
A new system of water pipes on the grounds of the Horne to
supply water for fire hydrants and for irrigation and watering lawns
and flower beds, to replace the piping now in use.
New wire fences for chicken ranch ; repairs to chicken sheds.
In conclusion I wish to extend to the Board of Trnstees my most
sincere appreciation of the confidence you have at all times placed in
me and to thank you for the _many kindnesses you have shown me.
To the officers and employes of the Home, I wish to express my
appreciation of their loyalty and good service.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK

B. HARTMAN,
Superintendent.

Covina Home-Superintendent's Report
'J'o the Board of Trustees,
Masonic Homes of California.

In making a report of the activities of the Covina Home for
the past year I find that there are so many things that have occupied our at~ention that I think it best to give only a brief outline
of ~cc?mphshments and recommendations. It has been a very
grabfyrng year to your Superintendent in that he has had at all
times the heartiest co-operation from the children of the Home
and ~he membe;s of the staff. It has been his attitude to try to do
nothing revolutionary but to build for the future on the foundations
established.
We've been called upon during the past year to care for an
.
rncrease of over thirty per cent in the residents of the Home. This
has nec.essitated new equipment and expansion generally. While the
Home is not filled to capacity, would like to recommend the addition of new buildings to the plant soon, because few children could
be added with the present equipment and still give them the care
an? advantages that the Masonic Fraternity wish to provide for the
children under their care. The local schools of the district serve
th.e n:eds of the Home very well indeed. Brother Ben S. Millikan,
District Superintendent, is a very progressive schoolman and is
particularly interested in the progress of our children. This coming
year it is the privilege of the Grammar School children to attend
school in a modern, up-to-date building just erected. The children
have made splendid advancement in their school work and hold a
high place in the Covina High School and the Charter Oak Grammar Sch~ol, where they attend. I would draw attention to the fact
that durmg the past year sixteen children have attended High
School, a
greater num.ber than we have had in the past. This
year we begm the term with twenty children attending. This adds
new r:s~onsi~ilities an~ new problems. Among these is the problem
of dec1dmg with the child the course he is to pursue to best fit him
for life. Therefore it would be recommended that after this year
~uitable. provisio.n be made to enter some of the older girls and boys
m special vocat10nal schools as some children would be benefited
more than through taking a regular high school course.
. 1:his year it has ?een possible with our new Manual Training
Bmldmg and Domestic Science Cottage to give the older children
additional training at home. The girls have enjoyed and profited
by l~arning the art of keeping house and have found a great pleasure m the very complete cottage donated by the Grand Council

fa;

121

Royal and Select Mass.ns of California. The Manual Trainin~
Building, a gift of the Grand Chapter Royal Arch Masons of Cah·
fornia, has served a splendid purpose in giving the boys a place to
·work off their surplus energy and at the same time receive instructions in the use and care of tools and learning to make projects
useful to themselves and the Home. In the carrying on of this
we've had splendid co-operation from various sources, Mr. George
Hargraves has very ably handled the manual training work and
has also given instruction throughout the year in physical training.
The past reports have covered very fully the watchful care that
is given to the health of the children. \Vith the assistance of the
several friends of the Fraternity this work has been carried on this
year .very satisfactorily. Our good Brother, Warren D. Gill, has continued his interest in the care of the dental work. After first examining each child personally and making recommendations as to work
needed the children were divided into groups and with the assistance of twelve other dentists their teeth have been kept in splendid
condition.
Dr. ]. M. Dunsmoor, for many years a staunch supporter and
friend of the Home, examined all the children and with the assistance of Doctors Nannie Dunsmoor, R. M. Dunsmoor, John B. Renfrew, James H. Beggs, W. R. Crane, Geo. R. Waller Jr., B. T.
Hastreiter and L. R. Linhart, cared for all minor operations such
as removal of tonsils and adenoids
Doctors W. P. Magan and S. S. Magan, resident physicians of
Covina, have been invaluable in caring for the ailments of the chi!~
dren during the year. They cheerfully respond at any hour of the
night or day that we need them and without thought of personal
remuneration give the best that is in them for the welfare of the
children.
A graduate nurse has been added to the staff and we are fortunate in having this position filled by a very competent person.
Throughout the year changes and improvements have been
made, but because of its bearing on the health of the residents
would mention especially that the dairy barn has been ceiled anrl
screened to make it more sanitary, and the milkhouse has been
enlarged and an aerator has been installed. The herd has been
increased and the tubercular test applied regularly so that we have
an abundance of wholesome milk.
The trip to Camp Baldy was made this year in trucks, which
enabled us to take a larger percentage of children than could have
gone in the usual manner. Seventy children made the trip and enjoyed four days of hiking to the various points of interest. The

November 20, Culver City Lodge No. 467 visited the Home. They

November 27, South Gate Lodge No. 320 and South Gate Chapter

June 18, Garvanza Lodge No. 492 and Garvanza Chapter No. 266,

June 18, Highland Park Lodge No. 382 of Los Angeles paid a visit

concert.
June 28, through the interest of 0. G. Beaman, of Albert Pike
Lodge No. 484, Los Angeles, the Home was given the opportunity to

July 2, a very pleasant visit from Torrance Lodge No. 447 and a
donation of fruit, jelly and candies.
August 13, Jinnistan Grotto and their families visited Camp Tucker at Balboa. Band music, picnic lunch for all and 20 gallons of ice
cream. A nice gift was given to each child and prizes were awarded the
winners of the various contests on water and land. Tom Wilson
awarded the prizes, and did much in making the day a very happy one
for all present, especially for the children of the Home.
Donations to Covina Home
A great many donations have been left at the Home for the pleasure of the children during the past year. While the Home is not dependent in any way on charity, yet these gifts have served to remind
us that the children of the Masonic Home have numerous friends among
the brethren and friends of the fraternity. We know that from the
spirit exemplified by the donors that they are not seeking worldly praise
and publicity for these presents, but we feel that it is only right that
suitable mention should be made.
Through the will of the late Brother Wm. Schulyler Moses, Golden
Gate Lodge No. 30, San Francisco, who was a Mason of high degree,
having been elected and installed 133 times to various Masonic offices
during the interval between 1850 and 1912, there was left to the children
of the Home one 8-inch telescope and globes.
The Los Angeles Times has furnished the Home with a Kennedy
audion radio set, with a two stage amplifier and magnavox for the year.
Wilshire Lodge No. 445 and Henry S. Orme Lodge No. 458 have
furnished educational and entertaining motion pictures at the Home
monthly throughout the year.

Mental Status
A total of 98 children (51 girls and 47 boys) are at the Home
at the present time, the youngest 5 years, 6 months, and the oldest
16 years. All children show a normal mental development with
the exception of four. These youngsters were greatly handicapped
in their former environment, and are somewhat slow in their
progress, but under the present opportunities offered are advancing
normally. It is very apparent that the Masonic child who has been
at the Home more than two years has a decided advantage over

155

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAN'D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the child who ha:s recently entered. On a visit to the Charter
Oak Public School, we were assured that our children were leaders
in their respective grades. The school enrollment in grades is as
follows:
High School ................................................. .20
8th Grade ........................................................ 13
7th Grade ........................................................ 8
6th Grade ........................................................ 12
5th Grade ........................................................ 12
4th Grade ........................................................ 10
3rd Grade ........................................................ 8
2nd Grade ........................................................ 8
1st Grade ........................................................ 3
Below school age .......................................... 3
Dental College .............................................. l

appear to be highly satisfactory the cause for the malnutrition
found must be looked for in other quarters such as have been suggested in another part of this report.
Conditions found in the nose and throat. were very satisfactory
with one or two exceptions. Tonsils and adenoids have been
removed almost universally excepting in the case of a few children
who have been in the Home but a short time.
The state of the teeth of these children was found to be extremely good. Teeth were white and clean and showed regular
and thorough use of the toothbrush. Such cavities as were found
were small and probably were formed during the vacation period.
This state of affairs is eminently satisfactory and worthy of all
praise.
The state of the skin in general was satisfactory. One rather
severe case of Impetigo was found and immediately reported for
isolation. Further remarks on the subject of contagious skin
disease will be found under "Recommendations."
As in previous years your examiner found a considerable proportion of children suffering from various degrees of flat-foot.
Out of twenty-six children specially examined for this point eleven
or 42.3% were found to have flat-foot varying from a slight to a
marked degree. The high incidence of flat-foot such as this is not
uncommon among children of similar age but is a condition which
is too often neglected and which demands prompt and thorough
amelioration. Further remarks on this subject will be found under
"Recommendations."

Total ........................................................98

Physical Examination of Children
A complete physical examination of all children admitted
since the survey of 1921 and of a number of the older children
whose condition required it was made. The present report deals
rather with the general findings of the survey than with individual
defects which were immediately reported to the Superintendent and
to the medical visitor.
The children had just returned from their summer vacation
at the beach and appeared to be in good muscular trim, tanned
and in good spirits. ,Eighty-four ~hildren were weighed and
measured with the results shown in the following table:
Normal weight or over ........... .24 or 42.9%
Below normal ............................48 or 57.1%
7% or more underweighL...... 19 or 22.6
10% or more underweight ........ 13 or 15.S
Comparisons were made by the standard tables of Wood. Since
the children were weighed without clothing a 4% correction was
made for this factor and due consideration was given to the fact
that after vacation many children show a certain loss in body
fat. Nevertheless the state of nutrition of the children cannot be
regarded as wholly satisfactory. Any well conditioned group of
children should show at least 50% at or above the normal average
and children 7% or more underweight_ must be regarded as in an
unsatisfactory condition. Since the diets given these children

Diet
Modern dietetic standards for growing children call for liberal allowance of fresh fruit, green vegetables, milk, butter and
eggs and a moderate allowance of starchy vegetables, breads, cereals
and meats. The diets observed in the Home were found to conform to these standards. The average consumption per child per
<lay approximated a quart of milk, two ounces of butter, an abundance of green vegetables and fresh fruit with a suitable quota of
the other foods mentioned. The quality of the food provided was
found to be satisfactory and particularly high in the case of meats
and milk. The cooking could only be classed as fair, with considerable room for improvement.
General Hygiene
The standards of housekeeping were found to be good. Recommendations previously made as to wash basins had not been

156

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

157

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

entirely carried out and further recommendations regarding bathtubs will be found in a later paragraph.
A matter deserving of special mention is the new dairy equipment installed under ,the direction of Mr. Drew, the new and
sanitary milking shed and milk house. This plant will now bear
comparison favorably with those devoted to the production of
certified milk and I feel that the Masonic Fraternity may be
reassured concerning the quality of milk now used at the Home,
a matter of the greatest importance in the health of children.
Recommendations
It is high time that a definite policy be adopted regarding the
shoes to be worn by the children in the Home. Specific instructions should be obtained from a competent orthopaedic specialist
as to the proper last or lasts suitable for the feet of growing
children with the prevention of flat-foot particularly in view. Haphazard buying of shoes inevitably leads to deformities of the feet
of one sort or another and the Home has not only an obligation
but an opportunity to prevent the occurrence of such disorders.
The revelation of the examinations for th~ draft during the war
showed how extensive and serious are such deformities of the
feet, interfering t:\Ot only with usefulness for military duty but
with the ordinary tasks and enjoyment of civilian life.
The second recommendation concerns the matter of bathing
facilities in the Honie. Any large group of children using the same
wash basins and tubs is subject to the danger of certain distressing
and highly contagious skin diseases, particularly that known as
Impetigo Contagiosa. It was recommended several years ago that
the spring faucets in the wash basins be changed and that the
children wash in running water. · It was found that while the
springs had been changed the children were still using plugs in the
basins and washing in the basins rather than in the running water.
It should be borne in mind that adequate cleaning between the use
of the basins by different children is manifestly impossible and that
the basins are not uncommonly used also for brushing teeth. The
remedy is extremely simple. Plugs should be entirely discarded.
It would also make washing more comfortable in running water
if a mixing pipe on the basins could be installed. The writer believes that stationary bath tubs have no place in institutions caring
for well children because of the impossibility of sterilizing or even
of adequately cleaning bath tubs under such conditions. The shower
bath is free from these objections and should be the only method
of bathing permitted. It is recommended that the present bath

tubs be discarded and extra showers installed. Special emphasis
has been laid oh the above points because of the extreme difficulty
of preventing or checking epidemics of Impetigo once a single case
has occurred in an institution. One such case was noted during
the examination of the children and it is understood that an
epidemic of large proportion occurred earlier in the year. Without
precautions such as have been above indicated another epidemic
may confidently be predicted.
An ever present danger in institutions for children is that of
diphtheria, an epidemic disease which is most serious both for
its own sake and the after effects. During recent years methods
have been developed both for detecting those individuals who are
susceptible to the disease (The Schick Test) and for immunizing
those who are susceptible. It is therefore now possible to protect the individual from diphtheria and to remove the menace of an
epidemic of the disease in any institution. It is therefore recommended that a Schick Test be given the children and that those
found to be susceptible be given the appropriate preventive treatment.
At present there are twenty of our children attending high
school for academic training which we do not deem necessary
excepting for those who intend to enter college as this requires
four years, which is partially wasted effort. Arrangements should
be made in Los Angeles, whereby the boys especially can receive
short and intense training in vocational schools. To accomplish
this it might be well for the Trustees to establish a home in Los
Angeles where boys and girls can live under proper supervision
and guidance. We believe that the present structures have reached
their capacity for housing the children, we would suggest that
additional buildings be erected of the semi-detached cottage plan
and in these should be housed the older children, thus effecting
a separation of the high school group from the younger group.
In our report of 1917 we suggested that a "follow-up" system
be adopted which has not been done so far; this we must recommend very strongly. The child going through the pubescent period
manifests a certain amount of instability, and during this time
requires careful guidance, especially as they have left the protecting influence of the Home behind them. It is during this period
that real constructive work must be done, to turn out a finished
individual based on the opportunities and education offered in
the preceding years.
We have carefully considered the almost weekly vfsi ts of
various Masonic organizations and Lodges to the Home, generally

158

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

on Sundays, and have given considerable stud.y to the effects of
these visitations on the children. Recognizing the value of the
interest displayed by the visitors to the Home, we feel that there
is great harm done to the children, by breaking off their regular
diet. It is a fact that they lose part of their time on Saturday
· in preparations necessary to receive the visitors, which could be
better spent in play; and to giving up of their Sunday to the
entertainment of a large group of visitors. If it is felt that this
custom cannot be discontinued we must recommend that the
children receive their regular meals in the dining room on Sundays as well as during the week. It is hardly necessary to point
out the physical and mental fatigue of undeveloped children following these performances.
We furthermore suggest that the older boys be in charge of a
male caretaker instead of a house mother. He should be qualified
to direct gymnastics, manual training and outdoor occupations.

Conclusions
While, in the present report, we have laid special emphasis on
the features which require correction it should be said emphatically
that we fou.nd the Superintendent and Matron not only willing but
eager to do everything in their power to bring the Home nearer
that ideal which has been consistently the goal of all those responsible for its direction. If faults have been found, it is but
fair to state that your examiners have never visited or known of
a similar institution whose standards were maintained at so high a
level as at the Covina Home, nor of a similar group of children
whose welfare was so jealously guarded.
HAROI,D K. FABER,

REPORT OF UNIVERSITY MASONIC CLUB
Brother William H. \Vaste, President of the Masonic Club
of the University of California, presented the following report, which was adopted:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on the University of California Masonic Club
House begs leave to submit herewith a brief report.
One year ago the Grand Lodge of California approved the erection
of a suitable club house near the campus of the University of California, for the use of Master Masons and the sons and daughters of
Masons at the University, and gave its consent to a statewide appeal
among the Masons for the necessary funds to erect and equip such a
building. By proper resolution this Grand Body also authorized the
formation of a corporation, or association, for the purpose of holding
title to the necessary property, and to administer the business affairs
of the organization, the plan of such organization to be approved by
the Grand Master, and provided always that the Grand Lodge be
represented on its board of directors, such representatives to be designated by the Grand Master.
Pursuant to the authority thus granted, the committee organized for
such campaign, with the following officers: Brother Edward A. Martin, Executive Secretary; Brother P. A. Brunk, Assistant Executive
Secretary; Brother William A. White, Director of Publicity; Brother
Carlisle Nielsen, Speakers' Bureau; First National Bank of Berkeley,
Treasurer; Brother Ira F. Thompson, Chairman for Southern California. A strong general campaign committee of fifty members of the
fraternity, and representatives from the Order of Eastern Star, with
the Most Worshipful Grand Master as ex-officio chairman, was
formed. It would be interesting to detail the features of this campaign
conducted by Brother Martin and his· able force of assistants, but
space forbids. vVe have time only for a statement of the general results. Much of the credit for the splendid showing made, however,
must be given to the enthusiastic support accorded the movement by
the student and faculty members of t~e University of California Masonic Club.
These young brethren have been untiring in their work. They have
saved the committee much expense in performing many of the minor
details, but their larger contribution has been in the generous giving
of their time in the visitation of Lodges all over the state, for the· purpose of presenting the cause to the brethren.
The campaign has been carried on very largely through the mails.
The preliminary educational feature, therefore, had to be accomplished

1

160

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

throngh the medium of circularization and printed matter, which has
proved to be the largest single item of the expense of the campaign,
which has been kept within reasonable bounds. In fact, the overhead
expense of the campaign to date has been remarkably low, taking into
consideration the large number of lodges and other bodies which have
had to be educated, following which the direct appeal has been presented. When it came to the consideration of the plans of the campaign, the Grand Master ruled that the use of funds of the various
Lodges in the Jurisdiction for the enterprise would not be for a Masonic purpose, and was, therefore, forbidden. Although the members
of the committee were somewhat disappointed at the attitude of the
Grand Master, we are of the opinion that the result has, on the whole,
been very beneficial, for the committee decided to ask for a contribution from every member in the state, the appeal to be presented to the
members through the individual Lodges. The Lodges were, therefore,
asked to secure a contribution of not less than two dollars from every
member on their rolls, the amount to be secured thus aggregating about
$180,000. This amount seems 1large, but for reasons to be presently
pointed out, it seemed necessary. The result of the appe<1l has been
wonderfully gratifying. We pause here to say that more than fifty
per cent of the amount has been realized, and that at the hour of
closing the campaign office in Berkeley last night, October 9th, the
sum of $90,346.56 has been actually subscribed. Many Lodges have
not yet reported any amount subscribed. A larger number have made
only a beginning. On the other hand, however, many Lodges have
"gone over the top."
As might be expected, the Lodges nearest the University have been
the first to get the vision of the work to be accomplished. In Berkeley,
for instance, the various Lodges, with a quota of $3900, have subscribed
more than $6000, an average of more than 152 per cent. The Sacramento Lodges have contributed an average of 105 per cent, Oakland
more than 65 per cent, San Francisco 45 per cent, Los Angeles 25 per
cent, while from far away Hawaii comes the report, that with a quota
of nearly $2600, it has contributed an average of nearly 85 per cent.
The Grand Chapter of Roya1l Arch Masons and the Grand Commandery
of Knights Templar ha;,e each made a generous contribution, which
has been paid. The various Scottish Rite bodies, Chapters of the
De Molay, Sciots, and Eastern Star Chapters, have also given generously from their funds. We have the assurance of the Grand Pyramid
of the Sciots and the Grand Chapter of the E.astern Star that they will
at their next sessions add substantially to what has already been done.
A complete statement showing the quota assigned to each Lodge within
this jurisdiction, the amount subscribed, together with its percentage,
accompanies and is made a part of this report.

Preliminary to the campaign, the corporation authorized by the
Grand Lodge, for the purpose of balding the title to the necessary
property and to administer the business affairs of the corporation, was
formed. Articles of incorporation of "The Masonic Club House of the.
University of California" were duly filed, and the committee takes this
opportunity to extend its thanks to Brother Past Master Milton T.
Farmer for the generous contribution of time and thought in the preparation of the necessary papers for such purpose. By-laws of the corporation were duly adopted, and the organization was completed with
the following officers and directors: President, Brother Willi.am H.
\Vaste; Vice President, Brother George F. Rodden; Secretary, Brother
Charles A. Adams; Assistant Secretary, Brother S. M. Shapero;
Treasurer, Brother WiiUiam B. Herms; Directors, Brothers Milton T.
Farmer, Phineas F. Ferguson, William P. Filmer, Francis V. Keesling,
Waldo F. Postel.
Owing to the steadily increasing values of available land for a
club house near the University, the first concern of the new corporation was the acquisition of a suitable site south of and near the campus. Several were considered. A rather significant feature of the
selection of a site was the very sincere desire manifested by various
holders of real estate to secure the location of the Masonic Club House
in their respective sections of the city. In one instance another organization offered to reHnquish one-half of its holdings, facing the
University grounds, "for the sake of having such a splendid institution
as its nearest neighbor." Another property owner made a substantial
reduction in the price of his holdings because he felt "whatever the
Masons did in the way of erecting a building would be an ornament to
the neighborhood and would advance the value of the rest of his
property." While several pieces of property were being investigated,
the owners of one, which was being very favorably considered, at a
price of $20,000, were suddenly forced to sell. The corporation made
a cash offer of $17,500, which was accepted, and the property became
ours. A few hours after the transaction was closed, other buyers were
ready to pay the original price of $20,000 for the property. This site
is a splendid corner, approximately 100 by 130, on the southwest
corner of Bancroft Way and Bowditch street, just across the former
street from the south end of the Athletic FieM. \Vhen the Memorial
Stadium is completed, the present bleachers and track will be removed
and that portion of the campus will be occupied, so we are informed,
hy a splendid group of University buildings known as the Science
Group. At the present time an old two story house occupying a portion of the site is rented for $35 per month, from which rental the
taxes and upkeep of the property are provided, the balance being
credited to interest.

Proper books and records showing the receipts and disbursements relating to the enterprise have been faithfully kept. They have
been examined by Brother Frank G. Hobbs of the Grand Secretary's
office. He also checked the balance sheet nresented herewith, and
found everything in proper form.
The statement of receipts and disbursements from November 15,
1921 to the close of business October 9, 1922, fo1'10ws:

The present concern of the Grand Lodge Committee and of the
corporation relates to the future of this enterprise. It was conceived
in the thought of Brother Past Grand Master Charles A. Adams, who
hoped to see some modest provision made for a center at the University
for social uses of the Masonic constituency, and as a possible incentive
for research along Masonic subjects. Brother Past Grand Master
George F. Rodden gave generous encouragement along a ,similar line.
The almost unexpected generosity of the fraternity throughout the state
under the present Grand Master has carried the cause far beyond the
anticipations of the two Past Grand Masters. Even with the amount of
money now on hand, which is but one-half of the expected quota, it at
once becomes apparent that the enterprise cannot be confined within
its original plans. Without offering what we are about to propose
as a final plan, we submit the following: The project must be carried
forward. This Grand Lodge and the Masons throughout the state are
now committed to the cause. No movement at the University within
recent times has perhaps aroused the same amount of favorable comment as has this one. Our own students, members of the faculty, and
others comprising the Masonic constituency at the University, will not
be denied what they have been led to hope for. It is now apparent
that something monumental, and yet of the utmost use, must result
from the enterprise. Aside from the social needs for such a club
house, a feature which has aliready been laid be.fore this Grand· Lodge
at its two past convocations, one of the urgent necessities at Berkeley
is suitable housing accomodations for the students. That need, and
the very apparent fact that this project is to be carried forward on a
comprehensive scale, offer a solution to both problems. No better site
could be found near the University for a modern system of dormitories.
Conservative estimates, based on actual knowledge and information,
lead your committee to believe that for an expenditure of $125,000, in
addition to the amount invested in the lot, a building can be erected
which will provide all of the social facilities required, an auditorium
of moderate size, a comfortable lodge room, and, in addition thereto,
fifty-five or sixty rooms for Masons and other students from Masonic
homes. Based on the occupancy of two students in each room, and
taking into consideration the two regular semesters, the Inter-Session
and the Summer Schools, such rooms will insure an annual income of
from twe'lve to fifteen thousand dollars. Rents from the lodge room and
the auditorium will add materially to this income. Other features which
it may be proper to include have been suggested along the same line.
Approximately $7500 per annum will be required for taxes, insurance
and maintenan;::e of the institution. The difference between this amount
and the gross income wou'id form a sinking fund, from which a bonded
indebtedness for the amount required to complete the enterprise over
subscriptions received could be gradually extinguished. That such an

FEE FOR AFFILIATES
Brother Thornber of Caledonia Lodge No. 486 presented
_the following :
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Whereas the Lodges of this state are being deprived of new members by affiliation on account of the Twenty Dollar fee required and:
Whereas the Masonic Homes of this state wou'ld eventually benefit
rather than suffer through the passage of this resolution,
Now therefore be it resolved that subdivision 1st of Section 41
of the Constitution be amended by striking out after the words "the
1st Degree" in the sixth line thereof, the words, "and for every member elected for affiliation upon a demit, or certificate of standing
or withdrawal from a Lodge of a jurisdiction other than California."

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

EXPENSES OF TRIAL OF NON-AFFILIATE
Brother Randall of Coronado Lodge No. 441 presented the
following:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Whereas, There are in California a great number of Masons of
other jurisdictions who believe, by reason of that fact, that they are
not subject to discipline, and with that idea in mind commit acts of
unmasonic conduct with impunity; and
Whereas, Such Masons ought to and should be brought to trial,
but owing to the fact that there are so many Lodges whose finances
are such that they are unable to stand the expense incident to such
trials, these undesirables continue to bring discredit upon our institution; and
Whereas, The discipling of such Masons is a matter in which the
fraternity, as a whole is interested and would be benefited; and be1ieving that proper legislation would tend to bring men of such character to trial, and thereby create in others a higher regard for our
obligations, as well as raising our standard in the eyes of the public
at large, I offer the following resolution:
Resolved: That a new section be added to read as follows:
"Sec. 200¥2. If the accused is a member of a Lodge in this jurisdiction, and a stenographic reporter is emp'loyed as provided for in
Section 200, the expense of such reporter shall be borne by the Lodge

176

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of which he is a member. If, however, the accused is not affiliated in
this Grand Jurisdiction, and a reporter is employed with the approval
of the Grand Master, the claim of said reporter shall be forwarded
to the Grand Secretary, certified to as correct by the Master and
Secretary of the Lodge in which the trial was had, and paid by the
Grand Lodge in the same manner as other bills, or claims; and
provided further, that the maximum amount of said fees shall not
exceed one-half ( 0) the fees allowed by law to stenographic reporters
in the courts of the State of California."

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and Finance.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ENDOWMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
We, the members of your Endowment Committee of the Masonic
Homes of California, appointed by the Grand Master at the close of
the last Grand Lodge, beg to report that owing to the fact our activities
have been decidedly limited, we have but a slight increase in our
Endowment Fund.
Immediat~ly following the appointment of this Committee, your
Chairman took up with the Grand Master the advisability of holding
a joint meeting of all the members of the Endowment Committee,
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes and Grand Lodge Officers.
This .suggestion was approved and the meeting was held in San
Francisco the latter part of December, last year.
At this meeting all phases of the situation were discussed, particularly the seeming criticism of continuing the active drive, and it appeared to be the consensus of opinion of those present that not only
members of the Fraternity, but practically all of our citizens had a
decided surfeit of drives of every kind and character. Furthermore,
an active campaign was being carried on through the lodges for the
erection of a Masonic Club Building in the 'Gniversity grounds at
Berkeley.
Another point brought up was that the amount raised by the
charge of $20.00 on each petition for the degrees had resulted in the
raising of large sums sufficient in size and importance to cause a
reduction in the per capita tax for the Masonic Homes. It was felt
that this increase of $20.00 for each petitioner would, before many
years, raise a sum sufficient for all extensions required and there
would be a surplus which could be added to the Endowment Fund.
It was therefore decided that a booklet be issued for distribution
to each member of the craft of this jurisdiction, setting forth the purposes and aims of our Masonic Homes, and that voluntary sub-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

177

scriptions should be made to the Endowment Fund and instructions
set forth how bequests could be made.
It was further decided that one day each year should be set aside
in each lodge, the date to be named by the Grand Master, to. be
known as "Masonic Homes Day," and that appropriate exercises
and entertainment features would be held; the evening program to be
of sufficient interest that the members of the lodges would be gfad
to attend.
This detail of facts, therefore, gives to the members of this Grand
Lod!je the reason of the inactivity or seeming inactivity of your Endowment Committee.
The Grand Treasurer advises that the condition of our Endowment
Fund as of July 31st, 1922, is as follows:

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren:
"A wise nation preserves its records, decorates the graves of its
illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures, and fosters national
pride and love of country by perpetual references to the sacrifices and
glories of the past."
With a feeling of profound regret in every heart we have assembled
here today for the purpose of paying a just tribute to our distinguished
dead and in a measure recalling the labors and triumphs of the past.
Out upon this \Vestern shore of the American continent, where
the ceaseless rolling billows of the Pacific ocean kiss the golden sands
at their feet, the pathfinders of liberty builded them a home. Here
on the 19th day of October, 1858, Alonzo Judson Monroe was born.

182

PROCJ:<JEDINGS OF THE

Nursed in the l~p of endeavor, rocked in the cradle of conquest, and
reared amid California's pathless world of woods-he naturally
possessed that rugged manhood which is a characteristic and the
priceless heritage of the pioneer.
His boyhood days were spent among men engaged in subduing a
forest-a forest whose trees were in the full vigor of youth when
"Abraham was about to offer up his son, Isaac, and when David met
and appeased the destroying angel."
At the time of his birth few people had found their way into
Northern California, and educational opportunities offered themselves
only to the most eager and persistent. But our lamented Past Grand
Master was most fortunate in coming nncler the direct supervision
of our late Brother James Berry Brown, who was his teacher, and
who became his boon companion for life. This wise, unfaltering
patriot took the plastic mind of his young pupil within the grasp of his
genius and formed a foundation upon which was erected a superstructure of human sympathy and moral! character; an imperial edifice
of ~onor, truth, and manhood that not only reflected credit upon
the mstruetor but assisted largely in giving us our late Grand Master
as we knew him, "the loved and loving brother, hushand, father,
friend."
'Ne will not recount his many deeds from his mother's knee to
manhood. Suffice it to say, he was a toiler in the mines, a sailor
before the mast, a hewer in the forest, a student in college, and finally
a member of the legal profession, honored and respected by the Bench
and Bar of the County and State in which he lived.

In August, 1888, he was united in marriage with Lucretia A.
Huntington. A partial and generous providence se1ected as his companion on the journey through life, one who, by her moral and intellectual attainments, enriched and embellished his proud nature·
reigned in his heart a queen sitting upon the throne of home th~
crown of virtuous motherhood upon her brow, ruling and guidin~· the
tempest of his life with the scepter of love. Thrice she went down
into the valley of the shadow of death that he might behold his
off-spring fresh from the hand of God and waiting for the breath of life.
Happy man! proud possessor of the most precious gift from the
bountiful hand of his divine Creator.
Measured by the shrunken rnle of this world's sordid wealth, in
the gathering of earthly riches he may not have been successful ; but
have you not read wherein it is written: "And Jesus sat over against
the treasury, and beh?ld how the people cast money into the treasury;
a~d many that were nch cast in much. And there came a certain poor
widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing. And he

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

183

called unto Him his Disciples, and saith unto them: 'Verily I say
unto you, that this poor widow hath cast more in than all they which
have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their ahundance;
but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.' "
Judged by this unerring standard, boundless. was his wealth; because he frequently gave abundantly of his scanty store that the needy
might be fed. Joy in the service of hu111anity was his wea!lth, and
love for all mankind was the legal tender of his soul.
He was made an Entered Apprentice, July 16, 1890, past to the
degree of Fellowcraft, March 24, 1891, and raised to the sublime
degree of ).faster Mason, April 21. 1891. He served as \Vorshipful
Master of his Lodge, Inspector of his District, Grand Orator of this
Grand Lodge, and on through the various offices to the. seat of the
Most Worshipful Grand ;\'faster to which he was elected October 13,
1911.
Always abounding in human kindness, courteous to his brethren,
faithful to the principles of our befoved fraternity, true to his country
and to his God, he has left a record of service as a man and as a
Mason to which his friends and brethren may point with pride. Having
all the degrees of masonry, except the thirty-third, and realizing its
influence in the advancement and defence of human liberty, he worshiped at its shrine, taught in its assemblies, and carried the purity of
its principles into his everyday life.
He viewed masonry as a mighty stream of wisdom and experiences
coming down to us through all the ages of the past, widening and
deepening and washing away the obstacles and stumbling blocks in the
pathway of right and duty; overthrowing the altars of false gods, and
in their stead erecting temples dedicated to the ever-Hving Goel;
hurling despots from their thrones; creating free governments; enlarging constitutional rights and privileges, and safeguarding the
liberties of the people everywhere. He believed that our institutions
were founded upon imperishable truths; he loved our schools and the
flag that floats over them; he was a foyal, eloquent, and fearless defender of all that is truly American ; he would not sit unconcerned
while the liberties of the people were being invaded nor look in
silence upon corruption in public service.
He loved his home with a fervency and zeal horn of· a great soul,
and from this source sprang his ardent love of country. He recognized
that the citizen has a duty to perform in harring up the ·countless
gateways which lure the youth of our country to destruction, and in
holding ajar the portals to an honorable life. Thus believing, he
attacked the liquor interest and other evils with ,a fearlessness and
devotion admired by all.

184

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

He was a firm believer in the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man; that we are our brother's keeper; that there is a law
above all the enactments of human codes, a 1Jaw written by the finger
of God upon the heart of man, which shall remain eternal and unchangeable for the guidance of humanity, and which admonishes us so ta
walk that we will not make our brother to offend.
In this solemn moment we reverently call him our late Past
Grand Master, Alonzo Judson Monroe; but to us who knew him
best and loved him most, Jud, the simp1e abbreviation of his middle
name, lingers on our lips mingled with a sigh of adoration to the
Deity for such friendship and brotherhood as was evidenced by his
conduct.
The tongue of man has infinite power to express the ideas which
the human intellect conceives; but when we seek to plumb the depths
of sentiment and love it then becomes a weak interpreter indeed. We
speak with all too feeble language of the virtues of our departed
brother ; but we will forever treasure in our hearts the memory of
his goodness. Eternal are the influences which his efforts to uplift
the world have set in motion. And as Almighty God is just, we know
that his reward wiM be unending.
SoNG................................................ Edward K. Hause, Jewel Lodge No. 374
EULOGY, Harvey Davis Loveland .... Geo. F. Rodden, Past Grand Master
Just one short year ago-on Wednesday in the second week of
October-the brethren of Grand Lodge were permitted to sit at the
feet of a master. For the greater part of an hour we sat, enraptured
and enthralled, under the sway of one man, willing subjects in the
dominion of wisdom and eloquence.
In lieu of a better, we must classify what was then offered us
under the general, if inept, title of Oration. But as he stood before us
in this beautiful temple, bathed in a flood of sunshine that strea1ned
upon and about him from above, exalted by the absorbed and
sympathic attention of his brethren, we who knew him best were
conscious that our beloved Grand Orator, Harvey Davis Loveland,
was, all unwittingly, but lifting the veil that we might peer into the
depths of his own soul-but laying bare his own heart that we
might discover its promptings. The principles and practices of his
daily life were easily visible in the rich truths of his message; and
they were offered to us with the modest hope that there might be
found something worthy of emulation, something that would bestir us
to finer strivings to the everlasting profit of the craft and all humanity.
Common experience will support the belief that, while listening to

185

some masterly discourse, attention is often diverted from the text by
one's admiration for the speaker or the technique of his art.
Thus do we rob ourselves of much that wouM be of rare value.
With that thought prompting, I have greedily read and reread
Brother Loveland's oration of last year, anxious that no toothsome
morsel of diction should be lost, that none of the scintillating gems
of poetry or philosophy should escape. While each exploration has
brought to light some theretofore undiscovered beauty, still have I
found myself most impressed by the absolute fidelity with which his
own splendid attributes have been reflected through his noble lines.
Modesty and a thread of self-depreciation as became one who
knowing so much realized that human limitations permit one to
know so little; delicate refinement and broad culture; adoration of
the beautiful as expressed in character, nature or art; a sane and
balanced philosophy, love of man and reverence toward God.
Those were the pigments with which he colored his discourse, those
were the outstanding-the salient characteristics of our friend and
brother.
Truth for truth's sake had become, with him, an obse.ssion.
He knew no compromise with equivocation or dishonesty in any
of its forms.
Truth, rigid and inexorablle, was a law of life.
I fancy there were no lines in literature which more definitely
impressed him, were more frequently quoted or which had done more
to shape his life than those of his beloved Whittier, "Truth should
be the first lesson of the child and the last aspiration of manhood. It
is the sovereign good of human nature."
And he had courage-that sublime courage born of faith.
He had courage to live as a man should live, despite temptation;
he had courage to· die as a man should die, with a smile upon his
lips.
Just before his passing, knowing that the end was near and in
anticipation of that event, he wrote:
"But unto those whose faith remains, death does but sever earthly
chains.
To spirits freed from this poor c1od, 'tis but to sleep, to wake
with God."
As the chemical elements of the soil in which it grows determine
the vigor and color of the rose and mark its destiny, so was it inevitable that the inherent qualities of this good man should develop
in him such love of humanity as would prompt him to dedicate his life

186

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF' THE

and talents to its service; and, with utter disregard of self or material
things, find his greatest happiness in the knowledge that happiness
had come to others.
Sacrifice and service. Those were the dominant notes around
which the most beautiful melodies of his life were written.
He was born in New York State on Ju:!y 19, 1853, and passed away
on Sunday, June 11, 1922, in his sixty-ninth year.
After finishing school he became a teacher in his native State
and later taught in Kansas, to which state he moved in 1876. While
thus engaged he studied law, and in 1881 was admitted to the bar.
In 1887 he came to San Francisco, where he became associated with
the Pacific Coast Jobbers' and Manufacturers' Association, of which
he was president for six years. He also served as president of the
Trans-Mississippi Commercial Congress. He achieved signal success
in both positions.
His work in collecting evidence and prosecuting suits before the
Interstate Commerce Commission in several well known cases stili
shows its effects· on western interests.
In point of service, it is said, Brother Loveland was the dean of
public utility commissioners in the United States, having been continuously since 1907 a member of the California Rai'iroad Commission.
In that year he was appointed by Governor Gillette to complete an
unexpired term. In 1910, he was elected to the Commission from the
second district, and afterward received appointments from Governors
Johnson and Stephens.
That his death brought both consternation and grief to his associates
of the Railroad Commission is evident by the following tribute to his
memory which was ordered inserted in the official minutes:
"In the death of Colonel Harvey D. Loveland, not only has the
Commission sustained a heavy personal and official loss, but the State
has been deprived of an able and faithful pub'lic servant. Colonel
Loveland served this State as a member of the California Railroad
Commission sine~ 1907. His career was marked by both public and
executive confidence and respect. He was elected once and received
four appointments by three Governors. He had the distinction of
being the public service commissioner of longest continuous tenure in
the United States. The hest part of his life was devoted to the work
of regulation of public utilities, ;md his specialized field of railroad
regulation was recognized as a national authority. His knowledge was
intimate and profound, his judgment was so1Jidly based on a rich experience, and his counsel was invaluable. During our intimate daily
association with Colonel Loveland we recognized in him a man of
the highest official and personal honor-unswerving in his duty, inde-

187

fatigable in his work. On the personal side he was the soul of courtesy, generous and ever ready to do a kindness."
His Masonic career was a distinctly impressive one. He was
initiated, passed and raised in Topeka Lodge No. 17, F. & A .. M.
in the State of Kansas in 1881. He became a member of San Franc~sco
Lodge No. 360 and served as its second Master. San Francisco
Chapter No. 1, 'Royal Arch Masons, conferred upon him his capitular
degrees and the Orders of Knighthood by Golden Gate Commandery.
He be;ame Commander of Golden Gate Commandery in 1901, and
Grand Commander of Knights Templar of the State of California in
1909. He was a 32nd degree Scottish Rite Mason, a member of the
Ca1lifornia Bodies in San Francisco. He was a Past Sovereign of
San Francisco Conclave No. 15, Knights of the Red Cross of Constantine and the Intendant General of the Order in California.
As Grand Master, I deemed myself most fortunate in that he
deigned to accept from me the appointment as Grand Orator of the
Grand Lodge of California.
And now he has gone, leaving nothing behind but cherished memories. Poet and philosopher, teacher and friend; a man whom the
best loved to honor, a man whom the Masonic world will ever revere;
a man, the nobility and purity of whose life can but assure us that
his white soul does "Live within the light of God."

Always cheerful and helpful, not only with his music, but ready
with a word, a smile, and a grasp of the hand for the incoming
brother; he was an inspiration to the succeeding generations of
Masons.
In the old Masonic days we seemed to get closer to the real heart
and spirit behind outward appearances at our banquets and ceremonies than now, perhaps because youth then called to youth:
As we, whom you might think old timers, look back on these old
days of ours, you must forgive us if we say that Sam Mayer's voice
was the sweetest we ever heard, that his music was the most appropriate on every Masonic occasion, and we leave it to you younger
brothers to feel the, same as to the voices and music of today, when
you look back on them after over a third of a century has .passed.
In thinking of our brother and speaking of him, a certain sadness comes over us, because we knew that never again here wil'l we
see his· face and never again on earth will we hear his voice; and yet,
if we are real Masons, we must know that hereafter, in a brighter
and better life, we shall see him again, know him again, hear his songs
again, in that celestial Lodge above, where the Supreme Grand Master
of the Universe forever presides.

AMENDMENT TO CONSTITUTION
Brother W. W. Abbott presented the following:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Proposing to add a new section to the Constitution, to be known
as Section 165A:

Section 165 A.-N o Mason in this jurisdiction shaiJI make a pplication for membership in any fraternal society, body or order in which
the prerequisite for membership is that he be a Master Mason, until
he shall be a member in good standing of some Lodge in this grand
jurisdiction for a period of two years. Provided, however, that he may
make such application after he has filed with his Lodge a certificate,
approved by the Master, and attested by the Secretary, under seal of
the Lodge, setting forth the fact that he has attended at least twelve
regular meetings of his Lodge; and it is further provided, that any
Master Mason who violates the provision of this section shall be
deemed guHty of unmasonic conduct and on conviction shall' be sentenced to no less than expulsion from the fraternity.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred Trial
Record No. 305, Santa Monica Lodge No. 307, respectfully report as
follows:
The ace.used w~s charged with deserting his wife in early part
of 1921: with leavmg her unprovided for, and with failure to give
her assistance when requested to provide same by the Master of the
Lodge. Summons was served upon the accused by mail, but he made
no appearance at the trial; either in person or by counsel. A trial was

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

191

held and the commissioners found him guilty on the "first" specification, and expuilsion was fixed as the penalty. The record, however,
fails to show that the Commission voted upon the charge of unmasonic
conduct, as required by Section 205 of the Constitution. While the
commissioners thus failed to comply with an important requirement
of the Constitution, it further failed in its observance of other pro·
visions relative to trials, for an examination of the record reveals that
the accused was found guilty upon absolutely incompetent testimony.
Letters and oral statements of third persons, and a written statement signed by the wife, but not even sworn to by her, compose
almost entirely the "evidence" received by the Commission, and this,
notwithstanding the provisions of Section 202 of the Constitution,
which precludes the introduction of hearsay evidence, and even the admission of affidavits.
The testimony of witnesses who are not Masons must be supported
by oath or affirmation made before some officer authorized to administer oaths. A little reflection should have convinced the Commission in this case, that the statement of the wife of the accused did
not even purport to have been made under oath, and, had it been
so made, it yet wouild have been merely an affidavit, inadmissible as
evidence. With the evidence, which was improperly admitted, removed
from consideration, the competent evidence is too meagre to support
the conclusion of the trial Commission that the accused deserted his
wife as charged.
The failure of an accused to appear at the trial does not justify
the abandonment of the wise regulations prescribed by the Constitution, for the determination of the guilt of the accused, and no brother
should be deprived of his Masonic rights and privileges, except upon
competent and sufficient testimony.
The Committee, therefore, recommend the adoption of the follow·
ing resolution:
That the action of Santa Monica Lodge, in case of Trial Record
No. 305, be and the same is hereby reversed and the case remanded
for further proceedings.

Adopted.

On the specification of unmasonic conduct the vote was "guilty" 1,
"not guilty" 8. No penalty was attempted to be fixed. How the

whidh at least constituted felonies under the laws of the land, is beyond the comprehension of this Committee.
However, as the provision of Section 205 of the Constitution requiring that each specification must be voted on separately, is mandatory,
the judgment of the Commissioners must be reversed, and the same
remanded for a new trial.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record No. 313 from Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, begs leave to report
as follows:
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct as set forth in
six specifications as follows: Charging the accused first with defrattding the wife of a brother Master Mason in the matter of an
exchange of real and personal property, in misrepresenting the amount
of indebtedness against the property conveyed by the accused; second,
by misrepresenting the value of personal property conveyed by the
accused; third, by other misrepresentations relative to the v<ilue of
certain of the personal property conveyed by the accused; fourth, by
concealing certain liabilities attaching to the property conveyed; fifth,
by failing to comply with or carry out an agreement made by the
accused to make good the loss sustained by the wife of the brother
Master Mason by reason of said false representations; sixth, by refusing to reconvey to the wife of said brother Master Mason the
property conveyed to the accused.
The accused entered a plea of "not guilty." Both accuser and accused were represented by able counsel and an exhaustive trial was
had on all the issues; the transcript containing some 460 pages of
typewritten matter.
Your Committee has examined said record with- great care and
finds no substantia•I error, provided the accusation charges a Masonic
offense. The trial commissioners found the accused guilty on the
first, second, fifth a!)d sixth specifications, and not guilty on the third,
fourth specifications; also guilty of the charge of t1111masonic conduct.
The commissioners then sentenced the accused to suspension. This
Committee is of the opinion that if the accusation specifies a Masonic
offense, the findings of the commissioners are amply sustained by the
evidence.
This brings us to the question : "Is it a Masonic offense to cheat,
wrong or defraud the wife of a brother Master Mason?" A diligent
search through our archives fails to furnish this Committee with a
precedent in the case for its guida~ce. Nor do our Masonic obligations seem to contain any specific declaration in that behalf. How·
ever, your Committee is of the unanimous opinion that, although not
stated in express terms, our Masonic obligations implicitly prohibit

194

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GR.AND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the cheating, wronging, or defrauding the wife of a Master Mason to
the same degree as they prohibit such conduct towards a Master
Mason. The effect on a brother Master :\fason may be as great if
the wrong is done to his wife, as if done to himself. Particularly
is that true, inasmuch as the State law requires the wife to support
her husband and minor chi1dren, if her husband becomes incapacitated
from so doing. Then, too, in the event of his death, she may be entirely dependent upon her own resources, or with her minor children,
become a Masonic charge; to say nothing of the confidence she has a
right to place in a Mason's integrity.
Your Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the specifications
in this case state sufficient facts to constitute a Masonic offense, and
as four of them have been found sustained by the trial commissioners,
and in the opiniol). of your Committee properly so, the judgment of
the trial commissioners should be upheld by this Grand Lodge. Your
Committee, therefore offers the follQ/wing resolution and moves its
adoption:
Resolved, That the judgment of the trial commissioners in Record
No. 313 of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, be, and the same is hereby
affirmed.

Adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 316 of La Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17, begs leave to report as
follows:
The accused, a member of Speranza Italiana Lodge No. 219, was
charged with unmasonic conduct, under four specifications. During the
trial the second, third and fourth specifications were abandoned, and
the case submitted on the first specification only.
This specification charged the accused with having on the 28th
day of September, 1916, been convicted of the crime of a violation of
Section No. 3,670 of the Penal Code,-that is, failing to stop and render
assistance to a person injured (in this case killed) in an automobile
accident, on the 5th day of January, 1916.
The charges in the Masonic trial were not brought until March
25, 1922, five and a half years after the conviction in. the criminal
courts and over six years after the offense was committed. No showing is made why so 'long a delay occurred before bringing the charges.
The accused and accuser were each represented by counsel.
The accused was found guilty on the first specification only, and
the penalty fixed at expulsion. The crime of which the accused was
convicted in the criminal courts was not one involving moral turpitude,
but was purely a statutory one.
The other specifications, which were abandoned at the hearing, deal
with entirely different matters, all but one of which are alleged to
have occurred prior to the trial in the criminal courts.
The evidence also shows that the accused was pardoned for the
crime of which he was convicted. Your committee are of the opinion
that had the other charges related to acts of unmasonic conduct on the
part of the accused, subsequent to the commission of the crime of
which he was convicted in the State courts, and such charges been
proven at the Masonic tria 1, evidence of the earlier conviction would
have been competent and proper to show a general course of conduct;
but the specification of such earlier conviction of a crime not involv~ng
moral turpitude, standing alone and without specifications and proof
of other acts of unmasonic conduct, should not after so long a time be
taken as sufficient to warrant a conviction of the accused. Your
Committee is not unmindful of the fact that there is no statute of
limitations in the Masonic law, but believes that in this particular case
the delay was unreasonable.
Your Committee therefore recommends the following resolution
and moves its adoption:
Resolved, That the judgment of the Trial Commissioners in Case
No. 316, of La Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17, be and the same is
hereby reversed.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial
Record No. 308, tried hy Acorn Lodge No. 494, upon charges presented
to the Master of Woodstock Lodge No. 491; begs leave to report
as follows:

In thi~ case the accused was charged with unmasonic conduct as
set forth m three specifications, the first charge being that the accused
attended Lodge in an intoxicated condition, and the other two that he
divulged his ballot on a candidate to two different individuals. The
trial co~mission found the accused not guilty on the first specification
and gmlty on the second and· third specifications. The commission
found the accused guilty of unmasonic conduct and sentenced .him to
suspension. The accused has appealed upon the ground that he has
not committed a Masonic offense in revealing the nature of his baHot

'

201

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

because the ballot is to protect him and he could waive that right if he
so chose, and that by telling of his act he is not revealing a transaction of the Lodge.
The uniform code of by-laws for Masonic Lodges in this jurisdiction provides in Article XI that "when a candidate for initiation * * *
is rejected * * * no member or visitor shall reveal directly or indirectly,
to such person, or to any other, any transactions which may have
taken place on the subject." The evidence in this case discloses that the
accu~ed told a Fellowcraft of his Lodge that it was he, the accused,
who black-balled an applicant (after the Fellowcraft had told the accused that he knew of the action of the Lodge), and that the accused
after the rejected applicant had been re-balloted upon, elected and
made a Master Mason, went to him and told him of the accused's
conduct and said he was glad to correct the mistake and welcomed
him into the Lodge. These two acts constituted the offenses charged in
the second and third specifications and were admitted by the accused
in his written answer filed at the opening of the trial.
Your Committee is of the opinion that while a strict and technica:t
interpretation of the above by-law might constitute these acts unmasonic conduct, yet the prevention of such was not the real purpose
of this provision. It is evident that its real purpose was to protect
each individual in his Masonic right to express his personal opinion
secretly, and that while the divulgence of affirmative ballot might by
process of elimination lead to the disclosure of the man registering
the negative ballot, yet if that man chose to reveal his secret and sustain openly the burden of his action, he has not committed a serious
infraction of Masonic law. Neither did either of these acts reveal
any transaction of the Lodge. However, in the opinion of your Committee, such acts should be discouraged.
The penalty was fixed by the commission at suspension. Under
all the circumstances and considering that in this instance there was
no divulgence to outsiders, as subsequent events developed, your Committee believes that the penalty was too severe and should he reduced
to a reprimand, and therefore recommends the adoption of the following
resolution:
Resolved, That the judgment of the Lodge be and the same is
hereby modified, and that the penalty be and the same is hereby fixed
to read as follows : That the accused be reprimanded in accordance
with the provisions of Section 206 of the Constitution.

The accused was found guilty by the trial commission of the charge
of having had adulterous relatio.ns with a married woman, and of unmasonic conduct, and sentenced to expulsion. The accused has taken an
appeal in which he sets forth at length how the accusation is the result
of a political difference and states that the testimony of the only witness
testifying directly to the offence can be completely refuted by the
testimony of a competent witness not available at the time of the
hearing, whose affidavit is attached to the appeal. The statement is
further made in the appeal, and is supported by the trial record, that
the report first filed by the police officer, who was the main witness,
was contradictory to what he testified at the trial, which report
absolved the accused from any wrongful conduct, and that by reaso1i
of this the accused was prevented from having a fair trial.

200

Report adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
Brother Robert E. Allan, chairman of the Committee on
Returns, presented the following report:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Californ.ia:
· Your Committee on Returns is very much gratified in being able
to report that the annual returns and the dues have been received
from every Lodge in the jurisdiction. The very great majority of
them we.re correct when they came in. For those that were not
correct, and for those that are late, our V. W. Grand Secretary appears
to have an infinite patience. Eventually he gathers in all the annual
reports and has them all correct.
The number of candidates raised this year is 8,771, or sixty !ess
than last year. Nothwithstanding the smaller number, this shows a
healthy increase and is evidence that the fraternity holds a high place
in the estimation of the community.
. On account of this increase, some of the members of Grand Lodge
are filled with direful forebodings and wonder what we are going to
do with the crop of new members. They are fearful we are making
members too quickh and Masons too slowly. When we had smaller
numbers seeking admission we were told the trouble was with the
Lodges, we had dry rot, and so forth. So there is always somethingo
to be dissatisfied over.
Your Committee believes there are as good fish in the sea as ever·
were caught. And we are catching the fish. We are also of the
opinion the character and membership· of the fraternity wa~ never
higher than it is today.

GEORGE WASHINGTON MASONIC MEMORIAL
Brother Harry L. Todd introduced the following:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Whereas, The George Washington Masonic "National Memorial
Association was organized in 1908 at the suggestion of Past Grand
Master Brother Oscar W. Lawler of California for the purpose of
erecting a suitable Masonic Memorial to Washington the Mason, at
Alexandria, Va.; and
Whereas, Forty-three States have indorsed the project and are
financiaitly contributing towards its realization; and
\Vhereas, The Grand Lodge of California has indorse<l the movement and has already appointed its State Chairman: and
Whereas, A feature of this Memorial will be the provision of a
place for each State in the Union to perpetuate the memory and
achievements of its most illustrious Masons; and,
\Vhereas, The erection of this Memorial is to be realized by a
contribution of one dollar for each Mason in the United States, which
plan has been adopted in forty-three states at last reports received'
from Past Grand Master Louis A. Watres, President of the Association; therefore, be it
Resolved; That the Grand Lodge of California, eager to do its
share to commemorate the memory of America's greatest patriot and
Mason, does appropriate' one dollar for each Master Mason in good
standing as of record October 5, 1922, payments to be made in four
equa1 annual installments.

Referred first to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, and if approved by that Committee, then to be referred
to the Finance Committee.
Grand Lodge was then called off until 9 :30 o'clock tomorrow
morning, for the purpose of giving the members an opportunity
to visit the Masonic Home at Decoto.

Thursday, October 12, 1922.
Grand Lodge was called on at 9 :30 o'clock, the Grand

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
Brother Jesse M. \Vhited, chairman of the committee on
Masonic Education, presented the following report:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Education beg leave to report as
follows:
Believing that any programme your Committee would outline must
necessarily be carried out by the Masters of the various Lodges assuming office January, 1, 1922, our active work was postponed until after
that time. Grand Lodges of other states had been or were about to
engage in the same activity. Our first step was to secure ·information
and advice from those sources. From data gathered, it was thought
that some programme similar to that outli'ned by the Bureau of Social
and Educational Service of the Grand Lodge of F. & A. M. of New
York was best suited for the pioneer work the Committee should
do to build a foundation for our future activities.
Following the New York plan, a questionnaire was sent to the
420 Lodges of this jurisdiction. This questionnaire, copy of which
is attached hereto, was a request for information as to how far the
respective Lodges were interested and wou1d co-operate in the idea
of the Committee in carrying out its work through District meetings,
Lodge meetings or other means; the time and place to hold the same
their past experiences, and the physical conditions applicable tci them~
selves and surrounding territory. Only 126 answers were received.
Of these, forty-eight stated they believed the plan of District meetings
was best; forty-eight that more good could be accomplished at stated
meetings and thirty were noncommittal or not inclined to follow out
atiy programme whatsoever. Those in favor of District meetings, in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

217

most cases, were from Lodges having a small membership and located
off the ~ines of travel. From three of the largest centers of population, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Oakland, wherein are located
over 150 Lodges, but thirty-four answers were received. The others
failed to reply from lack of interest or reasons unknown to your
Committee. Those who replied and were opposed to co-operating
with us, or lukewarm as to the movement, stated "they were too busy
conferring Degrees," or "cannot interest our members."
With this questionnaire was also sent a request that we be furnished a list of volunteer speakers in the communities, whom the
Master or Inspector believed were qualified to enlighten the members
on matters of interest to the Fraternity, either from a Masonic standpoint or upon other subjects. The names of 347 parties were furnished.
An invitation was sent to each to become a part of our Speakers'
Bureau. Seventy-four acceptances were received. The names of these
volunteers, some of whom were members of the Fraternity and others
not, together with information regarding each, was printed in a Roster,
copy of which is also attached. A supply of these were mailed to every
Lodge.
Whether the estab1ishment of this Speakers' Bureau served its
purpose can only be a matter of opinion. The Roster contained a
request that the Master, after a trial of the plan, favor the Committee
with his opinion as to whether or not the Roster was of any service
and also the character and value of the addresses given. \Vith but very
few exceptions, this request was not complied with. From oral
statements and the letters received, it would appear that the Committee
performed some service. This was, perhaps, best evidenced by the
fact that direct requests for speakers, by letter, telephone, or telegraph,
ceased after the issuance of the Roster.
Through the kindness of Brother Sidney Morse, Executive Secretary of the Bureau of Social and Educational Service of New York, we
were furnished printed copies and lantern slides of their excellent
illustrated Masonic lecture entitled, "The Civilian Patriots of the American Revolution." Through the Grand Lodge of Iowa, we were provided with manuscript copies and slides of a fine Masonic lecture entitled "The Birth of Old Glory." Requests for the use of the manuscript
and slides of these two lectures as well as the testimonials received
after their use are evidence of the value of this form of education.
We are advised that the Bureau of Social and Educational Service
of the Grand Lodge of New York spent $13,000 in the preparation of
their programme and the maintenance of the Bureau.
The Grand Lodge, F. & A. M., of Wisconsin has established a
Research Bureau, which issues bulletins and valuable papers in connection with Masonic history.
