GRAND LODGE OF CALil<'ORNIA

Brother Silas T. Shepherd, Chairman of this Bureau, has very
kindly furnished copies of these to all Lodges in this jurisdiction
desiring them.
It has been stated that th,e most effective means of education or
the dissemination of information, is through the eye. The numerous
requests for the above mentioned lantern s1ides and films, as well as
the attendance where they were shown, confirms our idea that this is
the best method for carrying out the ideas of the Committee and
especial attention should be given towards enlarging this method of
education.
While not a member of the Masonic Service Association of the
United States, your Committee and others interested, upon request,
have been favored with copies of all their bulletins and other Hterature
issued by them. We have been allowed the use of their excellent
picture entitled, "Equality of Opportunity in the American Public
Schools." This film has been shown at a number of meetings during
"Public School Week." It received favorable comment from the press
arnd demonstrates the value of this form of educational service.
The resuhs of the work of the Masonic Service Association were
placed at our disposal on the same terms as other Grand Lodges who
are members of the Association. The Committee is under obligations
to Brother George L. Schoonover, Educational Director of the Association, for many favors. From a financial standpoint, it will be less
expensive for us to avail ourselves of the privileges of membership
rather than the expenditure of money which would duplicate the
work performed by it, and we therefore recommend that the Grand
Lodge again consider the proposition of becoming a memoer of the
Masonic Service Association.
The San Francisco 1922 Shrine Committee kindly donated us three
sets of the reels of the Historical Masonic Pageant held in San Francisco on the night of June 15th. These were placed at the disposal! of
the various Lodges throughout the State and have been generally
shown with satisfactory results from an educational standpoint.
The resources of the "National Masonic Research Societv," and
its official publication, "The Builder," have been of material as~istance
to us. Our thanks are due Brothers H. L. Haywood and W. E.
Atchison in this connection.
Through Brother William P. Filmer, Lodges publishing monthly
bulletins have been fornished the weekly service of the "Capita1 News
Service." This is a Bureau maintained in \Vashington, D. C., by the
Supreme Council, A. & A. S. R., S. J., for the purpose of furnishing
news items and statistics in connection with general F..ducational matters and Masonic activities.

There are over twenty-five Masonic Educational Associations
operating in various States carrying out the educational. program;ne
of this Supreme Council. They are at present engaged m adva~cmg
the interests of the Towner-Sterling bill. We have also been furmshed
with the result of their work.
In connection with the M. W. Grand Master's Proclamation for
"Public School Week" one of the Bulletins of the Masonic Service
Association and the data collected by the above mentioned Associ~­
tions were embodied in a pamphlet entitled, "The Needs of Our Public
Schools." A supply of these were mailed to all Lodge,: and. we have
been informed were of material assistance during Public School
·week." Requests for this pamphlet, as well as copies of the Grand
Master's Proclamation, from other Grand Lodge jurisdictions, have
been quite numerous.
"Public School .week" is now an established part of the work of
the Grand Lodge. To successfully carry it out, more attention must
be given to the preparation of a programme
this activ~ty. Work
along this tine should be commenced at least nmety days m advance
of the designated time. Through lack of interest, a pr?gr~mme o~ a
guiding hand, a number of Lodges have neglected to assist m carrymg
out the wishes embodied in the Proclamation. It should be made
mandatory upon every Lodge to comply with the provisions of the
Grand Master's Proclamation.
The cilerical work necessary to carry out the work of the Committee aloog the above lines has been heavy. Appro~imately 339
letters have been received and of these, 208 were rephed to. The
length of these answers varied from ten lines to two pages and over.
In addition there has been a large amount of local and. long distance
telephones and telegrams.
With the above recapitulation, we believe if the work of the Committee on Masonic Education is to be of any future value, there must
be a method of handling it on practical and business-like lines.
We therefore make the following recommendations:
1. That the Committee on Masonic Education, as soon as possible,
adopt a programme covering Masonic and practical Educational topics
and put the same into effect.
2 That the State be districted and at regufar intervals meetings
be held in each District under the auspices of the Committee on
Masonic Education for the purpose of carrying out this programme.
3. That any expense to a Lodge necessary to carry out any request of the Committee on Education, be payable out of the general
funds of the Lodge and not out of that allowed for refreshments and
the promotion of Fraternal intercourse, but that where a Lodge or

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
Brother Arthur Joel introduced the following:
Whereas, As Masons we have ever cherished as one of the most
important institutions of this land the common school system of public
education; and
Whereas, Grand Lodge approves the policy of setting aside one
week of our year for devoted service in the cause of the Public Schools
of our Country: Now therefore, be it
Resolved, J?y Grand Lodge that one week of each year be designated
and set apart by the Grand Master as Public Schools Week, during
which all of the subordinate Lodges in this jurisdiction shall publicly
promote the welfare of the Public Schools; and be it further
Resolved, That a committee of five members .be appointed by the
Grand Master as soon as practicable to act under his direction, for the
purpose of effecting the most widespread observance of said Public
Schools Week; and be it further
Resolved, That the sum of $500.00, or so much thereof as may be
necessary, is ·hereby appropriated for the use of said Committee to
be expended under the direction of the Grand Master.

the preservation of the three-fold boon of citizenship-religious liberty,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on by-laws has had under consideration the bytlaws of Lodges. under dispensation, and begs leave to report:
That we have carefully examined the by-laws of said Lodges and
find the same in proper form with the exception of Azure, Bellflower,
Catalina, Smyrna:, Forest Hill, Utopia and Belvedere Lodges.
In the case of Azure Lodge, that portion of the by-laws which
should provide for the fees to be charged for the remaining degree, or
degrees, after the first or second degree has been conferred in ainother lodge, has not been properly filled in, nor any fee provided. 'We
therefore recommend that said omission be supplied by Azure Lodge,
and that a certified copy thereof be forwarded to the Grand Master
for his approval.
As regards Bdlflower, Catalina, Forest Hill and Utopia Lodges,
several of the charter members have failed to write their names in
full and have only used initials. vVe therefore recommend that their
full names be affixed as soon as practicable, and that the Secretaries
of said Lodges certify to the Grand Secretary upon proper completion
thereof.
We find that the same defect exists in the case of Smyrna Lodge
as to the charter members signing by initials instead of full name;
also that its by-laws have not provided for the fee to be charged for the
remaining degree or degrees after the first or second degree has been
conferred by another Lodge; and further, that Section 1, Article IX
should be changed so as to read: "Nine dollars, payable quarterly in
advance." We therefore recommend that the full names of the charter
members be affixed as soon as practicable and certified by the Secretary

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lo'dge of California:

\Ve, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, have had
under consideration the recommendations of the Grand Master in his
annual address, and beg leave to ·-report as follows:

Proposed Amendments
The Grand Master recommends an amendment to Section. 73 of
the Constitution, which recommendation is being considered by the
Committee on Jurisprudence, and a report will be made to the Grand
Lodge proposing amendments to Sections 73 and 74 to carry out the
spirit of the recommendation made by the Grand Master. This Com·
mittee concurs in the policy expressed in the amendments to be proposed by the Committee on Jurisprudence.

Adopted.

.251

The Grand Master recommends an amendment of Section 96 of
the Constitution to provide that a request for a waiver of jurisdiction
shall be made by the Lodge to which a petitioner intends to present
a petition instead of by the petitioner himself. It is tbe opinion
of your Committee that a Lodge should take no action '''i-especting a prospective petitioner, and should acquire .no jurisdiction
over him for any purpose until his petition has been presented to
the Lodge. We can easily conceive of embarrassment and perhaps a
dangerous situation that may follow the espousal of the aspirations
of a candidate prior to the time the Lodge obtains jurisdiction over
him as provided by our law, and we are of the opinion that the
recommendation of the Grand Master should not be adopted.

Adopted, and the proposed recommendation failed.
The Grand Master recommends that Section 112 of the Constitution be amended by adding after the last word in the section as it
now reads, the following: "Any number of eandidates may be examined
at any meeting, but not more than five shall be examined at any one
time; such examination shall be held in front of the East." We have
carefuily eonsidered this reeommendation and find that such an amendment to our law being obviously restrictive and conducive to the
orderly procedure in the Lodge room and to be. an adequate test of
the proficiency of the candidates, and therefore recommend that the
same be adopted.

Adopted, and section 112 was amended as above indicated,
by unanimous vote.
The Grand Master recommends an amendment of Sections 161
and 248 of the Constitution. An examination of the present provisions of our law leads your Committee to believe that no amendment
of said sections is necessary or expedient at this time, except to incorporate the valuable suggestion made by the Grand Master that a
member against whom charges are pending should not be entitled to
receive a certifieate of standing, and we, therefore, recommend that
Section 161 of the Constitution be amended by adding, after the words
"good standing," in the first line of said section, the following words :
"and against whom no charges are pending."

The Committee on Jurisprudence concurred in this report,
which was adopted, and section 161 was amended as recommended by unanimous vote.
The Grand Master recommends that our book of Constitution be
revised in order that laws which have been repealed by amendment
may be omitted, and that the subject matter be condensed and the

Sunday Desecration
1. Brother L. T. Cranz proposes that "No Mason or body of
Masons shal:l advertise in the. public press the holding of any meeting or gathering for any purpose whatever on a Sunday. other than
for funeral purposes; nor shall tickets be issued or posters displayed for
any public function except as hereinbefore stated." \Ve are of the
opinion that this proposal is entirely too sweeping and comprehensive
in its terms, mainly in that it includes bodies not under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge and would preclude the holding of devotional
services and perhaps other meetings that might properly he held on
the Sabbath; and we therefore recommend that the resolution be not
adopted. Your Committee believes that legisiation should be enacted
prohibiting the desecration of the Sabbath by Masonic organizations
and groups under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, and further
recommends that the Committee on Jurisprudence be requested to
formulate and submit appropriate legislation to this Grand Lodge.

Reducing Cost of Printing Proceedings

7. Brother Leo Bruck of the Finance Committee introduced a resoiution for the amendment of Article 4, Section 501 5th subdivision of
the Constitution, to add thereto the following words: "The same
shall be subrnitted to the Committee on Finance, and a summary thereof published in the Proceedings." The effect of this amendment is to
reduce the size and cost of the report of the annual proceedings of
this Grand Lodge by eliminating from the report the itemized list of
expenditures and receipts during the fiscal year. :No good purpose
is served by printing a transcript of the cash book. The items are
checked by auditors and are examined by the Finance Committee and
a summary thereof will give in a concrete and compact form the
information desired by the craft relative to the financial transactions
of this Grand Lodge. Vv e, therefore, recommend that the proposed
amendment to the Constitution be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

The report was adopted, and the Committee on J urisprudence immediately reported back the proposed amendment with
a recommendation that it do pass. Thereupon subdivision 5th,
Section 50, of the Constitution, was amended by unanimous
vote to read as follows:
"5th. To report, at each annual communication, a detailed account
of all moneys received by him within the year, with a specific statement of the source whence they were derived; and to present therewith the receipts of the Grand Treasurer therefor. A detailed and
itemized statement of the disbursements of Grand Lodge during the
year shall be submitted to the Committee on Finance and a summary
thereof shall be published with the Proceedings."
Withdrawal of Life Membership Fund
8. Brother Leo Bruck of the Finance Committee proposed that
Section 129 of the Constitution be amended to provide for the withdrawal from the life membership fund upon the death of a life mem"
her, of such sum as he shall have paid into such fund, which amount
when so withdrawn shall become a part of the General Fund of the
Lodge. Your Committee is not advised of any circumstance which
makes it either necessary or expedient to change our present law relative to life membership funds. It appears to your Committee that a
life membership fond gradually built up and its integrity maintained
is a valuable asset to a Lodge and that except in extraordinary circumstances no diminution should be permitted in the principal amount
of such fund. It is conceivable that in the future it may be proper to

Proposed Paid Instructor
9. -Brother Norton Langford of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296 has
proposed that a new section be added to the Constitution, providing
that two or more Lodges located within a city or Masonic district
may enter into compact providing for the employment of a brother
at a salary to instruct candidates in the three degrees of Masonry,
which instruction shall be given only in a building used for Masonic
purposes. Your Committee, after careful consideration, recommends
that this amendment to the Constitution be not adopted. The matter
of instructing candidates lies within the province of the Master and
it is his prerogative to commission qualified brethren to perform this
important duty. He should be the sole judge of the fitness and qualifications of the instructor and he has the power to make such arrangements as to him seems wise and expedient.

Report adopted, and the proposed amendment failed.

Dual Membership

Time Limit in Which a Mason May Appl y for Other Degrees

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has given the
subject of dual membership due consideration. It has investigat~d the
operation of dual memberships in other jurisdictions and found it successful and meeting with approval after years of usage.

There have been presented to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes several resolutions proposing amend:nents to section
165 of the Constitution pertaining to membership in Lodges, prescribing the time limit within which a newly created Master Mason may
apply for degrees in other bodies or organizations, wherein the prerequisite to member,ghip is that the person be a Master Mason.

Yom Committee, therefore, reports favorably on the principle of

for your approval.

District Deputy Grand Masters
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
re-referred the proposal to amend the Constitution to provide for
the creation of the office of District Deputy Grand Master, and the
commissioning of Deputy Grand Lecturers, beg leave to report that
this subject matter has been reconsidered by the Committee and that
it is now of the opinion that the action taken at the Session of 1920
(Proceedings 192D, pages 289-292) on this subject should be rescinded.

This matter was before Grand Lodge in 1921, at which time it was
suggested that action to accomplish the desired result would probably
be taken by the bodies'. above referred to, but since the closing of the
session of Grand Lodge of 1921 .no such action has been taken. It is
the opinion of your Committee that legislation on thi·s subject should
emanate from such bodies rather than from this Grand Lodge, although we recognize the undoubted right of the Grand Lodge to prescribe the conditions upon which a Master Mason will be permitted
to retain his membership.
Your Committee believes that detriment has come to some of the
Lodges i.n this jurisdiction by reason of the fact that candidates for
the degrees have been 1solicited prior to the time they have become
Master Masons to petition for membership in one or more of the organizations above referred to, and that too often newly raised Master
Masons have been weaned away from the mother Lodge by friends
particularly interested in the growth in the membership of some other
organization. The knowledge of our art, the contact with the spirit of
our Institution, and the understanding of our tenets and principles
require that more attention be given them during the brief time devoted to conferring the degrees. For this reason we believe that
affirmative action should be taken by this Grand Lodge at this time,
although we do not recommend the adoption of any of the various
resolutions which have been presented to us.

It appears to your Committee that the present system of Inspectors
is adequate and satisfactory, and that no change shou'ld be made
therein without greater reason than has yet been presented. We, therefore, recommend that the policy of creating District Deputy Grand
Masters and Deputy Grand Lecturers, be not adopted.

It seems to your Committee that the purpose sought to be accomplished can for the present be effectively served by requiring of the
candidate at the time he petitions for the degrees an express promise
not to petition for, or receive any of the degrees in any body, order
or organization the prerequisite of membership wherein is that the
person be a Master Mason, until the full period of six months shall
have elapsed after he shall have taken the third degree of Masonry.

The report was adopted, and the action of Grand Lodge at
the annual communication of 1920 proposing to create the office
of District Deputy Grand Master was rescinded.

We therefore recommend that the form of petition for degrees
prescribed in sectio.n 246 'of the Constitution be amended by designating
rhe pre.sent clause 13 thereof as 14, and adding a new clause to be
numbered 13, and to read as follows:
"13. Do you promise that you will not, within six months after receiving the degree of Master Mason, petition for or receive any degree

our Constitution was amended to its present form in order that the
decision of the question of physical qualifications was left to the wise
discretion of Masters of Lodges, and to avoid the necessity of decisions by Grand Masters pertaining thereto. Every Master is as well
qualified to determine the fitness of candidates as is the Grand Master.
and should assume the responsibility of so doing. The provisions of
the Constitution are mandatory, and neither the Grand Master nor
Masters of Lodges have the power to waive the requirement that an
applicant must be physicaUy able to conform substantially to what
the several degrees respectively require of him. We therefore recommend that the action of the Grand Master in denying requests for
such dispensations be approved.

Arrest and Return of Charter
Under the heading of discipline, the Grand Master reports that it
became necessary to arrest the charter of a Lodge in the jurisdiction
for an act of contumacy in returning a communication from the Grand
Master and criticizing his action in sending the same. Subsequently,
the Lodge made satisfactory apology to the Grand Master, retracted
its action, and the Grand Master restored the charter.
We have examined the record pertaining to this case, and we are of
the opinion that the Grand Master's action was entirely correct, and
we recommend its approval.

The recommendation of the Committee was adopted.
Long Beach Board of' Relief
We have examined the compact of the Long Beach Lodges in
the formation of a Board of Relief. We find no evidence that the
action of the brethren assuming to represent the Lodges was ever
acted upon by the Lodges in meeting, hence it cannot be said to be
a compact of the Lodges.
We recommend that when the Lodges have taken action approving
the formation of the Board and the adoption of its by-laws and certified such action to the Grand Secretary, the compact be approved.

Adopted.
Dual Membership in Organization of New Lodges
Brother W. E. Metz of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296 introduced the
following, which was referred to this committee, and to which we
have given careful consideration:
Whereas, The three principal tenets of Masonry, Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth, have been the foundation stones of our fraternity

262

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GHAND LODGE Ol<' CALIFOHNIA

for countless ages, but have in recent years, in thickly populated centers, commenced to crumble into decay, due to the bui1ding up of
Lodges of large membership who remain unknown to each other; and
Whereas, It is a fundamental fact that it is not in conformity with
the laws of nature to hold a sincere feeling of brotherly love for a
total stranger, and as the exercise of that principle can only be brought
about through contact, getting together, learning each other's faults
and virtues, and stimulating the practice of these tenets, it naturally
follows that we must have smaller Lodges and more of them. It is an
titgent need recognized by a11 Masons who have given the matter consideration, but owing to the arduous task of mastering the ritual and
lectures of the three degrees, and the reluctance (due to recognized
sentiment) of Past Masters to withdraw from their Lodges, the forma·
tion of a new Lodge is looked upon with trepidation; and
Whereas, Believing that the situation can and should be relieved
whereby the formation of new Lodges would be encouraged without
affecting a sentiment which is truly commendable, I offer the following resolution :
Resolved, That Section 161 be amended to read as follows:
"Section 161. A member in good .standing whose dues are paid,
who desires to affiliate with another Lodge, may apply for, and receive from the Secretary of the Lodge of which he is a member, a
duly attested certificate of his standing. By presenting such a certificate with his petition, a member may apply for affiiliation with an·
other Lodge in the manner prescribed in Section 98. If such applicant
be elected to affiliate with a Lodge he can become a member thereof,
only, after the issuance of a certificate of his withdrawal, which shall
be immediately issued upon due notice of his election from the Lodge
with whieh he desires to affiliate. Vpon the granting by the Grand
Master of a dispensation for the formation of a new Lodge the membership of any signer of the petition therefor in any other Lodge in
this jurisdiction ,shall not be affected; provided, however, that he shall
nevertheless be liable for and shall pay to such Lodge such unpaid
dues as may have accrued between the date of his certificate of stand ..
ing in such Lodge and the date of the granting of such dispensation,
and thereafter he shaU only be liable for dues in the new Lodge thus
formed; and provided further, that the old Lodge in which he shall
retain membership shall not be liable for Grand Lodge dues because of
his membership, said member being carried and reported in the Secretary's report to the Grand Lodge, as 'dual member'. A certificate
of standing in lieu of a demit may he received with the petition for
the formation of a 1new Lodge only when it emanates from some
Lodge of this jurisdiction, And be it further

Proposed Amendment to Section 97
It is proposed by Brother Norton Langford of Silver Gate Lodge
No. 296 to amend section 97 of our Constitution by substantially extending the jurisdiction of Lodges having concurrent juri.sdiction in
regard to rejected candidates beyond the one-year period prescribed.
Your Committee is of the opinion that our ancient laws have been
sufficient and are now sufficient as to the jurisdiction over rejected
material. This jurisdiction is absolute and complete for twelve months
and shou1d be sufficient to safeguard our Institution.
The Committee therefore recommends that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

The report was adop~ed and the proposed amendment failed.

Life Membership, Arcata Lodge
We have considered the action of the Grand Master in approving
the standing reso'lution of Arcata Lodge No. 106, establishimg the system of life membership. The original resolution introduced, and
notice of which was mailed to the members, provided for the payment
of $100.00 as a life membership fee. .At the meeting at which action
was taken upon the resolution it was amended so as to make the fee
$150.00, and was adopted as amended at that meeting. In 1915 we
established the rule that in the case of amendments of by-laws there
was no power in the Lodge to amend the proposed amendment, and
without notice to the members as required by the Constitution to adopt
the amended amendment. The same rule applies to life membership,
as notice of the standing resolution must be given to all the members of
the Lodge; and itll this case it cannot be said that notice of the resolution, which was adopted, was given to the members as required by
the Constitution. \Ve therefore recommend that the action of the
Grand Master in approving the >Standing resolution creating a life
membership in Arcata Lodge No. 106, be not approved, atlld that the
resolution be referred to Arcata Lodge for such further action as may
be deemed advisable.

Adopted.

and we recommend that his action be approved.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND
LECTURER'S REPORT
Brother Will H. Fischer, chairman of the committee to
which had been referred the report of the Grand Lecturer,
presented the following:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to which has been referred the annual report of
the Very \Vorshipfttl Grand Lecturer, has had the 1same under consideration, and begs to submit the following:
We note with satisfaction the prosperous condition of the Lodges
throughout the jurisdiction. It is particularly gratifying to observe
that, by the construction of new temples, and the re-modeling of old
ones, provision is being made by many of our Lodges for greater attention to those social features which, by bringing the brethren in closer
personaq relations, are so well calculated to promote true fraternal
feeling based on the mutual understanding, admiration and respect
which flow from intimacy of acquaintance.
The teaching of Masonry's sublime truths is, of course, as we all
recognize, the first function of our Lodges; but it is a fact well established by experience that social activities, when conducted along Masonic lines, conduce in a most important way to those attachments
which provide greatest opportunity for the exemplification, in the
practical every-day affairs of life, of the lessons we teach.
In this connection we approve the Grand Lecturer's implication
that Lodges should refrain from excessive degree work. A Lodge
which becomes a mere machine cannot devote to its members that
measure of individual a.ttention which is so highly desiraMe; nor
can the degrees be conferred with complete impressiveness under such
conditions. It 'were better that candidates shou~d endure a reasonable
delay than to feel, upon receiving the degrees, that the process of conferring the same iG mechanical and lacking in fineness of feeling.

271

PROCEEDINGS OJ.-' THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The report of Lodges show an increase of interest and attendance
in all cases where educational programs are carried on. vVe believe
the educational work should receive further and more substantial encouragement.
It is a pleasure to voice our concurrence in the Grand Lecturer's
approving references to the Inspectors of this jurisdiction. The 6ervice rendered by the Inspectors cannot be too highly appreciated. This
service requires constant study, attention to numberless detai1s, much
sacrifice of time and convenience, and above all a true and unselfish
devotion to the interest;; of the craft. Fortunate indeed is our jurisdiction in the character, ability and tireless devotion of these who serve
as inspectors of our comtituent Lodges, and we heartily join in the
sentiment expressed by the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer.
In conclusion, we congratulate this Grand Lodge and the craft on
the fact that Brother Thomas J. Baker continues to serve it as Grand
Lecturer. Few of us, perhaps, realize the energy, sacrifice and fraternal
fealty which enter the spirit of his work. May he long be with us,
and may he be ever conscious of the affection, support and appreciation of his brethren.
Fraternally submitted,

GEORGE WASHINGTON MEMORIAL

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes have given due
consideration to the recommendation of the most Wonshipful Grand
Master that the Inspectors of this grand jurisdictioin should be dothed
with a proper regalia, to become their personal property, and on the
retirement from office of the Inspector he be given past rank as su.ch,
and be permitted to wear his insignia on all Masonic occasions, including Grand Lodge communications.
The Grand Maister expressed th-e belief that by such means we
,
would lend dignity to the rank of Inspector.
Your Committee is in accord with the views of the Grand Master
on this subject. We feel that through this means the Grand Lodge
will be given a delicate, if belated acknowledgment of appreciation of
splendid service, aind that some tangible evidence of rank will increase
the respect for the authority which attaches to the important office
of Inspector.

We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the incoming Grand Master be requested to appoint
a committee of three whose duty it shall be to design, or cause to be
designed, a regalia that will be an appropriate insignia of the office of
Inspector, such desig.n to meet the approval of the incoming Grand
Master; and, further, be it
Resolved, that when in the judgment of the incoming Grand Master
a suitable design shall have been created, the Grand Secretary be directed to cause a regalia to be made, and to be presented to the 1several Inspectors of this grand jurisdiction, to become their personal
property; and, further, be it
Resolved that the I.nspectors shall be permitted to wear the regalia
of their rank on aH official occasions, including communications of
Grand Lodge.

Masonic Temple Association
The report of the Masonic Temple Association of California has
been carefully considered. The report shows that it has paid aiJI of its
current expenses out of its regular revenue and has paid $10,000.00 on
the mortgage, which with the $40,000.00 appropriated by this Grand
Lodge at its seventy-second annual communication to buy stock in
said Association, has reduced the mortgage a\S of October 1st, 1922,
to $90,000.00. Your Committee is of the opinion that the funds of
this Grand Lodge are sufficient to enable them to purchase additional
stock amounting to $40,000.00. We therefore offer the following
resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that this Grand Lodge subscribe a,nd pay for 4,000 _shares
of the capital stock of the Masonic Temple Association of California
at the price of $10.00 per share, in addition to the stock already owned.

South West Lodge
Your Committee has before it the request of South West Lodge No.
283, located at National City, for refund of $24.00. It appears from
the correspondence before us that on October 6th, 1921, a check wa's
drawn by South West Lodge in favor of the Grand. Secretary in the
amount of $40.00 on the Peoples N ationa'l Bank, National City. Said
check was deposited for collection in the Crocker National Bank of
San Francisco, October 29th, 1921; that on October 26th, 1921, three
days prior to the date on which said check was deposited for collection
the bank at National City closed its doors. From the correspondence
at hand we are unable to determine whether the check was held by
the Secretary of the Lodge after it was drawn or whether the Grand
Secretary's office held it for a number of day1s after its receipt.
Since the failure said ba,nk has paid dividends of 40%, which
amount to $16.00 on this check, leaving a balance of $24.00, which the
Lodge has requested this Grand Lodge to refund. As South West Lodge
has been laboring under heavy financial burdens, and there is some
question as to whether they were really at fault in this matter, we
recommend that they be reimbursed in the 1sum of $24.00. We there-fore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $24.00 be and the same is hereby appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge to reimburse South West
Lodge No. 283.

No. 425, located at Holtville, California, for reimbursement of the sum

John Maley of Chehalis Lodge No. 28, Wa1shington. It appears from

Holtville Lodge early in May of this year. At the time he arrived
there he was il'I ~nd had to be placed in a hospital and unde"r the
doctor's care. On communication with Brother Maley's Lodge, the
Lodge promised to pay the expenses and reimburse Holtville Lodge, but
so far no payments have been made. We believe that the Grand

Woodstock Lodge No. 491
Your Committee has had under consideration the claim of Woodstock Lodge No. 491, for the return of certain moneys expended on

and si1nce the brother's death has taken care of his widow, that several
hundred dollars have been expended on this case, and Balsack Lodge
has returned to Woodstock Lodge al'l the money expended with the
exception of $55.00. Also that Woodstock Lodge advanced and paid
on account of Tacoma Lodge $6.32, and as neither of these amounts
have been returned, we offer the following resolution and recommend
its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $61.32 be appropriated from the funds of

moneys expended for relief on behalf of Mrs. George W. Caswell,
widow of a member of Balsack Lodge of East Boston, Massachusetts,
and for a member of Tacoma Lodge of Tacoma, Washington.

Masonic Homes
The annual report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, together with financial reports certified by the accountants of
the Board, have been examined. It displays excellent management on
behalf of the Trustees.
During the year ending September 30th there was received from
the $20.00 charge for initiation the sum of $181,480.00. The 25 cents
per capita produced in addition thereto $23,171.00, or making a total
of $204,651.00 to be used for maintenance and other expenses of the
Homes. We believe that a tax for the coming year of 25 cents in
addition to the amount to be received from the $20.00 per capita tax oo
initiations will produce sufficient revooue for the maintenance of the
)fasonic Homes of California. The Committee therefore offers the
following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of 25 cents per capita be levied upon the
membership for the maintenance of our Homes at Decoto and Covina,
payable July 31st, 1923.

PROCEEDINGS OF: THE

U. C. Club at Berkeley
Your Committee has had before it the request of the Committee
on the proposed Masonic Club House at the University of California.
This Committee has made wonderful progress in collecting funds from
the brethren of this grand jurisdiction, and have secured sufficient
money and pledges to warrant us in believing that this enterprise will
be successfully consummated. We feel that this Grand Lodge would be
justified in appropriating $5,000.00 to assist in this noble undertaking,
the same to be used for the building and equiping a suitable Lodge
room or assembly hall in the Club House. We therefore offer the
following resolution and recommend its adoption :
Resolved, that the sum of $5,000.00 be appropriated from the funds
of this Grand Lodge foi- the purpose of aiding in the building and
equiping of a· suitable Lodge room or assembly hall in the Masonic
Club House at the University of CaHfornia.

Harry Sumner Johnson
The Assistant Grand Secretary, Harry Sumner Johnson, died
suddenly on October !st, 1922. He had held this position for about
twenty-two years and had rendered this Grand Lodge valuable and
loyal service: Your Committee is of the' opinion that this Grand Lodge
should, in a small degree at least, render some financial assistance to
his widow and orphans, and we recommend that his salary of $300 per
month for the mc.nths of October, November and December, 1922, be
paid to his widow, and we therefore offer the following resolution and
recommend its adoption :
Resolved, that the sum of $900 be appropriated from the funds of
this Grand Lodge to the widow of Harry Sumner Johnson, our late
Assistant Grand Secretary.

Public School Week
Referring to the proposed resolution introduced by Brother Arthur
Joel, providing that $500.00 be appropriated for the Committee in
charge of Pub'lic School Week, your Committee on Finance offers the
following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of five hundred dollars ($500.00), or so much
thereof as may be necessary, is hereby appropriated for the use of said
Committee, to be expended under the direction of the Grand Master.

elected Grand Master.

elected Deputy Grand Master.
The R.".W.".David J. Reese of San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214
was elected Senior Grand Warden.
The W.~.Albert E. Boynton of Oroville Lodge No. 103 was elected
Junior Grand Warden.
The V.".W.".William P. Filmer of King Solomon's Lodge No. 260
was re-elected Grand Treasurer.
The V.".W.".John Whicher of King David's Lodge No. 209 was
re-elected Grand Secretary.

INSTALLATION AND FELICITATIONS
Past Grand Master Charles L. Patton was appointed Master of Ceremonies, and the officers-elect and appointed, excepting the Grand Orator, Grand Standard Bearer and Senior
Grand Steward, were installed in due and ancient form by
the retiring Grand Master, Samuel E. Burke.
Immediately following installation, Brother Will H. Fischer
presented to Past Grand Master Burke a beautiful oriental rug,
the gift of Grand Lodge.
Past Master Hugh K. McKevitt of Presidio Lodge then
presented to the newly-installed Grand Master, with the compliments of Presidio Lodge, a solid gold gavel.
Brother Bain, Master of Presidio Lodge, not to be outdone
entirely, presented the Grand Tiler with a traveling bag.
A brief address was made by V. W. E. J. Brother Hudson,
Grand Secretary of the District Grand Lodge of Shanghai
(Massachusetts constitution), and at 1 o'clock, all business
being now completed, the seventy-third annual communication
of Grand Lodge was closed in Ample Form.
WM. A. SHERMAN, Grand Master.

REPORT
OF 11-fE

Committee on Correspondence
October, 1922
By JoHN FRANKLIN \Vi;;sT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.,
of the State of California.
Your Committee on Correspondence submits herewith its annual
report. The craft in several jurisdictions seems to have been greatly
affected by the unrest in world affairs. In some quarters, a more or
less definite desire has been manifest to have the organization take
part in outside affairs. I fear that the addresses of some of the
Grand Masters deal with questions that come dangerously close to the
border line of Masonry. One cannot help experiencing the feeling that
the proper affairs of the fraternity are too often overshadowed by
trivial bickerings in which Masons are not interested. It is, of course,
the duty of every Mason to become intelligently informed on all topics
that affect his lodge, his city, his state and his government. In fact,
he cannot be a good Mason unless he does so. Any topic which will
affect the duty one owes to God, his country, his neighbor, his family
or himself, is a proper topic for discussion within a Masonic Lodge, but
quarrels of nations and party strife should never be permitted to enter
the sanctity of the lodge. It is an inspiration to see how hearts of
thoughtful brethren respond to the messages to the craft, when they
are properly presented by those leaders who adhere to the faith of our
fathers. One writer has expressed the thought I have in mind, as
follows:
"Masonry has not outlived the ideals which gave it birth, though
some there may be who believe it has. Being uncomfortably difficult
to attain, as ideals are likely to be, they are and ever will be springs
of tnoughts and actions, which, expressing themselves in the lives of
Masons, will help mankind to find a way out of worries that disturb the
peace of the heart.
"The rapid growth in membership has brought into our ranks many
who have not yet found their way into the spirit of Masonry. Here,
no doubt, is to be found one chief reason for the restless searching
after strange fields of endeavor.

336

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"The plain duty would seem to be to strengthen the pillars of the
temple that they may not be torn down or weakened."
A determined effort must be made to instill into the minds of our
newly obligated brethren the true meaning of Masonry. The older members of the craft must be rejuvenated and all must be inspired with
a desire to know and live Masonry. 1fany Grand :.\Iasters have
sounded the call, and the loyal members of the. craft are responding,
for they realize that the principles taught in .)Masonry will make for
a higher type of manhood and the stabilizing of civilization.
The Masonic fraternity is essentially an educational institution, for
it stands whole-heartedly for at least four of the fundamental principles of education: viz., the development of
1. Character that is above reproach.
2. lnfeltigence that is broad, deep, sane and practical.
3. Leadership that is wise, efficient and masterful.
4. Citizenship that is iojal, devoted and unselfish.
In reading the reports of the various grand jurisdictions, I have been
deeply impressed with progress that is being made in the development
of Masonic education and the diffusion of knowledge among members of the craft. Let the good work go on and grow rapidly.
The following table contains the grand jurisdictions covered by this
review, as well as other data, which your committee hopes will prove
valuable to all who are interested in this report:

There were present at the One Hundred and First Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Alabama Grand Master Percy B. Dixon,
twelve Grand Officers, seven Past Grand Masters and representatives
from 451 of the 574 chartered Lodges. The Grand Master's address
is very interesting. The following extract gives an idea of the high
plane which he assumed in all his discussions:
"That the Peace, Progress an"d Enlightenment which we as Masons
have enjoyed may not only continue, but be shared by our fellow
citizens, thus carrying the principles of Fremasonry into practice,
this Grand Lodge should avail itself of every opportunity to be ever
in the vanguard of the Grand Army of Education in its warfare
against Ignorance and Superstition.
"At the Ninety-Fourth Annual Communication. in 1914, (see page
163, report 1914), this Grand Lodge passed a resolution calling upon
its members to enlist the support of the State Legislature in submitting
to the voters an amendment to the State Constitution, permitting the
several counties to tax themselves for local educational purposes; Alabama being the only State ?n the Union then prohibiting such local
taxation. The usual argument, presented by the foes of education, that
the State was not ready for such· legislation, and that the several counties were opposed to such local taxation was refuted when the State
by an overwhelming majority passed the Amendment, one of the very
few in recent years. 'Within a little over a year after the passage of the
amendment, sixty-two of the sixty-seven counties had availed themselves of the privilege, and at the present time every county save one
has adopted the Educational Tax, thereby permitting the ·state to
advance from the third lowest in the educational scale, passing a number
of other States in the upward progress. Notwithstanding this progress,
the work of advancement has just begun; the surface only has been
scratched, and much remains to be done if we would materially help
the future citizens of our State.
"As no State, even as the individual citizen, lives unto itself, so no
true progress can be made by the State unless it participates in the
national welfare. It is therefote incumbent upon this Grand Lodge to
urge its members to enlist in the Campaign for a proper education of
the nation. To this end your attention is called to a measure now before Congress, known as the Towner-Sterling Bill. This legislation,
if enacted, would create a Department of Education with it~ head as an
officer in the Cabinet. Practically every nation in the world save the
United States has such a department; in this country it is but a small
and inadequately supported Bureau.
"Through such a department it is proposed to strengthen and
support the Public Schools of the nation, not only by financial assistance

340

341

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

but by providing opportunities for properly equipping teachers as well as
other technical facilities out of the reach of the average community.
This assistance will be rendered both the children and the grown-ups,
so that immigrants also can be educated to become loyal citizens.
"Do not let the specious argument of demagogues or politicians, or
the ever present enemies of the public schools beguile you into
indiffei:ence or opposition. Each has a selfish motive for his opposition
no matter how thoroughly it may be disguised. You have but one
point for consideration ; that of making the best possible American
citizen in all that title implies."

"The action of this Grand Lodge in 1920 has been somewhat
criticized, possibly the criticism was just. As far as I can learn we were
alone in recognizing the Grand Lodge Valle de Mexico.
"We regret the controversies that have arisen among the Grand
Lodges of our Sister Republic. The subject should have earnest
consideration of this Grand Lodge as it is our aim and desire to
extend recognization to the most worthy.
"No doubt our Correspondence Committee after careful study of
::Yfasonry in Mexico will be in possession of sufficient data to make
a satisfactory report to this Grand Lodge at its next regular
Communication."

Again the Grand Master strikes an important note when he says:
"I therefore beg that each of you will give this subject your careful thought and prompt attention, and act before the opportunity is lost.
"The next important matter to which I wish to call your attention
is the fact that we are getting careless about the Constitution of this
Grand Lodge. Too little attention is paid to the study of the Constitution and Edicts by many of the Masters of subordinate lodges in
this Jurisdiction. While many boast that they are one hundred per
::ent. perfect in the Masonic Ritual, a. state of perfection in itself
worthy, yet many of these same ::Yfasters are either deficient in their
knowledge of the constitution, or what is still more reprehensible,
having a knowledge of the provisions of the law, seek in every way
to evade it."
The report of the trustees of the Masonic Home shows that the
home is being run in a very satisfactory manner, that it is turning
distress and want into comfort and pleasure. There are living at the
home at this time 13 men, 41 women, 121 boys and 109 girls.

ARIZONA (1921)
The Fortieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arizona
was convened at Bisbee, February 8, 1921. The Grand Lodge was
opened by Grand Master Henry G. Glore, with the assistance of the
Grand Officers. The Grand Master reported that he had visited all
but one of the Lodges in the jurisdiction.
MEXICAN GRAND LODGES
This grand Jurisdiction recognized the York Grand Lodge of
Mexico in 1914, and in 1920 recognized the Grand Lodge Valle de
Mexico.
The Correspondence Committee, Proceedings of 1913, in speaking
on Mexican Grand Lodges, in part says: " . . . but consider it
contrary to Masonic Law to recognize more than one Grand Lodge
occupying the same territory." In this I heartily concur.

W: .Bro. David Benshimol presented the following and moved its
adoption:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Arizona:
"R!!SOLV!\D, that there be incorporated into the proceedings of this
session a photograph of the Grand Secretary, together with the
telegrams received by him on his seventy-fifth birthday and fiftieth
anniversary as a Mason."
In accordance with this action a very fine portrait of Brother
Roskruge appears in the proceedings, together with eight pages filled
with copies of the telegrams sent to him at that time. Allow us,
Brother Roskruge, to join with your Arizona brethren in extending to
you our heartiest congratulations.

HAND IT TO HIM NOW
If with pleasure you are viewing any work a man is doing;
If you like him, or you love him, tell him now.
Don't withhold your approbation until parson makes oration
And he lies with snowy lilies o'er his brow;
For no matter how you shout it, he won't really care about it ;
He won't know how many tear drops you have shed;
If you think some praise is due him, NOW'S the time to slip it to him,
For he cannot read his tombstone when he's dead.
More than fame and more than money is the comment kind and sunny
And the hearty warm approval of a friend,
For it gives to life a savor and it makes you stronger, braver,
And it gives you heart and spirit to the end;
If he earns your praise, bestow it; if you like him, LET HIM
KNOW IT;
Let the words of true encouragement be said;
Do not wait till life is over and he's underneath the dover,
J:<'or he cannot read his tombstone when he's dead.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A sensible regulation was adpoted, permitting Lodges to expend
not over 10 per cent of this total revenue of the preceding year for
any purpose not "wholly Masonic." This includes suppers.
A proposal to tax $10. upon each initiate and affiliate, for Masonic
Home Endowment Fund was laid over.
On his 75th birthday and 50th Anniversary as a Mason, Brother
George J. Roskruge, was re-elected for the 39th time as Grand Secretary. We join in the large number of congratulations.
Again, $100. was donated to the Washington Memorial.
Apparently, any non-affiliate in Arizona, who does not within a
reasonable time "restore" himself by affiliation or contribution is
summarily declared suspended. No lodge is allowed to charge a 'fee
for affiliation.
One regulation reads :
"Hereafter, when a petition for the degrees, or an application for
affiliation in a Lodge in this Jurisdiction shall be received, the Master,
when appointing the Committee on Investigation, shall not announce the
names of said Committee in open Lodge; but shall privately inform the
Secretary as to the names of the said Committee. When this Committee makes its report it shall be to the Master, and he to the
Lodge, and after the vote has been taken, said reports shall be
destroyed."

ARKANSAS (1921)
The 80th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas
was convened at Little Rock on November 15, 1921, with G. M. W. W.
Magee in the East, all of the Grahd Officers and fourteen Past Grand
Masters and representatives of 432 of the 552 chartered Lodges present.
Three lodges were constituted and seven lodges were instituted.
The following resolution was adopted:
"That this G,rand Lodge recommend to the subordinate Lodges of
this Grand Jurisdiction that the order known as the Order of DeMolay
for Boys is an organization worthy of their encouragement, and moral
and financial support.
"It is further recommended that a chapter of DeMolay be organized
in each community where population will justify it, and that the
Lodge halls or meeting places of Lodges, whenever practical and
agreeable to the Lodg._, shall be tendered as a meeting place for this
organization."
The Grand Lodge refused to join the Masonic Service Associatfon.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

343

Brother Thomas C. McRea, Governor of Arkansas, delivered the
Annual Oration, which was received by all present.
The following. complimentary action was taken by the Grand Lodge :
"M.'.w:.Brother Jacob Trieber, Past Grand Master, called the
attention of the Grand Lodge to the circumstance that R. W. Brother
Fay Hempstead, Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge, had recently
been elevated to the high position of General Grand Master of the
General Grand Council of Royal and Select Masters of the United
States and suggested that recognition of the fact be made and the
appreciation of this Grand Lodge be manifested by greeting Brother
Hempstead as such, and expressing their thanks to the General Grand
Council for the honor thus bestowed upon the Masonry of Arkansas.
The craft .was called up and Brother Hempstead was presented and
was saluted with the private Grand Honors of Masonry. Brother
Hempstead responded with fitting appreciation of the courteous action
of the Grand Lodge, and of thanks for their cordial reception."
The Grand Lodges of Ecuador, Venezuela and Queensland were
recognized.

COLORADO (1921)
The Sixty-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
·Colorado convened at Denver, September 2, 1921. There were present
Grand Master Haslett P. Buske, the Grand officers, twenty past grand
masters and representatives of 125 of the 134 chartered lodges.
Under the· heading of "Improper Publicity" the Grand Master
well says:
"In many quarters there is to be observed an unjustifiable appetite
for Masonic Publicity. Newspaper advertisements of Masonic activities
are lamentably frequent. What seems to me a particularly flagrant
instance of this evil, in a locality where solicitation has been charged,
is called to your attention by the submission of numerous newspaper
clippings. These things are to be discountenanced and ought to be
discontinued. They constitute merely an indirect method of solicitation.
All their effects are evil and all their tendencies destructive. No
attempt should be made save 'by the regularity of our own behavior'
to popularize the craft. \Ve want no members who do not come of
their 'own free will and accord,' 'uninfluenced by mercenary motives
or the improper solicitation of friends.' The greatest danger which
today threatens the fraternity is the danger against which its sages and
leaders have warned it in Colorado and elsewhere from time immemorial- too much popularity. Our more active lodges should investigate
petitions more carefully and select their material more judiciously.

344

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Their growth is too rapid to be always healthful. We should cease to
worry about the enemy without. Now, as always, he is absolutely
impotent to injure us. Freemasonry can only be torn down from within."
The following is also timely :
"The Masonic world today exhibits marked evidence of a disposition
in many quarters to depart from the time honored principle of the
Fraternity to abstain from all participation in political activity. Lodges
and Grand Lodges are advocating the passage or defeat of legislation,
and inquiring into the fraternal and regilious affiliations of candidates
, for public office. This field has always been to our Fraternity a forbidden one. It cannot be entered without the utmost peril to that
internal harmony absolutely essential. to the existence of Masonry.
Th.is is the curse of Latin Freemasonry and, however seductive the
voices that lure us, the lessons of history are too plain for us to be
deceived. Let Colorado Masons remember the ancient landmarks
and be led into the worship of no false gods."
Colorado mourns the loss of their Grand Secretary, Brother Charles
H. Jacobson, who died February 20, 1921. Brother Jacobson served
for seventeen years as Grand Secretary. What his Brethren thought
of him is so beautifully expressed in the report of Committee on
Necrology that we quote from it:
"So lived and died a great man and great ~fason, who 'builded
better than he knew.' The foundation of his Temple was service;
service to his fellow-man, his country, and his God. Inspired by the
highest ideals and the most ennobling conceptions of life's duties he
gave to all who knew him a firmer and surer grip on the great
fundamentals of existence, broadening the intellectual horizon and
knocking the shackles from the soul. Under a somewhat stern
exterior beat as warm a human heart as the Great Architect ever
encased in clay. As has been written of the Master, whom he so
faithfully served, 'He went about doing good.' Holding himself to
the strictest accountability, he was ever patient and tolerant with the
weaknesses and errors of others. In his life he so exemplified the
teachings of the craft as to be the very personification of the spirit
of Freemasonry. With a powerful intellect, a profound understanding,
wide reading, a facile and busy pen, and a gift of eloquence vouchsafed
to few, his years of service to the Fraternity in our Jurisdiction have
left a mark that time will not efface. He was in very truth a mighty
builder, and his passing marks the end of an era.''
CONNECTICUT (1922)
The One Hundred 'and Thirty-fourth Annual Convention of the
Grand Lodge of Connecticut was held in the city of Hartford, February

345

1-2, 1922. In his address, M:.w:.Grand Master Charles Winthrop
Cramer approved daylight saving for all lodges in his jurisdiction that
desire to avail themselves of it. The Grand Master takes advance with
regard to carrying on the work of Masonic Education: He says:"The Executive Commission were painstaking in their effort to
place the Educational Programme before the delegates present and
that they were successful was evidenced in the unanimous rising vote
of endorsement at the end of a day and a half occupied in presenting
the Programme.''
The Executive Commission of the Association has prepared an
Educational Programme which "covers every phase of the right
relationship between man and man as expressed in the Masonic
Rituals and Charges." The problem of how to make use of it is
set forth in Part IV of the Commission's report, as follows:
"The great problem, therefore is how our States should be organized
in order to make use of that which is produced by this Association.
We feel that the experience of the past year demonstrates conclusively
that in order to accomplish this result each Jurisdiction must perfect an
organization able to present it in every lodge. In our experience
meeting the other evening we were privileged to hear the ideas of
those brethren who have been out in the field getting a personal
contact with the craft. We have ·all heard their reports. If our
deliberations have been successful we ought. now to be able to agree
upon the fundamentals of a plan which will bring results, and at the
same time leave each juridiction the settlement of the particular problems
which it has to face. Inevitably each Grand Lodge will utilize as
much as possible of the machinery already created for the conduct
of its affairs."
"Several Jurisdictions have already developed plans of their own.
A study of the features which they have incorporated seems to indicate
that to be effective certain requirements are essential. We have taken
occasion to go into some of these plans and suggest the following
features for consideration.
"As already indicated each Jurisdiction will have to determine for
itself the details of a plan suited to its use.
A. A Central Committee created by the Grand Lodge, to have
charge of the work in each Jurisdiction.
B. A Secretary of this committee, where practicable, to assume
responsibility for the details.
C. A Speakers' Bureau, composed of the best possible talent
available in the Jurisdiction, whose service shall he on a
volunteer basis.

346

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

D. District or Lounty Committees, to arrange the details of Lodge
meetings at which the programs are presented. These committees should be responsible to the Central Committee. Where
it is feasible to use District Deputies or County Chairmen who
can be placed on the mailing list of the Secretary, the
arrangements for local and district meetings can be more
readily perfected.
E. A consistent arrangement of dates, so that speakers, and
motion picture machines and films, where used, may be routed
on a definite schedule, thereby economizing both time and
money.''

DELAWARE (1921)
The 116th annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Delaware
was convened at ;Wilmington, October 5, 1921. There were present
Grand Master William J. Highfield, eleven grand officers, seventeen
Past Grand Masters and representatives of twenty-two chartered lodges.
During his term, the Grand Master visited every lodge in his jurisdiction. It is unfortunate that it was physically impossible for the Grand
Master of the larger jurisdiction to make a like record but the year
is entirely too short to admit of this.
\Ve quote as follows from the well-worded and business-like address of the Grand Master :
"The World War has ended. Our country gradually is working its
way back to a full peace footing and to a state of normalcy. It has
occurred to· me that at such a time of transition as this there is no
duty the discharge of which should bring to a Mason a greater degree
of satisfaction or to his country a greater amount of benefit than for
him to stand shoulder to shoulder with all other Masons to combat in
every proper way all efforts of harmful propaganda which he may see
in the life surrounding him. By propaganda I mean that dangerous,
deadly, insidious propaganda which strikes at American institutions and
which seeks to make those institutions subservient to interests which
are not truly American.
"Masonry stands for the Ten Commandments, the Declaration of
Independence, the Constitution of the United States, and the law of the
land. Masonry stands against anything and everything which menaces
American institutions and American national life.
"With a Mason in the White House, standing for everything that
is good and true in American life, and whose most ardent wish is for
earnest and intelligent co-operation from all good American citizens
in the matter of serving American interests, certainly there is no body

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

347

of nien which should rally more loyally to the work of combating any
revival of the disgraceful propaganda which was uncovered by the
World War, th= the brethren of the great fraternity which we love
and which we are pleased to call our own."
The Grand Lodge refused to recognize The Grand Lodge of France
and the Grand Orient of France.
The Grand Master visited every lodge in Delaware and attended
the annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania. He
recommended that Flag Day be observed annually by all the Lodges.
He urged that caution should be exercised in the admission of candidates to "protect the body of our craft against infusion of harmful
elements which will not assimilate with those life principles which
are the foundation of the existence and the well-being of Masonry."
He recommended that time be set apart at Lodge communications for
"the discussions of the fundamental truths and precepts of our craft."
The minimum fee for admission was made $40.00 outside of Wilmington and $75.00 in Wilmington.

IDAHO (1921)
The 44th annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Idaho
was held in the city of St. Maries, on September 13, 14, and 15, 1921.
During his Masonic year, the Grand Master visited. sixty lodges.
He urged the foundation of Masonic libraries, and many lodges
put his recommendation into practice. The Widows' and Orphans'
Fund, started several years ago, has $85,750.00 in War Savings
·Stamps and Government Bonds. Emphasis is laid on the importance of having investigating committees realize the duty entrusted to them:
"To my mind it is far better that a few good and worthy men
be denied than for one unworthy to be admitted."
Approval was given to the following resolution:
"That no candidate for the degrees of -Masonry shall be advanced to the second or third degree· until at least four weeks
have elapsed since taking the previous degree.
"Furthermore, no member shall apply for or receive any Scottish Rite or Royal Arch, Chapter degree until one year at least

351

The Grand Lodge voted to rejoin the Masonic Service Association of the United States.
On the subject of ritualistic ciphers, the Grand Lodge passed
on its first reading an amendment to its by-laws, reading as
follows:
"No Mason in this jurisdiction shall use or have in his possession any alleged key or cipher of the Masonic ritualistic work
except as provided on pages 57 to 60, Masonic Code and Digest.
Any violation of this section shall be deemed gross un-Masonic
conduct and the offender shall be subject to expulsion."
We wonder what the exception in question may be like. We
think it would be far better to have abolished ciphers utterly.
In an effort to curb the mad rush of candidates to break into
the Order, an amendment to the by-laws was submitted reading
as follows:
"No lodge shall advance a candidate until after a satisfactory
examination in open lodge, on the degrees already received; or
confer upon a candidate more than one degree at the same communication; or the first section of the first and second degrees, or
the first and second sections of the third degree, on more than
one candidate at the same time."
Another by-law was offered to the following effect:
"When a committee or any member of a committee, to whom
a petition for the degrees, membership or waiver or jurisdiction
over a rejected candidate, report unfavorably thereon, the Master
shall declare the candidate rejected without passing the ballot."

ILLINOIS (1921)
The 82nd annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Illinois
was convened at Chicago, October 11, 1921. ·There were present
M.".W.".Daniel G. Fitzgerrel, the other grand officers, nine
Past Grand Masters and representatives from 830 of the 902 chartered lodges. Immediately following the opening of the Grand

who died June 15, 1921. The following quotation is taken from

"It is impossible to specify and with precision to define those
traits, qualities and personal attributes which win and hold our
affection. They elude all effort at definition. They cannot be
segregated and scrutinized. Whatever they may be, Brother Cutter possessed those qualities in well-rounded measure. He brought
into this Grand Lodge and into all of its constituent lodges which
he visited, .and diffused among our Brotherhood generally, a genial and fraternal spirit. He breathed the atmosphere of genuine Brotherhood, and radiated from his personality an aura of
warmth and light that charmed and enriched all who came within·

him, and his generous heart with warm embrace held us all in

loss which now broods over all, are not to be attributed wholly

this, and forming the rigid framework upon which these more
graceful and engaging qualities were supported, were a stern integrity, and an earnest, persistent purpose to do each minute of his
life the very best that he could in the service of his fellow men.
To do his duty fully and to leave nothing undone that promptness and fidelity could accomplish, were the dominant thoughts
with him and guided and inspired him every moment of his life."

There were on September 30, 1921, one hundred and fortyfour happy and contented children in the Masonic Home at La

352

Under the heading of "Masonic Lotteries" the Grand Master
says:
"Masonry does not look with the least degree of allowance
upon raffles, lotteries of gift enterprises. The law as given in
Section 325 is so simple and positive that no one needs to err.
Yet, in a lodge in the State during the year past a regular lottery for the benefit of a building fund was promoted. An automobile and a number of other valuable articles were offered to those
who were the fortunate possessors of the proper tickets. The
District Deputy Grand Master very properly reported the case
to me. .I ordered all money returned and the whole scheme suppressed. If lodges cannot provide themselves meeting places
without resorting to plans and schemes which violate the Masonic
as well as the laws of the State and Nation they should be content
to rent lodge rooms indefinitely."
Sixteen lodges were constituted and nineteen lodges were instituted.

353

Past Grand Master Delmar D. Darrah submits his usual excellent report on Correspondence. Under the heading of "Too
Many Laws," in the foreword of his review, he says:
"One of the very best things that could possibly happen to
the Masonic fraternity would be to eliminate all existing laws and
regulations and return to Anderson's original Constitutions of
Freemasonry. It cannot be doubted that there are entirely too
many laws enacted for the regulation and government of the
society. One Grand Master found in counting up the laws of
his jurisdiction approximately three hundred. All this could be
greatly simplified by the use of a little common sense:
"It has been noticeable in recent years that in each meeting
of some of the Grand bodies, there have been a large number
of laws and regulations presented and enacted. Many of these
amendments have been offered by men not active in the work
of the fraternity but who have set themselves up as saviors of
the institution and who imagine that in order to keep the fraternity straight, a certain number of amendments must be adopted
each year."
The writer is fully of the opm10n that at the present time we
have all the laws, rules and regulations that the fraternity can
possibly need for the next hundred years and nothing can be
gained by the enactment of any more.
In a timely note of warning the Grand Master "pays his respects to those excrescences and parasites which of late have
shown a tendency to fasten themselves upon the Masonic institution and thus attempt o win honor, recognition and power by
claiming to be a part of our ancient institution, while, if the truth
were known, their glory is only reflected. Of these he says:
"One year ago J found it necessary to call attention to action
of bodies other than Masonic who make as a prerequisite membership in the Ancient Craft. Since then there has appeared almost an epidemic of other societies being formed on similar lines.
Considering all this the question is, where is it going to end?"
It will end in chaos and confusion and in the final demoralization
of the Institution unless those who serve and love Masonry· put
a prompt end to this sort of thing.

The Grand Master brings an excellent address to a close with
this poem:
"Not what we have, but what we use
Not what we see, but what we chooseThese are the things that mar or bless
The sun of human happiness.
"The things nearby, not things afar;
Not what we seem, but what we areThese are the things that make or break
That give the heart its joy or ache.
"Not what seems fair, but what is true,
Not what we dream, but what we doThese are the things that shine like gems,
Like stars in fortune's diadems.
"Not as we take, but as we give,
Not as we pray, but as we liveThese are the things that make for peace,
Both now and after time shall cease."
The fact nevertheless remains that unless we dream rightly,
look upward toward high ideals and pray in our souls for their
realization among men, we shall, after all, "die and leave our
errand unfulfilled."

the Brotherhood of Man as applied to good citizenship, and our
duty as Masons in the exercise of our rights of citizenship, especially in reference to our public school system.
"From our first induction into Masonry, the high ideals of loyalty and patriotism to our country and government have ever been
before us. We believe that true patriotism and loyalty to our
country and government can be maintained only by education of
the people and that such education can only be properly given in a
public school, the true 'melting pot' for Americanization. The
founders of our government early realized that some system of
universal education of all the youth of our land was essentially
necessary if this government was to continue, and provisions were
early made for such a system that has finally developed into the
great system of free public schools as we now know it-a sacred
trust for us to hand down to future generations.
"\Ve are heartily in accord with the views of our distinguished
brother, the author of the ritual of 'The Order of De Malay for
Boys' when he says, 'The public school system of our country is
the foundation of the universal enlightenment which is the crowning
glory of our institutions. Masonry has ever been the champion
of our educational institutions. Civil, religious and intellectual liberty are the triple temples of our country's greatness, but
they must stand alone, upon separate foundations and under separate roofs.' As Masons, we are unalterably opposed to the same
building housing a public school, a church and a seat of civil government. The public schools are America's Marne. Before their
door this Order takes its stand and says of all who would assail
that sacred citadel, 'They shall not pass.' "

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The following important decision was handed down by the
Grand Master:
"During the year several of our lodges have requested me to
inform them whether a lodge has a right to use its funds to purchase stock in an oil enterprise, use some of the lodge funds in
assisting in the building of a public tuberculosis sanitarium, or appropriate money from the lodge funds to assist in purchasing
robes for an 0rganization known as the De Molay. To all of th<;se
inquiries I replied that it was not proper to use the funds of a
lodge for any other than strictly Masonic purposes.
"Ouestions of a similar nature have been submitted to several ~£ my predecessors, and rulings and decisions made by them
covered only the particular case and the purpose for which the
lodge proposed to use its funds. One decision provided that the
funds could not be donated to an endowment fund for a cemetery
owned by a city; another provides that the funds of a lodge cannot be used in securing a location for a business enterprise apart
from lodge purposes.
"It is provided in a note by Past Grand Master Owen A. Bassett under Section 4 of Article VII of the Constitution, that 'A
!od~e holds all of its funds and property in trust for Masonic
uses * * *.' This has been for so long a period the general usage
that it has become a law, and on this our Grand Lodge bases its
right as the possessor of all the funds and property of a lodge
when it becomes extinct. It seems to me that neither the law nor
the decisions rendered are general enough in their character to
furnish the desired information to the craft, and I therefore feel
justified in submitting the following decision on this subject:
"Lodge Funds.-The funds of a lodge are to be used for Masonic purposes, which, as provided by Section 6, Article VIII of
the Constitution, includes the payment of any sum of money out
of the treasury for the support of the poor, for the relief of the distressed, or for any other purpose which shall tend to ameliorate
the condition of the human family or an individual."

"Can Hiram Lodge become a sustaining member of the Commission for the Blind upon payment of $12.50 per annum and appoint a representative to have an active voice in the affairs of the
Commission?
"I ruled that there being no law covering this specific case,
after careful consideration I could not give my consent for Hiram
Lodge to become a member of any such Commission for the following reasons:
"1st. The Grand Lodge of the State of Louisiana is a corporate
body, and, in my estimation, it is not the prerogative of the Grand
Master to permit a constituent Lodge, as a Lodge, to connect itself in any manner with any organization outside of Masonry.
"2nd. While I have no doubt that this particular cause referred to is a very worthy one, it would nevertheless, be setting
a precedent for constituent Lodges to ally themselves with other
organizations, since these alliances might afterwards prove to be
embarrassing should the organizations be unworthy. And another, or subsidiary reason for my refusal to grant Hiram Lodge
its request is that, in my opinion, such a request should be presented to the Grand Lodge at its regular session by resolution
or otherwise."
