MAINE (1922)
The 103rd annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Maine
was held at Masonic Temple, Portland, on May 2, 1922, and there
were present, M.".W.".Edward W. Wheeler, twenty-two grand officers and 269 representing 190 of the 206 chartered lodges of the
jurisdiction. In his annual address the Grand Master says:
"The Grand Lodge meets in a period of coqtinued industrial
depression and social unrest. While peaceful relations among all
nations have been restored and are now fully enjoyed, dangerous
domestic difficulties have developed. Defiance of law and disregard
to the personal and property rights of the individual have grown
to an alarming extent since last we met. From available statistics
it is estimated that the . volume of crime has increased fortyfive per cent in the last twelve months. The daily press has become a chronicle of criminal activities, the continuance of which
threatens the security of private rights and the stability of organized society. The prompt suppression of these evil and criminal
tendencies has become the imperative duty of the hour.
"We are all inclined to boast of our liberties, but are apt to
ignore the responsibilities which such liberties impose. Liberty
which is the freedom and privilege of the individual, is granted
and secured to us by law. Without this protection which the law
affords, the primitive doctrine that might makes right would hold
an undisputed sway.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

365

"The Masonic fraternity seeks no control over the processes
of government and the enforcement of the law, and, as an organization, it takes no part in the solution of industrial and social
problems except through the influence of its teachings upon the
character and conduct of its members. The primary purposes
of Masonry are to enlighten the mind, arouse the conscience and
stimulate the noble and generous impulses of the human heart.
It seeks to promote the best type of manhood and citizenship
based upon the practice of brotherly love and the Golden Rule.
When these results have been accomplished, the mission of
Masonry has been achieved."
With reference to guarding the portals to Masonry the Grand
Master says:
"In order to insure greater care and a more diligent inquiry
on the part of investigation committe~s, I believe that some form
of a questionnaire should be prepared under the direction of the
Grand Lodge afld furnished to the lodges in this jurisdiction, to be
used in connection with the regular application blanks whenever
it may be deemed advisable. The answer of the applicant should
be required to the question whether he has ever before applied to
any other lodge for the degrees, even though it is covered in the
application. Answers should also be required. to such other questions as will enable the committee to make an intelligent and
thorough inquiry regarding his past history and moral qualification.
"But while we must not lower the high moral standard we
have established, I am more than ever convinced that some modification may properly be made in our ancient decisions and ~egu~
lations regarding physical disqualifications, which are more
appropriate for operative than speculative Masonry and justify the
suspicion that we give greater emphasis to the external than the
internal qualifications of an applicant."

DEGREES BY COURTESY
"From the information I have received through the District
Deputies and otherwise, it appears that many of our lodges have
conferred degrees by request upon candidates elected to receive
them in other lodges in this state. This has resulted through ignorance of our Masonic law. Degrees by courtesy are permitted
only between lodges in different Grand jurisdictions. By the standing regulations of this Grand Lodge, with which the Master of
e~ery lodge should be familiar, a lodge may not confer a degree
at the request of another lodge in this jurisdiction, except after
accepting the candidate in the usual way and receiving its regular

366

PROC'EEDINGS OF THE

fees, the requesting lodge having waived jurisdiction. A candidate
receiving the degrees in violation of this regulation has no standing in any lodge and is not entitled to recognition as a Mason.
Having received the degrees irregularly, he must file a new petition with the lodge having jurisdiction; the lodge must obtain a
dispensation therefor, and then proceed in the same manrier as with
an ordinary petition and if the candidate is accepted he must be
re-obligated in all the degrees. This statement of the law is made
for the benefit and guidance of the Masters and Wardens of the
subordinate lodges here assembled and in the hope that the embarrassing consequences of the irregular and improper conferring
of degrees may hereafter be avoided."

"Ins'pired by this thought let us continue to labor whether

MICHIGAN (1921)
The 77th annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Michi·
gan was held at Battle Creek, May 24-25, 1920. There were present M.".W.".Ira A. Beck, Grand Master, thirteen grand officers,
sixteen grand masters and representatives from 452 of the 472
chartered lodges.
The Grand Master pledged the craft to give moral support to
the church organizations of the State and asked the Masters to
give practical support to the "Going-to-Church" movement by
recommending to the members of their lodges to attend divine service as often as possible. "The greatest duty in America today,"
he urged, is to "guard well the priceless heritage of Liberty, protected by the American flag," and that the Masons must form "a
bulwark of constitutional government, which makes secure those
institutions which we and all other American patriots love and
cherish." He instituted, constituted, consecrated and dedicated
new lodges, officiated at the corner stone layings of churches and
Masonic halls, issued an unusually large number of miscellaneous
dispensations and decisions, and disposed of a vast amount of
routine business. The largest lodge in the state became a subject for censure, its discords and arbitrary transactions causing
the Grand Master to say that the conditions complained of were
"a sad commentary upon large lodges,'' disregard for Masonic
law having been of frequent occurrence for twenty years and more.
A start has been made to erect at Detroit, "the finest Temple of
Masonry of its kind in the world," at a cost of four million dollars.

power of prayer. I knew, too, that there were kind, considerate

should I through ignorance wander from it. First, I want to thank

all the brethren of the Jurisdiction. And then I want to thank
those kind brothers who have given so generously of their time
and thought to assist me in my work I would also ask all of you
to bear with me in my shortcomings and mistakes. May the
broad mantle of Masonic charity cover them all."

Masonic Research and Study Clubs
"This good work, started a few years ago, has been growing
slowly but in a satisfactory manner. In a number of Lodges Study
Clubs have been formed, and meetings are regularly held and much
interest shown. A joint meeting of the Study Clubs of St. Paul
was held in May. Past Grand Master Schoonover of Iowa, Chairman of the Executive Committee, was present and addressed the
meeting, and much good will no doubt result from the meeting.
Brother R. E. Denfeld, Past Grand Master, continued the work
of lecturing and instructing the brethren in the different Lodges
of the Jurisdiction. It was my privilege to be present at several
meetings he addressed. His addresses were interesting, instructive
and inspiring and were much enjoyed by all. Now that Brother
Denfeld has passed away we must redouble our efforts to carry on
the good work so ably conducted by him. More responsibility
should be assumed by local brethren and an effort made to organize
more Study Clubs to .systematically follow the course of study
outlined by the National Masonic Research Society of Anamosa,
Iowa. There are wonderful opportunities for uplifting individual
Masons and Lodges by establishing and carrying on these Study
Clubs. The time seems ripe and I strongly urge that more
clubs be formed."
On the whole, the report shows that the year bas been one of
substantial growth, not only in numbers, but also in the enriching
of the lives of the Masons of that good Jurisdiction.

Grand Master Edward L. Fausette opened his annual address by
sounding a trumpet call to duty in these ringing words:
"We are passing through a period of unrest and discontenttesting days for Freemasons. Socialism, anarchy, greed, selfishness
and ignorance, parading in the name of democracy, are some of
the evil force.s that menace the foundations of government and civil
society. Every principle of Masonry, every virtue sacred to the
heart of our fellowship is being singled out for assault and destruction. Because of this fact Masonry finds itself confronted with
additional duties and tremendous responsibilities. A new atmosphere of brotherhood, liberty and equality must be produced. vVe
can be the builders of the great temple of democracy and the
educators to inculcate a true Americanism. vVe must seek to do
our part in making civilization better than it ever was, in making
the world a fit place in which to live, a place where the principles
of man's brotherhood will find lodgment."
Repeated utterances of this sort, gleaned from many volumes of
Proceedings, furnish evidence that the leaders of the craft are
fast coming to realize that a Mason's duty is not limited to the

mere rumor to that effect is of more or less harm to our fraternity.
The new United Grand Lodge of Queensland was recognized.
The following comment on the 1921 decision as to physical
qualifications seems to us sound and temperate:
"We have noted for some time and with something of concern
that the matter occupies the attention of many Grand Lodges, and,
as it seems to us, is decided rather by sentiment than by an appeal to
reason and ancient landmarks. · As we have often remarked,
Masonry was never intended as ·a popular institution and membership in the fraternity is not a necessity to any man. We may hold
a friend, even of kindred blood, in profound and tender regard, and
yet we should not be blind to the fact that his misfortune must
prevent him from being useful to the fraternity, and that he may
become a liability rather than an asset. ·However, we would not
criticize our brethren of this, or any other Jurisdiction, for their
attitude upon this subject. But we think this question, at present,
is the most serious, and possibly the most dangerous our order
has to encounter."

impaired in the end. As we have said heretofore, Masonry was
never intended to be a popular institution, and it is by no means
necessary that every man should be a Mason, especially as the
absence of such distinction involves no criticism upon his

MONTANA (1921)
The Fifty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Montana was held at Butte on August 17th and 18th, 1920.
There were present M.'.W.'.Robert J. Hathaway, the Grand Officers,
fifteen Past Grand Masters and the representatives from 119 of
the 130 chartered Lodges. It has been the custom to print in the
proceedings a sketch of the life of the retiring Grand Master.
This sketch was omitted at the request of Grand Master Hathaway
and in its place is published a report of a meeting of Montana
Army Lodge No. 1, whii;h was held at St. Aignan, Loir et Cher,
France, at which the worshipful, acting as proxy for Grand Master
Hutchinson, installed Brother Hathaway as Senior Grand Warden
of the Grand Lodge of Montana.
The minutes of the meeting read as follows:
"R. W. Brother Robert E. Hathaway was then introduced and
duly installed as R. W. Senior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge,
A. F. & A. M. of Montana. After the ceremony R. W. Brother
Hathaway made an address to the assembled brothers expressing
his satisfaction and pleasure at being installed into his high office

by a subordinate Lodge of his own Grand Lodge in France and
thanking the officers and members of Montana Army Lodge No. 1
for their efforts in his behalf. Ther'e being no further business to
come before the meeting, Lodge was closed in form on the third
degree at 10:30 P. M., peace and harmony prevailing."
In opening his splendid address the Grand Master expressed
the conviction that "Masonic influence is in direct ratio to the
exercise of that influence," adding this word of suggestion:
"As ancient Masonry was adapted to ancient conditions, so
must we adapt our Masonry to present day problems, and to do
this, Masonry must become an active, vital element in every
community."
He urged that every Lodge should have a committee "whose
duty it shall be to inform themselves of all cases of illness or
distress among Masons and their families occurring in their vicinity
and to see that these ill or distressed members are suitably remembered by the fraternity, by visitations, by flowers and in any
other way that may make more bearable such illness or distress."
From his noble concluding thoughts we select these:
"To us the most important, the overshadowing, paramount.
shining joy of this year is the glorious fact that in spite of all
infidelity, radicalism, rationalism, spekticism, agnosticism and all
the other isms and ologys and osophys that have tried, and that
will try to supplant God's law and Christ's teachings with their
own pigmy ideas, there still predominates that splendid, substantial,
reverential spirit of faith in God, manifesting itself in a thousand
ways of service and worship.
"Why not give government by Christ's principles a fair trial?
"Disregard His divinity if you will; forget that He is the Son
of God; grant only that He was a Man, a Teacher and a Statesman,
then study the principles of associated humanity laid down by
Him for social and governmental relations.
"Pay no attention to what either His own disciples or His
traducers may have said of Him; grant Him only the courtesy
shown your other famous men; consider only the principles He,
Himself taught and you will find His laws, His rules of life and
conduct make all succeeding statesmanship relative."
The volume contains a number of interesting photographs of
the beautiful Masonic Home and its attractive appointments.
The Grand Lodge reiterated its former declaration ~egarding
the York Grand Lodge of Mexico, which Montana as well as New

"We have made a net gain this year of 1,097 members-an
increase over the preceding year of 370 members, or a total for the
past two years of 1,824 net. All over our broad land men have
been knocking at the doors of Masonic Lodges for admission.
:Many have been the rejections, but in spite of this American Freemasonry has. advanced as never before. More and more the young
and old realize the fundamental teachings of this great order and
are hastening to enlist under the banner of our fraternity. Let
us here and now resolve to study and apply the teachings of Freemasonry in our daily walks of life and business. Let us strive
to prove to our less enlightened brethren that our spirit of
brotherly love and affection is not solely confined to Lodge walls,
but is part of our life, and that no matter who the individual may
be or what creed he may profess, we are here to work hand in
hand for the upbuilding of mankind and the glorification of 'True
Americanism,' thus demonstrating that our order is founded upon
the principles of equality and justice."

"Your Flag and Mine"
"On June 14th, 1777, the then Congress of the United States
met in old Independence Hall, Philadelphia, and adopted the
following resolution:
"'Resolved, That the flag of the thirteen United States be
thirteen stripes, alternate red and white; that the Union be
thirteen stars, white on a blue field, representing a new constellation, the stars to be arranged in a circle.'
"Thus was created the glorious standard of our beloved country
which has never been lowered to an enemy.
"On June 14th, 1921, National Flag Day was celebrated by
Masonic Lodges in nearly every corner of the State, and it is our
hope that this birthday of our Flag ·may every year be made a
veritable feast day in the Craft. Masonry inculcates loyalty to
State and Nation, and it is for us as citizens of our beloved country
to keep ever alive the wisdom, the loyalty and the patriotism of our
forefathers."

OHIO (1921)
The One Hundred and Twentieth Annual Communication
of the Grand Lodge of Ohio was held in Cleveland, October 19
and 20, 1920, and there were present 11,r.·.w:.John R. Flotron, Grand
Master, all of the other Grand Officers, all but two of the Past
Grand Masters and representatives from 450 of the 548 chartered
Lodges.
Sixteen Lodges were constituted and eleven were
instituted.
The Grand Master gives this very wise and timely admonition:
"I find a general laxity throughout this Grand Jurisdiction in
the matter of the business concerns of the Lodge. A large portion

383

of our members do not seem to be aware of the fact that the
business of a Lodge is just as secret as its ritualistic work, especially so with reference to the ballot, which is one of its most
sacred institutions. It is not
to all men to be honored by
becoming members, but Masonry does not contemplate placing
upon such men a mark of character in the community in which
they live. · Greater effort should be made to correct this condition.
Masters should familiarize themselves with the Ancient Charges
and the Code, and only such information disseminated as will tend
to build up a high regard for the obligations and law of Masonry."
Under the heading of "Protection of Ancient Craft Masonry"
the Grand Master recommends as follows:
~I recommend that the dignity, solemnity and importance of the
three degrees of Ancient Craft Masonry be protected by making
it a Masonic offense in this Jurisdiction to solicit or to recommend
a Master Mason to receive any degree in any organization or body
recognized by this Grand Lodge as Masonic for a period of not
less than three months after he has passed a satisfactory examination
in the Master Mason Degree; and, further, to solicit or recommend
a Master Mason for membership in any organization for which
that standing. is a qualification until the person so solicited or
recommended has been a Master Mason for a period not less
than one year after he has passed a satisfactory examination in the
Master Mason Degree."
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom the above recommendation was referred, reported as follows:
"The Grand Master recommends that it be made a Masonic
offense to solicit or recommend any one within three months after
passing examination in the Master's Degree for membership in
any Masonic Body, or within one year for membership in any
organization requiring as a prerequisite membership in Masonry.
There is much merit in the suggestion and much gravity in the
subject. So much, indeed, that the committee is unable at this
time to form an opinion from the knowledge we have on the
problem or within the time we have for deliberation. We, therefore, recommend that the whole matter be referred to a special
committee of five, chosen by the incoming Grand Master, who may
ascertain and report to the next Annual Session how such a step
may affect our welfare and relations with the other Masonic
bodies and suitable legislation to carry on any measure they may
recommend."
The Committee on Masonic History, of which Brother Robert
I. Clegg is chairman, presents a report containing a valuable refer-

ence to the Masonic initiation of Louis- Kossuth, the heroic fighter

OKLAHOMA (1922)
The Forty-ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Indian Territory, the Thirtieth Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of Oklahoma Territory and the Fourteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the State of Oklahoma were
held February 28 and March 1, 1922, at Guthrie. There were present
M. W. James Henry Patterson, Grand Master, sixteen Grand
Officers, twenty-two Past Grand Masters· and representatives from
367 of the 450 chartered Lodges.
Grand Master Patterson's home Lodge presented him with an
apron. We quote the following from Brother William Mack
Saxon's presentation speech:
"You received the lamb skin, or white leather apron, when you
were made an Entered Apprentice in the Blue Lodge, and you
have worn that apron all these years. I have known you for a
number of them, and during all that time you have never brought
discredit upon that apron. It is still white and pure. You have
labored hard among your brethren. You have given them the best
years of your life, because Masonry is in your heart, and you love
it from the very depths of your heart. We appreciate that fact,
and the brethren over at Prague wanted you to have this apron
here to wear when presiding over this Grand Lodge. They want,
by this silent testimony, to say to you that they love you and
your work, and that they appreciate the honor that your name has
brought to their town and their lodge. It is a synonym of strength
in Masonry in Oklahoma and your brethren appreciate it."
Brother Patterson responded (in part):
"Brother Sexson, Brethren, and Members of Prague Lodge:

385

You know that no man has the language adequate to express his
feelings on an occasion of this kind. Coming as does this from my
little Lodge, knowing that they have made a real sacrifice, makes
an impression upon me far more indelible than would be the case
if it came from a large Lodge that was wealthy so far as money
is concerned. Realizing that I have rubbed shoulders with those
boys over there for years and years, ever since I landed in Oklahoma twenty-seven years ago, I feel that this is done because I
have not failed in what I have been trying to do."

In his annual address the Grand Master says:
"Danger is surrounding us on every side, the most serious within
our own borders. Discontent is permeating our industrial system,
and the calm, unfavored judgment of our best minds is needed to
save us from anarchy itself. Here our duty as Masons lies; to lead,
to direct, to encourage men in the paths of right living, right thinking and sanity in action; to encourage them into following the
precepts of the Golden Rule as exemplified by the teachings of our
order. If we believe in our Masonic obligations, if we have faith
in our teachings, then we have a great duty and a great responsibility placed upon us.
"We need Masonry in our schools. The boy or the girl, or the
man or the woman, who reflects education, without the Church or
Synagogue, is a mental and intellectual slave. Our education should
be based on the enlightenment of the present, and not on the legends
and fables of the dark ages. A state or nation, as far as its intellect
is concerned, is no greater than the sum total of its individual citizens; and therefore it is our duty, because of the welfare of our
country-our country which stands boldly out today as the greatest
and most successful democracy which the world has ever seento see to it that our American children are educated in the only
school which should be recognized by a democracy, and that is the
public school (applause), under the supervision of proven American
teachers, who will make their appeal to the intellect and not to the
fear or to the sup~rstition."
In concluding the address the Grand Master says:
"Here in Grand Lodge are assembled the real leaders of the
Craft. in Oklahoma, and I beg of you to take inventory of yourselves and to try and see yourselves as your brothers see you, as
your neighbors estimate you in your community, and, finally and

OREGON (1921)
The Seventy-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Oregon was held in Portland June 15, 16, 17, 1921. There were
present M. W. \Villiam Jasper Kerr, Grand Master, sixteen Grand
Officers, eighteen Past Grand Masters and 130 of the 147 chartered
Lodges.
We quote from the Grand Master's address:
"The report of the Grand Secretary shows a membership on
January 1 of more than 21,000, an increase over that of the corresponding date of the preceding year of 2,944, or 16 per cent. There
has been a large increase, also, during the past six months, so that
the present membership probably approximates 23,000. Such
increase in membership is encouraging, as an indication of increasing interest in Masonry. It involves, however, a large responsibility. Under such conditions practically all of the energies of the
Lodges are consumed in degree work, leaving little opportunity
for a study of the fundamentals of Masonry. There is danger that
the work may become unduly formal, with little opportunity on
the part of members to obtain a comprehensive understanding of
Masonic principles and philosophy. ·with increasing numbers,
therefore, there is corresponding demand that time shall be found
in which Masonic duties may be made clear and emphasized.
"There is ample evidence that those now coming to the doors
of Masonry are actuated by varying motives. Most, no doubt, are
sincere and in every way worthy, but there are those who hope thus
to gain political advantage or social advancement, while others are
expecting that Freemasonry will aid them in their business ventures. For instance, a professional man who had recently been
admitted to membership in one of our Lodges expressed disappointment that he had not received the same relative increase in
his business from members of the Masonic Lodge as he had therefore received from other orders of which he was a member."
The Grand Master also made a strong plea for better Masonic
education. He urged visitations by the Grand Master or his official
representatives, and that special lecturers should be employed, and,
like a number of other Grand Masters, he favored the system of
the Masonic Service Association of the United States.
He paid fraternal tribute to the memories of deceased brethren,
including Past Grand Master Edward Elmer Kiddle.
From the report of the Committee on Necrology we learn that:
"Brother Kiddle was born July 15, 1862, in Warren, Illinois, and
was married July 27, 1884, to Miss Emma Walling at Hamilton,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Kansas. Soon afterward he removed to Union, Oregon, where he
soon became an active member of the Masonic Fraternity of

1920, aged 58 years, 6 months and 13 days."
Of him the Grand Master said:
"In all the relations of life Brother Kiddle has shown the
s~erling character of an honorable business man, a loyal citizen of
his country and a true Mason. An active member of the Masonic
Fraternity, always in attendance at the meetings of the Grand

PENNSYLVANIA (1921)
The printed report of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of
Pennsylvania contains the reports of the four quarterly meetings
as well as the report of the annual meeting. In as much as the
proceedings of the annual meeting covers the most vital points,
only the annual meeting will be reviewed.
The annual communication of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania
was held in Philadelphia, December 27, 1921. There were present
Grand Master John S. Sell, all the Grand Officers and representatives from 481 of the 533 chartered Lodges.
\Ve quote from the Grand Master's address as follows:
"Freemasonry in Pennsylvania is a fraternity. It is not a
religious body, it is not a political or social organization, and it
does not intermedd!e with or take part in political, business, social
or religious affairs. Lodges meet for Masonic purposes only-

390

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

namely, for transacting the business incident to the orderly cond~ct
of their affairs and for conferring degrees by and through winch
we endeavor to reach the hearts and minds of the members and
teach them the competency of the Divine wisdom, their relation
to Him and their fraternal duty toward each other and to all
mankind.
"Lodge meetings are not to be meetings for the discussion of
subjects of any kind, whether social, political, religious or topical
upon which there might be a difference of opinion; neither are they
to be places of entertainment, nor places from which there shall
emanate propaganda of any kind with a view to moulding Qr
influencing legislation or public opinion. Freemasons in Pennsylvania therefore should guard careful!y against innovations and
vigorously resist everything which tends to weaken or ahrogate
our Ancient Usages, Customs and Landmarks. They should always
keep in mind the fact that there is no new thing in Freemasonry.
"Any organization in Pennsylvania not recognized hy the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania and which uses a Masonic Lodge as a door
through which a man must first pass in order to become a member
thereof is not Masonic, and membership therein or affiliation
therewith by Freemasons should be prohibited. Some of our
brothers may say that Masonry has no right to interfere with the
right of its members to join any other organization, whether
fraternal or otherwise, and that their right to do so as citizens is
guaranteed by the Constitution. These seem to forget that they
have no inborn or inherent right to become Masons, and the
Federal Constitution does not guarantee this privilege. The privilege of becoming a Mason emanates from the Grand Lodge
operating through its subordinate Lodges. Therefore it naturally
follows that since they are Masons, under and by virtue of the
Grand Lodge, they must be obedient to its mandates."
With regard to investigation he says:
"I have therefore decided and required that absolute obedience
to this edict and to the requirements on this subject as laid
down· by Past Grand Master Watres must be observed, and, in
addition, it is now further required that in the case of every
petition~r the committee, or one of them, shall certify to t~e
·worshipful Master in his own handwriting, written on the margm
of the petition, that he, or they, personally visited the home of the
petitioner, and that the home conditions of the petitioner are such
as consistently\ belong in the home of a Master Mason.
"I have so decided for the reason that in many instances committees seem to have signed printed certifications _in a perfunctory

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

391

manner with but little, if any, thought of their -import, and because it was a prepared place to sign, which in signing cost them
nothing, while the facts certified to were of such wide variance as
should have at least caused some hesitancy before placing a petition
befor.e a Lodge for final action."
We do not agree with the Grand Master in his decision on
physical disqualification. In most cases the Grand Master would
not be influenced by local color. He says:
"During my administration f.3,s Grand Master I have been
requested to pass upon cases of physical ·qualification and have
invariably held that as Grand Master I had nothing to do, authoritatively, with a man until he became a Mason. I have always felt
that the Worshipful Master, officers and members of subordinate
Lodges are good Masons; that they know or should know the
essential physical and other qualifications of petitioners; that they
have and keep in mind the best interests of the fraternity in
general and their own Lodge and community in particular, and
that, therefore, they should be, as they doubtless are, quite as
well informed and quite as solicitous as the Grand Master in seeing
to it that no petitioner who lacks the necessary qualifications is
approved."
George Washington Memorial Association
"The collection of funds for the George Washington Masonic
l\ational Memorial Association, under the direction of· R. W.
Senior Grand Warden, Brother Samuel M. Goodyear, Chairman for
Pennsylvania, is progressing most satisfactorily. The members·

in Pennsylvania will in this, as in all other meritorious Masonic
demands, not be found wanting.''
The report of the Committee on Masonic Education is so fitting
and so well stated that the report is copied in full, as follows:
"Among the timely and important subjects· under discussion in
the Grand Lodges during the period covered by the foregoing pages
was Masonic education. To some extent it appears to have been
suggested by the mighty flood of petitions and the phenomenal
growth of the Craft since the war. It has been feared that this
tended to convert the Lodges into 'degree mills'; that the making
of actual Masons was neglected; that proper digestion of the vast

392

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

material was impossible, and that the initiates thereby lost the
opportunity to acq.uire Masonic light and knowledge.
"The awakening of our leaders to the demand that the members of the Craft shall understand what Freemasonry really is and
what are its aims is truly commendable, but we do not share their
apprehension that yielding to the sudden and widespread desire
to join the fraternity precludes the possibility or opportunity of
producing the educated Mason. Growth in membership is to be
desired. provided that unremitting vigilance is exercised in the
admission of candidates. There is strength in numbers.
"Few initiates get a grasp of the meaning of Freemasonry,
its symbolism, its principles and its functions in the ceremonies of
their initiation. From a retrospective view of our experience we
all know that the mind is not in an absorptive state at the moment.
When a brother becomes a Master Mason he is only at the
threshold of a vast exploration. It is then that the fraternity's
duty, as a guide to him, has just begun, a~d if the Lodge officers
are alive to that duty, methods will be pursued to perform it. It
is true that during the recent tide of new members there has generally been little time to bestow upon Masonic culture, but as the
tide recedes the process is next in order.
"It is not a newly discovered fact that Masonic education has
been sadly neglected. It is not only the brethren who have recently
come among us who require attention, but vast numbers of those
who joined the fraternity in the many years of the past. We
venture to say that the average Mason is not what may be termed
a 'well-rounded Mason' in a knowledge of the science of Freemasonry. We apply this statement to officers of Lodges and, to
a degree, to officers of Grand Lodges. They are not skilled themselves nor have they an adequate knowledge of what is to be
taught.
"What appears to be needed: First, schools of instruction to
train teachers and volunteers to attend them. This has been
accomplished in many Grand Lodge Jurisdictions so far as it
relates to correct and uniform ritual work, but it is obvious that
this is limited in its scope. Second, there should be a comprehensive
program of approved Masonic subjects and methods of instruction.
This requires 1ntellectual ability and leadership; it should be
organized by the best scholastic talent in the Grand Lodges and
passed on through the schools of instruction to the Lodges.
"The above crude outline is only suggestive of possible plans
to bring to the Craft a new and deeper meaning of the Masonic
institution. Whatever plan or method is devised, of this we are

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

393

confident: it will find the Craft responsive and recepti;·e and
eager to acquire Masonic light and knowledge. Is it worth the
effort; is it too complicated; is it too big a contract?"

PHILIPPINE ISLANDS (1922)
The Tenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Philippine Islands was held in Manila January 24th, 1922. There
were present M.'.W:.Edwin E. Elser, fifteen Grand Officers and
representatives from chartered Lodges.
We like the custom followed by this Grand Lodge and some
others of having the Grand Lodge opened by the Deputy Grand
Master and the Grand Master received with stately ceremony.
The Grand Master says:
"By the . infinite goodness of the Supreme Architect of the
Universe we are. permitted to again assemble in this our Tenth
Annual Communication, and to meet in this beautiful temple dedicated to progress, tolerance, charity and unselfish purposes, and a
perpetual monument to those brothers who by their altruistic efforts
and love of our fraternity made it possible for Masons of this
Jurisdiction to point with pride to another structure consecrated
to the betterment of mankind. May our deliberations at this time
be in harmony with the ideals to which this new home will be
dedicated, may brotherly love prevail, and may we accomplish
some good that will be of everlasting benefit to the Craft.
"One year ago in accepting this honor in your power to bestow,
I did so with a great deal of misgiving, ·realizing my many shortcomings, and appreciating the enormous responsibility attached to
the distinguished honor. It appeared appalling to me with so
little experience in this particular line of effort, but with my tru.>t
in Him, who directs us all, I accepted the gavel from my illustrious
predecessor, entered upon my duties, and with the assistance and
advice of many loyal brethren feel that I am surrendering the gavel
with the knowledge that though I may have accomplished very
little: yet I am sure that the fraternity has not suffered, and that
considerable progress has been made.

"One Lodge in this Jurisdiction passed a resolution endorsing

have grave doubts as to propriety of Lodges as a body passing
resolutions that will try to dictate or approve any laws being
passed by our Government. Some of our sister Jurisdictions have
already passed a similar resolution. It appears to me that we as
individual Masons should do all that is in our power to promote
and support proper laws for the maintenance of this Government,
but when we as a body try to do it we will be accused of entering
politics, and the world, without regard to creed or religion. will
turn against us. We must not be stampeded into politics, as a
body, on account of the activities of our enemies, for they will in
time fail, as we would do, did we but follow their tactics."

covered. I recommend that the incoming Grand Master be authorized to appoint a committee to prepare and furnish the necessary
data to John Trotwood Moore, director."

Under the heading of "Physical Defects" the Grand Master
quotes the law of the Jurisdiction as follows:
"In 1912 this Grand Lodge adopted the following resolution:
"\Vhereas, The perfect man is an ideal being, and absolute
perfection does not exist among men, either physically, mentally
nor morally; therefore be it
'
"Resolved, (I) That it is not obnoxious to the Ancient Landmarks and Charges of Masonry that slight maims or defects of
the body should debar an applicant for initiation or advancement
in Masonry; and (2) That an applicant for initiation must be sound
and hale, without maim or defect in his body that may render him
ineligible to be a Mason; that is, physical maims and defects
should be considered on the basis of his ability to receive, practice
and impart freely and without artificial or other aid all the rites
and .ceremonies of Ancient Craft Masonry, including Masonic
work in the lodge room, and shall possess the mental and physical
ability to earn his livelihood in his chosen occupation outside the
Lodge room; and
" 'Resolved, That when an applicant for initiation has a maim
or defect the Lodge to which the application is made shall refer
the case, with a faithful description of such maim or defect, to the
Grand Master, who shall thereupon rule upon the eligibility ()f
the applicant in the light of these resolutions."'

From the annual address of the Grand Master we quote:
"Masonry appears to have entered upon an era of unusual activity. The great increase in ).fasonic membership all over the
world is attracting much attention. The trend of the massthought is to Masonry. Why? Numerous rea.sons have been
assigned. The prime reason I deem to be the appeal to the
intellect and conscience of mankind, made by Masonry standing
unscathed and unchanged amid the wreck of nations, amid the
ruin, destruction and devastation made by the world war and
amid the bitter hatred engendered by and the deadly strife of
that war, giving to Masons neutral grounds where hatred ceased
and deadly strife is surerseded. by brotherly love,
"It has been gratifying to learn of the efforts being made in
some parts of the State to instill into the members a deeper
knowledge of the greatness of Masonry; efforts which are tending
to make Masons out of members. These efforts should be
encouraged.
"The forms and ceremonies of initiation and the lectures
furnish the alphabet only of Masonry. They do not, of themselves,
make any man a Mason, but only a member. Too often this
member docs not use this alphabet; he will not learn to spell and
then to read, and having read, to understand, and rushes 9n into
the so-called "higher degrees" with little knowledge or appreciation of those through which he has passed. It is this spirit that
seeks to change the alphabet, because of lack of understanding.
It would, through ignorance, tear down the very foundation
stones on which the whole superstructure of Masonry is erected.
"Nothing would do so much for the good of the Craft as to
awaken in the hearts and minds of our members a deep, unquenchable thirst for Masonic knowledge and an increasing demand
for such additional light as will reveal that great, underliyng.
living something which makes our Ancient Institution the most
vigorous arid helpful of all organizations for making its members
God-fearing, law-abiding, useful citizens of the great Republic,
founded by Masons 011 Masonic principles.'''

WEST VIRGINIA (1921)
The Fiftv-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of West Vi;ginia was convened in Masonic Temple, Parkersburg,
November 16, 1921. There were present M:.w:.Adrian C. Nadenbousch, Grand Master, twelve Grand Officers, fifteen Past Grand

At 12 o'clock, noon, November 16th, prior to the regular session

cornerstone of the Masonic Home.
From the inspiring annual address of the Grand Master we
quote:
"As we are about to enter upon the review of the work ~f the
year and to plan our activities for yet another, we are remmded
that today even as upon the opening of the First Annual Communicatio~ of this body in the year 1865, we are standing in the
slowly receding shadow of human tragedy. Then the veil of civil
strife had just been lifted from the face of national mourning
and the spirit of fratricidal hatred buried in a common impulse
to construct upon the ashes of human folly a governmental fabric
that would indissolubly unite a people destined, at no distant
day, to become the emancipators of the world. Now, not a nation

407

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

divided against itself; but so-called civilization is but emerging
from the pall of death and despair by which it was enveloped in
that awful cataclysm of cruel murder that deluged the sweet earth
with blood; now, this same civilization, through its most able and
accomplished representatives, is gathered about a conference table
in the City of Washington seeking earnestly to build upon the
ruins of international hatred and distrust a temple of international
comity and good-will, of international common sense and evenhanded justice, and thereby to translate into harmonious action
the universal decree that 'these dead shall not have died in vain.'
True to her destiny America unfaltering accepts the challenge to
leadership in service to humanity, and, standing with chastened
heart, but firm resolve, beside the open grave of her 'unknown
dead;' pledges herself irrevocably to the execution of her mission
in the ringing sentiment of her Chief Executive that ' there inust
be, there shall be, the commanding voice of a conscious civilization against armed warfare.' My brethren, let us as Masons remember that we also are citizens of a common country aroused as
never before to the senseless, silly, futile resort to arms for the
settlement _of our disputes, and accord to those charged with
the duty of annihilating useless precedent and setting up in its
stead a sane, honorable, equitable standard of conduct that meed
of sympathy and support so sorely needed at this fateful hour.
With the life-blood of the world slowly ebbing out at the behest
of unbridled passion and unholy lust, may we not vision in this
generous response to humanity's cry a new day whose glorious
dawn shall bring to us fulfillment of the prophecy that the sword
lately drenched in blood shall be beaten into a plow-share, that
the spear lately piercing a nation's heart shall be beaten into a prun- .
ing hook, that nations themselves shall· not lift up sword against
nation, neither shall they learn war any more and realize in truth, in
all the fullness of heavenly promise, that the Temple of the Lord's
House shall be established in the top of the mountains, and that
the reign of the Blessed Emmanuel, the Prince of Peace, shall be
universal and everlasting."

"Contemporaneous with the history of Wisconsin as a State
has been the building of the great temple of Masonry in this

of our Craft as it stands today-one of the most notable and
permanent contributions ministering to the stability and greatness
of the State.

vision, heroic endeavor and the spirit of sacrifice. v\T e feel today
the urge of past generations. Like coral islands built out of the
innumerable deposits of sea animals, the edifice of Masonry has
been built out of the endeavors and sacrifices of past generations
of Masons-men whose ideal was a house not made with hands,
but a fabric that is eternal.
"As Masons we stand for the open Bible, for the public school,
for the chance for every child to discover his soul and cultivate
his mind. We stand for America, for its institutions and for that
emblem of liberty, the American flag.

most practical things of life. In the evolution of things, operative
Masonry became speculative Masonry, and speculative Masonry
is something to be transmuted into real life. Great thoughts
produce great souls. The symbolism of Masonry is the golden
key that unlocks the treasuries of eternal wisdom. It teaches us
the immutability of law, the impregnability of truth and the
irresistibility of goodness. The men it has produced are its· best
recommendation. The contemplation and practice of the teachings of Masonry will make a man a gentleman, a dispenser of
happiness ·and an optimist."

The Seventy-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of Wisconsin was opened in ample form in the Scottish
Rite Cathedral, Milwaukee, June 14, 1921.
There were present M.".W.".C. E. Shaffer, Grand Master, fourteen Grand Officers, fourteen Past Grand Masters, representatives

+

The Grand Master visited sixty-one Lodges and found the
Craft everywhere in splendid condition. He commends the interests of the Masonic Service Bureau which, by action of the Grand
Lodge in 1920, was formed by consolidation of the Masonic Employment Bureau of Milwaukee County with the Masonic Relief
Association, and the hope is expressed that "it may attain a wider
and even more beneficent influence" throughout the Juris<liction,

408

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Attention is called also to the splendid work done under the
auspices of the Committee on Masonic Research. This committee has proved itself a most useful one. Its valuable pamphlets,
suggestions for lecture programs, study classes, Lodge libraries,
etc., have been circulated widely and are easily among the best
things which have been put in circulation for the encouragement
of Masonic education. New York has been favored by having
had the Wisconsin literature supplied to a number of organizers
of study circles.
The report of the Grand Lecturer, Past Grand Master David
B. Greene, suggests the formation of new Lodges in co11gested
parts of the field to take care of the large influx of candidates
whi~h is clogging the machinery of the existing bodies, adding that
the present crowding "robs work of its zest and pleasure" and
reduces the officers of Lodges to drudges, while "the finer elements
of friendship and fellowship" suffer in consequence.
One hundred and twenty-five Lodges in the State own their own
buildings, some of these jointly with other bodies of Masons.
The Masonic Service Bureau has a Field Secretary, who devotes
his entire time to looking after brethren in need of assistance and
trying to locate jobs for the unemployed. Seven hundred and
seven applicants for employment were registered during the year
(June 1, 1920, to May 31, 1921), and 309 were placed in positions.
The Grand Lodge adopted a recommendation made J::,y the Committee on Expenditures appropriating to the Masonic Service
Bureau a sum equal to three cents for each Mason of the membership of the Lodges. The report of the committee gives this
interesting bit of information:
"Not only have many deserving Masons been placed in employment, but substantial relief has been rendered to Masons in
distress and to their widows or dependents. The name Service
Bureau was adopted at reorganization in accordance with the
recommendation of this Grand Lodge last year. An attempt to
get the Relief Association to amalgamate with the Service Bureau
did not succeed, but the former organization was dissolved in
April and its funds, amounting to over seven hundred dollars,
turned back to the Masonic bodies, constituting its membership.
Some of these funds have been paid to the Service Bureau. The
records of the Relief Bureau were expected to be turned in to
the Grand Secretary, but so far he has not received them. They
would be of much value to the Service Bureau if they were
available,"

Under the caption, "Our Duty and Opportunity," the Grand
Master well says:
"Though some time removed from the immediate thought. of
the great World War, the usual results of enormous taxat10n,
extravagance, lowering wages, high rents and costs o! merchandise, and high rates of transportation and consequent ht~h cost of
living, and general disrespect for law exist among certam classes.
Worst of all, the young men and women who have gone from the
country to the city have thereby deserted the country town_ or
the farm and do not wish to return to either. Taxes have risen
to huge proportions, and money which would i,n normal times
have been invested in industry has found itself into non-use or
into non-tax-bearing securities.
"But these things always adjust themselves. The law of
compensation always works. We must always pay. If we have
driven from the world the Prussian idea that the Boches were
born to rule the rest of mankind, and the peoples who inhabit the
earth are thereby further advanced in civilization, those who gave
the supreme sacrifice will not have passed through 'life's greatest
venture' in vain. The keystone thought in this life is the greatest
good to the greatest number. Amassing of wealth is but secondary, and its possession is but in trust. From the ashes of th.e
burned temples, from the memory of the men who gave up their
material lives, there has arisen a unified spirit to push forw~rd
to greater achievements, to higher ideals, to a closer understan~mg
and kinship with Divinity, and the burdens of war are as no_thmg,
but are as the small consideration paid for a higher place tn the
onward march of civilization.
"All thoughtful people agree that civilization endures only by
providing food, clothing, warmth . and transpo.rtation for. th~
masses. These are economic questions. Education, accordmgly,
must direct itself to enlightenment along these lines. As these
necessities of life are supplied the mind is then in a condition to
study the meaning of truth, to climb upward in such quest. to
'heights by great men reached and kept' to the pinnacle to wh1ch
the finite mind cannot reach, to the knowledge of truth, to the
Infinite!'

doing., anxious to prove its metal, chafing against the curb of
rules and regulations, and sometimes even against our Ancient

because of the vision, the energy and ambition of youth."
He says the progress of Mason;y in Alberta continues to indicate prosperity .in every district, some of his Lodges conferring
from ISO to 190 degrees in twelve months. He asks the pertinent
qnestion, "Can a Lodge thoroughly assimilate so much material?"
Some Lodges can; our home Lodge conferred about a hundred
degrees in seven months; the degrees were not abbreviated in the
slightest particular, the lectures were always given in full, and
every candidate had to pass a most rigorous examination ere he
was advanced.

BRITISH COLUMBIA (1921)
The Fiftieth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
British Columbia was opened in ample form in the city of Victoria,
June 23, 1921. There were present M.".W.".Martin L. Grimmett,

412

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

sixteen Grand Officers, fourteen Past Grand Masters and representatives from eighty-six of the ninety-three chartered Lodges.
On June 22 the Grand Lodge was convened in extraordinary
session to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the founding of the
Grand Lodge of the Grand Jurisdiction of British Columbia. In
the evening, following the celebration, a magnificent banquet was
served in honor of the distinguished visitors present. The toasts
which followed the banquet were exceptionally good and extremely
interesting.
The following words of the Chairman of the evening express
the unanimous verdict of all present:
"Brethren, I think you will all agree with me that we have had
one of the most successful banquets ever held in British Columbia.
and that to add anything further to the remarks we have listened
to this evening would be to 'paint the lily or perfume the rose.'
We will now bring the proceedings to a close by singing the
National anthem."
From the Grand Master's address we quote the following item
of interest:
"Cariboo Lodge No. 4 first worked under a warrant from the
Grand Lodge of Scotland, issued in 1867. In this year a Masonic
temple was built which, however, was destroyed in 1868. A new
building was erected in the latter year, which still stands and is,
I believe, the oldest Masonic hall or temple in this Jurisdiction. A
very unique feature in connection with this hall is what a visitor
is informed is the Silent Tiler. As you ascend the stair to the
Lodge room on the second floor your guide will point out that
about half-way up the stairway is hinged; he will further tell you
that by means of a mechanical contrivance this part of the stairway
was raised and remained suspended in midair while the brethren
were at labor. For many years the Silent Tiler has been silent
indeed, as this means of tiling the Lodge has not been used for a
long time. The brethren are naturally proud of this unique feature
in connection with their Lodge building, as it is doubtful if any
other Masonic building in this or any other Jurisdiction can boast
of a Silent Tiler.''
An excellent historical sketch of the Grand Lodge was presented
by Bro. L. Watts Dorrey.
The Grand Master ruled that a petition from a returned soldier
who had lost his left foot could not be presented, and the Grand
Lodge sustained the decision. They cannot claim to be living up
to old law that "A man must be without maim or blemish," as they

did admit an applicant who had lost several of his toes. We know

A pleasing incident was the pres~nting by special committee of
a gold medal to the widow of the first Grand Master of British
Columbia, Israel W. Powell. We would be remiss in our duty
if we did not quote these beautiful words of Mrs. Powell in response
to those of the committee:
"As these pages of half a century ago are being unfolded I am
prompted to make an observation, if I may, on that attribute of
your noble society which has most strongly impressed me, and
that is the powerful, yet unseen, influence which, devoid of ostentation or display, wields such sway over the manifold vicissitudes
of its members in particular, and, indeed, shapes the destiny of
humanity in general. How like the manifestations of that Supreme
Power which accomplishes nature's transformations and wonders
in mystery and silence!
"Have you ever watched the rising sun creeping lazily over the
horizon? How the pink flush of dawn, scattering the night's gloom,
floods the eastern heavens with opalescent hues in seeming homage
to its Lord? Then the rim faintly appears, shadowy and ghostlike, climbing upward and ever onward until in its full effulgence,
tipping every leaf and flower with the marvel of color and magic
of fragrance, it stands revealed in all its golden splendor and
majesty, and yet this miracle is daily performed, not with outburst
or noisy demonstration, but in the hush of awe-inspiring stillness.''
Past Grand Master Begg of Washington was introduced as a
substitute for Grand Master Skaggs. After some real Scotch humor
anent how he was dragooned into the position in which he found
himself, he said:
"Brethren, it is both interesting and pathetic to me, with its
suggestions of double allegiance. Under this flag, the Union Jack,
I first saw the light of day. Under this other flag, the Stars and
Stripes, I first beheld that hieroglyphic bright which none but
Craftsmen ever saw. As I stand under these two flags and hear
of Freemasonry is it any wonder that I can scarcely find words to
express my feelings? It affords me great pleasure to give you the
greetings of the Grand Lodge of ·w ashington. The heart of that
Jurisdiction beats true with yours tonight, standing firmly on the
foundation on which this great institution is built. I feel that as
long as these two flags stand side by side the people of their
countries hold the peace of the world in the hollow of their
hands."

ONTARIO IN CANADA (1921)
The Sixty-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Canada, in the Province of Ontario, was held at Ottawa, July 20,
1921. There were present M:.\V.'.Fred W. Harcourt, Grand Master,
fifteen Grand Officers and representatives from 400 of the 481
chartered Lodges.
In opening his address the Grand Master referred to the historic
significance of Ottawa and the birth of the Dominion of Canada.
He spoke of the clanger of over-large Lodges, quoting "The imbecile
tyranny of numbers." He suggested the appointment of a committee to consider the advisability of forbidding the canvassing
of Masons to join the "Grotto." The use by women of the
designation "Masonic" for any organization of theirs is censured,
with this warning:
"I do not understand why Masons as Masons allow their names
to be used by organizations not Masonic, even to please their wives
or those they hope to call by that name. To my mind it is opposed
to the best traditions of the Craft and sails dangerously near violation of Masonic obligations."

The address is replete with striking thoughts set between
matter-of-fact reports. Here is a sample:
"May we not regard Masonry as a great spiritual fighting
machine? We must dare to drop that which is out of date and
effete in our methods, so as to be able to mobilize and unify the

415

The Grand Master visited many Lodges. lie will not tell how
many, else people might wonder how he earned a livelihood. He
adds this characteristic comment:
"l t is the right of a Lodge to have a visit from a Grand Master
some time during its existence. Many have told me that they
never saw one. Outlying Lodges, no matter how small or unimportant they may be, have rights equal to large Lodges. A list
of these visits should be in the hands of the Grand Secretary, and
the incoming Grand Master should make a point of favoring those
Lodges which have not been visited by his predecessors. To
Lodges in large cente~ it may seem a small thing to mention, but
a visit from a Grand Master is a veritable red letter day to a small
Lodge."
The printer says it would be a "latter" day, and the proofreader
let it go at that. Some of the small outlying Lodges might really
think the "latter" day had come, so great would be the surprise
if they had the honor of receiving a Grand Master.
The address is that of a plain-spoken, scholarly, vigorous man
with a keen sense of humor and a lovable personality. Brother
Harcourt is all this, and whatever he says could be none other
than himself.
The Semi-Centennial fund has grown to $104,217.28. The income
is used for benevolent purposes.
The Report on Condition of Masonry is an exceptionally fine
piece of work. It is so full of splendid suggestions that we are
tempted to make extensive extracts. Attention is called to the
most commendable record made during the year in the dispensing
of moneys for benevolent purposes. Sixty-six thousand, five hundred dollars was disbursed a.nd tberc is still a balance on. hand of
$31,000. The report closes with these words:
"Canada, as well as the rest of the world, is passing through a
stage of what is loosely called reconstruction, but which is really
one of transition and readjustment. We are beginning to realize
that peace is not in a proclamation or on a parchment, but in the
hearts and souls of men. There can be no peace on earth except
among men of good-will. We must have a set and resolute purpose
to seek the good of others-other men, other classes, other nations.
We must cultivate a spirit of mutual service and fellowship, of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

unity and good-will. There has been too much of the emphasizing
of class differences, too much criticism of each other and too little
desire to understand each other. Man has been trying to raise a
superstructure on the sands of discontent, distrust and discord. The
world today needs a change of heart and the spirit of optimism.
Let common sense take the place of hysteria and co-operation and
concession the place of sullen refusal in the settlement of disputes.
Let us practice and preach and teach the principles which our
beloved order promulgates: brotherly love, respect for the rights
and feelings of others, and let us carry a message of cheer and
encouragement to all men in all ranks of life. Then, and then only,
will we be doing our duty as Masons, and Masonry can stand in
the future as in the past, four-square to every wind that blows."

MANITOBA (1922)
The Forty-seventh Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Manitoba was held in Winnipeg, June 14, 1922. There were
present M:.w:. George N. Jackson, Grand Master, fifteen Grand
Officers, ten Past Grand Masters and representatives from all the
chartered Lodges.
In his annual address the Grand Master says:
"To many of us the Annual Communication has an appeal
because it is here that friendships are renewed, strengthened and
perpetuated. It is here also that new friendships are made, resulting, in time, in ties of love and esteem that shall last as long as
life itself. I trust that those of you who are here for the first
time will be inspired by this sentiment, that you will feel at home,
and that you will participate freely in our deliberations, bearing in
mind that sooner or later those of us who have been long in the
service must pass on, leaving the destinies of the Grand Lodge
upon your shoulders. Therefore, prepare yourselves to command
by learning to obey. As members of this Grand Lodge we come
here as the representatives of ninety-one Lodges of Masons, whose
membership now exceeds ten thousand. Your presence here is
fraught with special significance. You come not out of curiosity,
nor for entertainment, not merely for the purpose of listening to
reports and exchanging ideas, but to gain new impetus and ardor
for the work of the coming year. I trust that we may all return
to our Lodges imbued with a spirit of loyalty and devotion to our
institution that will impel us to emphasize and promote that great
fundamental principle of the Brotherhood of Man based on the
Fatherhood of God.

SASKATCHEWAN (1921)

Twelve Lodges were constituted and four Lodges instituted.

The Fifteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Saskatchewan was held in the city of Saskatoon, June 15, 1921.
There were present Deputy Grand Master George M. Wier,
thirteen other Grand Officers, ten Past Grand Masters and representatives from 100 of the 155 chartered Lodges.

The Grand Master, on account of poor health was unable to
attend the district meetings, but sent to each ~eeting through .
the Grand Secretary this special message:

The following beautiful words taken from the Deputy Grand
Master's address fittingly explains why the Deputy Grand Master
opened Grand Lodge:
"Now is the stately column broke,
The beacon light is quenched in smoke;
The trumpet's silver sound is still,
The warder silent on the hill."
"These words . spoken on the decease of a distinguished British
statesman, are fitting expression of the deep grief that fills the
heart of every brother Mason throughout the Grand Jurisdiction of
Saskatchewan. Under the pall of a deep bereavement for the loss
of our Grand Master, and with hearts sorely stricken, yearning
for the sound of a voice forever silent that should have welcomed
this Fifteenth Annual Communication to the U niver&ity Ci,ty of the
Province, we, nevertheless, bow to the inscrutable ways of the
Most High Master is still present in our midst, shedding its benign
influence over our proceedings and directing our deliberations along
higher levels of rectitude and wisdom.
"On May 19, 1921, M:.w:. Bro. Hon. Mr. Justice E. L. Elwood,
Supreme Head of the Craft in this Grand Jurisdiction, relinquished
the gavel to his successor at the summons of the Great Architect
to join the Grand Lodge above. Stricken down at the meridian of
his existence, at a time of life when he seemed scarcely more than
to have entered upon a career of splendid promise and attainment,
his loss is particularly hard to bear. His keen legal mind, sane
judgment and broad, human sympathy were .of inestimable value
to the Craft which he loved and served so zealously. During these
days of storm and stress, when the forces of reconstruction are
being assailed on all sides by the discordant elements of a greedy
and rampant individualism, when the ancient landmarks that form
the only enduring foundation of the social order seem at times none
too secure, his steadfast example, wise counsel, penetrating vision
and unwavering faith in the ultimate triumph of the powers of
righteousness were as an anchor and source of inspiration to all
with whom he associated."

"Masonry aims at building up character and assisting to make
us better men and better citizens. Not only better in our relations."
The Deputy Grand Master urged the need of encouragement
of the study of the substance of Freemasonry. District meetings
should do more than merely instruct in ritualistic matters. Initiative
and constructive thinking in Masonic philosophy needs to be cul. tivated. Instructors of Masonic vision, calibre and resourcefulness ·are required to meet the new conditions.
The Grand Lodge approved a plan for providing Masonic
scholarships to prospective teachers to encourage them to take the
necessary training at the Provincial Normal School at either Regina
or Saskatoon.
A brief but most interesting report on Foreign Correspondence
is submitted by Past Grand Master W. M. Thomson.

Bro. C. A. Elliott, chairman of the committee, submitted the
report on Foreign Correspondence. Of it he says:
"It has long been felt that it would be for the benefit of the
Craft if more of the brethren took an interest in what is being
done by Masons in other parts of the world. In the hope of interesting those whose time for the study of these subjects is strictlv
limited, the report has on this occ.asion been prepared in a condensed
and, it is believed, more attractive form. Any brother can read
the whole in a single evening. It is suitable for reading in Lodge
if there is no work to be performed, or a part may be read during
any hiatus in the work."

The foreword of the report is attractive as well as interesting:
"This year the committee is trying out a different plan. They
know that in the past their reports have not been widely read and
therefore, that these reports have failed to achieve one of 'thei;
principal objects, the education of the brethren. This year nine
short articles have been written, each dealing with an important
subject, and indicating what is being thought or said or done in
other Grand Jurisdictions. It is believed that these articles have
been written in a sufficiently attractive style to make them inter·
esting as well as instructive, so that every brother will enjoy
hearing one of these articles read aloud in the Lodge. It is hoped
that a copy of this report will be kept ready to hand in every
Lodge, so that the Master may be able to use every otherwise
unoccupied moment in affording light and guidance to the brethren
by telling them what is occurring in the big Masonic world, and
bringing to their notice the questions and problems by which it is
agitated."
The topics discussed are French Masonry, Bolshevism, Masonic
Education, Masonic Homes, Masonic Libraries and Museums
Physical Qualifications, Relief and Benevolence, the Washingto~
Memorial, the Masonic Service Association and Masonic Poems
the latter with some very fine samples.

NEW ZEALAND (1921)
The Thirty-second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of New Zealand· was held in Auckland, May 11-12, 1921.
There were present M.".W.". Thomas Ross, Grand Master,
twelve Grand Officers, four Past Grand Masters and representatives from 195 of the 217 chartered Lodges.
The following amendment to the constitution was adopted:
"Every applicant for initiation into Freemasonry shall be
handed by the Secretary of the Lodge the booklet on 'The Aims,
Objects and Teachings of Ancient, Free and Accepted Freemasonry,' sanctioned and issued by Grand Lodge, which must be
returned to the Lodge after perusal. On the applicant then deciding
to proceed with his application, it shall be considered by the
Investigating Committee of the Lodge or Board of Enquiry where
such is constituted,'" was, after some discussion, referred to the
Board of General Purposes for report.
It seems that Boards of Enquiry have been organized at several
points in the Jurisdiction by voluntary arrangements among the
Lodges. A proposition to establish them throughout the territory,
investing them with proper and necessary powers and authorities,
'was negatived by a large majority.
A careful study of the volume of proceedings reveals some
very interesting information regarding the matter of benevolence.
During the year covered by the reports there was contributer!
by the Lodges and brethren to the several benevolent funds the
following sums: To the Fund of Benevolence, £971; to the Widows
and Orphans and Aged Masons' Fund, £8,230; response to circular
appeals, £2,573; a total of over £ 11,750.
Sixty annuitants were beneficiaries of the second-named fund
in sums ranging from £26 to £52 per annum.
This Grand Lodge appears to have been organized in 1890, and
the report at this Communication shows the Widows and Orphans'
Fund to have reached the substantial sum of more than £46,000,
on which interest was received during the year of more than
£2,200. The third fund named arises from authorized appeals to
the Lodges in behalf of particular cases and the ·response each time
was quick and liberal.
Besides all this there is a Special War Benevolent Fund of over
£ 12,000, from the principal and income of which loans and donations are made to assist soldier members of the late war and their
dependents.

QUEENSLAND (1921)
The Seventeenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
Queensland was held at Brisbane, March 14th, 1920. There were
present M.".W.". James Stoclart, Grand Master, ten Grand Officers,
three Past Grand Masters and representatives from fifty-six of the
seventy-six chartered Lodges.
We quote from the Grand Master:
"Brethren. in the short address I propose to make to you tonight
it appeared to me an occasion in which the choice of a Masonic
emblem was particularly fitting on which to base my remarks. The
emblem I refer to is the Masonic Ladder. The Masonic Ladder
is said to originate in the vision of Jacob, where, as you all know,
it was depicted as connecting earth with heaven. Jacob referred
to the lower stave as the 'Gate of Heaven,' and other staves came
to be regarded as Faith, Hope, Charity, Strength, Beauty, Wisdom,
etc. In every Lodge the foot of the Ladder rests upon the Bible.
Masonically, when you once place your foot on the lowest rung,
then your steadfastness to our principles should enable you to
climb in easy stages to the mansions above."
The idea of the Ladder designates the ascent of the soul to
perfection, of ascending t'o heaven by means of the practice of
moral virtues.

The Grand Master's address was brief but comprehensive. He
fittingly says:
"The returns furnished show a splendid increase of membership
in all directions, but mere numbers is not the mark at which we
aim, unless it is understood that initiation is but a small part of
the work we have on hand when we make a man a Mason. Masonry
must meah more than the assembling in our Lodges or reciting
our ritual; it must mean the teaching of the truths of Holy Writ,
which treat of the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of
Man.
"\Vhile we welcome these new members to our ranks, our
efforts must not relax in the direction of retaining those already
in the Craft, and I hope some endeavor has been made towards
this end in the manner I indicated at our last Half-Yearly Communication by the discussion of Masonic history or the principles
of the order for a short period at our Lodge meetings whenever it
is possible to do so. I feel sure that if this course is followed it
will bring regular attendance and a prolonged interest.
"It was very gratifying to notice in the Report of the Board
of Benevolence the substantial increase in the amount contributed
by brethren at the annual installation ceremonies, and it is earnestly
hoped that this will be surpassed in the coming year as an e:idence that the brethren recognize the value of this opportumty
to assist the poor and distressed in our midst."

moreover, we do see it stated that a certain section of this community must not belong to Freemasonry, because it is an international, capitalistic and monarchistic secret society. That it is
international we quite admit, and that it has its ramifications through
the whole of this great globe of ours we cannot deny. We say that
Freemasonry is universal in its application, because it applies and
makes an appeal to human principles. It is cosmopolitan, international, comprehensive and wide-reaching in its efforts and effects.
To say that it is capitalistic is an abuse of terms, because the
humblest can enter our ranks, provided he is of good repute. We
fix no monetary value on our members. We recognize that in
Freemasonry there is co-equalness in citizenship. Our one common ground is our common humanity. \Ve say that every fine
character in Freemasonry is co-equal with another fine character;
that every fine character is independent altogether of rank or
position. We admit monarchs into our ranks, not because they
are monarchs, but because they are human, like ourselves. We
recognize no distinction of rank, but I hope and trust we will
always recognize distinctions of character, which should be the
mainstay of this organization."

The Grand Master in his quarterly address aptly says:
"We see Freemasonry constantly accused of being a secret
society. It seems to me that the accusers are really much more
secret than we are ourselves. Freemasonry needs no defense; it is
insistent .of those .eternal principles that are the inspiring note of
the world's humanity. Of course, we recognize that every successful institution incites individual hatred and uncharitableness, and,

The only other item likely to interest our readers was that a
law was passed that:
"No Lodge shall on the same day initiate into Freemasonry
more ·than four persons or pass more than four brethren or raise
more than two hrethren unless by a dispensation from the Grand
Master, which dispensation shall specify the total number to be
initiated, passed or raised, respectively."
The visit of the Prince of ·wales to Victoria was the occasion
of an elaborate affair. His being a Mason was a source of rejoicing
to the fraternity. Americans sometimes fail to grasp the attitude
of our British brethren toward royalty. With right-thinking men
there is no thought of personal cringing, and the King himself
merely represents the nation as does our flag to us. But when
we come to consider the place the Prince holds in the affections
of the British people, we run up against his personality. Charming as a young man, filling every station with entire satisfaction to
all, his record as a soldier stands out conspicuously. \Ve heard
a Canadian Major say that he met every danger he could get a
chance at, and had to be restrained almost by force from the most
reckless exposure on the battle lines. Remembering that the visit
to Australia followed soon after the war ended, it was not surprising
that the people went wild over him. \Ve in America were almost
as enthusiastic over him as a hero in a w·ar for civilization-our
war as well as theirs.

many of initiation. It is, or has been, the custom when there were
