been held on the 24th of February.
The Grand Master, in his address to the Grand Lodge, uttered
some noteworthy steadying thoughts regarding the stand of Freemasonry toward citizenship, from which the following quotations
are excerpted:
"The basic principles of our institution are the Fatherhood of
God and the Brotherhood of Man, and these, coupled with non·
interference in religion and politics, have distinguished the Craft
from other institutions in all ages and have given it a unique
place in the world. The duty of a Freemason is nowhere more
clearly outlined than in the charges of the First Degree, more par·
ticularly his duty as a citizen, and it is with the Freemason as a
citizen that I am at present concerned. He is enjoined to be
exemplary in the discharge of his civic duties; he is to discountenance every act calculated to subvert the peace and good order
of the community; he is to support the laws of the State of which
he is a citizen, and, finally, he is to act on the square. Therefore
a Freemason ought to stand for everything that will promote good
government and justice to all. Especially at a time when the
world is being torn asunder by class hatred, social unrest and a
total disregard for law and order on the part of a considerable
section of the community.
"I cannot see any good arise by the Craft, as such, taking part
in any public movement, however noble and praiseworthy, and I
am certain that such a course would be fraught with disaster and
would in the end eventually lead to strife and dissension in our
own ranks. With the Freemasons as individuals it is different. The
lessons he has learned in the Lodge fit him in a peculiar degree for
the discharge of his duty as a citizen, and if he has given much
thought to these he will be an asset to the community in whatever
capacity he may be called upon to serve. In other words, he will
practice outside the Lodge those duties he has been taught within
it, and so prove to the world the beneficial effects of our ancient
institution in the making of a good citizen."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Grand Master pointed out the obligation resting upon
Freemasons to "hold the scales of justice with equal poise," especially amidst the aftermath of war, with the resulting "terrible
tangle of industrial unrest," and to exert their best endeavors "to
harmonize conflicting views and to sow good-will among all the
peoples of the State." The "priceless heritage of civil and religious
liberty" must be defended at all hazards. Then follows this pleasing
reference to the United States:
"As an instance of the high regard in which the Craft is held
by some of the rulers of the world, and how it stands in their
minds as a symbol of moral stability in public affairs, the taking of
the Presidential oath recently by Bro. Warren G. Harding furnishes
a notable example. At his special request he used the old Masonic
Bible on which Washington took the same oath in 1792. The
Bible, which is the property of St. John's Lodge, No. 1, New York,
was taken to Washington in a special car by the Grand Master
and other Grand Officers. Bro. Harding opened the Bible at
precisely the same page as Washington when he took his oath
nearly 130 years ago. The fact that these two Presidents sent
to the Lodge room for the Lodge Bible to be used for such a solemn
purpose on such an historic occasion shows clearly that Freemasonry to them was a very real thing, and that they looked to
the Craft as a great, loyal and steadying force in the community."

The reports of the Board of General Purposes quite generally
related to matters of local interest, but during· the year several
matters of general interest to the Craft were presented in these
reports.
Both the Board and the Pro-Grand Master declined on behalf
of the Grand Lodge the invitation to participate in the International
Congress of Freemasons extended by Swiss Grand Lodge Alpina
of Switzerland upon the ground that the Grand Lodge of England
has never participated in a Masonic gathering at which are present
those who do not conform to those Ancient Landmarks of Freemasonry which demand an express belief in the G. A. 0. T. U.
and an obligatory recognition of the V. S. L. The Pro-Grand
Master adds to this that controversial affairs of state are not permitted to be discussed in Masonic Lodge.
The Board reported that it had made full investigation of the
Order of the Eastern Star and held that the provision of its ritual
that there shall preside at the meetings during the conferring of
the degrees an official styled the Worthy Patron, who has to be a
Freemason "in good standing," is considered by the Board to set
up a test the validity of which none but Freemasons can properly
judge, and the Board also held that no such test can be recognized
in connection with bodies which, contrary to the immemorial
practice of the United Grand Lodge of England, admit women to
membership. They say:
"The source of the danger thus indicated is brought home more
closely to the Board by the knowledge that Secretaries of some of
our Lodges have received a request from women Secretaries of
Lodges of the Eastern Star, asking for a categorical statement as
to whether certain persons named were 'in good standing' in that
particular Lodge-a request to which no Secretary of a Masonic
Lodge in such circumstances has a right to reply."

432

In closing his inspiring message, the Grand Master gave this
final caution:
"I am not at all sure but that the very fact that we keep quiet
and make no display, while the world knows we are united and
determined to defend loyalty, has not a greater power in the
community than if we proclaimed our determination from the
housetops."
The Charity Stewards system has proved most useful in the
fifteen years of its existence. Practically every. Lodge now has
a Charity Steward, whose duty it is to look after the interests of
the Benevolence Fund among his brethren1'

GRAND LODGE OF ENGLAND (1921)
At each of the Quarterly Communications the Reports of the

and widows, making a large total for the year. All this, in addition
to the support of the three great charities-the Homes for Boys,

433

The report then proceeds:
"As there are various bodies of great and apparently growing
popularity in the United States and some parts of the British
Empire which, while not formally claiming to be Masonic, are, at
the least, imitative of the Masonic institution, the Board thinks
it necessary to state the general principles upon which it feels
bound to act in regard to them. The Craft is not concerned with
bodies-whether composed entirely of men, of women or of both
sexes-which do not claim to be Masonic in either ritual or
practice, and do not make Masonry in any way a test of membership or of participation in their ceremonies. But it is clear that
a grave risk is incurred by brethren who enter into association

434

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

with bodies making Masonry in any way a test of admission to
membership, while admitting as members persons who would not
be qualified to join a Lodge under the Jurisdiction of the United
Grand Lodge of England. No Freemason is entitled to attend
any non-Masonic meeting at which Masonry by direct implication is
introduced, or to participate in any ceremony which is quasiMasonic or is held under pseudo-Masonic and unauthorized
auspices. The Secretary or any member of a Lodge who gives
to any one outside, and particularly to a non-Mason, information
on Masonic matters known to him because of his Masonic connection, commits a breach of discipline which, when proved, will be
severely dealt with."
The report was adopted,
The Masonic Peace Memorial for which contributions are being
received is to take the form of a new Masonic Hall in London the
present one having been outgrown to an extent to be entirely idadequate to the needs. Contributions to the fund for this purpose are
coming in from all parts of the Empire. The London Lodges have
already contributed £ 150,000.

IRELAND (1921)
This report must of necessity be very meager for all that one
receives from Ireland in the way of proceedings is a srirnll pamphlet

At the meeting in December, 1920, the Deputy (;rand Master,
R. W. Brother Colonel Claude Cane, drew attention to the fact
that during the year their losses by death or resignation had been
extraordinarily heavy.
Among those whose resignations are .reported were R. W
Brother Sir Charles Cameron and Lord Frederick Hamilton. The
former had surely earned the privilege of retirement, having reached
the remarkable age of ninety-one years, with his mental faculties
unimpaired. He first became an officer of the Grand Lodge in 1870,
and his official connection with Grand Lodge continued up to the
date of hs retirement, at which time he filled the responsible position of Deputy Grand Master.
The list of departed brethren also includes some very distinguished names, such as V. W. Brother John Baptist Crozier,
Grand Chaplain and Lord Primate of All Ireland; V. W. Brother

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

435

Lord Plunket, G~and Secretary, and W. Brother H. E. Flavelle,
Deputy Grand Secretary. ·
The Deputy Grand Master congratulated the Craft upon the
generally satisfactory condition of Masonry in Ireland. Although
eighteen new Lodges were organized in 1918 and twenty in 1919, he
was able to report the formation of nineteen during 1920, and the
actual membership of the Lodges has been substantially increased.
Nor is the gain in Lodges and in membership confined to the
North of Ireland, where it might be expected, but progress has
been made both in Dublin and in the South and West of the
country.
We are delighted to note the fact that the Grand Lodge of
Ireland does not favor the wholesale making of members by the
Lodges. In its constitution it is enacted that the First Degree and
the Third Degree must be given to each candidate singly, while
a regulation recently adopted limits the number that may be
. initiated or raised in any one day to three.
At the meeting held on St. John's Day, December, 1921, the
Deputy Grand Master reported the resignation of two other prominent members of Grand Lodge-Brother Joze, who had been their
Organist for thirty-three years. and R. W. Brother Lord Shaftesbury, Provincial Grand Master of Antrim.
The Deputy Grand Master stated that for the first time in its
history Grand Lodge had held one of its regular meetings outside
of Dublin, when in the previous October a meeting was held at
Belfast.
Although, as we have noted above, the past three years have
been remarkable for the increase in the number of new Lodges,
the year 1921 had_ surpassed them all, and the Deputy Grand
Master reported the formation of no fewer than twenty-eight new
Lodges. A surprisingly large number of these are located in the
city of Dublin, some in the Provinces and a few in foreign parts,
while one is a military Lodge attached to the First Battalion,
Duke of Cornwal'f>s Light Infantry.
"\Vhat of the night, Watchman; what of the night?" Conditions in Ireland when the Deputy Grand Master spoke were not
of the most cheerful character, and although the Deputy Grand
Master professes himself an optimist he could not conjure up a
particularly rosy picture of the future. He concluded his address
with these words:
"I suppose that I am almost bound to say a few words with
regard to the future. The future for us, at any rate, here in the
Soµth of lrel!lnd is one which we cannot look upon very lightly,

436

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

or without a certain amount of seriousness. Changes are impending. We do not yet know exactly what those changes will be,
but they have been foreshadowed, and, at any rate, the social state
of affairs is not going to be exactly the same as it has been in the
past. Probably not one of us in this room but looks forward with
a certain amount of apprehension to what may happen, and probably those changes are not such as recommend themselves fully
to any one of us. But I think there is no need for pessimism. I,
myself, frankly, am an optimist, and there is just one t.hing that I
want to say to you before I sit down, and that is: That whether
we like it or not, whatever form of government is established in
the country, constitutionally, and by the consent of all the parties
concerned, and under the sanction of the Sovereign to whom we
hold allegiance, we, as good Masons, are bound to make the best
of it. In the words of that Charge which is read, or should be
read, to every candidate on his initiation, we are enjoined 'to be
exemplary in the discharge of our civil duties, by never proposing
or countenancing anything which may disturb the peace and good
order of society; by paying obedience to the laws of the state
in which we reside and by which we are protected, and by never
losing sight of the allegiance we owe to the Sovereign of our native
land."
SCOTLAND
The reports of committees and Provincial Grand Masters indicate
that there are a large number of the younger men applying for
membership in the Lodges, and that the increase in numbers is
made up of that class of men who immediately take hold of the
spirit and activities of Masonry.
The formation of the United Grand Lodge, made possible by
the union of the Lodges under the Scottish Constitution with the
Grand Lodge of Queensland, has met with the approval of this
Grand Lodge, and directions given that the surrendered charters
granted by this Grand Lodge be returned for ca1'cellation, and then
returned to the Lodges to be retained as mementoes of their former
connection with this Grand Lodge.
During the year a large number of new Lodges were organized
in various parts of the earth.
The striking thing about the proceedings is the reports concerning benevolence. The income is derived from a variety of
sources-fees, donations and the like-and the expenditures for the
care of orphans and dependents are as widespread as the Lodges.
Our Scottish brethren give a great deal of attention to the matter,
and their benevolences keep pace with the growth and extension
of their Lodges and influence.

WILLIAM A. SHERMAN
GRAND MASTER
1922 1923
William A. Sherman, fifty-sixth Grand Master of Masons in California, holds the distinction of being one ot the youngest men ever so
honored by the Fraternity in this State. He was born in San Francisco
forty-two years ago. As a boy he moved with his parents to the historic old town of Sonoma, in the beautiful Valley of the Moon, where
he graduated from grammar and high schools.
Like scores of other men who have attained success in the business
life of the State, Brother Sherman began his career on a newspaper.
During two years spent on a San Francisco daily he laid the foundation
which has enabled him to cope with complex situations. Preferring a
business career, he abandoned journalism and became connected with
the Merchants Ice & Cold Storage Company. For the last twenty-one
years he has been identified with that concern; his ability and business
judgment, combined with his well-known characteristics of sincerity
and kindliness, winning him steady advancement until he became general manager of the concern. He is also on the directorates of various
allied industries. His standing in the business world has long been
recognized.
The same characteristics that won him success in his chosen line
of endeavor were successfully applied to the various problems presented for his decisions during his i::cumbency as Grand Master. The
success of his administration is recognized by all. As a business man
he brought to the office of Grand Master a cool, practical knowledge
that tlid much to make his year in office an outstanding success.
Brother Sherman was made a Master Mason in Presidio Lodge No.
He has been actively identified with
Masonry during the succeeding years. Jn 1908 he was clcctccl Master

MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Grand Lodge today begins its seventy-fifth year of constructive
work in California. The seventy-fourth Annual Communication is
now open. Nearly three-quarters of a century of progressive endeavor lies behind us. It is a record that should thrill each member
of the Craft with justifiable pride. Year by year since that memorable meeting in 1850, our Masonic edifice has grown in strength and
beauty. The stones of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth have been
used to erect our structure. It is, therefore, established on a permanent foundation. Its possibilities for the future are unlimited.
This is emphasized by the success attendant upon our <"ndeavors
during the last twelve months. Although our nation and state have
passed through economic and political turmoil in the last year, California Masonry has pursued the even tenor of its way, steadily advancing in membership and strength. It has been a year of splendid
activity and harmonious relationships.
At the present time there are 484 lodges, either duly constituted
or working under dispensation, which number on their rolls more
than one hundred thousand carefully selected men. During the year
dispensations have been given for the formation of 38 new lodges,
the largest number in the history of the Grand Lodge of California.
It is particularly pleasing to report that not all of the new lodges
have been formed in the larger centers of population. This in itseli
sptaks well for the activities of Masonry in all parts of our State.
At the time of my installation as your Grand Master I fully
recognized the grave responsibilities of the high office with which
you had honored me. In many ways I fear I have not measured
up to the opportunities presented, Im\ through the considerate and
whole-hearted support of the Fraternity I feel that my efforts have
not been altogether in vain. It is with a feeling of humility and
appreciation that I pass to my successor the gavel of authority,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

442

443

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

realizing that he will receive the same full measure of support that
was accorded me.
Visitations
If time and space would permit, it would give me pleasure to
record in detail each and every visitation made during the year.
This, obviously, is impossible, but I wish to express to each member of the Fraternity my deep and lasting appreciation of the many
acts of kindness extended to me during my many visitations.

While it has been physically impossible to visit every lodge or
even every district in the State, I have visited either collectively or
individually some 350 lodges and have found them all in a prosperous condition. In practically every community in the State, from
the cities to the remote mountain hamlets, Masonic Lodges arc
found, and their influence for good is generally admitted.
The visitations . and performance of public ceremonies have
necessitated my traveling in excess of twenty-seven thousand mile~
in the last year. It has also necessitated traveling by every method
of conveyance with the exception of the aeroplane, which was declined only because of the extremely bad weather. This trip by
aeroplane was to have been made especially so that I might spend a
Sunday with the children at Covina.
I believe that the visitations of the Grand officers to the various
lodges encourages the officers and brethren in their Masonic endeavors, and quickens their interest in the social and civil activities
of the various communities.
Corner Stones
During the year Grand Lodge has been convened many times
for the purpose of laying the corner stones of public schools, Masonic Temples and other public buildings. I have conducted eighteen of these ceremonies, and in each instance an effort has been
made to bring to the people a clearer understanding of the high
ideals for which Masonry stands. It has been a source of gratification to know that in many cases where the Fraternity has been
misunderstood, people not of our membership have been glad to
learn of the broad principles of Masonry, and have acknowledged
that a better feeling has resulted in the several communities.
The manner in which Masonry is officially recognized in California is well illustrated by the fact that two Governors requested
me as Grand Master to lay the corner stones of two important
State buildings. The first was the State Building in San Francisco.

At the request of Governor William D. Stephens, Grand Lodge conducted this ceremony. At the request of Governor Friend W.
Richardson, Grand Lodge laid the corner stone of the ~tate Building
in Sacramento. These ceremonies served to bring before the people
of the State the dignity and importance of our great Fraternity.
In connection with these ceremonies as well as many other
matters I am especially indebted to the Right Worshipful Arthur S.
Crites, who conducted several of these ceremonies, as did Right
Worshipful D. J. Reese, Senior Grand Warden, and Right Worshipful Albert E. Boynton, Junior Grand Warden.
It was impossible for the Grand Officers to conduct the ceremony. of laying the corner stone of a school house at Shasta, and
this was ably done by the Inspector of the district, Worshipful
Gustave A. Hutaff.

Hawaiian Islands
Indeed would this report be incomplete without reference to
my official visit to the lodges in the Hawaiian Islands. On May
2, accompanied by the Grand Secretary, our wives and my older
boy, I commenced a trip to the Islands which unquestionably will
be one of my most pleasant memories.
We were received by Inspector Lester Petrie and other leaders
of Masonry in the Islands. Then commenced a week of visitation,
hospitality and the extending of fraternal good will such as few
men are fortunate enough to receive. Superlatives fail to describe
the hospitality and sincerity of purpose of these Island brethren.
I visited all the six lodges in the group, and Brother Whicher
remained to investigate the feasibility of the establishment of another lodge on the Island of Kauai. During the visit to Schofield
Barracks Lodge, Grand Lodge was convened for the purpose of
installing Brother Petrie as Grand Standard Bearer.
In reference to Masonry in the Islands it may not be generally
known that six lodges exist there with a membership of nearly
1500. While there has been some talk of the establishment of a
Grand Lodge in the Hawaiian Islands a discussion with the leaders
of Masonry there developed a general belief that the lodges prefer to remain under the jurisdiction of California.
H owcvcr, as the Islands arc so far removed from the mainland,
I believe mnch good conl<l be accomplished if they were given a
Grand Oflicer with authority to grant dispensations and convene
Grand Lodge for public ceremonies and other purposes. I, there-

Masonic Education
School Week Observance
With the idea of calling the attention of all Masons in California to the public schools in the State, I directed that the week
commencing March 19 ·be observed as Public School Week. The
response of the Fraternity was enthusiastic and constructive. While
in some of the localities the attendance was not as large as anticipated, nevertheless on the whole the week was a success and demonstrated the positive interest and sincere desire of Masons in this
State to interest themselves in the public schools.
The observance this year was held in the springtime, as it was
believed-and events justified this belief-that greater interest can
be aroused at this season of the year than later, when the members
are occupied with a multiplicity of problems which control the
actions of those engaged in the various agricultural pursuits. It is
the judgment of your Grand Master that most of our Masonic
activities are given greater attention and bring better results in the
springtime than during the heat of summer or during the harvest
season, when the crops are demanding the attention of our brethren
engaged in agricultural and allied pursuits; also those brethren who
reside in the centers of population and who with their families spend
their vacations away from the reach of the Masters of the Lodges.
Too much praise cannot be given Brother Arthur Joel, together
with Brothers Warren D. Gill and Robert Greig, who worked with
him to make this
school week unquestionably the most successful ever held. The report on this subject will be printed in another part of the proceedings of Grand Lodge.
In connection with School Week, I believe that better results
can be obtained if one large meeting were held instead of several
small meetings in the larger cities. I also believe that in the smaller
communities individual meetings, either closed or open, are the most
effective as all reports show that the district meetings are largely
attended by those living in the immediate vicinity of the town where
the meeting ls held, while very few come from other communities
to the meeting.
I also hclicve it would he an excellent innovation if an educator
of national prominence were selected to address the meetings in

While the Committee on Masonic Education has done the very
best within its power, nevertheless I believe that the results obtained
have not fulfilled the expectations of the Craft. This, in my opinion,
is not due to a lack of earnestness or ability on the part of the
members of this committee, but rather to the faulty system of our
educational organization. Some of the brainiest men in the Fraternity have had charge of this work during the last few years, but
the results have not measured up to their expectations. The importance of this work cannot be over-estimated, and if properly
handled it would require the entire time of the chairman of the
committee. Naturally, this cannot be expected from busy men, and
only busy men have the capability and the vision for such respon,
sibility.
It is my recommendation, therefore, that the committee be continued, but that it be given a paid Executive Secretary to be appointed by the Grand Master. It would be the function of this
Secretary to work with the Committee on Education to the end
that programs could be arranged and speakers sent to the various
lodges. At the present time, if a lodge asks for a speaker, the first
man available is senf, no matter what his qualifications may be. It
is often the case that the man sent is not thoroughly conversant
with the subject to be explained. With an Executive Secretary, the
wants of the lodges could be ascertained and speakers could then
be furnished accordingly. In the selection of this man, great care
should be taken to ascertain that his educational and executive
qualifications are adequate, and this being determined satisfactorily
his compensation should be adequate.
'
During the year I have from time to time addressed the Craft
through the medium of a bulletin, in which I have endeavored to
give kindly aamonition and advice on matters of Masonic interest.
I believe the Committee on Masonic Education, under the direction
of the Grand Master, could enlarge upon this plan and that an instructive quarterly bulletin could be sent to every member of the
Craft. In order to do this economically a sufficient number of these
bulletins could he furnished to every lodge in the jurisdiction and
then distributed by the Secretary to the members.

Constitution Week
The week of September 16-23 I set apart as Constitution Week.
This was in keeping with the policy adopted in many parts of the
United States to bring home to the people of the nation the fundamentai guarantees upon which American freedom of speech, freedom of religious worship, security of life, liberty and property and
other important guarantees were based.
The response was splendid, and I believe that Masons realize
more fully the importance of this truly Masonic document. Both
School Week and Constitution Week observance aroused great iuterest among the Masons of the State as to their duties as citizens.
If we continue to stress these matters it can only be a question of
time when Masons will take a more active part in the economic and
political affairs of the State, which will mean improved conditions.
Roosevelt's definition of an American citizen should be well
known by everyone.
We care nothing where a man was born; we care nothing as to the land from which his parents came; we stand
for absolute freedom of religious belief, but we insist upon
one flag, one language, one undivided loyalty to this nation
and to the ideals of this nation. We are a new nation,
differing from all other nations, friendly towards them all
in so far as they will let us be friendly, desirous of helping
them, but resolutely bent upon maintaining our separate,
self-respecting, self-reliant national existence. We accept
no substitute for Americanism. We insist that all our people must be Americans and only Americans.
Masonic Service Association
At the last communication of Grand Lodge it was decided that
this jurisdiction should become a member of the Masonic Service
Association. This was done largely in compliment to the man who
presented the association plan to Grand Lodge and really contrary
to the judgment of many of our brethren who had given especial
thought to the matter and to the recommendation of .those who, at
the request of Grand Lodge, had thoroughly investigated the plans
and methods adopted by this association.
Without in any way minimizing the worth of this association, I
do not believe that California has received sufficient service to
justify the expenditure of so much money; in fact, I believe that if
this money were given to the Committee on Masonic Education,
that committee could obtain better results in the development of a

447

program consonant with the needs of California than could be
obtained liy following programs drawn up by those not in touch
with our local conditions.
After discussing this matter thoroughly with members of the
various committees of Grand Lodge, including the Chairman of the
Committee of. Policy and Purposes and the Chairman of the Committee on Finance, I determined to notify the association that with
the expiration of our year's membership we would cease to be members. This was not done with the idea of forcing my own opinion
upon Grand Lodge. It was done in order that the expense of a part
of the year could be saved, as the rules of the association require a
ninety-day notice before withdrawal.
Although I appreciate the fact that the association has had its
troubles during the year, nevertheless I do not feel that the material
sent out would justify the great expense of retaining our membership.
In matters of relief we are definitely on record as opposed to
its system. In this connection I might add that I received a telegram from the association on September 9, stating the urgency of
immediate relief for suffering Japan on the part of Masons of the
United States, and suggested our cooperation. To this I replied
that just seven days previous to the receipt of their telegram, California had recognized and responded to the call of suffering humanity in ] a pan. It has always been the policy of this jurisdiction upon
the realization of the enormity of a calamity to send relief and then
ascertain the details later.
Relief
During the year calamity has overtaken various parts of the
world to such an extent that financial aid was deemed advisable
from the emergency relief fund of this Grand Lodge. The first call
came early in the year when the city of Astoria was destroyed by
fire, making hundreds of people homeless. Fearing that the call
upon the Grand Lodge of Oregon might be too large, we forwarded
$1000 to their relief. It was later found that this was not needed
and the money was returned.
On the morning of September 2 the world was shocked at the
news of the terrible catastrophe that had befallen the cities of Tokio
and Yokohama. Realizlng immediately their great need and that
action should be taken at once, I directed that $2500 of our relief
fund be turned over to the Red Cross to be handled for the general
relief of ] apanese sufferers. While there are no ] apanese Masonic
Lodges, and it was probable that other jurisdictions having lodges
in the stricken area would send needed assistance, nevertheless I

felt that I was justified in my action by those lines in our ritual,
which say:
One to whom the burdened heart may pour out its sorrows; one to whom distress may prefer its suit; one whose
hand is guided by justice and whose heart is expanded by
benevolence.

Grand High Priest, William Penn Humphreys; the Grand Commandery through its Past Grand Commander, William H. Waste,
and its present executive head, our own beloved Junior Grand Warden, Albert E. Boynton, and the Scottish Rite through Illustrious
William P. Filmer, Sovereign Grand Inspector General for the
Northern Jurisdiction of California, and Perry W. Weidner, Sovereign Grand Inspector General for Southern California, and the officers of the various Shrine Temples have been most delightful and

this kind cannot help but win praise from all classes.
The Sciots, through their head, Brother E. L. DeLa Mater,
have always responded promptly to any suggestion on my part
relative to this organization.
In this respect, however, I suggest that action be taken by
Grand Lodge, through our Jurisprudence Committee, to exercise a
general supervision over any new bodies claiming to be coordinate
Masonic bodies and which make as a prerequisite for membership,
good standing in the Blue Lodge, with the idea of preventing the
formation of other organizations claiming to represent Masonry.
At the last session of this Grand Lodge, by resolution, the purposes and ideals of the Order of DeMolay were approved and members of the coordinate lodge:s requested to lend their moral support
to the extension of the order. The a,ction of this Grand Lodge has
been followed by a number of other Grand Lodges. Advices are to
the effect that the Order of DeMolay in this State has increased
over 25 per cent in the number of chapters organized, and SO per
cent in membership.
The individuals in charge of the movement in California, particularly Jesse M. Whited, as well as the sponsoring bodies, are
using every effort to counteract the impression that the Order of
DeMolay is a Masonic body.
The practical work that the Chapters of the Order of DeMolay
are doing as far as raising the standard of their members and holding
out an ideal to the communities where they are located has been a
source of satisfaction to the sponsoring bodies and the Fraternity
in general. The teaching of clean thinking, clean speaking and clean
living by the order cannot make for other than better citizenship.
Contrary to some prophecies, the members of the order who
have attained their majority are not making application to become
members of the Masonic Fraternity, and the fear that the DeMolay
might be a Masonic kindergarten or a proselytizing ground for
Freemasonry is not borne out by facts.

448

On the afternoon of September 17, fire destroyed a considerable
portion of the city of Berkeley, making homeless and destitute many
individuals and families, particularly among the professors and
students of the University of California. Immediate relief being
deemed necessary two thousand dollars was placed in the hands of a
committee composed of the Masters of the eight Berkeley Lodges,
together with Brothers William H. Waste and Robert Greig, representing the Grand Master.
It was believed that particular assistance could be given students in the purchase of books and other necessaries needed to cause
the least delay in the continuance of their studies. No report has
yet been rendered nor has there been a call for an additional contribution, but this important relief is in most competent hands.
In this connection it can be said of Brother Waste that with his
characteristic promptness of service to his fellowman he was endeavoring to communicate with the Grand Master almost before the
fire was under control.
Six Months' Inhibition
It is a source of gratification to report that not one complaint
was made of the failure of any individual Mason to live up to the
six months' inhibition in becoming a member of any of the coordinate bodies of Masonry, the prerequisite of which was that the
petitioner be a Master Mason for the above-mentioned period.
Immediately upon the adjournment of Grand Lodge, requests
were made for interpretation of this rule, and after a thorough discussion with members of the Jurisprudence Committee, it was decided that there might be some ambiguity in the language of the
resolution, nevertheless the spirit of the resolution was to be observed. In this I decided that the six months' rule did not apply to
members in the Masonic Club or to membership in the Acacia
Fraternity, but did apply to joining the Eastern Star.
Coordinate Bodies
During the year the coordinate bodies of Masonry have at all
times shown a sincere inclination to advance the interests of Craft
Masonry. The relationships of the Grand Chapter through the

Inspectors
Perhaps no body of men are doing more constructive work in
the Grand Lodge and receiving less recognition than the Inspectors
in the ninety-odd districts of the State. With very few exceptions,
they give their time and their ability in a quiet, unassuming way
that seldom receives the rec-ognition which they so manifestly merit.
Theirs is a labor of love for their work is done "without hope of
fee or reward."
They relieve the Grand :Master of many details which would
necessari.ly swamp an already busy office. At the present time
they a.re required to make a report to Grand Lodge and the Grand
Lecturer, showing the condition of their respective districts, on or
before September l. This I believe should be changed, as the reports
which they send in are too valuable to be passed over lightly, and
such is largely the case. These reports ar.e now made so close to
Grand Lodge that the Grand Master has not the time to act on their
many valuable suggestions. As a matter of fact, this report was
written before one-half of the Inspectors' reports were received.
It is therefore my recommendation that Section 56 of the Constitution be changed to so read that these reports shall be filed on
or before May 1. In this way the Grand Master will have sufficient
time to examine and digest the valuable suggestions of these conscientious and capable workers in the vineyard of Masonry. I also
believe that by receiving these. reports early in the year, much important data can be secured for the use of the various committees of
Grand Lodge, as most of the Masonic work is accomplished during
the early part of each year.
Grand Lecturer and Ritual
There are some individuals we meet in our daily lives who become recognized institutions. \Ve realize the tremendous amount
of good they are doing, and yet we frequently give them little recognition. Such a one is our beloved Grand Lecturer, Thomas J.
Baker.
He has worked among the brethren for the last sixteen years,
going quietly, correcting patiently, speaking kindly, and radiating
the true principles of Masonry up and down and across this great
jurisdiction. Few realize the hard conditions, the unusual hours and
the other trying exactions of his position. One of less rugged constitution and calm personality would have fallen under the strain
long before this. His service to the various Grand Masters as they
come and go is incalculable. There is never a detail of arrangement or the possibility of extending a service that is not anticipated
by this patient, kindly man.

451

I believe that as a slight reward for his sixteen years of faithful
service he should be given a three months' leave of absence with
full salary and expenses for a trip throughout the United
States, and that during his trip he be requested to visit various
jurisdictions in order that he may familiarize himself with their
methods and rituals, and perhaps impart to them some of the
spirit and details of our own work. Upon his 1eturn he should
be requested to call a meeting of the Ritual Committee of California
with the idea of shortening the work, this for the purpose of avoiding unnecessary repetition, and also that more time may be devoted
to social and educational matters. I believe he should also investi·
gate and report on the so-called group plan of conferring degrees.
Whatever change is made in our ritual, I am of the opinion that
we should be very careful not to change its individualism nor to
lose sight of any of the fine ideals and principles which are given
so splendidly under its present system. However, I believe that
much time can be saved by a careful consideration of the matter
by the Ritual Committee. In this connection I recommend that
this Committee should be instructed to make its report at the next
annual communication of Grand Lodge.
I also recommend that the matter of going from one degree
to another during the same meeting should be done by proclamation.

Jurisdic ti on
During the year the matter of jurisdiction of lodges has been
a source. of some argument, and is therefore a matter which may
be well considered by this Grand body. Jn some other jurisdictions, particularly Pennsylvania, the entire State is concurrent jurisdiction. However, when a man petitions a lodge not nearest to
the one where he resides, that lodge must be notified of his petitioning some other lodge, and such petition lies over sixty days before
it can be acted on by the lodge receiving it. This would require
a change in Section 95 of our Constitution, which would then
read as follows:
"Nor unless he shall have been a resident within the
jnrisdiction of the Grand Lodge during twelve months.
When a petition is received by a lodge other than that which
is nearest to the place of residence of the petitioner, the
lodge receiving such petition shall, under its seal, inquire
of the lodge within this jurisdiction, nearest the place of
residence of the petitioner, whether it has any Masonic
objection to the lodge to which the petition is. addressed,
acting thereon. The only Masonic objections arc physical
disqualifications and unfitness of character and habits. If
no reply shall have been received within two mouths from
the date of inquiry, it shall be assumed that no Masonic
objection is made by the lodge of which such inquiry is
made."

Peter Lassen
As a pioneer of Masonry in California, Peter Lassen heads
the list. That Masonry was very close to his heart is evidenced
by the fact of his bringing the first charter to California from
Missouri upon his return from a visit to that State, and organizing
the first Masonic lodge in this State.
His grave is located at Susanville, and according to reports

distinguished man and Mason, but lack of time made the visit
impossible.
I believe that the land where his grave is located should be
acquired by Grand Lodge and that proper care he given it in a
simpk, dignified way. Thh; could he done at a small expense
through the supervision of the lodge at Snsanville. I believe this
matter should be referred to the incoming Grand Master with
power to carry out this suggestion if it meets with your endorsement.

Warren G. Harding
On August second, in the city of San Francisco, our President
and Brother, vVarren G. Harding, was called to the Great Beyond.
Coming at a time when the nation believed his recovery was but a
question of days, the shock was all the more severe. Just an hour
before being apprised of his death, the Grand Master as the guest
of the Grand Commandery, k. T. Cal., had taken part in that
, splendid ceremony of the presentation to Hollywood Commandery
in behalf of Marion Commandery of the International Travelling
Beauseant. The President's message of fraternal greeting which
had been read to the assembled thousands by his private secretary,
George B. Christian, had inspired and rekindled their faith anew in
the brotherhood of man.
In his passing the nation lost a great and good man, one
whom the country had grown to love because of his kindness,
humility and humaneness. He was a man of noble and generous
impulses, presiding over the nation at a time when the world
needs a gospel of love and understanding between man and man
and nation and nation.
Reflecting the feeling of sadness of the entire Fraternity in
California a message of condolence was forwarded to his beloved
wife. I believe as a further aclrnowledgrnent of our reverence
for his memory, Grand Lodge should pass suitable resolutions, an
engrossed copy of which shall be forwarded to Mrs. Harding and
also to his aged father.
Probably no better tribute to his character can be paid than
to quote his creed as given to the employees of his m::wspaper.
It follows:
Remember there are two sides to every question. Get
them both.
Be truthful. Get the facts.
Mistakes are inevitable, but strive for accuracy. I would
rather have one story exactly right than a hundred half
wrong.
Be decent, be fair, be generous.
Boost, don't knock
There's good In everybody. Bring out the good and never
needlessly hurt the feelings of anybody.
In reporting a political gathering, give the facts. Tell
the story as it is, not as you would like to have it. Treat
all parties alike. If there is any politics to be played, we
will play it in our editorial columns.

George Clement Perkins

•

The dean of our Past Grand Masters, George Clement Perkins, died at his beautiful home, Palm Knoll, Oakland, Monday,
February 26, 1923, after more than eighty-three years of busy and
useful life.
The career of Brother Perkins ought to be an inspiration to
every young man. He was born August 23, 1839, at Kennebunkport, Maine, and at the tender age of twelve he went to sea, making several voyages to Europe. In 1855, while yet a boy, he
arrived in San Francisco from Liverpool as a sailor before the
mast. He went to Sacramento by steamer, thence walkmg to
Butte county, where he tried mining, without success. Afterward
he secured a job as clerk in a merchandising establishment at
Oroville, saved wages, and in a few years purchased the business.
By the time this young sailor was twenty-five years old his business operations amounted to more than half a million dollars a
year. Na tu rally his business affairs expanded and mining, ranching, merchandising and many other interests engaged his attention.
In 1872 he became a member of the firm of Goodall, Nelson &
Perkins, afterwards known as the Pacific Coast Steamship Company, with marked success.
The years of Brother Perkins were filled to the full with
Masonic and political labors in and for the people of California:
and the nation. He was made a Master Mason in Oroville Lodge
No. 103, December 15, 1859, before he had attained his legal majority, but long after he had served a hard apprenticeship in the great
"University of Hard Knocks and Experience." He was active in
lodge work, and served as Steward, Secretary, thence through the
chairs until 1864 he was made Master of his lodge, which office
he also held in 1865 and 1870. Tl e afliliated with Oakland Lodge
No. 188, in 1886. In 1871 he was elected Junior Grand ·warden,
and at the annual communication of 1874 was elected Grand Master.

458

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The political life of Brother Perkins began in 1869, when he
was elected to represent Butte county in the State Senate. In
1879 he was elected Governor of California, serving one term.
In 1893 he was appointed to the office of United States Senator,
succeeding Leland Stanford, who had died in his office. He remained eontinuously a member of the United States Senate until
his voluntary retirement in 1917. He was one of the great men
of the Senate and his advice and counsel were sought by his
confreres in that august body.
The late Edwin Allen Sherman, in his "Fifty Years of Masonry;'' wrote of our brother the following:
"There was never created a man and brought into the
folds of Freemasonry more courteous, genial, affable and
pleasant in manner, more generously disposed and charitable than George Clement Perkins, who always met even
the humblest and impoverished brother Mason on the common level of fraternal humanity, whether as Master or
Grand Master, Grand Commander, Governor or Senator;
and every one, from the highest to the lowest, in all walks
of society, has always been placed at their ease. Kind and
generous to a fault', ever true to sincere friends and charitable even to faithless ones; a born leader of men. He
was an honor to Masonry, to the nation, and especially to
California ·•

Charles Lewis Patton
Another active worker in the Masonic vineyard, Charles Lewis
Patton, died Wednesday morning, April 11, 1923, at the age of 58.
He was made a Mason in California Lodge No. 1, March 24, 1887,
and was Master of his lodge in 1894. At the annual election in
October, 1896, Brother Patton was elected Junior Grand Warden
and was made Grand Master in 1899.
'
Brother Patton was for so many years actively identified with
Grand Lodge as a member of the Committee on Jurisprudence, that
his splendid service as a member of the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes may not be readily recalled by the ·present generation. In 1895, Grand Master James Baunty Stevens appointed
Brother Patton a member of the Board to succeed Gustave Langford Spear, who had resigned. He was soon thereafter elected
president of the Doan!, and on October 14, 1896, he had the
pleasure of presiding at the ceremony of laying the corner stone
of the Home at Dccoto by Grand Master Preston. In October,

Albert Glenn Burnett
Another loss to the Fraternity and to the world was announced on the 15th of August, 1923, when word reached us that
the spirit of Past Grand Master Albert Glenn Burnett had left
its tenement of clay and winged its way to its eternal home. Brother
Burnett was particularly loved by your Grand Master, to whom
he was attached by the closest ties of affection. In his death
the Craft lost a man who was an ideal Mason-generous in thought
and deed, fearless in the execution of his duty, honest, kind,
thoughtful of his fellows, a brilliant orator whose mind and tongue
were ever attuned to the defense of every righteous cause,-a gentle
man in all that goes to make the best type of citizen.
Our brother was born in Polk county, Oregon, April 9, 1856.
His father, Glenn 0. Burnett, was a minister of the gospel, and
from this good father and a pious mother he inherited those
sterling principles of right-doing which characterized his after life.
His education was in the public schools and the Christian College
at Santa Rosa, and after leaving school he was engaged in teaching,
meanwhile studying law. In 1887 he was admitted to the bar,
and in 1888 was elected District Attorney of Sonoma county, serving in that capacity for two years. In 1896 he was elected Judge
of the Superior Court of Sonoma county, and re-elected in 1902.
In 1906 he was elected Justice of the District Court of Appeals
for the third appellate district, and again elected in 1910 for the
term of twelve years, and re-elected in 1922 for a like term of
twelve years.
Judge Burnett was married May 1, 1878, at Santa Rosa, to
Miss Hood, and there was born of that union three children, two
of whom-Albert' Hood and Alice Helen, are now living.
He was made a Mason in Sotoyome Lodge No. 123, Healdsburg, in 1882, subsequently affiliating with Santa Rosa Loge No.
57. In Grand Lodge he was Grand Orator, Junior Grand Warden,
Senior Grand Warden, Deputy Grand Master, and at the annual
communication of 1915 was elected Grand Master.
In his address to Grand Lodge in October, 1916, Grand Master Burnett uttered these words: "How forcibly the record of the
dead reminds us that we too, are passing away. The places that
know us now will soon know us no more forever. Whatever may
be the distinction we r.ow enjoy, we will soon meet upon the

460

common level of the tomb
Let us, my brethren, heed the
lesson of the grave; but may we also never close our eves to the
light that streams through its gloomy portals, revealing -the glory
ineffable that lies beyond. God grant that we may make the
most of the present life, that we may work while it is called
today, knowing that 'The night cometh when no man can work,'
that we may endure unto the end in the earnest, unremitting and
faithful discharge of our duties, and at the last great day recieve
the final judgment of the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe:
'Well done, good and faithful servant.'"

Recommendations
In addition to the recommendations made in connection with
matters already discussed, I make the following:
(1)

That the presentation of a copy of the Constitution and Ceremonies to each Mason, upon being given his third degree, be
discontinued and that a booklet to be published by the Committee on Masonic Education be given to every Mason, giving
the essentials that he should know. Investigation shows that
the Constitution is being continually changed and that the
members receiving the books are not reading them as they
should.

(2)

That each man petitioning for the degrees of Masonry should
be given a short outline of what Masonry is; its principles,
its aims and its responsibility-this in order that the petitioner cannot say that he did not know the character of the
institution he was joining. This could be made a part of the
petition itself, on a perforated form, to be torn off and retained
by the petitioner.

(3)

That the Grand Lodge will not recognize the claims of individual lodges in cities where there is an established Board
of Relief receiving re-ithbursement from Grand Lodge.
That the Committee on Policy and General Purposes give
careful and serious consideration to proposed projects for the
establishment of tuberculosis sanitoria for the benefit of members of the Craft, and to report at this Communication a tentative expression of policy thereon.

That requests for ruling by the Grand Master should be made
through the Inspector of the district and that his decisions
be given to the Masters through the Inspectors.
That elective and appointive Grand Officers of Grand Lodge
retain the past rank of the position which they have filled.

(7)

That lodges be prevented from advertising and selling tickets
for Sunday outings.
There can be no objection to a
quiet gathering of Masons and their families for an outing
on Sunday; nevertheless the promiscuous advertising or sale
of tickets is not in keeping with the dignity of our Fraternity.
(8) That the Grand Secretary be directed to revise the Constitution in order that its various provisions may be understood
by the lay members of the Fraternity.
(9) That waivers of jurisdiction be asked for by the lodge instead
of by the candidate if the matter of State concurrent jurisdiction is not accepted.
(10) One year has elapsed since the six months' rule became effective. A careful analysis shows that it has failed to accomplish
the purpose for which it was enacted-namely the increased
attendance at Illue Lodges. For this reason I believe the
wording of this amendment should be changed so as to place
upon a candidate a moral obligation to attend his lodge regularly during the six months' period and also that he must
secure his certificate of proficiency in the third degree.
(11) New Temples-The building of a Masonic Temple is most
commendable.
However, it often appears that plans are
adopted and lodges become obligated to construction plans
which result in burden far in excess of their financial capabilities. Without any purpose of hindering the building of
Masonic Temples, nevertheless it appears that much inconve111ence and anxiety might be averted if before a lodge
assumed any obligation in connection with the erection of
a Temple, that a general plan together with the scheme of
financing be approved by a committee composed of the Grand
Master, Grand Treasurer and the Chairman of the Finance
Committee.
(12) At the last session of Grand Lodge, Section 155 was amended
to make it mandatory that the first degree be conferred in the
lodge in which a petitioner was elected. This is unquestionably good legislation, but I believe that the Grand Master
should be given the authority to grant dispensations to confer
the first degree in other than the lodge in which the petitioner
is elected in cases where there is justifiable reason for doing
the same.

Conclusion
In conclusion I desire to emphasize the now generally recognized fact that Masonry has become a powerful factor in the
economic and political life of this land, and particularly so in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

462

463

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

California. By a political factor I refer to the influence for good
that Masons as citizens wield. A good Mason is a good citizen,
and a good citizen will watch with the closest attention the various
municipal, county, state and federal problems that are presented
for his determination at the polls. A good Mason, performing
his duty as a good citizen, will likewise watch closely such matters
as those that affect the schools of the land; matters dealing with
immigration; with the selection of individuals to public office, and
all these problems come within the scope of the duties of Masons
as good citizens. Let us bear in mind that this is a nation of
individual rulers; each citizen being a part and parcel of this
great government, thus forming a country with more than 110,000,000 rulers. Masons, as a selected class of men, should at
all times remember the words of our illustrious Brother Patrick
Henry when he warned that "Eternal vigilance is the price of
Liberty."
My closing admonition to this great body of California
Masonry is to "Watch" at all times; watch all political and economic problems and act upon them with the sole idea of benefiting our land and humanity, always remembering that "Like produces Like" is the eternal law of the universe, and that in the
end Right will prevail.
"Oh Liberty, white Goddess! Is it well
To leave the gates unguarded? On thy breast
Fold Sorrow's children, soothe the hurts of Fate,
Lift the down-trodden, but with hands of steel
Stay those who to thy sacred portals come
To waste the gifts of freedom. Have a care
Lest from thy brow the clustered stars be torn
And trampled in the dust. For so of old
The thronging Goth and Vandal trampled Rome,
And where the temples of the Caesars stood
The lean wolf unmolest• d made her lair.

ADDENDUM
At the beginning of the term the Grand Master announced he
would personally visit as many Lodges within the year as might be
physically possible. Meantime it was his purpose to communicate with
the brethren from time to time through the medium of printed circular
letters on matters pertaining to the Craft. The letters follow:
Bulletin No. 1
Masonry is today a vital force in the industrial, economic and
political life of California. Its tremendous influence for good has permeated every fiber of our social structure, resulting in noticeably improved conditions. It would be strange, indeed, were it otherwise.
The fact that nearly 100,000 men in California, past the age of twentyone, of high moral character and good standing in their respective
communities, are now enrolled in this Grand Jurisdiction is selr-evident
proof of the Fraternity's potential force in the state. I call these facts
to your attention, brethren, that all may fully appreciate and understand the great responsibility that devolves upon the 500 Masonic
Lodges in California, and upon each individual member of the Craft.
It is needless for me to attempt to voice my appreciation of the
honor done me by my elevation to the Grand Master's chair. But I
feel no elation; rather I assume my manifold duties humbly and with
a full knowledge of the great responsibility placed in my hands,
reverently hoping that the Gerat Architect of the Universe will so
guide my conduct that with the assistance of the Craft as a whole the
high standard of California Masonry will not only be maintained, but
the year's record will be one of progress, of constructive work, of a
fuller and clearer application of Masonic principles to daily affairs
than ever before recorded.
It is not, however, my pnrposc to foster or condone any radical
changes in established customs, nor to sanction any innovations not
consonant with the dignity, power and harmony of Masonic principles.
This does not mean that new ideas are to be frowned upon, for we
are early taught that Masonry is a "progressive science." In order to
keep pace with this progressive age in which we live we, too, must
be progressive in all things, particularly in reference to our duty as
inclividnal Masons.
Unfortunately, there is no gainsaying the fact that many members
of the Craft fail to realize what Masonry really means. They take
their membership as a matter of course, paying their dues, wearing an
emblem and by so doing feel that their responsibility to the Fraternity

has ended. This attitude is wrong and should be corrected. The
man who is raised to the sublime degree of a Master Mason immediately assuines responsibilities that cannot be lightly laid aside. Masonry
stands for Human Service; for the betterment of mankind; for a
broader and keener appreciation of the duty the good citizen owes to
his city, state and nation; for toleration and application of constructive
ideas. The Master Mason who fails to apply these principles to the
affairs of everyday life is false to his trust and false to the obligations he has voluntarily assumed. It can thus be seen that a good
Mason is perforce a good citizen. Also, we must remember that the
very foundation of our Institution is obedience to law and respect
for duly constituted authority. In this manner Masonry has from
time immemorial proved its constructive worth, for its aim is building, not destroying. Therefore, the Mason who by word or deed
deviates from this lofty line of thought and conduct deserves the censure of his brethren. It must not, however, be presumed that Masonry
seeks to restrict the individual Mason in regard to his social, political
or indu~rial activities; provided, of course, that he conforms to the
law of the land; nor is Masonry concerned with what other societies
the Master Mason may become affiliated, provided such organizations do not conflict with good citizenship. Masonry has no quarrel
with any organization, sect, creed nor race. Nor has Masonry any
desire to recognize, officially or unofficially, any organization, sect or
race, either by praise or adverse criticism. At the same time, however, the membership must understand that the Grand Master will
not tolerate any outside influence injecting itself in any manner into
any Masonic Lodge in this jurisdiction.
Harmony is one of the principal tenets of our faith, and it is the
duty of every member of the Craft to preserve this harmony in and
out of the Lodge. This means that every Mason should constitute
himself a committee of one whose duty it shall be to eliminate all
that savors of dissension. It is useless for us to close our eyes to
the fact that disturbing elements occasionally creep into our ranks.
Sometimes the discord is caused by mistaken enthusiasm on the part
of an over-zealous brother; sometimes it can be traced to professional
agitators who use their membership to foster personal projects; sometimes ulterior motives underlie the words of these misguided brothers,
and sometimes they are actuated solely by a wrongly directed desire
to help. No matter what the motive,· these brethren are a menace to
the peace and harmony of our ancient Institution and they must be
checked, even though it is necessary to discipline them through official
action of the Lodge.
The growth, development and reputation of the constituent Lodges
of the jurisdiction will always be uppermost in the mind of your Grand
Master. He believes, and wants the membership to appreciate the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

465

fact, that the whole Fraternity is but a reflection of the constituent
Lodges. The Grand Lodge itself expresses the combined intelligence
and sentiment of the Lodges composing it. Even though the most
beneficent and vital program possible were evolved in Grand Lodges,
unless it proved acceptable to the great body of the Order, it would
fail of accomplishment. So upon the character of the constituent
Lodges the greatness of the Fraternity depends. .Therefore, no problem is of greater importance than maintaining the quality and standing
of the constituent Lodges. While the Grand Lodge in the nature of
its powers must of necessity enact certain legislation for the guidance
and government of the Lodges, nevertheless the autonomy of the
Lodges should be closely and zealously guarded. Every energy of
Grand Lodge should be exerted to develop and encourage the constituent Lodges, so that through the enlargement of Lodge individuality each may become a greater agency for service to the membership,
the Fraternity and the several communities.
It is the opinion of your Grand Master that in these times of
rapidly increasing membership the ritualistic work of the Lodge should
be separated from the executive; that while the Master should be held
to accountability for the character of degree work, yet his energies
should be devoted more largely to the development of fraternal relations among his members, educational programs that will instruct yet
not disrupt his Lodge-in short, to do those things that will make his
Lodge a vital force for service and understanding in the community.
There are members who are peculiarly adapted to the conferring of
degrees and who delight in this work. In this they should be encouraged. However, there has gradually developed a tendency of progression in the line of officers in the constituent Lodges that should
be given very careful attention. Custom often becomes virtually law.
And while there is nothing in the Constitution to support it, nevertheless. it is practically a rule in most Lodges to promote officers from
the lowest appointive positions year after year until they reach the
Master's chair, regardless of their abilities or qualifications to discharge the important duties of the Lodge's chief executive. If the
appointive positions, as in Grand Lodge, became places of honor and
service rather than stepping-stones to the oriental chair, a greater
number of men of e"xperience in life's affairs would be attracted to
serve as officers. Under the present system efficient but busy men
often refuse to serve because of their inability to give the time to a
service requiring seven or eight years, while they would gladly and
enthusiastically serve three or four years. This is a subject I submit
for consideration in the constituent Lodges. It is a matter of custom
and not of legislation.

must the individual Mason be educated in the monitorial explanations

will be developed among men, to the elimination of all narrow jealousies and misunderstandings. Let Masonry have its day and play
its part in this new condition. The opportunity that is present should
be the inspiration fot: accomplishment.
Some Masons believe that the efforts of the Fraternity should be
expressed solely through the symbolic Lodges. This would appear
logical. Nevertheless, pending the acceptance and adoption of a definite
policy in conformity with that belief, other organizations whose memberships are composed entirely of Masons should not be discouraged
in honest efforts for good. One of the underlying principles of
Masonry is toleration, and if the Fraternity stands on that platform it
must extend toleration as well as demand it. Most of the social,
political and religious controversies of present-day Civilization are due
to intolerance, misunderstanding and sectionalism-influences which
Masons should seek to eradicate.

Bulletin No. 2-Christmas Greeting
Masonically, the message of "Peace on Earth, Good Will to All
Mankind," now ringing through Christendom, means "Brotherly
Love, Relief and Truth." And Jew or Gentile, Mohammedan or Hindu,
Brahmin or Confucian, kneeling together in perfect accord at the
common altar of Freemasonry, can and should at this particular season
return thanks to the Great Architect of the Universe for the many
blessings vouchsafed.
Peace is being restored throughout the world; the thoughts of
mankind are turning from destructive aims to useful pursuits. The
United States is entering an era of prosperity and our beloved California in particular is enjoying the Wessings of revived industry and
commerce.
Never in the history of Masonry in California has the condition
of the Fraternity as a whole been more satisfactory. Nearly five
huncw::d Lodges are flourishing and the individual members have
upheld the best traditions of the Craft. This is, however, a time for
retrospect and for the forward view.
We are concerned, each in his own position, that the Fraternity
may continue to make progress-that the mistakes and shortcomings
of the past may serve as warnings for the future. Always the wise
man profits by that which in his own experience has proven incomplete
or inadequate.
The year upon which we are about to enter will be big with events;
bigger still with possibilities for service .. A former contentment with
routine will not now suffice. Freemasonry in California must con-

468

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODG.HJ OF CALl.B'OHNIA

tinue to justify its existence and impress itself upon the common-.
wealth as a social agency of surpassing worth .. The impulse and purpose must come, not from Grand Lodge legislation, but from the work
of the constituent Lodges and the individual labor of every true
Mason. The Lodge must be, and be known as, a distinct asset in the
community life. It must be a rallying point for good citizenship, for
informed action-a center whence can be directed or re-enforced whatever movement may be for community good.
In each case and place the duty of the hour will be apparent to
those who earnestly seek out their required work.
With every Lodge taking up its full share of duty, and carrying
through its labor with single-minded and informed zeal, the Craft of
our great jurisdiction will be recognized as among those "foremost in
the ranks of time." The results depend upon you and your brothers,
according to the measure of opportunity and acceptance of duty.
And again, with the weight of responsibility resting upon me, I
wish for you and your Lodge, and for all good Masons, the best that
the Craft in its largest meaning can bring to you of good.
May Brotherly Love prevail and may the Great Architect of the
Universe bless and prosper you and yours.

Bulletin No. 3-0n the Problem of Illiteracy
Freemasonry is now recognized as one of the greatest educational
factors in the civilized world. In every land and clime it is waging
a constant and successful battle against bigotry and illiteracy. The
spreading of "Masonic Light" means lifting the yoke of ignorance from
the neck of the people. This applies to all problems, from that of
illiteracy to the various public questions that confront the voter. The
earnest and intelligent Mason, therefore, should realize and recognize
the vital civic problems that are continually arising and which should
be solved in accordance with the high principles of our Craft. These
problems, however, must be handled by the individual and not by the
Fraternity as a body, for Masonry's unchanging attitude is to keep
aloof from all matters not within its own particular sphere.
This does not mean, however, that a constructive program may
not be worked out and applied by the members of the various constituent Lodges under the direction of the Grand Lodge. It is, ih
fact, the duty as well as the high privilege of the Grand Master in
particular to call attention to the various pertinent questions .that
affect Masons as good citizens, and to offer certain suggestions calculated to correct abuses, improve conditions, inaugurate needed reforms or generally benefit th~ people as a whole.

lutely without learning must be added other millions whose edu?ation

been developed and sharpened are at the mercy of de:nagogues ~nd

su~~ .institutions have a considerable weight of facts to justify their
cnt1c1sms. But in most of the States, and especially in our own this

Bulletin No. 4-Public School Week
Grand Masters of California have in recent years directed attention of the Lodges and the brethren to the necessity for a concentration of interest upon the public schools of the State. These suggestions have been productive of great good. In every community it has
been possible for Masons "to arouse a spirit of inquiry and of intelligent action whenever matters affecting popular education have become

473

an issue. In again bringing the subject before the Craft of this jurisdiction your Grand Master does so with confidence, realizing that in
the desire to serve the cause and to safeguard future generations all
members of the Fraternity are united.
The President of the United States recently proclaimed an American education week. It was urged upon all the people to give consideration to the problems involved, to the end that popular education
might be furthered and the nation lifted from a position of admitted
inferiority to its proper place among the enlightened peoples of the
world. Other affairs of prior arrangement and relative importance
prevented the Craft of this State from joining, as Masons, in the discussions of that week. Yet we cannot allow that the manifest duty
shall be neglected, nor the year to pass without a concentration of
Masonic attention upon this all-important subject.
All good citizens are agreed that the wellbeing of the country,
and even its perpetuity, will depend upon the product of the schools.
The diminishing of ignorance, the fixing in the minds of the young
the great ideals of citizenship, of uprightness of life, and the necessity
for a grounding in the principles of integrity that human experience
has proven essential, are matters that cannot be neglected nor delayed,
except at risk to the very institutions upon which the security of the
nation rests.
It is not enough that the various communities shall join in the
erection of great school buildings, to which architects and health engineers shall contribute their most advanced ideas. The most perfectly constructed and completely equipped school building can of
itself give nothing of worth to the children gathered within its classrooms. It is only as the equipment and facilities are used by a teaching personnel of experience and peculiar adaptability to the work that
they become important and valuable. Therefore, it becomes the first
and most important matter of inquiry as to how. near the highest
standard the teaching force of a given school or system of schools can
reach. To expect the immature to furnish real instruction is folly.
The mere passing of examinations in book learning is not a sufficient
test of quality. There must be a rigid integrity of character, a knowledge of life and its manifold meanings, and a devotion to the profession. These are the qualities to be sought for. And with an insistent demand they will be forthcoming. The teaching profession is
not to be regarded as merely a stopgap in the lives of adolescent
young women, to be held to only until the opportunity for marriage
may present itsel_f. It is a profession demanding the utmost that men
and women can give of service, having influence for good more lasting than is possible in any other line of endeavor.

474

PROCEEDINGS OF' THI<J

With a perfect teaching force, concerned only for th~ presentation of truth and able to apply the proper tests, the question of text
books might' perhaps not come within the province of the community
or of those among the citizens having greatest concern for the betterment of the schools. But under existing conditions, with many influences at work to present erroneous ideas and ideals, with economic
falsities rampant, dangerous social heresies abroad, with .diverse p~r­
tisanships loudly advocated and sectarianisms of many kmds seekmg
expression the text books of the State and nation are being sought
as a subtle yet most effective means of propaganda. They_ are not
safely to· be left to the judgment of inexperienced teachers nor to
those who sometimes gain position of authority who may be the too!J,
whether conscious or unconscious, of designing interests. Other societies and institutions are analyzing the text books placed before the
children and young people of the land, and with some the motives
are not beyond suspicion. In this matter Masons can have but one
concern-that the truth, so nearly as is possible, shall have clear statement, to the end that the habit of free and untrammeled thought shall
be of the possessions of our future citizens.
In every community the school probiems will be particularly presented. There can be no set program for discussion. The duty· before
any body of brethren is to consider seriously the situation existing at
home· to consider the needs and to devise ways and means for betterme~ts as these may be developed by keen inquiry and open-minded
discussion. There can be no value to discussions that stop short of
the real truth. To shirk a situation because certain local interests
are involved or because certain individuals or groups may be offended,
is to lose all that may have value. It should be borne in mind that
the majority of people, in any community, are vitally concerned in the
public schools. And these will rally, without reservation, to support
of any who take up the subject of improvement without suspicion of
personal or institutional bias or unworthy interest.
With the idea of calling the particular attention of all Masons in
the jurisdiction of California to the public schools of the State, it is
hereby directed that the week commencing Monday, March 19, 1923, be
observed as Public Schools Week, and it is the order of the Grand
Master that all the Lodges in the jurisdiction, either singly or in
groups, foregather one evening of that week for the purpose of dis~
cussion and information on subjects relating to public education.
A suggested program will be mailed each Lodge by the .spe~ial
committee created by Grand Lodge at its last annual commumcat1on.
Dated at San Francisco, California, February l, 1923.
