REPORT OF TRUSTEES, MASONIC HOMES
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:
Brethren: We present herewith our report for the fiscal year ending July 31st, as to financial matters and to October 1, 1923, relative to
the general condition of the homes.
The board met immediately after the adjournment of Grand Lodge
and the Secretary announced that to fill the vacancy caused by the
expiration of the term of Brother C. M. Wollenberg, the M. W. Grand
Master ha~ reappointed him for a term of four years.
R. W. Albert C. Boynton, the newly installed Junior Warden was
also seated as a member of the board.
Brother C. M. Wollenberg was elected President and Brother
Jam es Gist, Vice President.
During the year, regular meetings were held at San Francisco and
Los Angeles, and weekly conferences by the Trustees living in the
vicinity of both cities.
There has been 110 change in the personnel at the Homes. Brother
· Frank B. Hartman at Decato and Brother Leland S. Drew at Covina,
who arc, as Superintendents, directly in charge of the homes, deserve
the commendation of the Grand Lodge for the efficient manner in which
the work of the H omcs is conducted.
Mention should also be made of Matrons Maude E. Miller and
Minnie Richardson and their staff of workers for their constant watchfulness and care of their charges.

548

549

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Building Operations at Decato

Work is now starting and it is hoped that the buildings will be
ready for occupancy by June, 1924.
The increase in the number of our children has been so rapid that
these buildings are urgently needed.

Our annual report for 1922 related that new buildings were beipg
constructed at the Decoto Home, and we now report that the new
dormitory of eighty rooms for women is completed and occupied; the
men's dormitory of one hundred rooms is so near completion that it
may be occupied within two months; the two wings added to the
hospital are now occupied.
To provide adequately for the growth of the Home it was found
necessary to reconstruct the dining room and kitchen, and also to provide for an assembly hall. This structure will doubtless be completed
before the end of the year. Meantime the basement of the men's new
dormitory is being used as dining room and kitchen.
The six wooden cottages now occupied by men residents will be
vacated as soon as the new dormitory is finished. These cottages are
little better than fire-traps, and your Trustees feel that our aged
brethren at the Home should not be subject to the constant danger
from fire.
As we reported last year, we all appreciate that the cost of building now is all but prohibitive, but we know our brethren of the jurisdiction will endorse the labors of the Trustees in their endeavors to
accord every proper care for the residents of the Home, whose suns
are nearly set, and who so patiently and cheerfully and calmly await
the day of their going to the "realm where the rainbow never fades."

Decoto Buildings
The cost lo date for new buildings and reconstruction, including
amounts to be paid on contracts not yet completed, is $602,099.

Covina Buildings
In our 1922 report we informed the Grand Lodge that the increase
in population at Covina would necessitate the erection of additional
buildings. Considerable thought was given to the type of building
to be erected and it was finally decided to continue the present plan.
Brother Robert Train, Past Master of Pentalpa Lodge No. 202 was
selected as architect and instructed to prepare plans for two buildings,
each to contain quarters for about 50 children (one for boys, one for
girls), matrons quarters, living room, study rooms, and isolation room.
After many revisions, plans were finally adopted and bids called for.
011 September 22nd, proposals were opened from 31 bidders and awards ·
of contract were made as follows:
General Contract, John Simpson Co., Los Angeles .................. $153,500.00
Plumbing and Steam }kating, Arthur Hess Corp.,
Los Angeles .........._. ....................................................................... .
20,760.00
Electric, Newberry Elect. Co., Los Angeles ............................ .. 4,836.00
Painting, A. S. Grant, Los Angeles .............................................. .. 5,300.00

Finances
The building program as outlined above indicates an expenditure
in a period of about three years of over $800,000 when we include
equipment.
This has been made possible by the $20 contribution paid by all
initiates. \Vhen this scheme was proposed in 1919 the report of the
Homes showed an annual deficit which had to be made up by Grand
Lodge.. Since this method of financing was adopted, we have reduced
the per capita assessment on the lodges from $1.00 to 25 cents per
annum, met all the running expenses and will have made the above
capital investment, all paid for by January, 1925.
Details of receipts and expenditures will be found in the reports
of the Secretary and Treasurer.

Physically Incapacitated
During the year the Trustees in accordance with the authority
granted by the Grand Lodge in 1921, have assisted various lodges in
caring for those brothers whose physical condition made their admission to the Ii ome impossible.
Our infirmary at Decoto, although enlarged, will not do more
than care for the residents of the home as infirmities creep upon them.
Again distance from a large center makes it difficult to get nurses and
other hospital employees, as well as medical specialists. We believe
the plan adopted is working out successfully and will continue affording this relief.
Visits and Visitors
We recognize the fact that no hrother can visit the homes without
receiving inspiration and that he carries that inspiration away with him
as well as the fixed purpose to do more in the fUture for Masonry than
he has done in the past. He carries a message throughout the state
and the effect of his visit cannot be easily measttred.
Welcoming visitors as we do and encottrag"ing visits of lodges
an<l other Masonic bodies, we have nevertheless found it necessary to
change some of the customs at the Covina Home. Nearly every Sunday in the year saw a body of Masons at the hnme, and in anticipation
of this visit thi: spare time of the chilclreu cluring the preceding week
was spent in getting up and drilling for an entertainment. This not
only took up the time of the tlome employees but also time that shonlcl
have been spent by the children in play or school study. We are still
inviting and welcoming visits of lodges and other Masonic bodies. on

550

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Sunday or any other convenient day, and our children will conduct
you through and explain the buildings; but as for entertainment, we
will expect you to bring that with you for the amusement of the
children.
We are sure that you will approve the change when you know
that now the children look forward to the coming visit with pleasure
and anticipation instead of apprehension.
Grand Lodge will visit our home at Decato this week. You will
see for yourself the magnitude of our building program, but more important you will meet our residents and from their happiness or discontent, form your own conclusion as to the success of our home.
We wish you could visit the home at Covina. All who are fortunate enough to do so come away inspired; and it is hoped that if
you are in the vicinity of Covina you will make it a duty to call at the
home.
Bequests and Gifts
We want to express our appreciation to the Grand Chapter of the
Eastern Star for the gift of furnishings for the social halls of the
new men's and women's buildings. They have appropriated $1000 for
each hall and are now engaged in installing the furniture in the
women's building. The men's social hall will be cared for as soon as
we are ready. W. Grand Matron Miss Stella Linscott is giving this
her personal attention. ·
Thanks also to the many local chapters that are always engaged
in sewing for the homes. Dresses for the girls, sheets, spreads, etc.
for both homes are largely produced by these chapters. We received
and have transferred to the endowment fund gifts and bequests as
follows:

Decoto Home Report of Superintendent

special meetings, and at times trips are made to Oakland San Francisco and towns in the vicinity of the Home.
'

To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California:
I herewith present for your consideration my fourteenth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decato, California,
for the year ending September 30, 1923.
The furnishings for the social room, a donation by the Grand
Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, have been selected by
a committee appointed by the Grand Matron and win be installed as
soon as delivery is made.
The first floor of the north and south wings of the hospital are
now occupied by men and women residents of the Home who are being
cared for there. The ladies' solarium has been furnished with wicker
furniture which was donated by the Guild to the Ladies Auxiliary to
California Commandery, No. 1, K. T. The first and second floors
of the hospital are connected with the women's building by two runways.
The new buildings, main building and hospital, all have elevator service.
There are now at the Home 88 men and 69 women. During the
year 41 persons have been admitted; 34 have passed away. The general
health of he family has been good with the exception of those who are
infirm and feeble owing to advancing years. There are 23 persons being
cared for in the hospital, where they are receivi_ng every care and atten•
tion our physician and nurses· are able to give _them.
The members of our family are encouraged to interest themselves
in the welfare of the Home and to render assistance in the general
routine work. A number of the brethren have assisted by their labors
in the carpenter and paint shops, in the care of the garage, mail, passenger and express service, kitchen, pantry and light work in a general
way.
The mending of linen, the making and marking sheets, table cloths,
pillow slips, etc., is done by the ladies of the Home. They also take
care of their rooms, halls, etc., and assist in light household work.
The water supply has been plentiful for household, garden, irrigating and building purposes. The deep well pump has been ove'rhauled and is now in good order.
There are now 3200 volumes on the shelves of our library. In
addition to this, our reading tables in the men's club rooms, the ladies'
social room and hospital are well supplied with daily papers and periodicals.
Each month arrangements are made so that members of the Home,
a few at a time, have an opportunity to visit Alameda Lodge, No. 167,
F. & A. M. and Orient Chapter, No. 177, 0. E. S. at their stated and

563

. The Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, at
their Annual Communication, 1922, appropriated $1,000.00 for the furnishing of the club room in the new men's building. This amount is
available as soon as the building is ready to be occupied.
As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been leased
either on shares or cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of fruit
for table use, the surplus being dried and stored for future use. The
hay crop has given good returns. The garden has supplied vegetables
for the table and plenty of greens. The chicken ranch has furnished all
eggs for table use, the surplus has been sold or put up in water-glass
for winter use.
·
All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The
sp_ecials were those held on New Year's Eve, New Year's Day, Lincoln's
Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day, Fourth of
July, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas.
Moving pictures and miscellaneous programs are given from time
to time in the Siminoff Temple. An orchestra, consisting of a violin
and piano take part in all of our entertainments. These programs are
given entirely by members of the Home. The Thursday evening socials
have been discontinued 1111til the new assembly hall is provided. Chorus
practice is held every Friday evening and the usual services are held
every Sunday afternoon, followed by a musical concert.
A number of literary and musical entertainments have been given
by generous volunteers from lodges, members of lodges and visiting
friends. The following is a list of the events which have contributed
to our enjoyment:
September 2: East Bay Lodge, No. 489, gave a luncheon in the
grove followed by an entertainment in the Temple.
September 14: Brooklyn Lodge, No. 225, accompanied by the Municipal Band of Oakland, gave a concert on the grounds of the Home.
September 16: Alcatraz Lodge, No. 244, Third Degree in the Temple, Smoker.
September 21: Illustrated lecture, "Washington, the Man and
Mason," by Brother Harry L. Todd.
September 23: Durant Lodge, No. 268, entertained the family with
a miscellaneous program.
September 30: McKinley Lodge, No. 347, conferred third degree
in Temple, Smoker.

En-

Most Worshipful Grand Master William A. Sherman and members
of the Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the Home, also
many of the brethren and friends interested in our welfare have spent
many pleasant hours with us.
I extend to the officers and employes my appreciation of the loyal
assistance rendered and the conscientious and painstaking efforts given
to the work in their respective departments.
I desire to thank the members of the Board of Trustees for the
kindly consideration always given in meeting the varied problems in
the Home, bringing to the work an influence which has in no small
measure shaped and moulded the moral and spiritual strength of our
family life.
Fraternally submitted,
FRANK B. HARTMAN,

Superintendent.

Covina Home Superintendent's Report
To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California:
The continued increase in the number of children at the Masonic
Home at Covina has complicated and increased the duties of every
member of the staff. However, each one seems willing to assume the
added burden and it is our desire at all times to strive for the highest
moral, mental and physical development of the children. As superintendent of the Home I feel that any success which has been attained
throughout ·the year has largely come as a result of the support given
by the Trustees and the various Masonic organizations and the cooperation of the various co-workers in the Home.
\Ve are anticipating with a great deal of pleasure the erection of
two new, modern dormitory buildings which will relieve the crowded
condiHon existing at the Home at the present time.
The International Sunday School Series have been introduced
and used in the Home throughout the year and have added greatly to
the interest and success of our Sunday School. General exercises,
directed by the children, are held each Sunday morning and special
music enjoyed, after which the classes repair to their respective rooms
to study the lesson more carefully. There are eight of these classes
and each is presided over by a competent teacher.
The children have shown excellent progress in their school work
and have taken a great interest in the school life and activities. \Ve
feel very fortunate in having such splendid schools at our disposal as
the Charter Oak Grammar school and the Covina High school, both
under the supervision of Ben S. Millikan, District Superintendent.
Bro. Millikan stands ready at all times to co-operate to the end that
each child. shall be served to his best interest. This fall school commences with thirty-three children enrolled. in High school and seventysix enrolled in Grammar school. Two are commuting daily to Los
Angeles, a boy in attendance at a trade school and a girl at business
college.
At the Home, special emphasis is put on music, domestic science,
physical training and manual training, besides encouraging the children
to keep up their home study in connection with their daily lessons.
This· is accomplished thru the efforts of our regular staff, a boys'
director having been added this year to handle manual and physical·
trammg and supervise the older boys.
·
Drs. W. P. Magan and S. S. Magan have continued their excellent
work as physicians for the Home. While their work is voluntary, we
are shown every consideration possible at all times. We are extremely
fortunate to have such capable and up-to-date men as the Magans to

579

watch after the health of the children. Most of the work is handled
thru office calls or calls by the doctors at the Home. Occasionally it
is necessary for operations to use the Covina Hospital.
Our good friend, Dr. J. M. Dunsmoor, has counseled with us
throughout the year and recently examined the children and recommended that several have tonsils and adenoids removed. This will be
attended to in a'ccordance with the recommendation very shortly.
Dental work has continued under the capable leadership of Bro.
Warren D. Gill. The children are divided into eleven groups. Following is a list of the very competent dentists, each of whom cares for his
group and is responsible for it.
Dr. Leo M. Baughman. Dr. Albert E. Saunders. Dr. Clarence M.

Dr. H. M. Barnhart has taken the responsibility for prophylaxis.·
The condition of the teeth of the children means a great deal to
their health and. proper development, and we are gratified to have the
above mentioned men take this active interest in the Home.
At the time of the writing of this report mental and physical surveys have been completed by our good friend and brother, Dr. Arthur
J. Ritter, physiologist of Stanford University Medical School, at~d ?r.
R. P. Sietz, assistant to Dr. Harold K. Faher, professor of pediatries,
Stanford University. A very thorough and conscientious analysis was
made of each individual child and we feel that with this knowledge to
assist us we can better understand each individual and be ahle to work
for his best interest.
This report would not he complete without mentioning the excellent work done by a member of the Fraternity, Dr. George H. Kress,
eye, ear and nose, throat specialist, who prescribes all glasses for the
children. He is always willing to serve us and will receive no remuneration for the work he does.

orange trees which require a great deal of care and which as yet yield

and vegetables are produced to supply the Home.

sufficient quantities and of the best quality to provide a very satisfactory
diet.
In regard to the hygienic surroundings, they are without fault.
The sleeping quarters are airy and each child has a bed of his own.
The children wash in running water and have individual towels, wnicn
the chance of spreading any infection that might overtake any
of the children.
A competent, trained nurse has been employed in the past year.
At regular intervals she makes inspection of all the children and anything that is not right is checked up before it has gotten under way.
The lavatories are kept. in quite a sanitary manner, and we have
not found that they have been a cause of spreading disease. The
larger percentage of the bathing is done with the shower baths. Bathtubs are still in use, however, but proper sanitary cleansing we believe
eliminates their spreading infection.
The children are well supplied with the proper clothing and shoes.
Cognizance is being taken of the fact that a number of the children are
flat-footed and orthopaedic shoes are being secured for them. Some
of the flat footed cases are undoubtedly due to their stay at the beach
in the summer, where they go barefooted practically all the time,
playing and romping a good deal on the sand. \Vhen they return from
the beach, it seems necessary to refit them, as their feet have broadened
out considerably.
'vVe wish to take this opportunity to express our appreciation of
the co-operation and courtesies which our superintendent, Mr. Drew,
and the matron, Mrs. Miller, and their associates have shown us at all
times. Whatever we feel is necessary, we have no trouble in securing,
and we deem it a pleasure, as well as a privilege, to be able to work
for these children who are in one way not so fortunate as some, yet
in other ways are far more so. We do not believe that the average
American home has as many opportunities and privileges to offer as
the Home for the children here at Covina.
V\.'ELLESLltY P. MAGAN,

. The usual outings! including a four days Easter vacation trip to
Camp Baldy, and six weeks summer vacation to Balboa have been
indulged in and appreciated greatly by all. It seems as the Home grows
our pleasures grow in like proportion. Of course the 'greatly increased
nu~ber o~ ~he larger children in the Home makes for a great deal of
socia! activity. A good many of these socials and recreations are
ment.10ned under visitations, but. these do not include the countless
evenmgs of pleasure which are spent at the Home.
Fraternally submitted,
L. S. DREW, Superintendent.

Resident Physicians' Report
This report takes into consideration only the things which have
to do more or less directly with the health of the children of the Home.
. The children, during the past year, have been more free from .
disease than in any previous year while they have been under our care.
Last year there were two or three severe epidemics, including influenza
a~d diphtheria, but with no fatalities. This year there has not been a
smgle case of diphtheria in the Home, and the only epidemic was a
small .one of scar.let fever, which we were able to control very satisfactorily and which did not become general throughout the Home.
There have been no epidemics of colds or influenza this year. In the
C~artei: Oak schoo~ and the Covina High school there was quite an
ep1dem1c of whoopmg cough. All the children at the Home were
immunized against this malady by a series of serum treatments with
the very gratifying results that, although some cases had star;ed to
develop, the disease made no further progress.
.
Generally speaking, the health of the children has shown a marked
improvement over that of the past years.
From time to time, we have endeavored to keep in touch with
the. diet of the children in one way or another; eating with them in
their dining room and inspecting the kitchen, dairy, etc. The diet
seems to be 11ourishi11g and well balanced, and conforms thoroughly
to the standard for a growing child. There is an abundance of fresh
vegetables and fruits at all times, and no combinations of "left-overs
are put together and served to the children. The food is plainly cooked
but appetizing, and the children seem to enjoy their meals.
The average consuniption per child per day of milk has been about
one quart, butter, two ounces, the green vegetables and fresh fruits in

MENTAL AND PHYSICAL SURVEY OF MASONIC
HOME FOR CHILDREN AT COVINA
By ARTHUR JoHN RITTER, Lecturer on Mental Deficiency and
M. D., Professor of Medicine and Executive
Head of the Division of Pediatrics, and

HAROLD K. FABER,

P. SEITZ, M. D., From the Division of Pediatrics of
Stan( ord University Medical School.

RoLAND

October, 1923.
MENTAL EXAMINATIOXS
There are at the present time 113 children, ( 62 girls and 51 boys)
at the Home, with the following enrollment in the Public and V ocational schools :
1 Below school age.
80 Grammar school.
29 High school.
1 Business college.
1 Trade school.
1 Auto training school.

The report was adopted, except the request for a 25-cent
per capita tax, which was referred to the Committee on

113
The mental development of ·the children varies from normal to
normal superior intelligence. There are a few youngsters slightly retarded. This is particularly noticeable in those who hav~ only recently
entered the home. It is a very striking fact that children who have
been at the home from one to two years have a decided advantage
over the newcomers, which is largely due to the adjustment, opportunities, hygiene, en~ironment and proper feeding.
The following table will show the comparative standing of the.
children, with ages in years and months, expressed in points, the maximum being 100; as well as the school grades 1922-1923.

The Board of Trustees. following our recommendation of 1922
appointed a Boys' Director, Mr. G. Dalager, who has had considerabl~
experience with boys. This arrangement has proven of great benefit
as they are supervised in play, athletics and· manual training.

It was most gratifying to your examiners to note the interest and
co-operation exhibited by your Superintendent and House-Mothers.
They were most anxious to know how and under what conditions the
best results could be obtained from the individual child and their welfare safeguarded.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION OF THE CHILDREN
All of the children in the Home were given a complete physical
examination. There follows a report of their condition as a group.
Individual recommendations are being prepared and will be forwarded
to the Superintendent and Medical Advisor. The weights and heights
of the children were compared, as in previous years, with the standard tables of Wood. A summary of the results of this comparison
shows:

The percentage was stated correctly.
These figures for the two years are strictly comparable, having been
calculated in the same way and by the same standard. The weighings
were made at about the same time of the year, after vacation. They
indicate a real and striking improvement in the nutrition of the children and are eloquent; testimony of improved conditions of diet,
hygiene and general health. It will be well for the general reader to
recall that good authorities do not regard an individual child who is
less than 10% underweight as necessarily abnormal, and it is therefore
extremely gratifying to find this year only two children more than
10% underweight instead of 13, as in 1922.
The examiner was impressed by the almost universal success attained by good dental hygiene. Of course, a few carious teeth were
seen but the dentists are already preparing for another annual examination. The posture of the children was generally very good and
this finding is almost a counterpart of the sturdy muscles the majority
posses. Tanned, healthy skins prevailed as a result of a six-week
sojourn at the beach. A single case of impetigo was discovered but
since it is receiving vigorous treatment, the patient was subjected to
a less rigorous isolation.
A relatively large number of the children were found to have conjunctivitis. Some of these cases were of a chronic nature, while
others, fewer in number, had acute attacks of the type popularly

DIET
The food served in the Home is of good quality, and the clean,
sanitary way in which it is handled is commendable. The cooking
still remains mediocre and this deficiency is best seen in the meats
The diet is not well balanced and there seems to be a preclominanc~
of starchy foods. Green vegetables might be offered in greater abundanc~ than .at. ~resent. Consultation with and regular supervision by
a tramed dietitian would do much to eradicate the faults mentioned.
GENERAL HYGIENE
No criticism can be directed towards the housekeeping and the
cleanliness of the dormitories is praiseworthy.
'
RECOMMEND A TIO NS

. In. a h.ome of the type dealt with in this report the dangers of
ep1clen11c. disease are constantly present. Because of the contact with
other ~h1lclren .at. s~hool, in the cities and elsewhere these clangers are
~nly slightly m~nnm~ecl by the high sanitary plane on which this home
is . run._ ~f prune importance as an efficient safeguard against such
e~1dem1cs is the ~ver-watchf~l eye of one sufficiently trained to recogmze
early the
.
. evidence of disease and promptly initiate suitable isol a _
ti.on. ~recaut10ns to prevent its spread. Such action will certainly
d1mm1sh the freq.uency of colds, tonsilitis, conjunctivitis and many
more dangerous diseases. Among these last, diptheria may be quoted

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

617

as an example; only efficient treatment averted at least one fatality
from this disease in the Home during the past year. A trained nurse
with special experience in the diseases of childhood could isolate cases
early and irt many instances initiate routine treatment before the arrival of the physician. She could care for minor illnesses and do
many of the simpler dressings. The proper woman for such a position
would possibly command a larger salary than is now paid but she
would more than repay the expenditure with the services performed.
While discussing the transference of contagious disease attention
is drawn to the poor facilities at present afforded the care of towels.
In the girls' dormitory individual towels are hung in contact with
those adjacent and thus all the disadvantages and dangers of the
common towel are retained. Similarly, individual containers are advised for the care of toothbrushes.
Finally, the value of the shower bath is once more emphasized and
the writer urges reconsideration of the plans for the new buildings
which, it is understood, call for bathtubs.
The conditions of overcrowding that have followed the increase
in number of the children in the Home necessitate larger quarters and
these we are pleased to hear have been provided for by the decision of
the Board of Trustees to erect two more buildings for the high school
children.
A word should be said about the records of the children which
should be provided at the time of admission to the Home. These
should include completer family and environmental history as well as
information regarding school progress and standing up to the time of
admission.
We wish to congratulate the Superintendent, Mr. L. S. Drew, on
the efficiency with which the Home is evidently conducted and which is
reflected in the improved condition of the children who have been
under his care long enough to show the benefits. In Mrs. Miller, your
examiners feel that the Home has a matron of unusual qualifications
for the place and whose motherly solicitude for the children under
her care is highly commendable. Mrs. Avery, the assistant matron,
has capably filled her position and has ably seconded Mrs. Miller's
efforts to make the care of these children as nearly that which would
be given in an ideal home as possible.
Such crisicisrns and recommendations as have been made are in the
main matters of deta ii and are offered with the intention of helping to
uphold the high health standards at which the Home has always aimed.
The general policies of the Home and the manner in whfoh they have
been carried out merit high praise.

The Board of Directors of the Masonic Temple Association of
California are again pleased to report a year of progress. All the
stores on the ground floor have been rented, and the Masonic Halls
well filled. The annual expense of operation has been reduced. The
net earnings, .exclusive of the interest charge, amount to $13,615.43,
which, in view of the fact that the location of the Temple is yet distant from the general business activity of San Francisco, is regarded
as satisfactory. It will be remembered that the old Masonic Temple at
'Montgomery and Post Streets, which was so remunerative to its stockholders in tater years, did not pay dividends for over twenty years
after erection, while the new Temple began making payments in liqt1idation of its mortgaged indebtedness some three years ago.
The trend of business out Market Street is now beginning to be
felt near the location of our new Temple. We are confident that in
a very short time increased rentals may be secured for the stores on
the ground floor, as they will be more and rl\ore in demand as the city
steadily advances commercially and in population.
The present indebtedness on the Temple consists of a mortgage of
but $40,000.00, which, if paid, will reduce our annual expense some
$2,400.00.
If the mortgage were paid off dividends could be paid, small at
first, but constantly increasing. The Grand Lodge is by far the largest
stockholder and therefore will be the largest beneficiary from its income.
We suggest therefore that the Grand Lodge subscribe for the
amount necessary to pay off the mortgaged indebtedness ($40,000.00)
and by so doing clear the Temple of all incumbrance.

EULOGY BY DR. JACOB NIETO
Most Worshipful and Brethren: It is meet and proper that we
• should .set aside an interim in the midst of our business that we may
the better be enabled to consecrate our own lives for the great and
glorious purposes which we have undertaken to perform.
For the dead we can do nothing. To them we can render no service.
But we, judging by their example an<l taking pattern by what they
have done, may be enabled more strongly and more thoroughly to
plan our own lives in accordance with the dictates of righteousness
and to make it possible for us to improve our own personal condition,
that we may be better as men, as Masons and as citizens.
Memory comes to us at a moment like this, and while it rededicates
us in a measure to the great purposes we have in view, it arranges a
panoramic scene before our eyes and we see in our· mind's vision
familiar faces peering in upon us, familiar forms go trooping by, the
men that we loved and honored, the men whom we criticised and
were unkind to, the men whom we slighted or whom we thought of no
consequence, one after the other they pass us by, and we are bound
to question ourselves as to our own conduct toward them and toward
all other men whom we meet day by day.
• Involuntarily a searching investigation is going on within ourselves,
and we are trying, if possible, to analyze our own feelings and to
bring our reason to bear upon the things that we do and say day by
day, forced upon us as a recognition that we ourselves are not faultless
and are guilty very often of many things we should not have done and
of speeches we should never have delivered.
Conning over our own censure of those who, now dead, had
earned at our hands, we question whether we were right. And it is

622

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

right that we should always question ourselves when it comes to a
matter of censuring a fellow being. We realize quite fully, and should
always keep in mind, the fact that impulse and reason never keep pace
with one another, and that we do things impulsively that reason
condemns immediately afterwards. And we deplore the fact that our
reason is not present with us all the time; and under the excitement
of either great affection or the feeling that should never exist in a
Mason's heart, we have done something ourselves that we should
never have done, and for which we. sincerely regret the performance.
We question ourselves as to our actions toward our brethren. \Ve
love to praise a man when he does something good. We should,
without envying him the honor and distinction which have come to
him through his own endeavors. And we should never allow our
feelings so to enter into our analysis of the things done or said by our
fellow beings that we prejudice our judgment against him one way
or the other.
Affection sometimes leads us to exaggerate the value of deeds or
words of the men whom we love, but hatred or dislike should never •
lead us to unnecessarily and unjustly condemn any one. We feel these
things at a time like this, and we deplore our weaknesses when we recall
the names and the faces of those with whom we have been intimate
in life, and who have had some effect upon our existence, as we hope
we had had upon theirs.
In this great and distinguished Fraternity we ought to be able to
question ourselves very severely and to take ourselves to task earnestly
in regard to the course we have followed. in the Fraternity, for the
Fraternity, and that for which the Fraternity exists; the promotion
of education, enlightenment and democracy in the world.
\Ve should question ourselves very closely as to whether, as Masons,
we have taken our proper place and stand in regard to all the public
questions that have arisen in our country, whether we have proven
true to standard, whether we have been conscious of the great work
that has been done by those who founded this Institution, in this
country at least, and ·whether, following their example or taking
license from what they have done, we have striven in the degree to
which we were able to strive to do something for the great cause for
which they struggled and for which they perhaps had to suffer.
It is no small thing to dedicate yourself to a great and glorious
cause, the cause of humanity. It is no small thing to be able to
include yourself amongst a band of men who are supposed to throw
aside every personal consideration and to labor for the welfare of
others, to put aside all idea of self-promotion or self-adulation and
to give one's self over entirely for that which may be done to further
the interest of your fellow creatures, to do in some degree, in some

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

623

slight degree, or to strive to do that ~hie? th; gr~at -fathers of this
country and the founders of this orgamzat1on m this land have done
before us ; to try and loosen the bands of oppression and to make the
thongs that bind not chafe while binding; g~adua!ly to loosen them,
that freedom may come in time, and progess1vely ; .and not to g<; to

It is a wornlt·rful spirit that pervades our country. NOW and again
a bigot will arise here and there, or a group of bigots will arise
here and there about the country, but of the general tone and tenor and
spirit of the population of this, our blessed country, there can be no
doubt but that it remains pure, glorious and splendid in its character of
absolute toleration towards all religious faiths and towards all sorts
and conditions of men.

this jurisdiction have done great work in their time. One saw that
a school was founded that might take charge of boys whose opportunities were not of a character to promote th.cir welfare in life, who
lived perhaps in environments that were destructive of the best that
was in them, and the Preston School is an example of that. We have
had men prominent in educational matters, life Foshay of Los An~eles.
\Ve have had men in other walks of life, that have been promment
at the bar, who have promulgated laws and statutes in .the State, that
have done good to everyone. But we have had besides, my good
brethren, hundreds of others who were not known by us, the great
mass of the unknown, who, without any fame being showered upon
them or any compliments being rendered them for what . they ?ad
done, or the hope of any reward moving them, have made. It possible
for these men and for others to go forward with strength, with courage
and with determination to accomplish the great things that have been
done by this Fraternity, in the name of Masonry and for the benefit
of humanity. For them also let us have a kindly thought. But for
them we could not flourish. But for the hundreds of those who
mod~stly and humbly come forward and contribute their individuality,
whatever it may amount to, to our cause, we could not proceed. And
bear in mind that there is no man so humble that he is not of some
value in the up-building of a great institution or a great cquntry.
Never overlook what you might consider the meanest of mortals,
whether in or out of your Lodge. Remember that God has moulded
us all for a purpose, and though it may be trne that we blindly grope
and never seem to find the purpose for which God had made us, yet
in the design of Providence, which is beyond our human concep:,
we all fit in and fill a place where we perform some useful task, tf
not for our own benefit, at least for the benefit of others.
At a time like this we ought to feel a debt of gratitude to those
who have left us a rich harvest which we are garnering today. These
men who labored and have gone to their eternal rest have left us a
rich heritage. Shall we prove worthy of it? Shall we endeavor to
prove worthy of it? Shall we strive with all our power and might to
do things which as good men, Masons and citizens, we ought to do?
Shall we not determine at a moment like this, shall we not make
a solemn resolve that from this time forward we will not he lackadaisical, we will not be indifferent to the things that are happening in
our country, in our city or anywhere else in the world, when a word
from us or a little act performed hy us may add to the sum total of
·good <lone for humanity at large? Shall we not determine now that
from this time forward all the things that should he done in our
country w~ will regard as personal, individual obligations settling upon
ourselves? Shall we not do that in order to make ourselves worthy

\Ve are .a generous people ; we are generous to the entire world;
we arc anxious to help; not only anxious to help, but we do help;
and whenever necessity arises anywhere in the world for assistance to
be afforded, no matter what the cause of the disaster might be or
the source of the trouble, we never ask any questions, but with tiue
religious spirit we go forward to help.
You would not ask a hungry man how it came about that he had
no food; you would not if you were a true American citizen and a
true Mason; you would feed him because he was hungry, just as God
feeds us all.
The dangers. in this country can only be fostered where education
is lacking. With wider information and knowledge afforded the
growing population, our institutions and our country will remain
secure.
Our children are the great assets of this country; our children;
all the children; they are the future citizens, the future promoters
of all that is good, the future defenders of the institutions of our
country. And we have taken a firm stand on the proposition of
education, and we owe it to the forefathers of our country, and to
the founders of the organization of Masons here, we owe it to them
to be sincere, to be earnest, to be energetic, to be watchful, to be
alert upon this proposition of the education of our children. It must
be an education where a child is taught to think, and not the kind
of education where a child's mind is crammed with a lot of facts
and its mind never urged to exert itself in thinking.
This is the proposition which we have before us at this time. A
thinking population can accomplish wonders, but a dull and stupid
mass of people, who can be moved by any demigod that comes along,
is a great menace to the institutions that we love. \Ve want to know,
as we question ourselves at a solemn moment like this, whether we
are measuring up to the high stan<lards possible to us, whether we are
doing our full duty, whether we keep a consciousness of that duty
with us constantly, or whether it is only on special occasions, when we
have public school week, that we engage in a little conversation about
the matter, and forget it ever after.
We have sacred and solemn duties to perform. The great men
that have been Past Grand Masters and Past Masters of Lodges in

of the great and glorious things that we now enjoy? Shall we not
then be able to come and say "Oh, ye spirits of the departed, if it
be so that you are still conscious of mundane affairs, will you not
look down upon us and decide for us whether we are proving ourselves
worthy of all the good things we enjoy, of all the blessings that have
come to us, of all the rich harvest that has been tendered us through
your efforts? Are we blundering unnecessarily, oh, Good Spirit, or if
it be that you are able to inspire our thoughts or that you really live
again in us, will you not direct us so that we ·may not keep on making
unnecessary mistakes, so that we may strongly, in the future, be able
to. carry on as you did, and even more greatly than you did, that we
may be able to do the work that is our hearts' desire, that we may
be able to help this great and glorious demoeracy of ours to shine yet
more resplendently as the beacon light of the world, that we may be
able to take into our arms, metaphorically speaking, we, the people
of the United States, the wounded and the bruised of all the world
and carry them as God carries us, as a shepherd carries the wounded
lamb, in our breasts, that we may be able to pour upon them floods
of affection and love-not maudlin affection and love, but the kind
of affection and love that makes men of them again, that gives them
back the courage they have lost, that removes the fear from their
hearts which is killing them day by day, and which will give them
the opportunities of re-establishing themselves and re-habilitating their
country, that we may be able, in the sight of God and the spirits of
the departed, to say we have done our duty to the best of our ability,
we accepted our obligation in a serious way, we understood what was
required of us and we believe. we have done it? Bear us testimony,
oh, ye departed ones, that we have not wasted our opportunities or
squandered the good fortune that you left us here. Mav God bless
the memory of our departed brethren, and may God cau;e His spirit
to dwell with us and guide us to deeds of goodness and greatness,
Amen.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Charters has had under consideration the peti·
tions for charters of the Lodges, for the formation and opening of
which dispensations were issued within the past Masonic year:
Your committee has carefully examined the records of and interviewed the delegates appearing for the Lodges under dispensation with
very gratifying results. Outside of minor variations, which have been
promptly corrected for the Committee, the records in all instances
substantially comply with all the requirements and show a sincere
desire to comply with our ::Vfasonic regulations.
The results attained by some Lodges in the neatness and accuracy
of their records would serve as worthy models to follow. All this, your
Committee feels, reflects credit as well upon the conscientious work
of the Inspectors and the efficiency of the past year's administration.
Your Committee finds that the thirty-nine lodges under dispensa·
ti on have been conducted in due Ma sonic manner that speaks well
for the progress of Masonry. We therefore recommend that charters
be issued to them in the order of their dispensations, with the following
names and numbers:

The testimony of the man who paid the money to accused is direct
and certain, as is that of the Secretary of Golden West Lodge that

The trial commission found accused guilty and fixed the sentence
at expulsion. The evidence was ample to sustain the judgment and no
error in procedure appearing, the action should be sustained.

Resolved, That the action of Golden West Lodge No. 455, be and

Report adopted.
Your Committee to whom was referred Trial Record No. 336, from
Crockett Lodge No. 139, respectfully reports as follows:
The accused was charged on two specifications, and the trial commission found the accused not guilty of the offense charged, but did
find him guilty of unmasonic conduct and ordered that he be reprimanded. He has appealed from the judgment of the commission.
It is apparent that if the trial commission found that accused was
not guilty of the offenses charged, he could not consistently have been
found guilty of unmasonic conduct.
Your Committee therefore offers the following resolution and
recommends its adoption:
Resolved, That the action of Crockett Lodge No. 139 in the matter
of Trial Record No. 336, be and the same is hereby reversed.

The report was adopted.

Respectfully submitted,

w ARREN E. LIBBY

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee to whom was referred Trial Record No. 329 of
Golden West Lodge No. 455, respectfully reports as follows:
The accused was charged with having received a petition for the
degrees of Masonry in Golden West Lodge together with the fee of
$100.00, neither of which was ever received by the Lodge.

Your Committee to which was referred Trial Record No. 349 of
Hollywood Lodge No. 355, respectfully reports as follows:
The accused was charged in two specifications: The first, that
on divers occasions he accepted certain money upon the consideration
that the person paying the same would not be prosecuted for unlawfully possessing or selling intoxicating liquor and upon the further
consideration that the accused would give notice of any contemplated
search of the premises when st1ch liquors were stored; that accused
was during all of said times a police officer.
The second specification 'charged accused with having accepted $50
upon a certain day upon the consideration that the person paying the
same would not be prosecuted for having in his possession and selling
intoxicating liquors; the said accused being at the time a police officer.
At the hearing before the trial commission it appeared that accused
was a fugitive from justi<;e and that the charges were sustained by

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

656

657

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

abundant evidence. He was found guilty on both specifications and
the penalty fixed at suspension.
This Committee is of the opinion that as there are no extenuating
circumstances the accused should have been sentenced to expulsion.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the decision of the trial commissioners in finding the
accused guilty of the charges be sustained but that the penalty be
changed, and the penalty be and is hereby fixed at expulsion.

The report was adopted.
Your Committee to whom was referred ·Trial Record No. 350,
being a member of Redondo Lodge No. 328, who was tried and
suspended by Ocean Park Lodge No. 369, on appeal by the accused,
recommend that the action of Ocean Park Lodge, No. 369, be reversed.

The report and recommendations were adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 345, from Moneta Lodge No. 405, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct, the case regularly
heard, and testimony was taken in the regular way. The accused was
found gnilty by the commissioners.
An appeal was taken by the accused. The examination of the transcript of the record shows that in addition to the testimony of the
complaining witness, further testimony was introduced to substantiate
the guilt of the defendant, and the Committee is of the opinion that
the judgment should be sustained.
Therefore, the Committee offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption :
Resolved, that the judgment of the Trial Commissioners in Trial
Record No. 345 of the Moneta Lodge No. 405 be and same is hereby
affirmed.

The report was adopted.

Lodge No. 486 that he had been a petitioner for the degrees in
Coalinga Lodge No. 387. The evidence disclosed that Coalinga Lodge
had not acted on his petition by ballot, but that the Committee to
which the petition was referred, reported unfavorably thereon, and
petitioner's money was returned to him. That before he petitioned
Caledonia Lodge he consulted two Master Masons in whom he had
confidence; that these Master Masons informed him that under the
circumstances, he need not state in his petition to Caledonia Lodge
that he had been rejected; that- acting on their advice he did not
do so in putting in his petition; that about three days before his
petition was acted on by Caledonia Lodge the accused, having learned
that the advice was wrong, went to the Master and Secretary of
Caledonia Lodge, informed them of his having put in his petition in
Coalinga Lodge; stated he was sorry he had made the mistake, and
asked leave to withdraw his petition.
He was told he could not do this. The fact of his having filed the
former petition in Coalinga Lodge became known in Caledonia Lodge
before a ballot was taken on the petition of accused. In spite of this
fact, Caledonia Lodge elected him to take the degrees. He took his
first degree, when the matter again came up. The Master appointed
an investigating committee which reported in favor of the advancement of the accused, whereupon he received his second degree. After
this the charges in question were preferred and the trial had. The
Trial Commissioners failed to find on the specification, but found the
accused guilty of unmasonic conduct. Upon the vote being had on the
penalty to be imposed, the Commissioners voted unanimously in favor
of imposing no penalty. An appeal was taken by the accuser.
While the Commissioners should have found on the specifications,
and while it was somewhat of an anomaly for them to find the accused
guilty of unmasonic conduct and then fail to impose a penalty, under the
provisions of Section 205 of our Constitution it was clearly the right
of the Commissioners to vote "no" on each of the three propositions
of fixing the penalty to be imposed, submitted to them by the Master.
What may have actuated the Commissioners to find the accused guilty
of unmasonic conduct, we can only infer. From the record we are
inclined to think they wanted to fix the stamp of disapproval on the
act of ,stating in the petition that he had not been rejected by another
Lodge, and yet were of the opinion that accused had done all he
could to right the wrong before the Lodge acted on the petition. In
our opinion the Master of the Lodge should have suggested or permitted
an amendment to the petition. While we do not desire that this case
shall be taken as a precedent, we nevertheless feel that the evidence
under all the circumstances warranted the Commissioners in their failure
to impose a penalty ..

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

659

We, therefore, offer the following Resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, That the action of the Trial Commissioners as disclosed
by Trial Record No. 365, be and the same is hereby affirmed.

The report was adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 362, begs leave to report:
The accused. in this case was charged with unmasonic conduct as set
forth in six specifications. The Trial Commissioners found him guilty
of the first and third speclfications, to-wit: Deserting his family and
breaking up a Master Mason's home by stealing the affections of the
wife of the accuser, all of which is charged to have occurred about
ten years ago.
The pen,alty imposed was that of suspension. The accused appeals
from the judgment. In our opinion the findings are not sustained by
the evidence. The record clearly shows that the accused was justified
in leaving the wife whom he is found to have deserted. Likewise on
the charge of breaking up a Mason's family, the accuser himself
testified that he and his wife separated through a disagreement on
financial matters, and not by reason of acts of the accused. This is
further sustained by the pleading in a divorce case had between the
accuser and his wife. No reason is given by the accuser why action
on his part was delayed nearly ten years.
We are, therefore, of the opinion that the action of the Trial
Commissioners in finding the accused guilty on the two specifications
in question and fixing the penalty at suspension is not sustained by the
evidence, and we therefore offer the following resolution and move
its adoption :
Resolved, That the action of the Trial Commission in Trial Record
No. 362, in finding the defendant guilty and fixing the penalty at suspension, be and the same is hereby reversed.

The report was adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 364, tried by Hawaiian Lodge No. 21, respectfully r-eport as follows :
The Trial Commission found accused guilty upon the specification
in the charge and upon the charge of unmasonic conduct, and fixed
the penalty at suspension. The record discloses that the accused had
sailed to San Francisco on or about April 26, 1923, which act was
known to the Lodge. The charge was preferred on May 1, 1923,
summons issued and returned unserved on May 7, 1923, and trial had on
May 16, 1923. It does not appear that the address of the accused
was unknown, and no diligence or even attempt is shown to ascertain
his address after discovery that he had left the jurisdiction of the
Lodge. The information that he had left was obtained for the first
time on May 7, 1923, when the Tiler attempted to serve him at his
former place of business.
Section 199 of the Constitution requires summons to issue at least
ten days prior to the day appointed for the trail, or a longer time
if the accused is without the jurisdiction of the Lodge. It affirmatively
appears that the summons was issued only nine days prior to the day
appointed for the trial, at a time accused was supposed to be within
the jurisdiction of the Lodge. Your Committee is of the opinion that
the judgment of the Commission must be reversed and the same
remanded for a new trial, on the ground that jurisdiction was not
obtained in the manner provided by our Constitution.
Your Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:
Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by Trial Record No.
364, be, and the same is hereby reversed, and the case remanded for
a new trial.

. Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 376, from Argonaut Lodge No. 461, begs to report as follows:
The accused was charged with unmasonic · conduct under two
specifications. The certificate of the Secretary is to the effect that
he forwarded by mail the summons and copy of the charges to the
address of the accused in San Francisco, which is within the jurisdiction
of the Lodge. Had the address of accused been without said jurisdiction, such forwarding by mail would be deemed sufficient service, hut
if the accused be within the iurisdiction of the Lodge, Sec. 199 of the
Constitution requires that the summons and copy of the charges shall
he served personally by the Tiler or some other member of the Lodge
authorized by the Master for that purpose, or shall be left at his
ordinary residence or place of business. Service as certified to, therefore, does not give the Trial Commission jurisdiction to proceed with
the trial.
The record shows, however, t·hat "the accused not being present
nor having made any reply to the summons, the Master ordered the
trial to proceed at once upon the testimony ex partc."
This procedure is authorized without service by Sec. 199 of the
Constitution in the single instance where the address of the accused
be unknown. Service is very essential to assure that justice be done

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

665

the accused, and to justify proceeding without it, the fact that the
address of the accused is unknown can only he established by a clear
showing of exercise of due diligence to find the address of accused.
The certificate of the Secretary in this case affirmatively shows that the
address of the accused was known and that it was· in the jurisdiction
of the lodge. Your Committee is therefore of the opinion that the
judgment of the Commission must be reversed and the same remanded
for a new trial on the ground that jurisdiction was not obtained in
the manner provided by our Constitution.
The first specification set forth in the charge inferentially charges
accused with embezzling $500. The second charges that he was a
fugitive from justice and that in leaving the city he had abandoned
his wife and family. Both specifications are poorly drawn. On the
trial only one witness was heard, but the Trial Commission utterly
ignored the requiren;ents of our Constitution as to qualifying him to
testify. The witness, without having qualified, gave slight hearsay
testimony that accused had admitted to his employers that he had
taken their money. There is no testimony offered at all as to the
second specification. The Trial Commissioners, however, unanimously
found the accused guilty on the first and second specifications and of
the charge of unmasonic conduct, and sentenced him to expulsion.
These errors are called attention to so that they may be corrected
on a new trial when jurisdiction is properly obtained.
Your Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption :
Resolved, That the judgment in the case covered by Trial Record
No. 376 be, and the same is hereby reversed, and the case remanded
for a new trial.

The report was adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 371, tried by Lexington Lodge No. 104, respectfully reports as
follows:
The Junior Warden of the accusing Lodge, by direction of his
Lodge, charged a brother with unmasonic conduct as set forth in three
specifications. The Trial Commission unanimously found the accused
not guilty upon all of the specifications in the charge, from which finding
the accuser appeals.
The Constitution under Section 205 requires that the Master, at
the next stated meeting of his Lodge after the trial is concluded, shall
announce the result and direct the Secretary to record a copy of the
record and finding as the judgment of the Lodge. The form of the
record of finding is provided in Section 257. Section 207 fixes the date
of the announcement as the date from which time to appeal runs.
The record discloses that the Master did not at the next or any stated
meeting of his Lodge direct the Secretary to record a copy of the
record and finding as the judgment of the Lodge. There being no
judgment recorded, there is nothing from which the accuser can appeal.
At said stated meeting, as appears from the record, the Master's
announcement was the result of the trial of a brother for unmasonic
conduct declared "not guilty." This does not comply with Sections
205 and 257 of our Constitution. Hence there beipg no proper announcement of the result, even had the judgment been recorded, your Committee is of the opinion that the appeal is premature and cannot be
considered.
Your Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:

Resolved, that the Lodge in which trial was had be directed and
required to have the proper entry and announcement made and the
records corrected in accordance with Sections 205 and 257 of the
Constitution.

The report was adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic Education begs leave to report as follows:
While the results obtained from the work of this Committee during
the past year have, perhaps, not fulfilled the expectations of the Craft,
still we feel that substantial progress has been made. The building of
our educational work is not a matter of one year or two years, but
that of a generation. Habits and customs are not easily changed, and
the construction of a real educational program within our Fraternity
means intensive development over a long period of time.

In the last analysis the work must be done in the constituent Lodge
itself, and your Committee feels that during the past year great strides
have been made in this direction. At the outset a bulletin was sent
to all Masters and Wardens, containing suggestions to this end. One
of those was that an Educational Committee should be appointed in
each Lodge, and we are pleased to report that this suggestion was
accepted by many Masters, and during the year a large number of
Educational Committees have been functioning, looking after the programs for the various Lodges.

670

PROCEEDINGS OF' '.rHE

It was also suggested that meetings be advertised more generally
than heretofore, and this suggestion has also been adopted in many,
many instances, and our membership as a whole has been better informed as to the activities of the Lodges.
Music and community singing was suggested as a method of promoting good fellowship, and there has been more of this element in
our Lodges during the past year than in any year prior.
Quite a number of subjects for discussion were presented to the
Masters and the suggestion made that as far as possible they secure
speakers from their own membership or in their own community to
handle the subjects. The following out of this suggestion relieved the
Committee of much of the onerous responsibility of securing speakers
and likewise developed within the Fraternity many speakers who had
not theretofore appeared before the Lodges.
It was our hope that we would have reported to the Committee the
names of these speakers and the subjects treated by them, but this
co-operation was not as generally extended as it was hoped, and in
more instances we heard the reports in a round-about way rather than
direct. To have followed up this particular phase of the work would
have required far more time and clerical help than was at the disposition of your Committee, and we have not been able to do as much as
we should liked to have done in this direction.
There is a great wealth of ability within the Lodges that has as
yet not been taken advantage of, and it is our hope that the future •
will find a way of bringing out this latent talent and interesting it in
the welfare of our Fraternity.
A number of new Masters' and Wardens' Associations have been
organized, particularly in the central district or San Joaquin Valley,
and special commendation should be given to Brother Henry E. Verble,
chairman of that District, for his efforts.
The older Masters' and Wardens' Associations have continued to
function, and their work has resulted in a larger acquaintance between
the Masters and Wardens of the various districts and cities and the
general promotion of good fellowship and friendship between the
Lodges.
The need of a short, comprehensive statement of the history and
purposes of our Fraternity, together with the duty of a Mason toward
it, has long been felt, and at the suggestion of our Grand Master the
Committee has prepared such a statement and has had it printed, ready
for distribution. It had been the expectation that this would be in the
hands of the Masters before Grand Lodge, but unexpected delays held
it up and it has now just come from the printer. Copies will be mailed
to all Lodges within the week, and it is the wish of our Grand Master
that a copy be presented to each candidate after he has received his

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

671

third degree. The booklet is not intended to be at all complete, but to
give information that the newly initiated as well as older members
should know and to inspire them to a further study of the history and
philosophy of our Craft.
·
We heartily concur in the recommendation of our Grand Master
that the Committee be continued and given a paid Executi~e Secretary
to handle the detail work of the Committee, and the following observa-·
tions as to the type of man to be secured for this work we feel to be
in order.
He should first be thoroughly familiar with the organization of
Freemasonry and qualify from an educational standpoint to handle the
work.
He should be entirely free from responsibility in other branches of
Freemasonry, holding no offices that would divide his time or attention
from th is work.
He should have no ambition in Freemasonry other than the development of our educational program. He should have the ability to
teach as well as to direct and execute the plans and purposes of the
Committee.
Adequate compensation should be provided by Grand Lodge, and, if
this recommendation is adopted, we do not hesitate to predict that the
man selected will make as large a place for himself in the hearts of
our Fraternity as has our good friend and brother, Tom Baker, in
his supervision of the ritualistic work, and as has also our beloved
Grand Secretary, John Whicher, in the performance of his many duties
and labors for the upbuilding of the Craft.
It would be the duty of the Executive Secretary to visit the various
districts at intervals, see that Masters' and Wardens' Associations were
properly organized and functioning, develop and maintain a list of
speakers in all districts who would be available for service ta the Craft,
prepare and distribute to the Lodges suggested programs for special
events and for quarterly meetings of districts, to prepare and distribute
at stated intervals bulletins similar and along the lines of the splendid
Bulletins prepared by our Grand Master during the past year.
It would also be his duty to correspond with the Committees on
Education in other jurisdictions and to arrange for an exchange of
ideas and programs that would be found to be mutually beneficial. In
fact, it is so easy to sec the things that could be done by one whose
entire time would be devoted to this work that it is needless to enumerate further.
To sum up, we would, therefore, make the following recommendations:

673

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

That the Committee be continued in its present form of organization; that an Executive Secretary, appointed by the Grand Master, be
provided for the Committee; that the sum of seventy-five hundred dollars be appropriated for the use of the Committee on Masonic Education, the sum to be expended upon authorization by the Grand Master.
Fraternally submitted,
CHAS. H. Vrc'rOR,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND LECTURER'S
REPORT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to which was referred the sixteenth successive
annual report of the Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer, deems it not
only a pleasant duty but a distinct honor and privilege to commend the

675

GRAND r,ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

674

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

courtesy and affability, the kindness and condescension and the zeal
for our Institution which have won for our beloved Thomas J. Baker
our warm regard and high esteem.
With self-effacing modesty, which is one of his outstanding characteristics, he has generously attributed to others credit for the pronounced success which has characterized his highly appreciated efforts
to impart to the Craft an intelligent conception of our ritual and a
keener appreciation of the fundamental principles which it is the purpose of our Institution indelibly to impress upon the hearts and minds
of those who are subject to its influence.
Your Committee concurs most heartily in the views of the Very
\Vorshipful Grand Lecturer regarding the importance and value of the
unselfish service. which, constantly, is being rendered to the Fraternity
by a most able and efficient corps of Inspectors. They are the instrumentalities by means whereof officers of constituent Lodges are trained
and inspired. It is through their devotion to service that uniformity
of ritualism is insured. They are, and should be, the media through
which divergent and conflicting views regarding words, forms, ceremonies, policies and purposes can best be harmonized and authoritatively determined. To the extent that the responsibility and authority
of our Inspectors is minimized is the potency of our Institution as a
stabilizing force for good impaired. They are the guardians of those
priceless treasures which it is our purpose to transmit, unimpaired,
through our l\fasters and \Vardens, to those who will follow after us.
It is, therefore, just and proper and in the interest of our beloved
Institution that through them should be communicated to those in
charge of the affairs of the constituent Lodges the views, the rulings,
the policies, of those to whom, for the time being, are entrusted the
administration of our affairs and that to them Masters, Wardens,
officers and members alike, should at all times yield that obedience,
submission, honor and respect to which the personal representatives of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master are entitled.
The observations of the Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer regarding
our growth and t,he prosperous condition of constituent Lodges affords
less cause for gratification than does the outstanding fact that there
has been developed throughout the jurisdiction a better spirit of genuine
fraternity. It is apparent that there is a widespread and growing realization of the value and importance of affording members easier and
more frequent opportunities to become better acquainted with each
other.
· The timely remarks of our Grand Lecturer regarding the proper
conduct of l\fasonic funerals deserve serious consideration, and merit
some comment. Whether there are particulars in which our burial
service might, to advantage, be simplified, modernized, better adapted

to present conditions and surroundings, and. rendered more in k:eping
with a Masonic conception of the true significance of mortal dissolution, are matters which might, with propriety, be respect~u_lly recommended to the attention of the Committee on Ritual as mer1tmg prompt
and serious consideration. A familiarity with the spirit as well as
with the wording of our service is essential. to a proper and impressive
Masonic funeral. The thought and h1'Pe that his Lodge may never be
calle°d upon to perform this solemn duty does not justify a failure
upon the part of a Master to be adequately pre~ared, should oc.cas~on
arise to respond in a way which will reflect credit upon our Institution
and ~void criticism. If, for any reason, he finds it impossible to make
adequate preparation a Master should, at the very outset of his administration, delegate to some officer or member of his Lodge definite
responsibility of being prepared to conduct services impressively.
The formation of thirty-nine new lodges during the past year, while
gratifying, imposes enlarged responsibilities not only upon officers and
members of these new organizations, but also upon officers and members of old and well-established Lodges, which are under obligation to
·exercise fraternal interest and fostering care.
Reference to interest in and attendance upon schools of instruction
is indicative of widespread desire upon the part of officers to benefit
to the fullest extent by the frequent opportunities afforded them by
our Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer.
The tribute to the value and effectiveness of the work of our Grand
Lecturer which is contained in the message of our Most Worshipful
Grand l\Iaster, expresses the views of the Committee regarding his fine
qualities and the worth of his services, and we are pleased t? con~ur
most heartily in the recommendation regarding the manner m which
Grand Lodge should evidence its appreciation.
That the past year has been one of outstanding accomplishment and
that our activities hav·e resulted in a better functioning of constituent
Lodges and a keener realization of the aims and purposes of our Institution is attributable in no small degree to the tireless efforts, the
vision, the tactfulness, the spirit of genuine co-operation and the devotion to service of our Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer is respectfully
submitted as the conclusion of your Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
PAUL BURKS,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns is pleased to note that most of the
Lodges, by far, sent in their returns promptly, and they were correct.
Some Lodges sent in their returns in good time but they were
incorrect and corrections had to be made.
At the opening of Grand Lodge correct returns of the following
Lodges were not in:
Reedley Lodge ::\' o. 304,
Gardena Lodge No. 372,
Calexico Lodge No. 412,
Kerman Lodge Ko. 420,
Westwood Lodge No. 501.
The reports from these Lodges were incorrect, and repeated letters
from the Grand .Secretary have failed to bring even a response from
the Secretaries, so the corrections could not be made.
Each one of the Secretaries of the above Lodges shows one of
two things; either great incompetence ·or gross negligence. Your
Committee is of the opinion that an incompetent Secretary, or a
careless one ought to be remo.ved from office.
The Master of a Lodge is responsible for the annual report being
forwarded to the Grand Secretary promptly, and, if the report is
returned for correction, he should be diligent in seeing that the
necessary corrections are made and the report sent back to the Grand
Secretary immediately. IN e also recommend that when 'the Grand
Secretary has to send a report back for correction, he notify the
Master of the Lodge of this fact.
Your Committee has once more to congratulate the fraternity on
the healthy growth in membership. \Vhile the increase is not a·s great
as last year it is still a large addition to our numbers. So long as a
high standard of quality is maintained we need not concern ourselves
particularly about mere numbers.
\Vith the increasing nnrnber of Lodges we must look for large
additions to our membership. Remember, when we cease to grow we
commence to die. \Ve know that our great Fraternity is going to
increase in strength and stature in the years to come, and we are
glad of it.

delivered in person by Past Grand Master Henderson, regarding the
Masonic cemetery of San Francisco which has been referred to the
Committee of Policy and General Purposes; and
Whereas, the matter is of moment and should be met squarely,
therefore be it
