REPORT OF RELIEF COMMITTEE, BERKELEY
FIRE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your special representatives in the matter of the relief provided by
the Grand Master from the special funds of Grand L-Odge in connection
with the Berkeley fire, beg leave to make a brief report of what has
been done in that connection:
The fire occurred on the afternoon of Monday, September 17th
last. The Grand Master was in Berkeley that night for the purpose
of ascertaining the extent of the losses and what should be done in
the way of relieving the distress of Masons and those dependent upon
them who resided in the burned district. The next day, at noon, at
a meeting in San Francisco, attended by the Grand Master, other
Grand Officers, and a number of brethren, relief plans were formulated.
As a result of this prompt action, an organization was perfected
in Berkeley on Tuesday night. There were present at this meeting
Brother William A. Sherman, Grand Master; Brother Frank G. Hobbs,
Assistant Grand Secretary, and Masters or Wardens of the eight Blue
Lodges in Berkeley. A committee was quickly formed for the purpose
of administering the Masonic emergency fund set aside by the Grand
Master, with the following officers: Brother Frank M. Shick, Master
of Berkeley Lodge, chairman; Brother Merle Randall, Senior Warden
of Henry Morse Stephens Lodge, vice-chairman; Brother Claude S.
Downing, Master of Durant I,odge, treasurer; and Brother C. G. Ames,
Senior Warden of Francis K. Shattuck Lodge, secretary. The Grand
Master designated Brothers Robert Greig and William H. Waste as
his special representatives on the committee. Assignments were made
to Masters of different Lodges to visit hospitals and to search out
in every way possible Masons and members of their families who
were in need of aid. Special effort was directed toward administering
to the temporary need of the students of the University of California.
Campaign headquarters of the University of California Masonic Club
House were turned over to the committee for this last purpose.
Whifo it is known that several hundred Masons and members of
their families were among those who lost all, or practically everything,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

691

by reason of the destruction of their homes, there has been very
little call for the administration of the Masonic relief fund. One of
the hardest features of the work of the committee has been to induce
those who have been discovered to have been in need to accept financial
assistance. Such has been the independent spirit and, in the large,
the fortunate circumstances of those burned out, that there has been
a surprisingly small amount of actual need, and but little suffering
r:aused by the great fire.
What has been accomplished is fully attested by the report of the
Relief Committee, which is attached to and made a part of this report.
The Committee of •the Berkeley Blue Lodges having this work in
charge feels that as the fire sufferers reach an adjustment of their
affairs there will undoubtedly be yet other cases calling for the
administration of this relief fund. The committee and your special
representatives agree and recommend that it will be well to continue
this matter in the hands of the Committee under the direction of the
incoming Grand Master.
Following is the financial statement of the Masonic emergency
relief fund as of October 10, 1923:

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY ANO

Masonic Service Association
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

This Grand Lodge is now a member of the Masonic Service
Association, and the Grand Master notified the Association that at the
expiration of our year's membership this Grand Lodge would cease
to be a member of said Association. The Grand Master took this
action prior to the meeting of Grand Lodge _because the rules of
the Association required a 90 days' notice before withdrawal. The
facts are stated in the Grand Master's message.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred the foregoing subject matt'er, have fully considered the same.
This Grand Lodge deferred entering the Masonic Service Association
for several years and finally joined, as the Grand Master states, largely
as a compliment to the very able and accomplished Secretary of the
Association who honored this Grand Lodge by a visit at its last Annual
Communication and spoke to us eloquently regarding the aims and .
purposes of the Association. We hold the Association in high regard
and have a profound respect for the able and earnest Masons who
are carrying on its work, but your Committee is of the opinion that
the Lodges of California prefer to work out the educational program
to which we have been committed for several years, and that the
financial support of this Grand Lodge should be given to that program
rather than be diverted in whole or in part to the Masonic Service
Association. The Association has not had the co-operation and
wholehearted support of the officers and Masons in this jurisdiction to
which it was entitled, but the Committee is of the opinion that a
discontinuance of the membership will better the prevailing conditions.
It is hoped that the work of the Educational Committee of this Grand
Lodge may be of some service or help to the Masonic Service Association and that the Association will realize that the withdrawal ·of the
Grand Lodge of California from its membership does not imply in any
way a lack of confidence in either the methods or purposes of the
Association, but rather that California desires to continue its educational
work, and is disposed to make its contribution for educational work
through that source. Under these circumstances and for the foregoing
reasons the Committee recommend the adoption of the following:
Resolved, that the action of the G.rand Master in giving notice of
the withdrawal of this Grand Lodge as a member of the Masonic
Service Association be approved.

After full discussion, the report failed of adoption.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

693

Booklet for Presentation to Masons
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
recommendation of the Grand Master that the regulation requiring
the presentation of a copy of the Constitution and Ceremonies to each
Mason upon his receiving the third degree be repealed, and that the
Committee on Masonic Education publish a booklet of pertinent information to he presented to newly-created Master Masons.
It is undoubtedly true that the present regulation requiring the
presentation of a copy of the Constitution does not have the result
expected by Grand Lodge and that a sufficient time has elapsed to
prove the experiment to be of doubtful value. We, however, do not
believe that the practice of presenting this book to our new members
should be discontinued until we are prepared to substitute it with
something of practical use and value to our new members. We think
that a booldet could be prepared which would contain in a small
compass much practical information of an educational and inspirational
value to our initiates.
The Grand Master also recommended that a short outline of the
purposes, aims and responsibility of Masonry be prepared for presentation to a petitioner at the time he solicits the privilege of presenting
a petition to a lodge for the degrees.
Your Committee thinks this recommendation worthy of earnest
consideration.
Inasmuch as no booklet or other literature has been prepared for
submission to this Grand Lodge to be substituted for presentation in
place of the Constitution, and no form of outline to be presented to
a petitioner has been prepared, we respectfully recommend that the
Committee on Masonic Education be authorized and directed to prepare
or cause to be prepared a booklet to be presented to the newly-created
Master Masons, and that they prepare or cause to be prepared a
statement of the outlines of Masonry for presentation to petitioners,
and that they report the result of their labors at the next communication of the Grand Lodge.

The report was adopted.
Leave of Absence for Grand Lecturer
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes fully concurs
with the Grand Master in his recommendation that a three months'
leave of absence, with salary and expenses, be given to our faithful
Grand Lecturer to enable him to make a trip throughout the United
States and to visit various Masonic jurisdictions.
This Grand Lodge has long been appreciative of the valuable service
rendered by the Grand Lecturer, and your Committee feels that his

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

694

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

closer contact with our sister jurisdictions, their rituals and activities,
would be reflected in his greater usefulness to our brethren.
V.fe therefore recommend that the Grand Lecturer, Thomas J.
Baker, be given a leave of absence for three months for such a trip and
that his salary and expenses be paid during such time.

The report was adopted.
Exemption From Grand Lodge Dues
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration a resolution reading as follows:
"Resolved that Section 41c of the Constitution be amended to read
as follows : ' All subordinate Lodges shall be exempt from paying
Grand Lodge dues on account of any member whose dues have been
remitted by said subordinate Lodge at any stated meeting during the
preceding twelve months prior to July 31 of said fiscal year."
The purpose of the proposed amendment is to permit any Lodge
at any meeting during the year to remit the dues of a member and to
claim exemption from Grand Lodge dues on account of such members.
By our system of reports and accounting, the subordinate Lodges
render to the Grand Secretary a report of their membership as of
July 31 of each year, and Grand Lodge dues are paid by the subordinate
Lodges at a fixed rate per member. Dues cannot be remitted in
advance, and if dues are remitted at any stated meeting prior to July
then the member will stand on the rolls of the subordinate Lodge as
a dues-paying member of July 31, and since the Grand Lodge exacts
dues on an annual basis instead of monthly, quarterly or semi-annual
installments, it is not practicable to change the present law on this
subject. The Committee recommends that said resolution be not
adopted.

The report was adopted, and the proposed amendment
was lost.
Courtesy Degrees
The Grand Master recommended that the law of this Grand Lodge
be amended to permit the Grand Master to grant dispensations to
confer the first degree in any other than the Lodge in which the
petitioner is elected to receive the degrees, in those cases in wh~ch
the Grand Master believes a justifiable reason exists for the grantmg
of such dispensations.
your Committee concurs in the recommendation of the Grand
Master, and the Committee on Jurisprudence has prepared and will
present an amendment to the Constitution to confer this power on
the Grand Master.

The report was adopted.

695

Fees for Affiliation
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration the following resolution introduced by Brother Willard
Clark:
"Resolved, that section 165 of the Constitution be amended by
inserting in line 21, after the words 'he may apply', the following:
'and by paying the sum equivale~t to the dues of the Lodge to which
he may apply for affiliation, said sum to be computed from the termination of the two-year period to the date of presenting his application
for affiliation.' "
It is no doubt true that it occasionally happens that a non-affiliate
who has carried a dimit for a number of years makes application
for purely selfish purposes; and it might be only reasonable to exact
something more than six months dues now required. It is to be
remembered, however, that during the time he has remained unaffiliated
he has not been entitled to any of the benefits and privileges of
Masonry; furthermore, he must petition for membership and the Lodge
may, and should, reject the application of one whose. motives may be
reasonably open to suspicion.
The most compelling reason, however, against legislation of the
sort proposed is the fact that by our law it is made the duty of every
Master Mason to be a member of some lodge ; and it seems to the
members of your committee tmwise to impose upon any non-affiliate
terms that might be deemed onerous. An applicant for affiliation from
another jurisdiction is now compelled to pay not only the affiliation fee
required by the lodge, but also the sum of $20 for the support of
the Homes; if in addition to this he were required to pay an amount
equal to three or four years' dues the total amount would be, if not
prohibitive, at least such as would afford a non affiliate a reasonable
excuse for not acquiring membership in a lodge in this jurisdiction.
We, therefore, recommend that the proposed amendment be not
adopted.

The report was adopted, and the proposed amendment
was lost.

Revision of Constitution
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration the recommendation of the Grand Master that the Grand
Secretary be directed to revise the Constitution.
This matter has been the subject of comment for several years,
and some of the criticisms of our present book of Constitution are
justified. The subject, however, is one of as much difficulty as importance, and should receive more careful and deliberate consideration
than can be given during the few clays of a Grand Lodge session.
Your Committee, therefore recommends that the Grand Master appoint
a Committee of three to consider the subject of the revision of the
book of Constitution and report thefr recommendations at the· next
annual communication of the Grand Lodge.

The report was adopted.
Recognition of Foreign Jurisdictions
We, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, have had
under consideration requests for recognition of Grand Lodges which
were before the Committee at the last Communication of this Grand
Lodge and for lack of time for investigation the applications were
continued until this session of the Grand Lodge. In addition to
these, other similar requests have been received during the year and
will be considered in this report.
At the outset, we desire to inform the Grand Lodge that many
difficulties are encountered in any investigation of the status, conditions
and regularity of some of the Grand Lodges seeking recognition. Correspon<lence is delayed or remains unanswered, Masonic histories are
not trustworthy in all respects, and there are no established precedents
for our guidance. We have collated from many sources such facts
as were available, and upon them we base our recommendations, fully
realizing that some of our conclusions may be unsound because of
misinformation or lack of greater knowledge. We feel that some
progress should be made in the great work of establishing Masonic
regularity and bringing about a recognized universal Masonry. In

697

The Masonic powers of the world fall under two classifications,
viz: those derived directly or indirectly from the Grand Lodge of
England and those derived from Scottish Rite sources. Practically no
difficulty is experienced in determining the legitimacy and regularity of
the Grand Bodies situated in the English-speaking countries and the
tests for recognition adopted by the Grand Lodge of California in
1913 (Proceedings, page 162) furnish a fair standard by which to
measure the claims of Grand Lodges seeking our recognition. In
1918 this Grand Lodge, in considering the Grand Orient of France and
the Grand Lodge of France, adopted a recommendation:
"That the principles enunciated by this Grand Lodge in 1913 as
tests for the recognition of other Grand Lodges be and the same are
applicable only to Grand Lodges of English-speaking countries, and
that as to the Grand Lodges or Grand Orients of other countries
each application be considered upon its merits with relation to th~
situation of the applicant and with a view to doing full and complete
Masonic justice."
Several Grand Lodges established under the Scottish Rite system
and domiciled in the Latin countries are seeking our recognition, and
under the policy of this Grand Lodge adopted in 1918 it is our duty
to examine into their respective merits, and it is our right to recognize
them if it appears to this Grand Lodge that a Grand Body exercises
authority over the three degrees of symbolic Masonry and is recognized
as a sovereign power over its Lodges and members and exhibits its
~dherence to the principles of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth, and
is engaged in the promotion of the happiness of mankind and the
brotherhood of man, and respect·s the territorial jurisdiction of the
American Grand Lodges. Such a Grand Lodge must be lawfully
organized b:) three or more regular Lodges and must be independent
of any other ~1asonic power. The Grand Lodge of Massachusetts
adopted an amendment to its Grand Lodge Constitution in 1922 on
th.e subject of recognitions which shows a profound study and careful
thought on this subject, and while not applied in its entirety in every·
case, has been helpful in pursuing om: examinations and in arriving at
our conclusions. This Massachusetts amendment is as follows:
"Fraternal recognition may be extended to a foreign Grand Lodge
when (a committee having first considered and reported theeron) it
appears to the satisfaction of this Grand Lodge:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

698

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

L That the foreign Grand Lodge in question represents a substantial
unity of the Freemasons of the territory over which it assumes
jurisdiction; i. e., the Country, Province, or State.
2. That it has been lawfully organized by three or more regular
Lodges.
3. That it is independent, having entire dogmatic and administrative
authority over resident Masons and the symbolic Degrees within its
territorial jurisdiction.
/
4. That its ritual. is fundamentally in accord with the ancient landmarks, customs, and usages of the Craft. This involves:
A. Monotheism;
B. The Volume.of the Sacred Law a part of the furniture
of the Lodge;
C. Secrecy;
D. The symbolism of the operative art;
E. The division of symbolic Masonry into the three
degrees of Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft, and Master
Masons;
F. The legend of the Third Degree.
5. That it makes Masons of men only.
6. That it is non-sectarian and non-political; i. e., that its dominant
purposes are charitable, benevolent, educational, and rdigious."
Your Committee is indebted to the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts
and the Grand Lodge of Alabama, as well as to other Grand Lodges,
for the careful and painstaking work that has been done by them in the
matter of recognitions, but your Committee feels that it is altogether
deplorable that there should be so many inconsistencies and so much
confusion among the Grand Lodges regarding this subject. It is usual
to find that a Body applying for recognition is recognized by one
or more American or other English-speaking Grand Lodges and is
not recognized by many others. It seems anomalous that a foreign
Mason can visit and receive fraternal courtesy in one jurisdiction and
is regarded as irregular and unworthy of Masonic consideration in
another jurisdiction but a short distance away. This, however, is the
usual case and not the exception, and there is no method by which this
unfortunate condition can be corrected.

GUATEMALA

The Grand Lodge of the Republic of Guatemala was organized
in 1903 with eight symbolic Lodges which theretofore had yielded
obedience to the Supreme Council of Central America. In 1871 the
Supreme Council formed symbolic Lodges in Guatemala, which then
was unoccupied territory. In 1908 the Lodges in Guatemala were
"forced to stop working owing to the armed forces on the part of the
then President," and that condition remained until 1920, in which
year the Grand Lodge was reorganized and claims now to be on a
firm footing. It maintains and holds tmdisputed sway, and is the
acknowledged Sovereign Power in Ancient Craft Masonry in the
Republic of Guatemala. It does not hold allegiance or render obedience
to any other Masonic power and it recognizes the exclusive jurisdiction
of all other Grand Lodges in their respective territories. It confines
its authority to the three degrees of symbolic Masonry and supports
the ancient landmarks, including particularly the Three Great Lights,
belief in God and the· immortality of the soul, the Legend. of the
Third Degree and the Division of symbolic Masonry into three degrees.
This Grand Lodge now has under its obedience ten Lodges with 650
members, nine of which work ii1 Spanisl; and one in English, and it
has been recognized by Louisiana, Maryland, New York, New Jersey
and the District of Columbfa, as well as a number of foreign Grand
Lodges. Jn its territory there is no other Masonic power claiming
any authority over symbolic Masonry, and it has no disputes on the
subject of jurisdiction in the Republic of Guatemala. The Grand
Master is M. W. R. Felipo Solares and the Grand Secretary is Edward
B. Coffey.

VENEZUELA

Masonry has had a troublous career in Venezuela for almost a
century, and the difficulties are not yet sufficiently composed to permit
your Committee with confidence to make any recommendation at this
time. Although the Grand Lodge of the United States of Venezuela
claims to be independent of the Supreme Council, yet in respectable
quarters there is doubt that the claim is valid. The Sovereign Grand

Lodge of the East in the United States of Venezuela are entirely

PJlRU

The Grand Lodge of Peru was organized by five Lodges in 1882,
and is an entirely independent body controlling the first three degrees
of Masonry, which it works according to the York Rite ritual. While
the Grand Lodge was originally constituted of Lodges belonging to
the Supreme Council, yet it owes no obedience to the Supreme Council
and denies its right to form or govern symbolic Lodges within the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge. It requires a belief in Deity, displays
the Bible upon the altar, and appears to comport itself in an entirely
regular manner. This Grand Lodge had some difficulty in 1897 by
reason of a decree issued by the Grand Master substituting the Book
of Constitutions on the altar in place o( the Bible, and its fraternal
relations were severed with a number of Grand Lodges. The offensive
act was repudiate.d in 1898, when a decree was promulgated a-brogating
the decree of 1897, and thereupon fraternal relations were re-established
with England and many American Grand Lodges. This Grand Lodge
is not strong in the number of Lodges or members, but proves itself
to be entitled to our recognition. M. W. George E. Thornberry is
Grand Master and Dr. Luis Felipe de las Casas is Grand Secretary.
Your Committee respectfully recommends the adoption of the following:
Resolved, that the Grand Lodge of California hereby recognizes
the Grand Lodge of Peru, and the Grand Master is directed to arrange
for an exchange of representatives.
BRAZIL

In Brazil there exists no Grand Lodge of symbolic Masonry, but
the Craft is ruled by the Grand Orient of Brazil, which is a powerful
body exercising control over all the State Grand Lodges. This Grand
Orient has about 330 Lodges with a membership in excess of 20,000.
::\1any of the greatest patriots and statesmen of Brazil, including a
former King and several Presidents, have been numbered among the

members of !the Grand Orient, and it is so firmly intrenched in its
jurisdiction that there is no probability that any other Masonic power
will be able to dispute its sway in Brazil. The Grand Orient of
Rio Grande do Sul, founded in 1893, is a clandestine body and may
be considered a thorn in the side rather than a rival of the Grand
Orient. The Grand Orient has the organization peculiar to the ·Scottish
Rite, and it is the opinion of your Committee that if Masonry in
Brazil is to be ever recognized, then the Grand Orient is the only
power entitled to our consideration. The objection to the Grand
Orient is that it exercises jurisdiction over more than three degrees
and the Supreme Council is in control of symbolic Masonry. Your
Committee believes that the history of the Grand Orient proves that
the organization. suits the people of Brazil, that it is successful in
its Masonic work, that it is promulgating and practicing the fundamental
principles of Masonry and it has received recognition of American
Grand Lodges with which this Grand Lodge is in fraternal accord.
Under these circumstances we see no good reason why recognition
of the Grand Orient should be postponed for further consideration
of conditions that are not likely to change, and th~refore respectfully
recommend the adoption of the following resolution :
Resolved, that the Grand Lodge of California hereby recognizes
the Grand Orient of Brazil, and the Grand Master is directed to
arrange for an exchange of representatives.
CHILI

The Grand Lodge of Chili was established in 1862, and is independent
of the Supreme Council and exercises control over the first three
degrees only. It respects the ancient landmarks, requires a belief
in Deity, and displays the Bible on its altars. The Lodges originally
forming the Grand Lodg·e were derived from Scotland and the
Argentine and the ritualism and customs reflect the influence of
Scotland, although the Scottish Rite practice generally obtains in the
Lodges. More than fifty Lodges owe obedience to the Grand Lodge,
and notwithstanding the persecutions of the Government in the past,
the Grand Lodge seems to be flourishing and a new era of progress
and success has opened before it. Our communications indicate that
many of the chief men in the political and civil life of Chili are members of the Lodges belonging to the Grand Lodge. We ·believe this
Grand Lodge to be entitled to our favorable consideration and we
therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution;
Resolved, that the Grand Lodge of California hereby recognizes the
Grand Lodge of Chili, and the Grand Master is directed to arrange
for an exchange of representatives."

Life Membership Funds
In accord with the instructions of the Grand Lodge given at its
last Annual Communication, your Committee on Jurisprudence reports
the following proposed amendment of Section 129 of the Constitution,
prescribing the form of resolution to be adopted by a Lodge in establishing life membership.
As the section now stands, it provides for. a resolution under
which the income only of the life membership fund may be used by
the Lodge, the original amounts paid in for life membership to be

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

706

707

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

forever kept and maintained for a Permanent Life Membership Fund.
The design of the proposed amendment is to so change the ·resolution
that under it the sum paid in for a life membership for any particular
person may, upon his death, be withdrawn therefrom and become a part
of the general fund of the Lodge.
At the last Annual Communication the Committee on Policy reported
against the proposed change, and this Committee concurred in the view
of the Committee on Policy. We still adhere to the view then expressed
by both Committees, and present the proposed amendment without
recommendation, for such action as the Grand Lodge desires to take.
In doing so we think it proper to state that it is necessarily prospective
in effect and applicable only to future resolutions.
The proposed amendment is as follows:
"Amend Section 129 of the Constitution by inserting after the
words 'forever kept and maintained as and for a Permanent Life
Membership Fund,' the following words, viz: 'Provided, nevertheless,
that upon the death of a life member, such sum as he shall have paid
into said fund may be withdrawn therefrom and become a part of the
general fund of the Lodge.' "

The resolution quoted above, as originally presented by
Leo Bruck, was adopted, and Section 129 of the Constitution was amended in accordance therewith by a five-sixths
vote.
Cour,tesy Degrees
The Grand Master recommends that Section 155 of our Constitution,
which, as now written, allows a candidate elected to receive the three
degrees in a Lodge in this jurisdiction, or any or all of the degrees
in a Lodge in another jurisdiction recognized as regular by this Grand
Lodge, to receive the second or third degree, or both, but not the first,
in another Lodge upon the request of the electing Lodge, be so amended
as t.o allow him to so receive also the first degree upon permission
of the Grand Master under special circumstances. We can see no
objection to this, for we can readily see that the circumstances of an
exceptional case may make such a course advisable and proper. We
are authorized to say that the Committee on Policy concur in this view.
We, therefore, propose the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that Section 155 of the Constitution be amended by inserting after the words, "but not the first," the following words, viz:
"except under written permission from the' Grand Master.''

The report was adopted, and Section 155 of the Constitution was amended in the respect reported, by unanimous
vote.

Sunday Desecration
Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully report that at the
last Annual Communication the matter of proposed legislation prohibiting Sunday desecration was referred to this Committee; and in
his message at this Communication the Grand Master has recommended
that Lodges be prevented from advertising and selling tickets for Sunday outings.
It is not in keeping with the dignity of Masonry, or in conformity
with our law, that Masons should assemble as a Lodge or as Masons
on any Sunday except for some such purpose as attending Masonic
funerals or other purely Masonic purpose. Section 78 of our Constitution prohibits the holding of any meeting of a Lodge on Sunday
except for funeral services, and Section 115 prohibits the conferring of
any degree by any Lodge on Sunday.
We ·believe that all Masons, upon serious consideration of this
matter, will recognize the great impropriety as well as the discredit
to Masonry, involved in gatherings advertised or heralded as Masonic
for other purposes than funerals or other strictly Masonic work.
It is difficult to define with absolute precision in written law
the duties of Masons in this regard, and in any event we cannot
believe that anything beyond bringing this matter to the attention of the
membership is essential. It goes without saying that such acts as are
mentioned by the Grand Master in his recommendation (Recommendation No. 7), viz: the advertising or sale of tickets for Sunday pleasure
outings, are clearly opposed to the principles and teachings of Masonry.
We heartily approve the sentiment expressed by the Grand Master in
this regard.
We respectfully submit this report for the approval of the Grand
Lodge.

The report was adopted, and the Grand Master's recommendation was approved.
Dual Membership
At the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge in 1922, the
Jurisprudence Committee was directed to prepare legislation providing
for dual membership.
In obedience to the instruction of the Grand Lodge and without
commitment of any member of the Committee for or against the
proposal, your Jurisprudence Committee herewith submits, without
recommendation, the following resolutions:
Resolved, that Section 157 of the Constitution be amended to read
as follows:

709

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"A Mason may be a member of two or more Lodges at the same
time, subject to the provisions of the Constitution regarding application,
reference, report and ballot, if such membership be permitted by the
law of the jurisdiction of any Lodge of which he is a member at the
time of application for affiliation in another Lodge, and in such event
he shall be entitled to the same rights and privileges and be subject
to the same duties, prohibitions and liabilities in each Lodge as attach
to membership therein ; provided, that if he shall be expelled or
suspended for any reason by any Lodge of which he is a member, he
shall thereby stand expelled or suspended from all such Lodges and
shall not be reinstated in any Lodge until the Lodge by which he was
expelled or suspended shall have reinstated him to membership; and
provided further, that he may withdraw from any Lodge of which
he is a member." Resolved, further, that Section 161 of the Constitution be amended by striking out the last sentence of the first paragraph
thereof and inserting in lieu thereof the following :
"If the applicant be elected, he shall become a member of the Lodge
so electing him by signing its by-laws; provided, however, that an
applicant for affiliation who has given to any Lodge of which he may
be a member, notice of his intention to withdraw therefrom, shall not
be permitted t-0 sign .the by-laws and become a member of any other
Lodge until after the issuance of the certificate of his withdrawal from
such Lodge, which shall be immediately issued by the Secretary upon
due notice of his election by the Lodge with which he desires to
affiliate; and provided further, that every applicant shall state in his
application for affiliation whether or not he desires to withdraw from
the Lodge of which he is at the time ·a member."
Be It Further Resolved, that the second paragraph of said Section
161 be amended by inserting after the words "ipso facto cease" the
following words: "unless he indicate upon the petition for dispensation that it is his intention to retain his membership in the Lodge or
Lodges of which he is a member."

An examination of the applications and records submitted to the
Grand Master in requesting these various dispensations, reveals the fact
that Secretaries of I,odges are too prone to substitute their own opinions
and conclusions for. the statements of fact required by our organic
law. For example, where our law requires a request for dispensation
to ·oe authorized by a two-thirds vote of the Codge and to be so
certified by the Secretary, we cannot say that the Secretary has strictly
complied with the law when he certifies to the Grand Master that
the Lodge duly and regularly· voted to ask the Grand :\faster for a
dispensation. The Grand Master should be put in possession of the
.facts and then draw his own conclusions· as to the regularity and
lezality of the acts which the facts show.
Apart from s11ch irregularities as these. which your Committee is
inclined to regard as errors in form rather than in substance, the
records in all the applications for dispensations show that the Lodges
took proper action and made their applications for dispensations in substantially proper form.
\Ve, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of the Grand Ma~ter in approving the
applicaticns for dispensations of the various Lodges be and the same
hereby is approved.

Dispensations Issued by Grand Master
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
various dispensations granted by the Grand Master, to hold election
of officers at other than the statutory times, to re-hallot upon rejected
candidates, in less than the statutory time, and to receive and act upon
petitions for degrees by members of the Army or Navy who have been
unahle by reason of such service to acquire a legal Masonic residence.
Our laws provide a specific procedure where dispensations are
sought in any of the foregoing cases, and it goes without saying that
this prescribed procedure should be strictly followed.

Jurisdiction of Lodges in College Cities
!\ recommendation to amend Section 95 of the Constitution of the
Grand L9dg'e has been referred to your Jurisprudence Committee. The
purpose of the amendment is to permit students and professors of

710

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

universities and institutions of similar standing within the jurisdiction
of the Lodge to apply for membership therein after having been enrolled
in the college or university for a period of six months or more continuously preceding the application, provided, of course, that the
applicant shall have the necessary Masonic residence in California.
This could be accomplished now by selection of residence and loss of
home residence. It merely permits application without loss .of legal
residence elsewhere in the State. We have prepared the requisite
legislation to accomplish this purpose. We offer the following resolution
amending Section 95 of the Constitution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that Section 95 of the Constitution be amended by adding
the following :
"If, however, the jurisdiction of a Lodge shall include a college,
university or other institution of like character and standing, the
jurisdiction of such a Lodge shall include jurisdiction concurrently
with any other lodge or Lodges having territorial jurisdiction over
any candidate who at the time of application is an officer, instructor
or student therein, and who, in addition to having Masonic residence
in California, shall have been regularly enrolled in such college,
university or similar institution for six months continuously preceding
the date of his application. The special jurisdiction conferred by this
section shall not be subject to waiver on the part of the Lodge
enjoying it."

The report \vas adopted, and Section 95 of the Constitution, as set out in the report, was amended by a fivesixths vote.
Request to Enlarge Jurisdiction of East Bay Lodges
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred the resolution of the East Bay Masters and Wardens Association requesting
this Committee to prepare and submit to Grand Lodge amendments to
the Constitution permitting concurrent jurisdiction to the Lodges in
the cities of Berkeley, Oakl;nd, Piedmont, San Leandro and Hayward,
respectfully report that section 92A of the Constitution now provides
the procedure to be followed for enlarging the territorial jurisdiction
of Lodges, and no special legislation is necessary. \Ve therefore recommend that the said resolution be not adopted.

Whittier Lodge, Naval Lodge, Needles Lodge
Your Committee has had under consideration the application of
Whittier Lodge No. 323. Naval Lodge No. 87, and Needles Lodge No.
326, for reimbursement for relief given in the following cases:
It appears that Whittier Lodge No. 323 has been assisting for the
last three years an old lady, seventy years of age, daughter of a member
of Sanger Lodge No. 129 of Waterville, N. Y., and on accom;it of the
Lodge refusing to reimburse them, have been put to the expense of
$1,005.00, which is a heavy drain on their Lodge, and although we
deplore the lack of knowledge on the part of the Masters of Whittier
Lodge in allowing this to accumulate through a period of three years,
we cannot help hut commend them for the Masonic spirit shown in
caring for this aged woman.
Your Committee had also under consideration the application of
Naval Lodge No. 87, for reimbursement to the amount of $159.50,

expended for the relief of Harley E. Glover, a member of Wm. H.
Upton Naval & Military Lodge No. 206 of Bremerton, Wash. All
their efforts to receive reimbursement from said Lodge have proven
of no effect.
We have also had under consideration the application of Needles
·Lodge No. 326 for reimbursement to the amount of $275.00, expended
for Dan R. Ballanger, a member of that Lodge. Brother Bal1anger
has been an invalid, totally disabled, and this is really a case for the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes, and we recommend that Needles
Lodge apply immediately to said Trustees for admission of Brother
Dan R. Ballanger to the Masonic Home, so that they may be assisted
through the Trustees in the care of this brother. But inasmuch as
the Trustees cannot make their action of assisting retroactive, we
believe that Grand Lodge can with propriety assist this Lodge in
carrying a heavy burden.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $1,439.50 is hereby appropriated from the
funds of this Grand Lodge to be paid as follows:
To Whittier Lodge No. 323, the sum of $1,005.00 for reimbursement
for the relief of Sarah Snow;
To Naval Lodge No. 87, $159.50, reimbursement for relief ·of Harley
E. Glover;
To Needles Lodge No. 326, the sum of $275.00, assistance in the
relief of Dan R. Ballanger.

Adopted.
Orosi Lodge No. 383
Your Committee has had under consideration the application of
· Oro5i Lodge No. 383, for assistance in enabling it to meet a final
payment of $900.00 due on its Lodge building. It appears from its
report that on July 4, 1922, the main buildings of the town were
destroyed hy fire, and that there was no suitable hall left for it to
meet in, and having been presented with a suitable building site, it
·has erected a hall which cast $11,000.00 This has been financed
by the members with the exception of $900.00, which they find them·
selves unable to borrow. and they therefore ask Grand Lodge to
assist them to the rxtent of loaning them $900.00, so that they should
not lose their hall.
We think this Grand Lodge justified in a case of extreme necessity
like this, to give a helping hand to these good brethren, who have done
all in their power.

Masonic Temple Association
The Committee has examined the report of the Masonic Temple
Association of California for the year, which shows that it has paid
its current expenses, besides paying off $10,000.00 on the mortgage,
which leaves a balance still due on the mortgage of $40,000.00.
While we are of the opinion that the fonds of this Grand Lodge
;i.~e sufficient to. enable us to wipe out the balance on this mortgage,
still we think that the Temple Association is well able to care for
some of this, and if Grand Lodge shall purchase $30,000.00, the Temple
Association should out of its revenues during the coming year pay
the balance of $10,000.00.
We therefore offer the following resolution, and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that this Grand Lodge purchase 3,000 sha~es of the
capital stock of the Masonic Temple Association of California at
$10.00 per share, in addition to the stock whi.ch we already own.

Adopted.

Purchase of Temple Stock
Your Committee have had before them the applications of Humboldt
Chapter No. 52, R. A. M., of Eureka, and of Franklin Lodge No. 143,
F. & A. M. of Courtland, to buy stock held by them in the Masonic
Temple Association of California, located at San Francisco.
It appears that these bodies purchased SO shares of stock each in
the Masonic Temple Association of California, amounting to $1,000.00.
This they did in good faith to assist a worthy cause.
It also appears that they have erected building·s in their own communities since that time, and now wish to assist in financing their own
homes.
While it would be obviously impossible for Grand Lodge to take
stock off the hands of all those who subscribed for it originally, yet
we cannot help but feel that in the present instances we should
relieve these brethren who generously assisted us.
We therefore offer the following resolution, and recotnrnend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $1,000.00 is hereby appropriated from
the funds of this Grand Lodge for the purpose of buying 100 shares
of stock from Humboldt Chapter No. 52, R. A. M., and Franklin
Lodge No. 143, F. & A. M.

Masonic' Homes
The Annual Report of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, together with financial reports certified by the accountants of
the Board, have been carefully examined, and they display excellent
management on behalf of the Trustees of the Homes.
Your Committee on Finance is of the opinion that a per capita tax
of 25 cents, in addition to the amount that will be received from the
$20.00 charge on initiations and affiliations, will produce sufficient revenue for the maintenance of the Masonic Homes of California. We,
therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of 25 cents per capita be levied upon the
membership for the maintenance of our Homes at Decoto and Covina,
payable July 31, 1924.

Adopted.
Masonic Education
Your Committee on Finance has had under consideration the recommendation of the Grand Master, William A. Sherman, that the Committee on Education be given sufficient funds to employ a paid executive Secretary, to be appointed by the Grand Master. After thoroughly
considering the needs of the Committee on Education, your Committee
on Finance has approved an appropriation of an amount not to exceed
$7,500.00, and offers the following resolution, and recommends its
adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $7,500.00, or as much thereof as may be
necessary, is hereby appropriated for the use of the Committee on
Education, in the employment of a paid Secretary and otherwise, the
same to be expended under the supervision and with the approval of
the Grand Master.

Adopted.
Masonic Club of the University of California
Your Committee on Finance has considered the request of the Board

its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $5,000.00 be appropriated from the funds

building and equipping the Masonic Club at the University of California.

Sojourners' Club at Fort Bayard, New Mexico
Your Committee on Finance has had under consideration the resolution introduced by Past Ma·ster William Rhodes Hervey, that $500.00
be appropriated for relief of the Soi ourners' Club at Fort Bayard,
New Mexico. From the information available it appears that this club
or hospital is being conducted in the interest of Masons, and its roster
discloses the fact that its sojourners are ex-service men who hail from
all parts of the United States. Your Committee feels that this is a
worthy cause and one in need of relief. We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $500.00 be appropriated from the funds
of this Grand Lodge to assist the Sojourners' Club at Fort Bayard,
New Mexico, in conducting its work, and that this check be made payable to Alpheus A. Keen, Grand Secretary of New Mexico.

Adopted.

REPORT
ef

Committee on Correspondence

REPORT
OF THE

Committee on Correspondence
OCTOBER, 1923
By JESSE M. WHITED
To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
I submit my fourth report on Foreign Correspondence.
A survey of the proceedings of the various Grand Lodges show
that the following are the matters engaging the attention of the
Craft.
First: Masonic education and the desire to furnish to the
newly raised Master Mason information and instruction as to the
·symbolism, history and ultimate purpose of the Fraternity.
Second: Impressing upon the members of the Fraternity that
Masonry stands for law and order, and that the individual as a
Mason and a citizen must live up to this ideal.
Third: The. relationship that the Blue Lodge should assume
with the co-ordinate bodies of Masonry or so-called "higher degrees."
Fourth: The association in the popular mind of the Masonic
Order with the "Ku Klux Klan."
Fifth: The advisability of limiting the membership of Lodges.
,
Sixth: The undesirable publicity that is now being given the
Fraternity, both by members and others.
Seventh: The advisability of requiring from applicants full and
complete data, by means of a questionnaire and a more rigid investigation by committees.
Eighth: That perfection in ritualistic work or increase in
membership should not be the ultimate aim of a lodge.
Ninth: That a set time should elapse between the conferring
of the degrees on any one candidate.
Tenth: The interest taken in the Order of DeMolay.

2

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

As in the past, the form of this report, which is generally
known as "topical" has been criticised. In the past it has been
favorably received by brethren of the jurisdiction of California. The
same style has, therefore, been followed. One of the objections
to the "topical" form of report is that it does not show what is
being done in other jurisdictions. To meet this criticism, therefore,
under the title, "Found in the Rubbish of the Temple," has been
summarized the events of interest and importance in the Masonic
world.
Acknowledgment is again made of the obligation we are under
to the Secretaries of the Grand Lodges and several Grand Bodies
of the United States, the Editors of Masonic publications and other
writers who have mat:!rially added to whatever value this report
may have.
It is, of course, understood that the opinions expressed
throughout the report are the individual ones only of the Chairman.
BALLOT
The strength and stability of the Fraternity, like that of our
Republic, depends upon the intelligent use of the ballot. Too often
this has not been the case, as is shown by the records of suspensions and expulsions. In some cases it has been used to serve private
ends or satisfy personal animosity. Educating a newly made Mason
in this detail might be profitable not only to him, but to the lodge
in general.
Canada:
Perhaps no topic has received more attention than the caution
to be exercised in dealing with the acceptance or rejection of applicants for admission. On one hand we have the warnings of those
who feel that the popularity of the Craft is leading it into dangerous
channels and that sufficient care is not taken in the selection of
proper material. On the other hand we are conscious of the fact
that in some cases personal prejudices, local jealousies, and thwarted
ambitions lead to a misuse of the blackball and to the exclusion of
men whose eligibility is beyond question. The malicious blackballing of desirable applicants, when once determined upon, is a difficult
matter to deal with, because it is usually the work of one whose
identity is concealed and who cares not whether he stains a brother's
honor with the stigma of his own infamy. Rut it is doubtful whether
this unmanly method of wreaking a petty revenge has done more
harm to the craft than the easy and complaisant attitude frequently
adopted in investigating the claims of applicants. The admission of
one whose public and private life is wholly at variance with our
teachings brings discredit on the good name of the institution and
repels many whose influence would give it a tone and a character in
keeping with its ideals.

HE.POW!' ON UORH.ESPONDENCE

Utah:
Grand Master called attention to the disregard of secrecy of the
ballot. An instance had come to his notice in which the result of a
ballot was known and discussed on the streets the morning following
the lodge meeting at which the same had been spread. There will
always be those who cannot hold their tongues, particularly when
some evil report or unpleasant action may be reported. If we dared
suggest it, and at times when we are properly protected, we venture
much, we would say there are men who can keep a secret almost as
well as a woman and we have met men who could talk almost as
glibly and fluently as some good women. In spite of this fact we
are not quite of the same opinion as the one who wrote that "Women
are words, men are deeds," for we have now and again, once in a
great while met a man ·who seemed to be mostly words.
Western Australia:
During the past year some trouble has arisen in connection with
the rejection of candidates on the ballot, and in more than one
instance has resulted in a very bad feeling being introducecf into the
lodge. The Masonic ballot has from time immemorial been held
to be a very sacred thing, and Grand Lodge has, very properly,
strongly discouraged any attempt to violate its secrecy. The rule
generally followed is for the brother who has an objection to a
candidate to state his objection to the Master, who will treat his
communication as strictly confidential, and the Master in turn will
recommend the proposer to withdraw his candidate. If the proposer
is disinclined to adopt this course then he must accept the consequences. Sometimes it happens that a brother knows something
regarding a candidate that he is unwilling to make public, and may
decide upon using· the machinery of the ballot box to record his
objection. This is perfectly constitutional, and perfectly Masonic,
for the blackball is just as legal as the white one. But this if often
the starting point of the trouble, and frequently great ingenuity is
displayed in the endeavour to trace the alleged offending brother
who deposited the blackball. Needless to say", conduct of this kind
is very improper, and should be sternly dealt with by the Master.
As the question of the ballot has been before Grand Lodge on different occasions, and the need for secrecy emphasized, I will quote
from the report of the Board of General Purposes in connection
with a case in which a brother was accused by several of his fellow
members of having blackballed a candidate: "The board desires to
impress upon all brethren, and particularly on Masters of Lodges,
the fact that the main character of a ballot is that the voting shall
be absolutely secret and independent. To his own conscience alone
has the brother to answer for the vote that he gives. A lodge is
not entitled to know how any of its members voted. No enquiry
on the subject can be entertained, and no information can be received. It is therefore essential that the ballot shall be secret. Not
only has no member a right to enquire how his brethren have voted,
but it is wholly out of order for him to explain or indicate, directly
or indirectly, his own vote. So soon as the ballot has been declared
the lodge should at once proceed to other business, and it is the
bounden duty of the \¥ orshipful Master in the chair peremptorily,

CIPHER RITUALS
While a number of Grand Lodge have strict regulations
against the use of Cipher Rituals, like a number of other laws, there
may be more honored in the breach than in the observance. In a
review of the various proceedings we have yet to note a case where
this rule has been violated and the offender punished. An example
might be of lasting benefit.
Iowa:
Indiana has a "written" ritual, of which there is but one copy,
which is in charge of the Grand Secretary and is never out of his
office. A "help" to the ritual is printed and distributed, as stated.
This help is simply the first letter of each word of the work and is
not iu.telligible to any one not knowing the ritual. It is a very satisfactory arrangement.
Iowa forbids even this, for we believe that the ritual should be
in the head and not in a book.
The unholy and unlawful practice of the use of ciphers by
officers of lodges is still lurking with us, but I am pleased to say
to you that its shadow is growing less, and now as it is on the
retreat it is hoped that the brethren will give it a vigorous kick.
Elect no officers who will not learn the work, and impress upon
them that you would rather they would resign than disobey Masonic
law in this matter,

CLANDESTINE MASONRY
This jurisdiction, principally through the efforts of the brethren
of Utah, is now happily free from the activities of the "American
Masonic Federation," Matthew McR Thomson and others of his
kind. Our Grand Secretary, John Whicher, also assisted in the
prosecution of these swindlers. The following excerpt from the
Proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Utah will give the reader some
idea as to the extent of this swindle.
Utah:
Somewhat more than twenty years ago a shrewd hard-headed
Scotchman, Matthew McBl(lin Thomson, b~ name \l.n'd by trade a

14

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

painter and paper-hanger, began, in a small way, peddling wh'.1t
he called Scottish Rite Degrees. Was he not a Scotchman, and did
he not have documentary proof of his right and "authority" to do
this very thing from three Scottish Grand Bodies, one of which
dated "from time immemorial?" And was not the "Charleston
Body"-as he was pleased to designate the Mother Supreme Council
of the World__:organized in the city of that name, and no longer
ago than 1801? What more could be expected or required?
Thomson lived in a little town up in Idaho at the time, and he
seems to have done a fairly profitable business. Railroad men, some
professional and business men, and at least one Past Grand Master,
bought of his wares. All this time, he was a member of a regular
lodge in the town where he lived; he had joined by affiliation, from
a lodge in Scotland on a frandulcnt demit; it lack"ed his own signature and the necessary confirmation of the Grand Secretary. He
atte~ded the Grand Lodge of Idaho as a proxy for the Worshipful
Master of his lodge, was appointed Grand Orator and came up the
next year also as proxy and delivered an oration!
In the meantime, however, Grand Lodge, had learned of his
activities in the matter of selling degrees, and action was taken
which very seriously affected his degree business, but it came only
after a prolonged fight on the floor of Grand Lodge, during which
Thomson spoke several times and at length in his own defense.
Thus far Thomson had not meddled with the first three degrees,
but, with the action of Grand Lodge which cut off his supply of
dupes, he turned his attention to devising ways and means of securing "authority" for conferring the symbolic degrees. Unless he succeeded in this, he would have no material for his "higher degrees."
The story is too long to be told here, hut at last he succeeded and
organized his own Grand Lodge-"Inter-Montana." This was in
January 1907, then came the American Masonic Federation, which
received into its bosom sundry clandestine organizations in the
country. This was incorporated during the summer of 1907, under
the laws of Idaho. Soon after Thomson moved his headquarters
to Salt Lake, and later as business prospered, a building was purchased a pr in ting plant installed, a monthly magazine issued, several b'ooks and numerous pamphlets published, and manifold
activities throughout the country were directed from this point.
During all these years this work went merrily on with little in
the way of interference or opposition. To be sure, now and again
one of his organizers would be arrested, and in some cases, jailed or
fined, and Thomson himself was expelled by the Grand Lodge of
Scotland. But this did not check progress and Thomson was quick
to capitalize such incidents, as persecution!
But finally the operations of one of Thomson's henchmen were
brought to the. attention of the Post Office Department and an
inspector was assigned to the task of investigating the organization.
That was in 1915. Hut progress was slow, for there was much
territory to cover in the investigation and Thomson had played his
game with shrewdness worthy of a better cause-and then the war
came on, for us, and the case put aside for the time being. With
the war ended, the inspector took up the trail once more, and he did
not lose it or leave it till he had evidence sufficient to present to a
Federal Grand Jury-that was in April 1921. A merry chase that

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

15

inspector had. Repeatedly, back and forth he swung across this
cc_rnntry, over to England and Scotland, and the Continent, but he
didn't once lose the scent, and the indictment of the four chief conspirators was the result. These were Matthew McBlain Thomson,
the head and organizer of this gigantic fraud scheme; Thomas
Perrott, ~ecretary general; Dominic Bergera, treasurer general (who
neve: hancllecl a dollar of the federation funds !) , and Robert
J am~son of Scotland, the foreign working partner in this scheme.
J am1son of course could not be brought here for trial. The arrest
of the three officers first named came in November following, and
the trial in May 1922, in the Federal Court of. Salt Lake City.
The men were tried for using the mails to defraud; the., indictment contained ten counts, and the defendants were each found
guilty on all ten counts and were sentenced, each to pay a fine of
$5000, to serve two years in the Federal Prison at Leavenworth and
to pay Government costs. Two furnished $15,000 bail and appealed,
Perrott, unable to give bail is serving his sentence at Leavenworth.
The existence of this far-reaching, increasingly vigorous clandestine organization, and the outcome of the trial concerned every
Masonic lodge in this country. Had this fraud been successful at
the trial, .conditions not unlike those which culminated in the United
Grand Lodge of England in 1813, might have been repeated.
It is easy to pooh, pooh, when ignorance of the actual situation
has blinded the eyes, and we have not taken any trouble to inform
ourselves. But to those who know, who were close enough to see
the possibilities of failure, who went through the weeks and months
of stress and strain of preparing to counter every possible move of
this arch-conspirator; who, again and again were balked, when seeking witnesses among men of national prominence by the well
known: "I pray thee, have me excused," having done all, still faced
seemingly almost insuperable obstacles, presented in the environment in which the case would be tried-to these brothers, at least,
the one big event which stands out in real importance above, and
beyond any other which marked the Masonic year 1922, was the
trial and conviction and final crushing of this gigantic Masonic fraud.
CLUBS
The fact that the clubs composed of the members of the Masonic Fraternity continue to multiply and flourish is perhaps the
best evidence that they serve a purpose. Like all other institutions
they may be subjected to criticism by the reason of the ill-advised
actions of some. These exceptions we do not believe should be
taken as a basis for sweeping condemnation. Masonry in its final
analysis is nothing more or less than Fraternity and Friendship,
and any means which will serve those ends should be commended
rather than censured.

The Grand Master desires to add his official approval and
commendation of the great Masonic club movement which the

brethren of this jurisdiction have been so largely instrumental in
bringing into a state of virile and beneficent activity all over the
land. I am aware that opposition ·to the Masonic club as a separate institution from the lodge has been voiced in some jurisdictions,
but it is my sincere belief that the opposition has been founded on
a false conception of the principles, objects and purposes of the
Masonic club, which are entirely constructive in their character
and in every aspect supplement, strengthen and support the work
of the lodges in spreading the doctrine of brotherly love, in affording immediate relief in many cases in which the lodge and its
officers might be impotent, and in bringing about intimate aquaintance and establishing enduring friendship among brethren who

Illinois:
A subject which has caused me much uneasiness during the
past year is the growing evil resulting. from· the formation in the
lodges of various kinds of athletic clubs, such as baseball clubs,
basketball clubs, bowling clubs, etc. At the inception of these
organizations it was believed that much good would come from the
form of innocent and healthful exercise which these friendly contests between the members of the lodges would produce. Instead
of promoting the generous and brotherly emulation which was expected, these contests have degenerated into the keenest and bitterest rivalry which in many cases has led the players and their
adherents into the most disgraceful quarrels, some of them resulting
even in fistic encounters.
In many cases, in their intense partisanship, the members have
forgotten not only the ordinary principles of sportsmanship, but
the requirements of decency and gentlemanly conduct as well.
Vile, abusive, and vulgar language has been frequently indulged in,
and disgraceful rowdyism has been not uncommon, and spectators
not Masons, have often been amazed, and naturally wonder what
sort of a fraternity it is whose members indulge in such ribald,
insulting and scandalous language and conduct toward each other.
With the formation of these clubs there has developed in the lodges
a sort of class spirit injurious to the welfare of the lodges, and, thi~
clannish class spirit in many cases has led to a bad kind of lodge
politics, such as the demanding of politicul recognition for the
athletic members in the selection of the officers of the lodges.
Moreover, in many cases, lodge funds have been used to finance
these clubs, to buy uniforms, etc. In every case which has come
to my attention where lodge funds have been so used I have advised that such uses cannot properly be called Masonic and are
therefore illegal.
All in all, greater evil than good has resulted from these athletic
clubs and craftsmen's leagues, and I have heen gradually, although
reluctantly forced to the belief that all these forms of clubs or
organizations within our lodges should be strictly forbidden.

The phenomenal growth of Freemasonry is reflected in the
Almost every

city or town in the Commonwealth which contains any considerable

has led to a situation which demands the consideration of the

hy the clubs.
From a close observation of the activities of the clubs I am
prepared. to emphasize an opinion expressed in a previous address
by a definite recommendation to the Grand Lodge, that in the
future no other organization except those recognized by the Grand
Lodge as Masonic shall be permitted to use the word Masonic in
its designated title and that those organizations already chartered
with permission to use a Masonic title take early steps legally to
change the same. There are numerous symbolic words that every
Mason would immediately understand as indicating a Masonic
connection, such as Ashier, Trowel, Square, Temple, and numerous others.
There is, however, in my judgment, an element of danger to
the Fraternity in too great a multiplying of these clubs and in the
encouraging of any idea that they are to take over or become the
center of Masonic social relations. * * * * If such club membership prompts a less frequent attendance at lodge meetings or
a less cordial support of lodge work or activities, then it becomes
harmful and not helpful.

CORNER STONES
A review of the Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges
show that laying of. corner stones seems to be one of the principal
functions of a Grand Lodge. While each jurisdiction has its own
particular laws, still we believe that the rule that the Fraterntiy
should officiate only at the corner stone layings of public buildings
is the most reasonable one a.nd calls for the least amount of objection or complaint.
Maine:
We note with especial favor the reference of Bro. Lucas to the
ceremony of laying corner-stones of churches on Sunday, an action
rather strangely prohibited by Grand Lodge, "fo mv judgment it
is high time to depart from this puritanical stand. W c say to our
church-going members, it is all right for you to go as a church
man and do these things, but you can't go as a Mason. It serves
to destroy our effectiveness by being criticized as narrow, while
our teaching and purpose is to the contrary." The old prohibition
-(we have had that word in Maine for many a long year before
Volstead was born) was on the ground of Masonic labor being
involved in corner-stone laying, but now it is a religious ceremonial especially as respecting Christian churches and especially
appropriate on Sunday.
Massachusetts:
I wish to bring to your attention something of the antiquity of
the ceremony of corner-stone laying. It is a necessary part of
our building and it should be of exceptional interest to the younger
brethren present who are to carry on the work in years to come.
Our ceremony of corner-stone laying dates back into the dim
ages of the past, beyond the beginning, even, of written history.
The earliest evidence discovered of anything showing a cornerstone laying is dated nine hundred years before the Christian era,
in Assyria, the first Temple.
Down through the ages, this custom has been followed whenever a building of
importance was to be erected-these ceremonies
attended the laying
the first stone. Throughout Europe are
nillcent edifices built as temples and brought down to us for our
miration. Unfortunate it is that so many have been destroyed during
the last six or seven years.

DECISIONS
Practically every Grand Master in his annual address calls attention to the fact that he is required to make decisions or rulings
on a number of questions which could easily be solved if the inquirer would refer to the printed law. While this is impliedly passing the problem to the party making the inquiry, in the final
analysis we believe it properly comes back to the Grand Lodge itself by reason of the multiplicity of laws, regulations, decisions and
statutes that are now on the books or that are regularly enacted
at each annual communication.

EDUCATION-MASONIC
A person after becoming a Master Mason is anxious for knowledge. We do not believe that this can be communicated by attendance at lodge, listening to the ritual and such fragmentary
information as can be picked up from time to time, and from
soi.trees that at the best are questionable. To supply this demand
the Educational Committee in a number of the jurisdictions are performing a service that cannot be estimated in dollars and cents.
While the fundamental ideas or basic teachings of Masonry are
communicated through the ritualistic work, still to supply the demand for "more light" there must be supplemental instruction. How
to furnish this to the greatest number at the minimum expense and
the maximum results is the problem. The idea embodied under
North Carolina we believe offers a solution of this question.

District o.£ Columbia:
The need and usefulness of a committee on Masonic education,
it is believed by this committee, is apparent. The present sources
at which such education may be obtained, and the advisability of
such sources for all desiring to use them, are indeed very limited.
The work of such a committee in disseminating and imparting, in
particular, Masonic history, law and philosophy, through various
means of publication, should be productive of much benefit to the
fraternity, not alone in the enlightenment of the initiate but in the
education of those amongst us who are unable to take advantage of
the limited available means now offered for ohtaining such knowledge. Your committee, therefore, earnestly recommends that the
Grand Lodge authorize the appointment of such a committee, with
duties as outlined in the recommendation of the Grand Master.

Pennsylvania:
That Masonic education is a present-day need and demand of
the Craft, there is no doubt. But what is Masonic education; where
should it begin and where end; what does the term embrace? The
!vfasonic Service Association has answered these questions in an
analysis of the "Brotherhood of Man;" and has divided this general
subject into five heads for discussion, viz: Religious Liberty, Equality Before the Law, Equality of Opportunity, Dignity of Labor,
Charity. The discussion of these subjects is intended to cover and
interpret Masonic ritual and charges, as applied to present-day human
relations. They cover a wide range: religion, political government,
economics, philanthropy, and, by implication, a long series of the
rights and duties of men as members of society, to be elaborated
ad infinitum. It is an ambitious program and, to a degree, comprehends a liberal education. It has been evolved by brainy leaders
of the Craft; and, therefore, it may be presumptions in an humble
private in the rear rank, like this writer, to question their conception of what is actually demanded in Masonic education.
The program outlined requires the expenditure of large sums
of money and sustained, voluntary effort which, experience shows,
wanes into desuetude after the first excitement. Our belief is that
the Craft-as such-should be expected to absorb only elemental
Masonic education, which may be imparted with a minimum of
expense and effort. The trouble with the present situation is, that
the average Mason does not know what Masonry means, although
he may he well informed on "Religious Liberty." He has joined
the Fraternity, lured by its mystery, a desire for social intercourse
and partly by certain motives of self-interest. After going through
the "degree mill" he knows about as little of its science and philosophy as when he started-unless he is the exceptional student who
relies UP.on himself for progressive knowledge. He has not established a basis for thought on the relation of Masonry to "Religious
Liberty," etc. \Nhat he actually needs are elementary Masonic
definitions and concepts; the history and traditions of the Craft;
its symbolism; and something of its jurisprudence, hindmarks,
customs and 11sages. The average Mason knows little about these
things. Tt seems to us that some plan may, lie devised to impart
lrnowkclge of them as a routine function of the lodge, in schools
which the newly-made lfason, at least, must attend before he is
vested with all the rights and privileges of membership.
.After these fundamentals are acquired, plans may be adopted
for advanced study, the application of Masonic principles to the

EDUCATION-PUBLIC
Practically all Grand Lodges have taken the stand in favor
of education and the support of the great Public School system
of our Country. We believe this end can best be accomplished
by elevating the public school. to such a standard of excellence
that there will be no necessity for private schools of any kind
whatever.
The report of the State Superintendent of Public Instruction
of California shows that there are approximately 800,000 children
of school age in this state; 42,000 are being educated in private
schools. In a number of cities the pupils are being housed in
temporary shacks and tents, the teachers are underpaid and pupils
are being taught only half-time. If Masonry has a mission in every
day affairs it is perhaps to make a change so that every boy and
girl will have the great American privilege of "Equality of Opportunity."

He must oppose all influences, be they ecclesiastical or otherwise

Towner-Sterling Bill, now pending. 'This is Educational Week.

the right to an education is the inalienable right of every child from
which no parent, much less an outside agency, can rightfully deprive him. Our State has the right to compel the parent to educate
the child, and the fact that private schools instead of public schools
have been allowed as a privilege and not as a right, means that
when this privilege is abused, it can certainly be withdrawn. There
are now agencies in our country that attempt to subvert the rights
guaranteed by our laws and constitution, and even the rights of the
parents themselves in dictating the education of our children by
saying that "education is none of the State's business." Surely no
church or sect has the right to place their authority over the State
in the matter of compulsory education in our public schools, for
when they attempt to take this prerogative from our government
then we no longer have a free government with the power to insure
the protection of our rising generation.

South Dakota:
The Grand Master tells us that:
Masonry in this jurisdiction has been instrumental in passing
two great laws which will materially advance education in this
State. One of these, requiring every teacher to take an oath to
support the Constitution of the State and of the United States
before they can obtain a certificate to teach. The other is what
is known as the Language Bill, passed by the last Legislature, requiring every child of school age to attend the public schools, during the time of the term in the school district, until they shall have
reached the eighth grade, where only the English language is
taught. This last bill was fought very hard by the patrons of
parochial schools, but the Legislature being composed of more
than fifty per cent Masons, it was passed and passed with a clause
of compulsion that has teeth in it.
Tennessee:
Two years have passed since Freemasonry in Tennessee took
official cognizance of educational conditions in the State. At the
historic session in January. 1921, educational committees were
created by the Grand Masonic bodies with authority to develop an
organization within the Fraternity for the purpose of awakening

The two years just passed have been eventful in the educational history of our State, and your committee is bold enough to
believe that no small part of this great forward movement should
be credited to the activity of our membership in the tremendous
cooperation given the school movement.
At the close of the school year in June, 1922, Tennessee had
struggled upward from )he 44th to the 42nd place among the 48
states .from the standpoint of educational efficiency.
\Ve have re<luced our one-room, one-teacher schools from 4729
to 3422. During the last two years we have added eighty-six consolidated schools, and we now have a total of 482 such schools in
the State, or an aver;i.ge of five for each county. The cost of this
development was $750,000. A great building program is now under
way and the coming years should show even better progress.
During the past year only one county had a rural school
term of less than one hundred days, while during the preceding
year fourteen counties failed to reach that mark.

While we may perhaps question the advisability of making the

District of Columbia:
Had politicians been kept out of the temperance movement the
drink habit would have continued to diminish, and in a few years,
would have been negligible, for it was growing less and less.
In 1804 there was more money estimated. for grog on a United
States frigate than for beef and pork together. In 181 Z there were
delivered to one (\Vashington) Navy Yard alone, "120 barrels of
good whiskey, at 52 cents a gallon," for issue to the ships of the
navy, but after the Civil \Var began grog was discontinned as part
of the ration, and only wine and malt liquors permitted on board.
This was effected through the temperance movements, and with
common consent.
No constitutional amendment was needed,
sought, nor suggested.
But by the 18th amendment the Government loses a round billion dollars in revenue annually, and has to spend $88,000,000 in its
effort fo enforce prohibition, while the sale of narcotics, insidious
drugs (substitutes for grog) has increased 300 per cent., and !:(overnment reports show that Americans have become the head of the
list of addicts, or "dope-fiends." Arrests for drunkenness have diminislwd, hut murders, bank rohhcries. highway rohheries, and defalcations have become greatly on the increase. The horrible examples exhibited by the "prohibs" were probably true, but their own
relatives should have been punished instead of the 98 per cent. of
temperance people.

New South Wales:
When a lodge apr,lies for a charter on the plea that it is fo be
a "temperance lodge,' I have always made a point of making a
special endorsement upon the warrant to that effect. I recently
received a letter from a country lodge applying for permission to
have this endorsement waived, on the grounds that "many of the
brethren consider that they should be temperate away from the
lodge as well as in the lodge, and, as most of them take" a glass,
they feel that they should not belong to a temperance lodge; in
