All this would be amusing if it did not cast a deep reflection upon
the Masonic spirit of the inhabitants of this particular locality.
Masons who will not attend a lodge only because they cannot there
imbibe their alcoholic beverages, are better far outside the institution
altogether. I endorsed this application as follows: "I regret very
much the evidently changed ideas of the brethren of this lodge.
They applied for a charter for a 'temperance lodge,' and got it. If
they now desire to abandon the principles upon which the lodge
was founded, they must decide to surrender this charter, thus closing
the lodge, and petition for a totally new lodge." I have had no
further correspondence upon this subject.
w·e think the Grand Master's view rather narrow. \Ve do not
question his ruling, hut his reflection on the "Masonic spirit of the
inhabitants." It is one thing to go to a lodge because you may
there get something to drink, and another thing to find that the
success of the banquet which usually follows a lodge meeting is
imperilled by the absence of a "modest quencher." The banquefroom is the place where the brethren get together and learn to
know each other, and no stigma shoul4 be placed upon those who
wish to make it attractive, so long as the law is not infringed, and
there is no excess. In our experience in Canada, before we "went
dry," there never was anything like excess at Masonic banquets.

EMBLEMS
It is written "On This Theme We Contemplate." In so doing
we are minded to inquire whether the desire to wear an emblem
has not produced a number of conditions against which Grand
Lodges are now called upon to legislate. The button Mason is
usually very much in evidence and through him the general public
form their estimate of the Fraternity. Perhaps Masonry might
mean more if it could be judged other than by this form of publicity.
Colorado:
By Section 296 of the Hook of Constitutions, we have forbidden the
use of Masonic emblems for advertising purposes, and the letter of the
law is generally obeyed. There is, however, a general violation of its
spirit by the indiscriminate use of the word "Masonic" in the same
connection. Commercial concerns are using it, not only to attract attention to their business, but in a manner and with the purpose of conveying the impression that their enterprises are connected with, or approved by the Fraternity. Insurance and accident companies are the
most notorious violators thereof. If the use of the square and compass,
which at most can but imply an association, be forbidden, then certainly
the use of the term "l\fasonic," which asserts that association, should
be banned.
District of Columbia:
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of Mississippi give its cordial and

South Carolina:
Grand Lodge (Tasmania) went on record as discountenancing the

Virginia:
He noted that Grand Master Galt ruled that a Mason whose conduct is immoral should not wear a Masonic pin, and wants to know
how we are to enforce our Virginia civil law forbidding it. Our law
only forbids those not members of a society wearing the emblems, and
when a l\'Iason is so immoral as to have his conduct notorious we can
only rejoice that his wearing the square and compasses serves to lower
his repute among ·Masons. We have no other remedy except that discipline we all avoid when possible.
Washington:
We have been struck with the fact that none of the brethren
whose portraits adorn the volumes we have thumbed over for so long
wear the emblem of Ancient Craft Masonry. If you omit the Grand
Masters of the English Dependencies, who always have their photographs in fu!l Masonic regalia, you will find everything, almost, except
the square and compass-Shrine emblems, Scottish Rite, Chapter and
Commandery are in evidence, but among those which are distinguishable one searches in vain for the lowly insignia of the lodge. Probably not one of them values these organizations above their lodges. In
fact many of them have spoken of the super-eminency of Ancient Craft
Masonry and not one of them has failed to voice his appreciation of the
honor bestowed in electing him to preside over the Craft; but the
visible mark of his Masonry does homage to some other institution. Of
those who wear nothing in the way of jewelry we have no criticism,
but we do think the others might at least don the square and compass
when they sit for their photo for the Grand Lodge proceedings.

to open up, or a sufficient number of proficient men to do the work.
There are a number of competent, capable, efficient workers in the
city who go from lodge to lodge, and fill the place of absent
officers. From four to ten of these men will be found at all lodge
meetings, ready to fill almost any position that they may be called
upon to take. Their ritualistic proficiency is very nearly perfect,
and they are at home in all of the several stations. They may, perhaps, work with such speed that they do not give proper expression
or interpretation to the ritual, but they are regular "bears" for
work, and many Masters have cause to bless them for aid when
badly needed. These men are called "rounders." They will work
uncomplainingly through the long afternoon with no reward in sight,
other than a lodge supper and a cigar or two. They are emphatically not the "knife and fork brigade," meaning members
who arrive just in time for supper, but who are too busy to stay
for the evening work. These men are really good Masons, as their
work or business is such that they are free during the day, or they
ate not compelled to labor daily, and most of them are members
who have an abiding love for Masonic work. Nearly every Master
in Chicago knows these "rounders." They are a bunch of good
fellows, but it is doubtful if thev receive credit commensurate with
the value of' their service in the cause of Masonry.

Georgia:
A most unusual anq affecting incident occurred when the
mother of Grand Master Bass was admitted and received in the
East. She was presented with the Past Grand Master's jewel intended for her son. The presentation speech was made by Grand
Correspondent Raymond Daniel, whose chaste English and beautiful thoughts brought tears to the eyes of the 1200 Masons who
heard him. In response Grand Master Bass said: "My brethren,
words are so weak when love is so strong. You have placed the
jewel where it most belongs, for if there be aught of good in me it
is due to mother. I thank you. God bless you." The Grand Secretary closed the incident with these words: "Would that an artist's
brush had touched this scene, that the world might have received
its impress. Words are so weak when love is so strong.".

Iowa:
\Ve are informed that Nova Scotia's was the first home established by the Masonic Fraternity in British America.
It seems that there has been some considerable gambling going
on at Masonic picnics, which caused the Grand Lodge (Kentucky)
to adopt a resolution to the effect that all wheels of chance, or
devices of chance of any character or description, where money or
anything of value is lost or won. upon the payment or deposit of
money or anything of value, shall be prohibited for use, operation.
exhibition, or display, at any picnic, outing, or gathering, held
under the auspices of a Masonic Lodge or auxiliary.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

The Grand Master (Iowa) reports that there is an increasing
number of Masonic picnics being held. Your committee believes
that these occasions are not only highly enjoyable, but that they
are productive of much good in that they promote acquaintance
and good fellowship among the members of the Craft, and their
families as well. We be Ii eve that every county should have a picnic
association, and heartily endorse the Grand Master's suggestion for
increased activities in this direction.
Kan.sas:
He (New Jersey) recommends setting aside N av ember 4 as a
celebration day, commemorative of the initiation of George \Vashington, which occurred on November 4, 1752. Upon his recommendation a number of lodges celebrated on this date, at \Vhich
time addresses were delivered, church services held, and pageants
given. We are for George Washington all right and respect his
virtues, but so far as Masonry is concerned we have never found
anything from an historical viewpoint which would warrant Masonic lodges setting aside any particular day of the year because of
the fact that he was an honored member of the Craft.
They (Montana) have a new form of voting for their grand
officers consisting of a slip heing prepared by the Grand Secretary
on which is printed the offices to be filled, and each representative
not only votes for a Grand Master, but on the same ballot votes
fbr all elective grand officers. A sort. of short cut, we might
term it.
The Grand Lodge (Mississippi) endorsed a bill pending in their
State Legislature, fornidding the wearing of emblems by persons
not authorized to do so. We note from the proposed bill it indicates the organizations covered in this protective proposition. The
wisdom of the Grand Lodge lending its endorsement, however,
might be questioned by ·Masonic scholars.
The Grand Lodge (Kentucky) determined to purchase and
present to each Past Grand Master a solid gold button to be worn
on the lapel of the coat of suitable design to advertise the fact
that the wearer is a Past Grand Master. An appropriation of
$150.00 was made to cover the cost of fifty buttons.
Few Past Grand Masters care to wear a large and expensive
jewel, except on rare and infrequent occasions. An inexpensive
button of this kind would be worn at all times with great satisfaction.
A resolution of a former Grand Communication requiring the
flag to be carried around the lodge room, brought before the altar
and saluted by the brethren at the opening ceremonies of a lodge,
was repealed, and the following substituted in lieu thereof:
The American flag should be exhibited in every lodge upon a
staff, or be hung in a suitable place in the lodge room, during all
its meetings. Its use in the opening ceremonies is recommended,
hut the extent of such ceremony shall be optional >vith the lodge.
It is apparent that the Grand Lodge of Kentucky does not look
with favor upon the idea of promiscuous circular letters being
sent to the lodges of the jurisdiction for it requires all requests
to circularize to have the approval of the Grand Master.

North Carolina:
It was reported that two Shrines had pledged 50 cents per
member for two years to build a swimming pool and fitting up
athletic grounds at the Oxford· Orphans Home. The per capita
expense of maintaining the asylum was $211.58 per year.
The singing class of the Oxford Orphan Home earned, net,
during the year $35,563.94; they gave 185 concerts, an average of
$192.24 per concert. Giving 185 concerts in different parts of the
State and elsewhere means that the class was absent from the
home. the greater part of the year, and we wonder how the education of the boys progressed during that period.
Another educational scheme was adopted by Grand Lodge
called "a Masonic Educational Loan Fund." Its purpose is to
make loans to boys and girls in NoFth Carolina to helo them
to obtain higher education, they to sign notes, endorsed by two
parties acceptable to the committee in charge of the fund.
The Smith-Towner educational bill was endorsed.
By action of the Grand Lodge each subordinate lodge failing
to file its returns with the Grand Secretary by Septen1ber first
annually shall be liable to a fine of $2.50, while failure to make

tine of $5.

Quebec:
The question wa~ asked, "Can a lodge work by virtue of the
presence in the lodge room of a photograph of its charter, the
original having been destroyed, or removed?" I ruled as follows:
"A lodge can work only by virtue of a charter from Grand Lodge,
or a dispensation from the Grand Master, and the presence in
the lodge room of that charfer or dispensation is indispensable.
The photograph of a charter can no more carry the authority of
a charfer than the photograph of a man can perform the functions
of a man."

principles of our great Fraternity to allow gambling or games of

they are legal or simply winked at by the authorities. The ultimate
result cannot be other than bad.

Michigan:
On March 20, 1923, I felt it my duty to issue the following order,
and had a copy mailed to the Worshipful Master of each constituent
lodge:
Being firmly convinced that the practice of holding circuses, fairs
and bazaars, the raffling of automobiles, or any other commodity, and
the use of punch boards for the distribution of prizes in connection
with and under the auspices of constituent lodges, is a reflection on Masonry and not in keeping with the principles of our great Fraternity, I
deem it my duty to issue this order prohibiting such practice by any
lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction on and after March 23, 1923.
If there is any one thing that Masonry stands for it is the upholdjng of the laws of our Commonwealth, and I am sorry to say, many of
the things being practiced today are in· direct violation of the law.
Michigan:
It is my firm conviction that the membership in our Grand Jurisdiction will never be found wanting when money is needed for any truly
Masonic enterprise, and I am sure you will agree with me that we
will have manifested in onr Masonry a far greater spirit of harmony,
with these undesirable things eliminated, than could possibly exist under
the present conditions.
While to some this order may seem very drastic, I am firmly convinced that as a Masonic institution we have no right to do things
under the guise of Masonry that we as individuals would not be permitted to do, and I do not believe there is a brother present who can
conscientiously say that the practices employed by many lodges during
the past in reference to the things as set forth in this order has not in
a sense been a detriment to Masonry.

THE GRAND LODGE
The Grand Lodges being the source of all authority must
necessarily be judged by the results of their work. The view expressed under the subdivision of Colorado we believe summarizes
the matter along practical and consistent lines.
Colorado:
In view of what has been hereinbcfore stated, and considering the
apparent confusion in the Masonic world, the. time seems ripe for the
re-statement by this Grand Lodge of the following fundamental principles:
I-The government of the Grand Lodge is neither a monarchy,
ali oligarchy, nor a "pure democracy." It is a representative, constitutional republic. Every attempt to graft upon it any of the distinguishing characteristics of the first three forms named is forbidden by the
injunction against "innovations upon the body of Masonry."
2-The Grand Lodge, which is but the entire body of the Craft in
the jurisdiction, acting through its duly chosen representatives, and
restricted only by the landmarks, has the sole power and authority to
determine what is and what is not "Masonic," and to fix the conditions
under which a petitioner may enter Freemasonry, or, having entered,
remain. Its only guide is its best judgment as to what is required by
the good of the Craft, and from its decision there is no appeal.
3-The only title to Masonic oftice is the best judgment of the
brethren voting or the officer appointing, uninfluenced hy improper
solicitation and exercised with no consideration in mind hut the highest good of the Craft.
4---This Fraternity, its activities, titles, ceremonies, symbols, and
emblems, are not to be used for political or commercial purposes. It
repudiates all solicitation for its degrees, all advertisement. all unseemly publicity. lt tolerates no foreign meddling in its affairs. It
interferes with no man's religion and will not concern itself with matters of political or legislative policy.

GROUP INITIATION
The objections to group initiation, we believe, are based on
sentimental reasons rather than personal ones. So far as we have
been able to ascertain, group initiation would not violate any of
the "Ancient Landmarks." It is a question that is engaging the
attention of a number of Grand Lodges. In the long run the practical workings of the system should be the guide ratheT than individual cases. Some of the largest jurisdictions use this method
and as they have prospered and thrived it appears to be a question
of expediency. Part of the ritual of all three degrees)s now grouped
and we do not know that it has had any bad effects on California
Masons.

Utah:
From the Grand Master's (Western Australia) address at the
quarterly communication, January, 1921, we learn that it has been
the general practice when initiating candidates to take them together
all the way through the ceremonies. Occasionally we learn of jurisdictions in this country adopting this practice but there are not
many such. Grand Master Reily very properly said: "As the ceremony of initiation is likely to create in the mind of the novitiate
more lasting impressions than any of the other degrees, it seems
to me desirable that it should be made as solemn as possible." And,
again, "As a man is only made a Mason once,· every care should be
taken to make his entry into the Craft as impressive as possible, and
I am convinced that this cannot be done when candidates are crowding around the altar." With these sentiments, we are in hearty
accord. In Utah and in nearly all other jurisdictions in the United
States, candidates are taken singly up to the point where the lecture
is given. A plan similar to this, the Grand Master wishes to have
adopted in Australia.
HIGHER DEGREES
Whether the Symbolic Lodge is to be used as a stepping stone
for "higher degrees" is a question that has been under consideration by practically all of the Grand Lodges of the United States.
There are two views: First, The Grand Lodge is concerned only
with the Symbolic degrees. Second, By reason of the connection
between the so-called "higher degrees" and the Symbolic Lodge,
where it works to the detriment of the Fraternity, the Grand
Lodge has a right to legislate upon the matter, either expressly
or by implication.
The statements of the Grand Masters of Oregon and Pennsylvania represent one extreme, while that of the Committee of the
Grand Lodge of Wyoming represents the other.
It has been said that the Masonic system may be likened to
the educational system of the United States. Symbolic Lodge
represents the common school, the Ancient and Accepted Scott'sh
Rite the University system, the Knights Templar the military idea
and the Mystic Shrine the fraternal or "playground" idea. Each
division has its place and function. Training in the common
school is essential to the success of the entire system. The value
of the individual Mason, both in public and private life must, therefore, depend upon the education that he receives in the elementary
school, to wit, the Symbolic Lodge.

Colorado:
At our last annual communication we were obliged to repudiate
one of those fraternal parasites which sought to fasten itself upon
the body of Freemasonry, appropriate its degrees and march beneath its banners. Others are appearing and causing much concern in this, as well as other grand jurisdictions. The same principles apply to all. and if we could turn back the pages of history
and write it anew, we might discountenance all. This, of course; at
the present time, is impracticable. We have a condition to meet,
due largely to our easy tolerance, and not a theory to vindicate.
But we should take no additional step down the road we have
mistakenly traveled in the past.
Delaware:
It is our sincere judgment that Masonry is suffering in these
modern days from two serious diseases. The first of these is the
anxiety on the part of the majority of the members of the Craft
to know the mysteries of the so-called "Higher Degrees." There
are no higher degrees. There can be nothing higher than the three
degrees of Blue Lodge Masonry and nothing holier than to attain
to that moral eminence which is involved in the term Master Mason. A Master Mason has the mastery over himself. His passions
have been subdued, his ambitions have been brought into harmony
with truth and justice, his powers are directed into the channels of
duty to God and his fellow men, selfishness has been conquered.
He is a man, a ma~ter, the noblest work of God.
It is a serious mistake for our members to come into our lodges
and i-mmediately upon receiving the Master Mason Degree,. rush a
petition into the Chapter, or the Consistory, and on into the Mystic
Shrine, before they become acquainted with the basic principles of
Masonry, all of which are to be found in the Blue Lodge.

Illinois:
Every now and then some Grand Lodge pulls off a piece of
legislation that is not only nonsensical but wholly without the pale
of common sense.
During the last year Colorado startled the Masonic world by
passing a law that no Master Mason could receive the so-called
higher degrees until after one year following his initiation. This
action· shows, in a measure, the general inconsisteney of Grand
Lodges. In one breath they will declare that the sum total of
Ancient Craft Masonry is concerned in the three degrees conferred
hy the lodge. Then in the next breath they will commence to
legislate against what are alleged to be the higher bodies of the
Fraternity. If Grand Lodges are disposed to hold that all there
is to Masonry is confined to the three degrees then why the legislation against the Chapter, Commandery and Consistory which in
a measure are declared to be clandestine?
A good many Masons lose sight of the fact that Freemasonry
is a principle and not a group of individuals. If this fact could be
realized, a great deal of trouble arising at the present time would
be obviated and done away with. The spirit of the times demands
co-ordination. If the Fraternity is going to get anywhere it means
that not only Ancient Craft Masonry but those organizations associated with it must join hands and work together.
For fifty years we have had in our midst, the Chapter, Council
and Consistory and we can see no reason why at this late date,
legislation should be directed against these bodies. If any of their
members are doing things which are disposed to refi.!'Ct upon
Ancient Craft Masonry, all it is necessary to do is call the attention of the proper authority to the sins of commission and it is
believed everything will be rectified and straightened out.

HISTORY-MASONIC
Napoleon said that history was fiction upon which liars agreed.
There are too few Masonic historians and the utterances of Grand
Orators, public speakers, ill-informed talkers have presented to the
general public a misconception of the history of Freemasonry. A
statement once uttered can never be recalled, and too often these
fictions take the place of absolute facts.

65

If there is one service that an Educational Committee of a
Grand Lodge or the Grand Lodge itself could perform it would
be to preserve for posterity a record of Masonic activities, etc., by
securing the historical facts in connection with the life of the lodges
in their particular locality.
Alabama:
Und.er a resolution adopted in 1918, Brother Street had essayed
the wor~ of ascertaining, by means of a questionnaire, designed to
get pertment facts, from every organized Grand Bodv in authentic
Masonic existence, upon which to decide upon justification for recognition, or warrant its denial, and he had succeeded beyond expectatio? in securing information, which en bloc he presents in an
admirable report, which takes the place of a review of proceedings.
In a story covering 376 pages we have a comprehensive statement of facts or of evidences of legitimacy procured by his intelligent and painstaking industry, to which he adds value by lucid
comment, and in fine, as the end which crowns his work, delivers
to the reader the best epitome of Masonic status in the civilized
world that it has been our good fortune to peruse under one cover.
Nevada:
The oration incident to Grand Lodge meeting was delivered by
Edward A. Ducker. It was Masonic and historic in character. In
one paragraph he says: "Freemasonry is hoary with age. Traditionally it is older than the sphinx." Seriously speaking, we wish
he hadn't said that. The non-thinking Mason will fail to take into
consideration the meaning of that word "traditionally" and the
result will be a misunderstanding of what the orator really meant
to say or rather, should have said. \Ve are now Jiving in an age
when Masonic writers and speakers must be careful what they say.
The present century is demanding the truth concerning the origin
and development of our Fraternity.

pamful to exhaust efforts to find the exact facts as to those whom we

HOMES
The question of the advisability of establishing Masonic Homes
is one upon which practical Masons may differ. Those jurisdictions that maintain homes are, of course, committed to that plan.
Those that distribute relief through a general Charity Fund are
as strongly in favor of that system.
It is. a question that should be considered from a business
standpoint. On this basis after a review of the reports of the
various Homes we are somewhat inclined to agree with the opinion
of that held by the Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence
of Colorado, particularly taking into consideration the investment,
overhead and the number that are actually benefited.
In some States the investment runs into hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the wants of a very limited number.
Maine:
The Committee on Masonic Correspondence (Colorado) has
this vital thing to say in its report, relative to Masonic Homes,
which amply justilic.:s our own-and their own-attitude toward
the5e institutions: "After a review of the moneys expended in
the erection and !icing· spent in the maintenance of Masonic Homes
throughout the United States, we arc reminded of the statement of a
Past Grand Master of our hocly that it would be very much cheaper
for us to board our .indigent aged ;.it the Brown Palace Hotel."

New South Wales:
One of the most interesting features in the proceedings of
th~ various grand lodges consists of the reports concerning Masonic Homes and kindred institutions. These indicate that year
by year Masons throughout the world are giving more practical
help to their aged and indigent brethren and their wives, and to ,
the widows and orphans of brethren who have been unable adequately to provide for their families. There must be thousands
of men and women who are spending the evening of their lives
protected and comforted by Freemasons, and there are thousands
of orphan children being clothed, housed and educated who, without
these homes, would have a poor chance of development, but who
under the fostering care of our Craft, are being prepared to face
the battle of life well equipped, mentally, morally and physically,
to become useful citizens. A large proportion of these children
would, if not brought under our guardianship, probably qualify
for that grade of society which sooner or later becomes more or
less a charge on the state, and it can therefore be confidently asserted that this great work is of national importance, apart altogether from the fact that it is an outward and visible sign that
Masons· are giving practical exemplification of the fact that they
are not unmindful· of their duty to relieve distress and succor
the afflicted and helpless.
A marked feature of the reports is that applications for admission exceed the room available, but in most instances this
position is being faced by an extension of existing buildings or
the erection of new homes. The growth in the cost .of upkeep
of these institutions is remarkable, especially in recent yearswhich brought with them an era of high prices-and although
there has been a general reduction in the prices of necessit11::,,,
the cost of maintenance seems to be on the increase.
Quebec:
The third great hranch of Masonic achievement to which Iowa
points with pardonable pride is that of her relief work. If there
is a single worthy case of Masonic want, deprivation, misery, or
suffering in the state of Iowa, says Brother Block, that is not
being promptly and efficiently relieved, the writer has not been
able to discover its existence, and he believes that he is in a
position to know. All this is being accomplished by means of
a highly organized charity system that has rendered satisfactory
service for many years past-a system which delivers the goods
without the necessity of establishing either a home, a hospital,
a sanitarium, or an asylum. There is not a single one of the
recipients of Masonic relief in the State of Iowa, who is being
"institutionalized"-and yet each and every charity case-be it man,
woman or child-is being cared for in a quid and efficient way,
that relieves the recipient without making him a subject of public
pity, and without sacrificing one bit of his personal pride or selfrespect. By Masonic statute the three principal officers of each
local lodge are constituted a Committee of Charity whose duty

North Dakota:
Fort Bayard, New M cxico, is the largest Tubercular Camp for
service men in the United States. Among these sick soldiers are scores
of Master Masons. Practically every Grand Lodge is represented. The
Grand Lod!le of New '.vTexico has been active and generous in its efforts
to bring relief to these brethren. They have maintained a brother to
act as representative of the Craft there and have clone everything in
their power to relieve the situation, contributing $300.00 monthly. The
Grand Master Brother Francis E. Lester, presented the situation to the
Masonic Service Association and also issued an appeal to the Grand
Lodges of the United States, asking for help in the erection of a Soiourners' Club designed to care properly for the needs of the Craft at
Fort Bayard. One or two of our lodges asked that this Grand Lodge
do something. This was brought to the attention of the trustees of
the relief fond, who very promptly authorized a contribution of $500.00.
This w~s sent and a <Irateful acknowledgment was received from
Grand Master Lester. Very reccntlv. the Grand Commander of the
Northern J nrisdiction of Scottish Rite. Past Grand Master Leon N.
Abbot, has authorized the contribution of $25,000.00 for this purpose.

Connecticut:
The Grand Masters of New Mexico, ::vfissouri and Iowa, sent out
encyclicals warning against the .Ku Klux Klan. From this, we judge
tbat their pernicious activities are plainly apparent there. There is
also some evidence that they are carrying on an active propaganda
among the Masons of Connecticut. vVe understand that they boast
that eighty per cent 'of their members are Masons. vVhile we cannot
believe this statement, it is a matter for alarm if any Masons
are lured into the spider's web of joining this gang, who announce
their intentions to at times override law and order. This latter
explains their shame to have tven the names of their members
known.
Whatever excuse there may have been in the south for the
existence of this organization in the days of reconstruction after
the Civil war, there is surely none· now. \¥hile we believe that
the "Klan" will ultimately break down within itself, we earnestly
hope that all Masons will keep out of it, and thereby avoid a
source of later bitter self-reproach.
Cuba:
The ](u Klux Klan is still attracting public attention. Since
Iowa and Missouri started the campaign against them the innovators of Atlanta have suffered many deceptions, until the Grand
Lodge of Texas gave them the final blow. As Texas is a southern
state and near the offices of the K. K. K. she has mighty reasons
for her doings. Many of the members of the K. K. K. were among
the Texan Masons and so they pretended to capture the Grand
Lodge completely, but, happily they met with a Grand Master as
was necessary. He waited for them with full preparations, and
without insulting or belittling them, but only by spreading a circular letter explaining the intentions of the Knights of the Luminous Cross, he overturned their plans, hindering them from using
Masonry for improper ends, that, together with the law against
lynching, at present being discussed in the American Congres"with a sure success. make us the most incredulous about the societv
of the hooded members. Let them rest in peace.

District of Columbia:
In the jurisprudence report there is reference to the Ku Klux
Klan which says: "It is a secret organization with a secret
111e111hership, therefore wholly irresponsible to the very government
whose laws it claims to uphold." Without questioning this, we
wonder if the American Federation of Labor and the Knights of
Columbus and the Ancient Order of Hihernians do not come close
to the same thing?
There are more laws on om statute books than on similar
hooks in Germany and England together, and from these the lawyers are able to discover their technicalities. These are probably
the reasons the Ku Klux think some law, better adapted to our
safety, is needed. But we must bow our heads in submission to
the law.

On the twenty-second day of June, 1922, having read in flaming headlines that the Ku Klux Klan were claiming that their
ranks in certain localitites were being largely recruited from Freemasonry, I issued a statement expressing my opposition to, and
disapproval of, any connection between Masonry and the Klan,
and ::\mong other things said:
Masonry does not undertake to regulate or interfere with any
outside matter. Its long life and great usefulness are due to the
fact that it has never allowed any deliberation or discussion in
its lodge room regarding any subject not concerning Masonry upon
which might be developed a controversy.

vVhile we have no concern with the K. K. K., or any organization as such, we may have a vital concern, regarding the conduct
oi Masons in joining that, or any other society, whose activities
may be regarded as a menace to Jaw and order.
In answer to your last question, I will say that my personal
attitude is folly expressed in my attitude as Grand Master. I
regret to say that the Klan has boasted, in more than one public
way, that their ranks were being recruited largely from the members of the Masonic fraternity. I cannot believe this to be true.
I feel that I know that it is not true of the Masons of Maine.
Did I conceive it to be true, I should feel that the germs of
disintegration had found their way into the heart of a Fraternity
that has existed for hundreds of years and at all times commanded
the confidence and respect of the community, in which it has

Washington:
This organization, which has received very much notoriety
in the public press, is likely to become a serious thorn in the side
of Masonry. It seems quite evident that it is making much of
the Masonic affiliations of many of its members, and though we
have never been solicited we have been told by some of those
who have been approached that this fact was prominently put
before them in the suggestion that they become affiliated therewith.
The writer has heard them eloquently defended on the floor of
one of the concordant orders, and it is extremely likely that they
have a large affiliation among our membership. A discussion of
its methods is unnecessary here, as most of you know as much
about it as the writer. In California a raid which resulted in murders seems to be definitely settled upon the organization, according to the public press, by the acknowledgment of the officers
of the order itself. The public press also brings the word that
the Grand Miaster of California has issued an edict forbidding the
reception of members of that institution into ours. Certain it is
that the spreading of a belief that an institution working under
cover as it does is closely related to Masonry can do us nothing
but harm.
The Grand Master of Wisconsin says:
Early in my administration as Grand Master I was made
acquainted with the secret solicitation of members of our Craft
in this jurisdiction, to join or affiliate themselves with an organization known as the Ku Klux Klan, or the "Invisible Empire." I
felt it imperative to warn all members of the Craft in this jurisdiction against being drawn into the meshes of an organization so
un-American and un-Masonic in its methods and practice.
Freemasonry stands for law and order, for good government,
for our flag and the United States of America. For each and
every individual to worship God according to the dictates of his
own conscience. Any sect, klan or organization that seeks to
interfere with these sacred rights of the individual is obnoxious
to society and a menace to the peace and dignity of the state.
I have faith in the Masons of Wisconsin. I believe that they
will refrain from becoming aligned with an organization so heinous
in its workings that it is compelled to strike in the dark. Affiliation with .an organization of this kind can only bring themselves
and Masonry in disrepute.

Quebec:
Some of the lawless horde known as the Ku Klux Klan,
having attemped to shield ·themselves under the pretense that
they had the sympathy and even the cooperation of Masons,
several of the Grand Lodges in the United States have come out
openly in repudiation of their false pretenses, notably those of
Connecticut, Idaho, Nor th Dakota and Oklahoma, and the Grand
Masters of New York and Massachusetts. The Grand Lodge of
North Dakota has not only prohibited all Masons of the jurisdiction· from connecting themselves with the Klan, but has ordered
every North Dakota Mason who may chance to have become a
member of the organization in consequence of its misrepresentations, to at once sever his connection therewith. None are more
entirely opposed to the teachings of Freemasonry and. are more
deserving of exemplary punishment at the hands of their colll;itry
than either individuals or organizations who take the law mto
their own hands, and nothing is ~ore prepostero~s than _the
supposition that the authors of lynchings and other crimes agamst
law and public order can by any possibility have the sympathy
or support of Masonry.
Not only is the organization in question un-Masonic, but it
is claimed that it is in open violation of the laws of the country
in which it exists. If this be so, and the statement is publicly
made that it is so, then it cannot be too severely condemned by
Masons everywhere.

up or sustain the Klan or any other organization, is a Masonic

LARGE LODGES
Whether a lodge should be restricted as to the number of
members it should have is a matter that is receiving serious consideration in a number of jurisdictions. From a practical standpoint
we believe there is more real and applied Masonry in a lodge
with a small membership. Masonry originally was a convivial society where all met upon the level, and carried out the Masonic
ideas through the work of the individual. The small lodge is conducive to this idea.

78

REPORT ON COHUESPONDENCE

The building of temples, the increase in membership calling for
expenditures for entertainment, relief and education necessarily call
for large lodges. This perhaps means the development of a lodge
to the neglect of the individual member. It resolves itself into the
proposition of "the greatest good for the greatest number," but
personally we are in favor of the small lodge.
District of Columbia:
The controversy as to the relative advantages of large and
small lodges is unending and every man is entitled to his individual
opinion on this subject; but it must be conceded that the good
Mason is an active Mason, and that effective activity in service
must be through co-ordinated effort. It follows, therefore, that if
an individual lodge is so large that the physical limitations of its
meeting place preclude the possibility of accommodating as much
as one half of its members, the other half will be debarred from
active participation in the work and counsels of the lodge and be
wholly <leprived of the benefits of fraternal intercourse.
I am persuaded, therefore, that under the peculiar conditions
existing in this jurisdiction it is desirable that the normal increase
in the fraternity be encouraged through the formation of new
lodges that may be effectively enthused with the desire to serve,
rather than by piling up unavailable. and in many cases disinterested, additions to the already over-grown lodges.
It is realized that this is a probkm which is difficult of satisfactory solution, hecause of the fact that it is not feasible by law
or edict to place a limit on the membership of the individual
lodges, nor is it possible to arbitrarily break up the lodge organizations; but I am convinced that if the brethren can be
brought to realize the great opportunities for effective service to
the Craft, to the community, to the nation. to the peoples of the
world, hy relatively small, well co-ordinated bodit's of men working to a common purpose. they may he indl1ced to favor and promote the estahlishment of many additional lodges in the jurisdiction.
Manitoba:
There are careful observers who maintain that such lodges
\vith large membership entertain a false impression of their usefulness by reason of the fact that they have so many hundred
members on their roll and have credit at the bank. Vine believe
that in such lodges members generally miss the sympathetic
friendships which make a man love his lodge and those intimate
associations whicl1 should unite himself and his fellows into one
great family. Naturally the majority of its members become indifferent and the average attendance when considered in proportion to the resident membership falls away steadily.

large lodges, they should be divided into groups of ZOO members,

would he divided into 16, which alone involved serious housing

q_uestio_ns, including the . matter of the readjustment of property
rights m temples and eqmpment. The committee however sets out
the following as the advantages of the smaller lodge, as' they appear from reports and correspondence which your committee has
had, may be grouped under the following heads:
(1) Greater opportunity for social life and a development
of the spirit of Masonry.
(2) A development of competent officers under the stimulus of the ambition to serve as Master of a lodge.
(3) The closer cementing of the ties in the individual lodge.
On these points the committee finds that any lodge can provide facilities for the first point, irrespective of its size, by limiting
the amount of degree work done at a meeting, and that, where
any lodge by reason of becoming a "Degree Mill," uses all its
time for ritualistic work, there can be no development of the
~ocial or cultural side.
Let the local lodge, says the report, be
1t large or small, spend more time in educating its Entered Apprentices, Fellow Crafts and Master Masons in the true meaning
of Masonry, and in spreading true Masonic light, and that lodge
will have a homogeneity and solidarity such as we all desire.
The committee also points out that the great amoui1t of ritualistic work prevents many good Masons from seeking preferment
as officers, as it is no small sacrifice for the type of man we desire
to head our lodges to spend three or four evenings a week in
merely ritualistic work of the Order, for a period of four to
seven years, not to mention the great amount of outside work
which necessarily devolves upon officers. Many of the best workers
also driit into the work of the other Masonic organizations. The
ties of Masonic brotherhood are close, however, whether the lodge
be great or small. but is it not a fact (the committee asks) that
each of us has a very limited circle of friends, in any organization which goes beyond our closest associates?

North Dakota:
Large lodges this year come in for more than their usual
amount of comment and criticism. The immense number of applicants for our degrees have brought about in many city lodges
so called collective work or the grouping of candidates for degrees
at one and. the same time. The large lodges are degenerating
into mere "degree mills" and the spirit of fellowship, which is
the most prized thing in Masonry, is absolutely lost in the great
aggregations of individuals. It is generally admitted now by thinking Masons that large lodges should be split up and that some
limitations be placed on the size of constituent lodges.

While it is the opinion of many that lodges with a membership
of less than 400 are closer together, enjoy an atmosphere of fraternity, not so apparent in some of the larger lodges, still if the
principles of Freemasonry are recognized and adhei·ed to as thev
should be, the question of numbers would be uncalled for. The
suggestion is made that if the spirit as well as the letter be adhered
to in conferring the degrees, and the candidate and brother be given
some attention outside of the conferring of the degrees, that they

Texas:
A great many lodges are sorely afflicted with what might
be termed (for want of a more descriptive name) chronic elephantiasis.
There are perhaps more than a hundred and fifty lodges in
the United States having more than a thousand members.
We are glad to see a note of warning in the addresses of
many Grand Masters against this growing evil. Some Grand Masters recommend that membership in the lodges be limited to not
more than five hundred. While there is more work in the large
lodge there is more Masonry in the small lodge with a hundred
members. The small lodge does not make so many members.
but it makes more Masons.
Washington:
The question of the size of lodges has come to the front for
some years with increasing frequency. While there is something
to be said in favor of the range of activities, the amount of charity
work which is made possible by the larger means, and the splendid
character of the work performed by many of these lodges, yet
when all is said and done it is the oninion of many thinking
Masons that the finest principles of Masonry are largely eclipsed
by the machinery which comes to be a necessary part of the
operations of a big lodge. Acquaintance, real brotherhood, is almost
al'I. impossibility. Have you not had the experience of coming in
contact with some brother Mason whose affiliation with your own
lodge was a matter of utter surprise to you? Then, too, the
benevolences of the large lodge come largely to be a matter of
spending money for help, not helping your brotherhood's sake.
Wisconsin:
The existence of very large lodges in some Grand Jurisdictions
has been felt to be detrimental to the best interests of the Fraternity
and means have been sought looking to the prevention of their further growth. Of course no Mason desires that good material should
be denied the privilege of becoming Masons. What has been desired
is that new lodges should be created to take care of the influx of
new members. The difficulty and expense of obtaining and maintaining suitable lodge rooms demand that in large cities the lodges
should be strong numerically. Jn many places new lodges, it is felt,
would be formed were it not for the very natural reluctance felt by
the older members from severing their connection with their mother
lodge, rich with its associations of former years. Two measures
have been proposed and are being tried in some Grand Jurisdictions.
First, that of permitting dual membership, so that a brother could
retain his membership in his old lodge and at the same time have
membership in a new lodge. This would result, it is claimed, in the
formation of new lodges to take charge of and relieve the old lodges
in a measure from the pressure felt by the great volume of petitions
that are being presented for the degrees. In connection with this it

LEGISLATION
It is a tendency in the United States when any c·ondition
arises which is not governed by regulation to pass a law governing it. Afterwards it is forgotten and our statute books are
burdened with obsolete l:;.ws. We sometimes wonder if Brother
James D. Anderson, one of the founders of the Grand Lodge of
1717, and the author of the Constitution of 1723, would not be
amazed at the additions, embellishments, changes, etc., that have
been added to his original work;
Georgia:
We exclaim "Amen" with him when he says that "one of the
very best things that could possibly happen to the Masonic Fraternity would be to eliminate all existing laws and regulations and
return to Anderson's original constitutions of Freemasonry."
Illinois:
The writer has been very much impressed in reviewing the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Ohio in noting the small amount
of legislation enacted. This shows that the Grand Lodge of Ohio
has become stabilized and does not propose to be carried off its feet
by various amendments presenting new-fangled ideas on Freemasonry. The greatest need of the Fraternity today is a fixed
policy. We have enough laws, rules, and regulations to last us for
a long time, and it is refreshing to find one Grand Lodge whose
proceedings are not overburdened with changes of various sorts.
One of the very best things that could possibly happen to the
Masonic fraternity would be to eliminate all existing laws and regulations and return to Anderson's original constitutions of Freemasonry. It cannot be doubted that there are entirely too many
laws enacted for the regulation and government of the society. One
Gran.d Master found in counting up the laws of his jurisdiction approximately three hundred. All this could be greatly simplified by
the use of a little common sense.
It has been noticeable in recent years that in each meeting of
some of the grand bodies, there have been a large number of laws
and regulations presented and enacted. Many of these amendments
have been offered by men not active in the work of the Fraternity but
who have set themselves up as saviors of the institution and who
imagine that in order to keep the Fraternity straight a certain number of amendments must be adopted each y~ar,

82

RBPOHT O.N COHHBSPO.NDBNCE;

The writer is fully of the opinion that at the present time, we
have all the laws, rules and regulations that the Fraternity can possibly need for the next one hundred years and nothing can be gained
by the enactment of any more. The greatest need of the time is a
return to the fundamental principles of the society and less disposition on the part of certain members of the Fraternity to throw restrictions around the working elements of the institution. If the
present tendency, to enact laws keeps on, it is questionable just
where the Fraternity will end, and it is almost impossible to conceive
what new legislation will be devised in order to safeguard the Fraternity.
Kansas:
Lodges are in a great many respects not unlike individuals when
it comes to a matter of law. If there is not enforcement, of course
there is no compliance with the statutes. The whole thing rests
upon the Grand Master.
Kentucky:
If we have not miscounted, he (Oklahoma) granted twenty-nine
dispensations authorizing the conferring of degrees without regard
to statutor.y time. It is not for us to criticize the laws or enactments
of another jurisdiction when within the scope of Masonic regularity,
but we modestly suggest that it were better to repeal a law that requires to be so frequently disregarded. It does not breed respect
for law.
Missouri:
A number of amendments to Grand Lodge by-laws were presented and adopted. A Grand Lodge session without some amendments would be a curiosity.
North Dakota:
For fifteen years the writer has been privileged to be a member
of the Sanhedrin of the Grand Lodge of North Dakota and he knows
the atmosphere which surrounds this revered body. He knows that
many zealous brethren introduce freak resolutions and propose fool
legislation which, if adopted, would make the jurisdiction the .laug~­
ing stock of Masonry. He knows further that the lack of time 111
which to properly consider some matters of apparent merit requires
that they be discarded or postponed over the communication. He
knows still further that this same Sanhedrin is composed of many
men of widely varying views and temperament; that to reconcile
these is a difficult task. Yet, to quote the Ohio committee, "we
should not put a straightjaeket on progress." That, however, is
just the result in too many cases. The fear of going wrong or acting the part of the path-finder makes many otherwise forceful men
cowardly, and recommendations of undoubted merit are frowned
down in consequence.

I think it is easily possible to legislate too much. The laws

MISSION OF MASONRY
The "Mission of Masonry" can be considered only from three
angles. First, as an Organization; Second, as a Philosophy; Third,
as a Fraternity. As has been said: "Yesterday is .only a dream,
tomorrow is only a vision, and our todays if rightly lived will
make every yesterday a dream of happiness and every tomorrow
a vision of hope." That perhaps is the true "Mission of Masonry."
British Columbia:
Vile confess we do not agree with the Grand 11astcr of Idaho.
Masonry is not on trial today more than it has been at any time
since it b<;gan, but Masonry has trials of its own, and one of them
is the ill-advised actions of certain members of the Craft who, not
content with Masonry as they found it. would like to see it in
rivalry with certain organizations which take particular pains to
let not only their left hands, but the whole world, know what their
right hands are doing.
Colorado:

activity. Lodges and Grand Lodges are advocating the passage
or defeat of legislation, and inquiring into the fraternal and religions affiliations of candidates for public office. This field has
alwavs been to our Fraternity a forbidden one. Jt cannot he entc:red without the utmost peril to that internal harmony absolutely
.:ssential to the existence of Masonrv. This is the curse of Latin
Freemasonry. and however seductive the voices that lure ns, the
lessons of history are too plain for us to be deceived.

The only remedy for this situation is to bring light and yet
"more light" to the members of the Craft. \Ve have received into
our membership an enormous number of young men in the last
few years. They are selected from the best of our American
youth and manhood. They are attracted to us from various reasons, but I believe all of them are sincere in their desire to
strengthen the Fraternity and make it of service in its chosen field.
But they are in the position of a crew of a ship, sent to sea without a rudder, chart, anchor, or sailing directions. In the path
of the storm, they drift with the wind and tide in whichever direction it blows the strongest. It. is our duty, now, to supply the
sailing directions and they will do the rest. In them rests the future
destiny of this association, and if we fail to give the proper inspiration and information now, they will drift in the wrong direction. If we do not change them, they will change us.
The mission of Freemasonry is to build character in men that
will find its truest expression in private and public morality; that
will make of the brotherhood of man more than a phrase; that
will prove that the truth is free and a power to overcome all evil;
and that will exhibit in all human relations the divine wisdom
of love.

North Dakota:
Boiled down to their essence these statements by the Grand
Master of Pennsylvania mean that a Masonic lodge is nothing
more nor less than a "degree mill." It may meet to confer degrees, dispense charity and bury its dead, but nothing more. It
must not attempt anything "with a view to moulding or influencing
legislation or public opinion."
If this narrow interpret2.tion of Masonry and its mission is
right, then for thirty-five years we have been wholly wrong in our
conception of the reason for its existence. If the Masonic ideal of
Most Worshipful Brother Sell is correct, its upkeep in time, talent
and treasure is woeful waste.
We realize that Masonry, or for that matter any other organization, must make its influence in a community felt largely through
its product. Clean-living, God-fearing. high-minded, charitable men
are the perfect product of Masonry; but neither Masonry nor the
Church of Christ will have much effe\;t for good through the product above described, because it is non-existent. Good men made
better through the symbolism and teachings of Masonry can by
their example do much, but associated together as lodges thev
ean espouse the cause of civic righteousness and by their united
efforts work miracles. As we understand Grand Master Sell, Masonic lodges or Grand Lodges mav not unite for action no matter
how righteous the cause.

Minnesota:
I have endeavored to present to the brethren during the past
year the necessity of lining up with the idea of a single standard
of morality. \Ve are living in an age of enlightenment, an age in
which we realize that the time has come to make a practical application of the teachings that we have promulgated. \Ve know
that there is no justice in a double standard of morality, and it is
time that we wake up to the fact, that we, the Masons, are the
ones to first demand that single standard from among our own
members. There is no reason why any man, particularly a Mason,
should be permitted to violate the moral law, and be taken back
into society to mingle with the mothers, sisters, wives or daughters,
while his sister, if she break lmt one, becomes an outcast.
Montana:
First and most important, we felt the necessity of impressing
upon the Fraternity the conviction that Masonic influence is in
direct ratio to the exercise of that influence. That, as ancient
Masonry was adapted to ancient conditions, so must we adapt our
Masonry to present day problems and that to do this, ~fasonry
must become an active, vital element in every community.
Nevada:
It may be said that political and civic problems should not be
discussed within the lodge room. That is very true when those
discussions relate purely to matters affecting the best method of
government or civic progress, hut when there is an attempt by people as members of our commonwealth to subvert our institutions
our existing system of law and order and displace it by anarch~
and a doctrine that might is right, then it is our duty as Masons
and as a Masonic institution to put ourselves before the world
openly, fearlessly and unitedly as discountenancing any such false
ideals.

Pennsylvania:
Freemasonry in Pennsylvania is a fraternity. It is not a religious body, it is not a political or social organization, and it
does not intermeddle with or take part in political, business, social
or religious affairs.
Lodges meet for Masonic purposes only, namcly, for transacting the business incident to the orderly conduct of their affairs,
and for conferring degrees by and through which we endeavor to
reach the hearts and minds of the members and t"ach them the
competency of the Divine wisdom, their relation to Him, and their
fraternal duty toward each other and to all mankind.
Lodge meetings are not to be meetings for the discussion of
subjects of any kind whether social, political, religious, or topical
upon which there might be a difference of opinions; neither are
they to be places of entertainment, nor places from which there
shall emanate a propaganda of any kind with a view to molding
or influencing legislation or public opinion.
Freemasons in Pennsylvania therefore should guard carefully
against innovations, and vigorously resist everything which tends
to weaken or abrogate our ancient usages, customs and landmarks.
They should always keep in mind the fact that there is no new
thing in Freemasonry.
Any organization in Pennsylvania not recognized bv the Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania, and which uses a Masonic ·lodge as a
door through which a man must first pass in order to become a
member thereof is not Masonic, and membership therein or affiliation therewith by Freemasons should be prohibited.
Some of our brothers may say that Masonry has no right to
interfere with the right of its members to join any other organiza-

tion whether fraternal, or otherwise, and that their right to do so
as citizens is guaranteed by the Constitution.
These seem to forget that they have no inborn or inherent
right to become Masons, and the Federal Constitution does not
guarantee this privilege. The privilege of becoming a Mason
emanates from the Grand Lodge operating through its subordinate
lodges.
Therefore it naturally follows, that since they are Masons
under and by virtue of the Grand Lodge, they must be obedient
to its mandates, and any brother who cannot cheerfully submit to
all the rules, regulations and edicts as promulgated by the Grand
Lodge should sever his Masonic relations or be compelled to do so.
In a number of instances, I have prohibited lodges from carrying out a program arranged in connection with a banquet or other
lodge, or assumed lodge occasion; these generally being "lectures,
stereopticon exhibitions, concerts by brethren, dances, card parties,
Past Masters' night, ladies night, social hours, etc.
Most of these were the result of over-zealous, perhaps misguided Worshipful Masters who wished to distinguish their administration by doing something different from their predecessors,
without regard to their obligation and the ancient charges to which
they submitted when installed.

Scotland:
We can do good to our country from the social point of view,
without any propaganda, by our mere existence; and perhaps you
will allow me to illustrate and give you one little example which
will illustrate my meaning. All of you are acquainted with a substance which is largely used in building, in architecture, at the
present day. It is known as reinforced concrete, and it was only
in recent years that the discovery was made, that by embedding
a thin network of wire or a few slender steel rods in the midst of
the conglomerate mass of stone and cement that made the concrete, it added immensely to its endurance. Brethren, can we not
adduce from that analogy that the network of Freemasonry which
has spread over the whole of the British Isles-because we have a
large number of Freemasons in almost every town-acts in the
same way as the wire netting in the re-inforced concrete. and hold
together that national spirit which is cemented by patriotism.

South Dakota:
One lodge in this jurisdiction passed a resolution endorsing the
Smith-Towner Bill, now called the Towner-Sterling Bill, and asked
the Grand Master for permission to submit the same to all other
lodges, and to the Grand Lodge for endorsement. I commend the
zeal which prompted the adoption of this resolution, but have grave
doubts as to propriety of lodges as a body passing resolutions that
will try to dictate or approve any laws being passed by our government. Some of our sister jurisdictions have already passed a similar resolution. It appears to me that we as individnal Masons
should do all that is in our power to promote and support proper
laws for the maintenance of this government, but when we as a
body try to do it, we will be accused of entering politics and the
world, without regard to creed or religion, will turn against us. We
must not be stampeded into politics, as a body, on account of the
activities of our enemies, for they will in time fail, as we would
did we but follow their tactics.

Vermont:
The word Masonry even among laymen has come to mean
a close and secret bond of union, or brotherhood, between friends.
This belief, more than any other thing, among all classes the world
over, is the cause of the present increase in membership. Men are
not joining the Masons because the Masons are seeking to do Red
Cross work. Such men can join the Red Cross directly, if they
wish to. .Nor are they joining the order that they mav become
better citizens. Economic and good government club•· are open
to all. Nor are they joining because thereby they can do much
to redeem the world. The church invites such and is seeking
members. The fact that it is a secret brotherhood is the strongest
reason why it should abstain from all interference with outside
matters; because its motives are in danger of being misunderstood.
Virginia:
We regard Masonry as an unchanging and unchangeable system of pure morals, using the word pure as it is applied to pure
mathematics. Only in the last thirty years has this unrest for
change and the effort to use Masonrv in directing civic affairs
arisen. Previous to that time any such effort would have been
universally condemned as unwise innovation, and we think it equally
true today. Masonry's field of activity is large enough, and has
been all down the ages, without its being brought into specific
activity in "present dav problems." Its very nature is general and

condemn, nor for a moment question the purity of motive actuating

West Virginia:
It has been well said that "there are four classes of Masons in
this world: First, those who are Masons neither in name nor nature;
second, those who arc Masons in name only; third, those who
are Masons only by nature; and, lastly, those who are Masons both
in name and nature, and this class are God's noblemen. But if I
could not be numbered with them I had rather be a Mason by
nature-that is, at heart-than a Mason only in name."
Wyoming:
We have made many new Masons, we have conferred the degrees in excellent manner, and our new members have learned the
lectures so· as to pass their examinations. But is this the real
purpose of Masonry? Have we done all that we could to teach
these new members. and for that matter the older ones, the real
meaning of Masonry? Have we shown them how to lead better
and more useful lives? Have we impressed on them their duty to
their government, their state, their city and their fellowmen? Have
we done what we could to help them understand the deeper, truer
meaning of life? To increase the number of our members is a thing
to be commended, but to improve our members is much more commendable. To do good degree work is an excellent thing, but' to
do good for mankind is much better. How much more important
it is to teach a new brother how to live rightly than to teach him
a lecture in perfect form.
These thoughts are filling the minds of many Masons, not only
in "Wyoming, but in all parts of the United States. There is a
feeling that Masons should do more in a practical way. \Ve know
there is much we should do, but to put the thoughts into a more
concise and definite form is more difficult. It is a problem that demands the best thought of all of our members. Each must do his
share.
NEGROES
The position of the Negro in Masonry as far as the Grand
Lodges of the United States are cqncerned, is not legislation
against his admission, but by custom he has been excluded. Lodges
working under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of England
take opposite position. While we are told that Masonry "unites
men of every country, sect and opinion,'' in the practical application theory generally gives way to sentiment.

Mexico:
It is said that the pos1t10n of a negro in Masonry is unique. It
is more so in Mexico than in any other country. Under Mexico's
common law there is absolutely no distinction placed upon color;
the negro and the white man are on the same level, and to discriminate between them is to bring upon yourself the penalty of the law.
In the Mexican lodges, by which we mean native lodges, they have
upon their roster a large number of negroes. The York Grand
Lodge of Mexico has, by the exercise of judicious tact, preserved
itself from this contamination. I believe that a good negro may be
a perfectly good Mason, and I am perfectly ready and willing to give
him his just due, but I do not want him sitting in my lodge any
more than I want him sitting at my table with my wife and my
children.

ORDER OF DE MOLA Y
In the report of the Committee on Correspondence for the
year 1920, attention was called to the above organization and a
brief history of the same given. At that time it was practically
only an inspiration of Brother Frank S. Land of Kansas City,
Missouri. From the small beginning of three yers ago this organization has now grown from one chapter in Kansas City to 1096
chapters, embracing the United States, Canada, Panama, Porto
Rico, the Philippines, Paris, Rome, and Milan with a membership
of over 150,000.
Every Grand Lodge and Grand Master in the United States,
as well as Canada and Australia, have commented favorably upon
the organization. The excerpts from the different proceedings
total over fifty pages of solid printed matter. Colorado, Kansas

93

and Oregon are the three jurisdictions who have been somewhat
adverse to the Masonic Fraternity, as an organization, interesting themselves in the Order of De Molay.
It has been the constant aim of the Grand Council of the
Order of De Molay to remove the impression that the Order has
any connection whatsoever with Masonry other than that it labors
under the shadow of the Fraternity through the sponsorship of
the individual chapters.
The Order has for its purpose the building of clean, patriotic
young manhood as the best preparation for future citizenship in
our great Republic, and which must be clean and patriotic if it
is to be effective in perpetuating our national institutions.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
While we are not a great admirer of some of the "Ancient
Landmarks," we believe that changes made in the one requiring
physical qualification has perhaps produced more harm to the
Fraternity than if it had been strictly complied with. As stated in a
previous Report, it should be remember~d that in lifting the ban
you do so not only for the individual who might be an exception,
but for every other crippled person otherwise eligible.
Where the decision is left open there is often a tendency to
think more of the particular case in question than the subject
as a whole.
The statements expressed by the Jurisprudence Committee
of the Grand Lodge of Idaho shows this both from an individual
and a collective standpoint.

PROCEEDINGS-GRAND LODGE
After reviewing the Proceedings for four years of practically
seventy-five jurisdictions we believe too many carry detail that
is ~f little use, either to the members of the jurisdiction or the
Masonic world in general. While the publication of the extended
reports, lodge statistics, rosters, etc., are a financial gain to the
·printers, still they are of little value to the average member.
Some jurisdictions such as Alabama, Massachusetts, New York
and Tennessee have made it a practice to embody, through Committee Reports valuable treatises on American and Mason'c History and these are of more value than the remainder of the volume.
Alabama through Bro'her Oliver D. Street, in its last year's
Proceedings embodied one of the most complete Masonic histories

gone years the Masters and Ward ens of all our subordinate lodges
always wore their own regalia to Grand Lodge. And while this was not
obligatory at all, it was a nice custom which we would very much like
to see revived. As to the proceedings being marked "private and confidential," so far as the jurisdiction of Nova Scotia is concerned, this
does not appear necessary, for nothing of a private nature is published
and, judging from the proceedings now before us, this also applies to
the Grand Lodge of Scotland. However, no doubt, that is their regula·
tion, so it goes at that.
Utah:
\Ve note that our brother fails not to call attention to the-to usunwise and uncalled for printing of details in the reports of committees on grievances and appeals. Like him, we can think of no justification for this, even if there were no ever watchful malignant enemies
to distort such procce<lings. P!:rsonally, we bracket together the printing of these details and those relating to charities in which the full
name of the beneficiaries and the name and location of the lodges
whence they come, are given. The "family wash" on a line, one end
of which is attached to a 40-foot pole, may be fine, for linen, but M.asons may be excused from emulating this custom.
Wisconsin:
The volume of proceedings for 1921 (Massachusetts) is a bulky
one of over seven hundred pages. It is always a great privileg·e aml a
great responsibility to review the proceedings of this Grand J urisdiction. A great privilege because we are always sure to find in them
many things of great interest; inspiring instances of Masonic charity,
eloquent addresses, historical matters of thrilling interest not to be
found elsewhere, witty remarks interspersed with sound philosophy, etc.
A great responsibility because all these things are so interspersed with
dry matter that one fears he may overlook the pith of the whole. The
pr.esent volume is no exception to the rule. We have here accounts of
special communications of the Grand Lodge to lay corner stones, dedicate Masonic temples, conduct funerals, constitute lodges, observe centennial celebrations, hold quarterly communications, the grand feast,
together with historical discu~sions and splendid orations by conp:ressmen, bishops, college presidents and great orators, all mixed together
with routine matters so that it seems almost as if some one had placec1
all the manuscript in a huge cauldron and stirred it up with a stick before
printing it. The redeeming feature is that as they never publish a correspondence report, they cannot come back at a reviewer and call him
down for his errors and oversights.

The proceedings (Kentucky) form a bulky volmi1e of over eight
hundred pages, of which more than one-half are devoted to the publication of a list of members of the subordinate lodges, Such a list of
substantial citizens is very useful to those having advertising matter or
propaganda of any sort to distribute, but its value to the Grand Lodge
is a very negligible quantity. This was proven in \Visconsin many
years ago when we abandoned the practice, thus cutting our printing
bills in two.

Oklahoma:
An instance of leak somewhere was manifested a few days ago,
while the writer was on the train, talking to a lady. She asked
if the Masons were going to try Mr. Blank, who is a member of
Hugo Lodge. This was the first news the writer had of any such
trial, though he had been summoned to be present one week hence
at the lodge meeting.
Pennsylvania:
The Grand Master (Alberta) expressed a timely warning against
furnishing the public press with items of news relating to transactions of the lodges. It is a reprehensible practice, too common and
by no means confined to Alberta. Conveying news-gossip-is
a bent of human nature; we like to broadcast it, and find the newspaper a ready medium. But a Mason should ever have in mind
that secrecy is an essential requirement of the Craft, not only of
the forms and ceremonies of the lodge, but of its transactions in
every particular. VV'hat takes place behind tiled doors does not
concern the public and should be withheld from it.
Quebec:
I have noticed with deep regret an occasional incipient desire on
the part of a few of our lodges for publicity through the columns of
the press. Naturally reference to Masonic activities will, to some
extent, find its way into the press without the assistance or connivance of any Mason, and there are such newspaper notices that
have nothing in them deserving of censure; but when we find in our
morning papers the substances of an address delivered the night before in the body of a lodge, or items of information that could have
been supplied only by someone who was present, we feel that there
is a distinct departure from the ancient traditions of the Craft and
a violation of one of its fundamental principles. The desire for publicity is unhealthy and un-Masonic. To advertise one's self or one's
lodge is contrary to the teaching of our order. Freemasonry is
farther removed than the poles from those societies that think they
will be effective because of the noise they make.
South Dakota:
Several times during the year my attention has been called to
spurious questions and answers published in some of our papers.
Usually under a heading something like this: "Masons will recognize this." Sometimes this will be found in a paper published bv
a member of the Fraternity. Really I can not understand such
man. Every effort should be made to put a stop to it, and I trust
that every Mason will make it his duty to call the attention of the
officers of his lodge, that they may take the proper steps to eliminate this abominable practice.

a large number of the members, as well as the general ~ublic
are inclined to believe that the Institution is not only a charitable

Illinois:
It is noticed that the Grand Lodge of Vermont has been having
some trouble with the Grand Lodge of California concerning the care
of an indigent member by the Masons of the western state. The matter appears to have heen amicably adjusted. It frequently happens that
our brethren of the west are quite liberal in the matter of caring for
the needy. Sometimes their generosity is not appreciated by some of
the eastern jmisdictions who are not quite so liberal in the dispensing
of Masonic aid. Hence, an argument.
Louisiana:
'While the great Order of Freemasonry is not an organization for
charity, it is a charitable organization, and has alwavs extended a helping hand to the needy and has endeavored to restore peace to the
troubled bosom of the worthy. But it is a regrettable fact that some of
our members seem to think that the small fee which they necessarily
pay to get into the lodge entitles them not only to a letter of credit, a
passport to a sanitarium, if feeling bad, and an insurance policy containing a sick and disability clause, hut also to an annuitv to their
families ever afterward if they die.
Of course, such cases are the exception and not the rule.
Maine:
The average income of the lodges of Maine is not sufficient to enable them to
necessary and unexpected calls for relief, while the
dues of many
are so low that they detract from the dignity of
Masonry. The several lodges should establish dues which will enable
them to meet their usual and ordinary expenses and provide a substantial sum each
for charitable uses. Every lodge should undertake
the creation
a charity fond which would make special assessments
and voluntary contributions for such purposes unnecessary. It should
be constantly remembered, -however, that no financial contribution by
a lodge to a distressed brnther or those dependent upon him can be
regarded as a substitute for that personal attention and sympathetic
interest in a brother's welfare which adds so much to the sentiment and
joy of life.
Manitoba:
I have no recommendation to make, but call your serious attention to the good points of l\fasonic practice as established by our
brethren of the Grand Lodge of England, particularly with relation
to the social side of Masonry, which they deem of more importance
than the ritualistic side. They teach enough of ritual to inculcate in
the minds of their novitiates that Masonry stands first and foremost
for the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man; for personal
righteousness; for law and order for good and orderly government
by orderly men; and that man is
brother's keeper. At their social
gatherings they aim to, and do, bring to the surface the good qualities
of their members-and never lose sight of their obligations to the poor

and distressed in their mid~t. The matter of relief is not referred
