New South Wales:
In the course of our investigations regarding the various activities
of other Grand Lodges, we have been struck by the fact that, in numerous cases in America, at least, there have been set up what are termed
Masonic employment bureaus, the object being to assist members c;if
the Craft, or their dependents, who may be out of employment, m
securing suitable work. This contingency has become a very real one
during the past year or two, and during the ~urrent year particularly,
in America as well as in Australia. The existence of these bureaus
must have been of special value in some of the industrial states where
there has been a slackening of the wheels of industry, and numbers of
men and women have been thrown out of work.
North Dakota:
One question which seems clear to your scribe ca.used considerable
discussion. The Grand Master ruled that "when a widow of a Master
Mason married a profane she forfeited her right to aid and assistance
from the Fraternity." The Grand Master was clearly right in this. The
widow gained her right to aid through marriage with a Master Mason.
When she married a Eecon d time she forfeited this right for the protection and support of the man she married. The fact that her first husband was a Master Mason in good standing at the time of his death gave
her the right to Masonic aid. This right remained valid and binding
on the Fraternity so long as shr remained the widow of the Master
xiason. Her subsequent marriage to a profane changed her legal status,
and it also automatically released the Fraternity from further obligation. The Grand l\Iaster wa8 sustained by the Grand Lodge, but the
Committee of Jurisprudence in a hair-splitting report, held the decision
faulty.
Pennsylvania:
It would seem to the Grand Master that if more of our unemployed brethren were willing to accept a job rather than insist on filling a position, there would be little, if any, need for the Grand Lodge
operating these enterprises; which will, I believe, eventually become
inadvisable,
RELIGION
Under the Ancient Charges Masonry had no concern with the
Religion of its members, other than "they be good men a,nd true."
Any attempt to interject, into the ritual or the activ;ties of the
Order, anything connected with this subject should be strictly
"taboo."

of the human race. No, she chose the religion of that remarkable
race, the Jews-chose not the religion of a man, but the religion of
a race. Buddha was a man, Ccnfucius and Mohamet were men
but the Jewish religion was the religion of a whole people. It i~
strange that throughout all the centuries today we cannot find a
people so permeated with the religion of God, the great Creator, ·as
t)'iat of the Jews .. It. has colored all their poetry, all their art, their
literature, all their hfe. Even today, when so many have drifted
from the ancient ideas, to them this religion is the one great factor
of human life.

RITUAL
There undoubtedly is a tendency at times to consider the
Ritual as something holy handed down from time immemorial rather
than view it as a means to an end. There must be certain forms
and ceremonies, but to make them the standard and ultimate end
means that sooner or later the Institution itself will be only an
observance.

\Ve want to preserve the fundamentals, but be free from the

We learn from his address that in this jurisdiction (British

attainment. There may be situations similar to this in other Grand
Lodges, but we are not cognizant of them. Uniformity of ritualistic
work appears to us of fundamental necessity.

Utah:
Our law provides that every \V. M.-elect before he is installed
shall receive the Past Master's degree. Yet in every issue of
annual proceedings is given a list of \V. 1\1'.'s who have not been

Wisconsin:
The so-called "degree" (Past Master) is entirely unnecessary,

_th~ requir,ement a nuisance, and as the degree is usually conferred,

1t is a farce. Some years ago \Visconsin had a similar requirement.
which was frequently disregarded. The grand lecturer conceived
the idea that this could be obviated by adding many clauses to the
obligation and elaborating the ceremonies of the degree. The result
was that outside of the grand lecturer and two or three brethren
whom he had specially instructed, no one in \Visconsin knew how
to confer it in accordance with his requirements. To get rid of the
whole matter the Grand Lodge promptly repealed the requirement
making its reception a prerequisite for installation of the Master, since
which very few Masters have received it.

Virginia:
The forms and ceremonies of initiation and the lectures furnish
the alphabet only of Masonry. They do not, of themselves, make any
man a Mason, but only a member. Too often this member does not
use this alphabet; he will not learn to spell and then to read, and
having read, to understand, and rushes on into the so-called "higher
degrees" with little knowledge or appreciation of those through which
he has passed. lt is this spirit that seeks to change the alphabet,
because of lack of understanding. It would, through ignorance, tear
down the very foundation stones on which the whole super-structure
of Masonry is erected.

The Grand Master of Indiana found some trouble on account of

but introduced variations. He said:
"I do not believe such degree teams have any place within this
grand jurisdiction or serve any good purpose. I therefore recommend that the organization and work of such degree teams be forbidden, unless all of the members of each degree team are members,
in good standing, in. one lodge. Such degree team must be authorized
and approved by the lodge, and the lodge of which the degree team
are members must be responsible to the Grand Lodge for the work
and activities of the degree team."
The work of some of these teams sometimes becomes a decided
nuisance. Teams made up of men from certain trades or corporations come to feel, sometimes, that they are more important than the
lodge. The writer is cognizant of one instance where they took the
Master to task because he had conferred the third degree on one of
"their candidates." They are nearly always willing to leave to the
officers of the lodge the conferring of the first and second degrees,
and all they ask is to have an opportunity to spread themselves on
the third degree, and at that they rarely stay for the lecture in that
degree. It is largely an advertisement for the group conferring the

of having the team composed of members of some organi7-ation based

The establishment of scholarships is an example of Masonry

Georgia:
Resolved, First, that the Masonic Grand Lodge of Georgia regards a citizenry educated to its privileges, duties and responsibilities
as essential to the welfare of our state.
Second, that in order to make a higher degree of education
available to many who otherwise could not afford it the Grand
Lodge of Georgia does establish a permanent and revolving Students' Masonic Loan Fund, which shali be increased by annual appropriations from this body.
Third, that suitable parts of this fund shall be lent to worthy
students upon proper application and recommendation, loans to be
made primarily to Masons or those dependent upon Masons.
Fourth, that the committee to which this resolution shall be referred shall recommend the amount of appropriation necessary for
the establishment and maintenance of this fund, and the method of
obtaining it.
Fifth, that this fund shall be in charge of a permanent committee of three appointed by the Grand Master this year, one of which
committee shall be appointed for a term of one year, one for two
years and one for three years. Annually after this year the Grand
Master shall appoint one member of this committee for a term of
three years. This committee shall direct the distribution of this
loan fund and shall make annual accounting of its condition to the
Grand Lodge.

SMOKING
Smoking in lodge or during the conferring of degrees is a
matter of local regulation. If we consider the institution historically as it was, a social and convivial society, there can be no
objection to the practice.
Viewed from the standpoint that a lodge is a temple of
lea.ming or a place of sanctity, smoking is entirely out of place.
This is a matter that should be left to the individual lodge rather
than for legislation by a Grand Lodge.
Cuba:
Let us refer now not only to English lodges, where due respect
is paid to the Masonic temple, but to others in many countries where
culture is commonplace, in them smoking is not allowed to members
in the lodge room. In Cuba no particular attention is paid to that
matter, but it seems that in the jurisdiction of an American Grand
Lodge things have gone worse. Idaho is a proof of our sayings,
the Grand Master of which in a true Masonic style, and by no mean's
of energetic decree, has forbidden the· custom of smoking in ope11
lodge, as he was able to observe that at the moment of obliging a
candidate, he (the candidate) had a _cigar in his mouth.
vV c think the decree very well applied, as the rules of good
breeding were forgotten. The l.fasonic temple is a true temple, and
if we do not consider it so either take off the name it bears or the
importance it has.

Master of a lodge. :reeling that every law of the Grand Lodge

personal preferences of the lodge or the Grand Master, I caused a

Utah:
In our judgment smoking should not be allowed in a Masonic

TEMPLES
The desire to erect magnificent temples, perhaps with the
idea of financial profit is a matter that vitally affects the Fraternity.
Too often the commercial idea becomes the main objective.
If some happy medium could be reached whereby no temple
could be erected until the necessary funds to pay for it were in
hand, difficulties would be prevented.
Florida:
There is a wave of legislation going the rounds of the Grand
Lodges, on the subject of restricting the use of the Masonic lodge
rooms and halls. Their is a wide divergence of opinion, the extremes ranging from those Grand Lodges which do not concern
themselves with the use made of the halls at such times as they are
not actually occupied by the Masonic lodge, to those who are clinging to the theory that a Masonic lodge room or building is a "Holy
of Holies" which must not he used for any other purpose whatever.
In some cases restrictions are imposed on the use of the rooms for
any other than lodge meetings, and in one case the use of the room
was refused for a Methodist Bible class on Sunday afternoon. In
some cases the Grand Lodges have forbidden the use of the rooms to
the Order of Eastern Star, and we have one case where the Eastern
Star is permitted to use the room, but it is refused to the \Vhite
Shrine, although the membership in the order is confined to members of the former. In some States the use of the room is given to
Odd Fellows, Knights of Pythias and similar organizations, and in
some cases even the ownership of the building is joined by the
lodge with another or both of the above mentioned. We have a
few cases where the Grand Lodge has refused the use of the room
for a banquet hall in a Masonic temple, and in some cases where
the use of the banquet hall for dancing parties, to be used exclusively by members has been refused.
In Florida the use of the banquet room is permitted for dancing
parties for members and their families only. The Order of the
Eastern Star is permitted to occupy and use the lodge rooms, and
we ~ve several cases where the lodge building is owned jointly
with other organizations. The lodge rooms have been used fo~
church services and for the giving of lectures upon Masonic subjects. The use of the room by the Shrine is also permitted.

protesting against the proposed bill. It is apparent in the State of

as other real estate. ~ o doubt the question of taxation of lodge
property will be taken up and definitely settled either by State
Legislature or by Congress. Freemasonry claims to be an eleemosynary institution organized to care for its indigent members,
their widows and orphans. Freemasonry is in no sense, a profitmaking institution and for that reason it should be exemot from

maintains magnificent homes for the aged, infirm, widows and
orphans thereby taking off the state a certain burden which would
be thrust upon it were it not for the fact that Freemasonry makes
it possible to care for its own.

I realize all the many difficulties that some of our lodges have to
contend with, and would not plead for more expensive rooms or
elaborate furnishings. I do not care how humble or unpretentious
the meeting place is, but I do plead for cleanliness. The entrance

the members themselves without expense, and much more has been
done by some. In addition to that, everything that is possible
within. reason, by way of decoration and furnishing to make th~
Masomc lodge room and surroundings the most attractive place in
the community, should be done. Smoking should not be allowed
in the lodge room until the lodge is closed. As men who "fear
God, love the Brotherhood, and honor the king," we cannot do our
best work unless our surroundings appeal to us, as well as to those
whom we would teach. Congenial and attractive surroundings have
a great influence on the lives of our members and help them to set
that example which is expected to attract the very best manhood
in th~ land. Our symbolic flag, the "Union Jack," finds its appropriate and honored place in all our lodge rooms.

THIRD DEGREE CATECHISM
The idea that a candidate after be:ng raised to the degree of
Master Mason should pass an examination would be a concession
only to those who make proficiency in ritualistic work the ultimate
end of Masonry. There are some things that every Mason should
know but whether or not he can impart them depends upon the
individual rather than on a catech:sm. We have known a number
of good Masons who do not care to visit lodges unless they
can be vouched for simply by reason of their hesitancy to endeavor
to answer a set of categorical queslions. It is the substance rather
than the form which should be adopted as a guide.
If a Mason can prove himself a member, the method Ebould
be such a one that the average person can meet.

That no candidate for the degrees of Masonry shall be advanced to the second or third degree until at least four weeks

elapsed since taking the third degree. ~ violation of thi.s requjrement is hereby declared to be a Masomc offense and will subject

Illinois:
It has been quite the fashion in any number of jurisdictions to
require all newly raised Master Masons to pass an examination upon
the catechism of the third degree before they will be permitted to
assume their prerogatives as members of the Craft. Just what inspired this particular legislation is not known. One Grand Lodge
adopted it. Possibly other Grand Masters. hunting for somet~ing
out of the ordinary to recommend to their Grand Lodges seized

fiEPOHT ON COHHB8PONDENCJil

123

upon this idea as a wise one. Now, this writer hasn't any objection
to any Master Mason who wants to do so, learning these questions
and answers, but he docs think that it is going too far when the
matter is made one of coersion and the idea of freewill and accord
is eliminated. One trouble with the Masonic Fraternity at the present time is that with its exact system of ritual the dotting of I's,
crossing of T's and skillful manipulation of rods, many business men
who would like to participate in its affairs feel they cannot give time
to mastering the intricate details incident to ritualistic work. Many
of these men would like to attend the meetings of their lodges and
take an active part therein, but when the major portion of our assemblies are devoted to ritualistic exploitation there is very little
offered these men except a seat on the side lines where they may
witness what is going on without participating therein. It is noticeable that whenever anyone wants to improve the society he turns
to the ritual as the vehicle for making the improvement. When
a man attains the degree of Master Mason he should receive some
information relative to the society, its origin, history, object and
purposes. Ko one seems to have conceived the idea of preparing
a catechism along this line which the Master Mason might be required to memorize in order that he be placed in possession of
knowledge of those essentials of the Fraternity which are so vitally
necessary in its constitution. There is much about Freemasonry
that the average Mason knows nothing of. Perhaps this is one
reason for his rapidly waning interest in the society and the fact
that the average lodge attendance is limited to about ten per cent
of the total number on the rolls. The average candidate will be
required to learn the catechism of three degrees, but it is only the
active lodge worker who retains them and can make any use of
them whatsoever. This writer believes in intellectual Masonry, but
wants that intellectuality to he derived outside of the ritual.

On the apnroval of the Committee on Jurisprudence, the Masonic Code was so amended as to provide:
Every Mason hereafter raised to the degree of Master Mason
in this jurisdiction shall become proficient in the Master Mason's
degree as required in former degrees and give proof thereof by examination in open lodge, which fact shall be entered of record.
Provided, however, that such examination may be had and record
entered in any lodge which may be designated for such purpose by
the lodge in which the Master Mason was raised. The secretary
of each subordinate lodge in this jurisdiction shall include in his
annual report to the Grand Lodge the names of all Master Masons
who have taken, passed and failed to pass an examination upon the
Master Mason's degree, in such subordinate lodge.

TIME BETWEEN DEGREES.
Throughout a number of the jurisdictions one of the complain ts is that lodges are becoming nothing more or less than
"Degree Mills." This is due t~ the fact that there have been
a large number of applicants in waiting and each individual Master
is desirious of measuring the work of his lodge and its standing
by the numerical game. "That which is easily gained is lightly
held." Perhaps if a limit could be fixed requiring a C'ertain fixed
time to elapse between conferring the degrees upon any individual

126

Ullll'OHT ON COHI:l<;Sl'ONDBNC1~

it would work a great good. The degrees assume a far greater
value when the candidate is given more time for preparation and
as a result the membership would become better Masons, with less
petitions influenced by cupidity or curiosity.
Iowa:
He suggests that some way should he found to relieve the con-gestion of ritualistic work which the great rush to get in imposed
upon the lodges. But it is a question in our mind whether it is
worth while to make the initiates' road one bit easier to travel than
it now is. vVe doubt if it would result in making better ~fasons.
In our judgment the only way that will be safe for the Order is to
make candidates wait and keep on in our steady, regular way and
thus, in the end, shape strong and true and square the blocks that
are used in the building of our :Masonic edifice.

Maine:
There is a growing sentiment among leading Masons that our
constitution enables our lodges to advance candidates from one
degree to another without any, much less suitable, proficiency in
the preceding degree. A candidate may, under the present law, be
advanced to all three degrees in forty-eight hours. Such haste
countervails one of the f\lndamental requirements of the ritual.
does an injustice to the candidate and is detrimental to the Craft.
I therefore suggest an amendment to the constitution, inhibiting
advancement from one degree to another in less than two weeks
except upon dispensation; and also a rule that, when practicable,
the candidate shall be examined in open lodge upon the preceding
degree.

TOWNER-STERLING BILL
Under the Ancient Charges the discussion of POLITICAL
questions had no place in the Masonic lodge. This was a wise
regulat'.on, but we do believe that the discussion of questions of
Civic interest affecting the N'ation, the State, the -county or the
Municipality is not "politics" and have a proper place in a Masonic
lodge. Each individual should be left free to determine as to
wheth'.!r or not he is in favor of any measure in question. The
purpose of the discussion should be simply one of enlightenment.
Any attempt, by resolution, law, or otherwise, to bind a Member
or the Fraternity to the support of a particular measure is outside
of the scope of authority of a Grand Lodge or an individual lodge.

Montana 1921:
The great interest manifested by the Craft in the SmithTowner Bill appeals to us strongly as a true index of the signs
of the times; Masonry must stand as a guardian of our free public
school system and protect it from all open or insidious onslaughts;
without being intolerant let us tolerate no attempt to belittle the
usefulness of, or retard the growth of our national educational
system; let no ecclesiasticism shape our paths of learning language,
art and science; let there be a distinct and high barrier between
Church and State; let us watch and watch and frustrate all attempts
to enslave our God-given intellects and consciences by pretended
divine authority from whatsoever source it may emanate; there is
a God Divine in each of our hearts, and let us follow His teachings
and our impulses will be guided in the right direction.
New York:
Much, for instance, is being said about the alleged. centralizing
tendency of the Towner-Sterling Bill and the danger that Federal
aid will lead to Federal control of education. This argument is
just a smoke screen. The language of this bill expressly eliminates
any possibility of Federal control. No intelligent person who has
read the bill can use this argument with sincerity. This is a mere
man of straw.
The usual arguments against this program on economic
grounds are nearly as baseless. The principle of Federal aid does,
of course, mean that the more populous and wealthy states contribute to assist those less favored than themselves. This objection, however, applies equally to all taxes levied for the common
good. By the same token, we ought to scrap our navy because
New York contributes more to its maintenance in proportion to
population than Mississippi. This objection is narrow, sectional,
and selfish. It is directly contrary to the Masonic teachings of
brotherhood, universal enlightenment, and relief.
After the mask has been stripped off, there remains only the
naked truth that there are .those who do not want to have the
American public schools strengthened.

WOMEN AND MASONRY.
Since the edict of the Grand Master of Pennsylvania against
the Order of Eastern Star, the relations that this organization
bears to the Masonic Fraternity has been a subject of comment
and discussion. As we understand it, the Eastern Star does not
claim to be a part of the Masonic Fraternity or connected with
it other than a desire to assist. Such being the case we do not
believe that there is any great cause for alarm.
When criticising the activities of the Order in question it
should be remembered that it is composed of the mothers, wives,
daughters, sisters of Master Masons, and they are endeavoring
to put into operation, by precept and example, the ideals of the
Craft.
District of Columbia:
In our last report we gave the correspondence with the Grand
Lodge of France on the subject of the admission of women into
Freemasonry. Their Grand Lodge had passed the ordinance by
a majority, but to be effective it would require a two-thirds majority. There was, however, much discussion over it. It was
referred to an "international" congress of Masons, billed fo meet
in Rome in April, but we have learned that it met in Geneva instead. \Ve have not learned the result.
The writer's belief is that it was more a "feeler" than a settled determination. In the discussion it was shown that they feared
interrupting fraternal relations should they adopt the bill.
But, after all, it should not be a surprise. The progress English women have made in acquiring the privilege of voting, which
they got by criminal assaults; the complete walkover the women
in the United States had in the eighteenth amendment to the Constitution, has encoura'{ed them, and they would not be human if
they let it rest at that. They have the same ambitions that men
have.· Not only the French women, but their men, seeing how
easily European governments "touched" the United States for loans
with no security, of more than $10,000,000,000, have attempted exploitation. We have before us a letter from a "frere trois points,"
as the French newspaper men call the Masons, which is addressed
to our grand secretary, inviting him to bring to our notice his
sale of stock in a series of hotels he is building in the Riviera.

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States
are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite.
Properly speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and
the Scottish Rite, for the one commonly called Yori< is peculiar in
its organized proceedings only to the l:nited States.
·
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instrnction
'is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent
Master and the Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degrees of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests
upon those who have been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular because
they are conferred in a Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning
"done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take
the temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In. the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory .south ·of the Ohio River and west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to
14°, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix. 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh,
19° to 30°; Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33 °.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mi<"sissipni River) ; the degrees·
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and
18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

Ancient Craft Masons-Commence their era with the creation
of the world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.) "i nthe year of light."
Scottish Rite-Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish cluonology is used. Anno Mundi (A.M.), "in the year of the world.''
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple
was commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno Inventionis. (A. Inv.), "in
the year of discovery."
Royal and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.),
"in the year of the deposit."
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organiZlltion
of their order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order.''
Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of tho ble11ln1
of Abraham by the High Priest Mclchizedek, Anno Bc11t'dlrtlonl1
(A. B.), "in the year of the blessing."
